articles.title: EA Sports FC 27 incorpora gratis al AFC Richmond femenino de Ted Lasso en su nueva actualización
articles.text:
EA Sports FC 27 incorpora gratis al AFC Richmond femenino de Ted Lasso, una ampliación que suma a las Lady Greyhounds a los clubes disponibles en el videojuego y extiende la colaboración con la serie de Apple TV. La actualización permite utilizar al equipo en Patada Inicial, además de añadir contenidos para Ultimate Team y el Modo Carrera.
Ted Lasso vuelve a EA Sports FC
La incorporación del plantel femenino abre una nueva opción para quienes siguen la serie y busca trasladar su universo a más modos de juego dentro de EA Sports FC 27.
El AFC Richmond ya había formado parte de la franquicia en FIFA 23. En aquella ocasión, los jugadores podían seleccionar al equipo masculino en Patada Inicial y disputar encuentros con figuras de la serie como Ted Lasso y Dani Rojas.
La actualización de FC 27 amplía esa propuesta con las Lady Greyhounds, el equipo femenino vinculado al club ficticio. De esta forma, los usuarios podrán escoger una plantilla inspirada en los personajes femeninos de la producción de Apple TV dentro de la lista de clubes para partidos rápidos.
La inclusión refuerza el vínculo entre el videojuego y la serie, que convirtió al AFC Richmond en una referencia reconocible para seguidores del fútbol y de la ficción televisiva. El club ficticio vuelve a los campos virtuales con opciones para el fútbol masculino y femenino.
El contenido estará disponible sin costo adicional para los propietarios del juego. La actualización no se limita a un cambio visual ni a la presencia de uniformes y escudos: incorpora variantes jugables vinculadas a distintos modos, con Ted Lasso como una de las piezas centrales.
Ted Lasso podrá dirigir equipos en Ultimate Team
Uno de los contenidos de la actualización es Ted Lasso’s Masterclass, una serie de retos que permite obtener al entrenador como recompensa para Ultimate Team. El personaje podrá incorporarse a la plantilla y aportará química a los futbolistas estadounidenses.
La recompensa tendrá disponibilidad limitada, por lo que será necesario completar los objetivos durante el periodo habilitado por el juego. El sistema traslada al modo de cartas uno de los elementos que definieron la identidad de la serie: el papel de Ted como entrenador y gestor de un vestuario.
La presencia del técnico en Ultimate Team amplía el tipo de colaboración que EA Sports había utilizado en entregas anteriores. En lugar de limitarse a incluir jugadores, indumentarias o elementos decorativos, FC 27 incorpora al personaje dentro de una modalidad competitiva que reúne a gran parte de su comunidad.
El entrenador podrá obtenerse a través de desafíos temporales, una fórmula que añade un motivo para volver al modo y completar objetivos relacionados con la colaboración.
El Modo Carrera tendrá animaciones especiales
El regreso de Ted Lasso también alcanza al Modo Carrera. Los usuarios podrán elegirlo como entrenador al iniciar una nueva partida, dentro de la opción de entrenadores reales y en el apartado de equipos femeninos.
Esta elección activa animaciones específicas durante los partidos. Las retransmisiones virtuales mostrarán reacciones del personaje desde la banda, con planos de cámara que buscan reproducir su papel en la serie.
La decisión de ubicarlo entre los equipos femeninos conecta de forma directa con la llegada de las Lady Greyhounds. El contenido plantea una trayectoria desde el banquillo que permite gestionar al club ficticio en una competición y construir una temporada propia dentro del videojuego.
Una colaboración que vuelve después de FIFA 23
La relación entre Ted Lasso y los videojuegos de fútbol comenzó con FIFA 23, cuando el AFC Richmond entró como equipo seleccionable en Patada Inicial. Aquella aparición llevó a la franquicia a personajes que ya formaban parte de la cultura popular, pero con un alcance limitado en comparación con la nueva actualización.
La serie se estrenó en 2020, durante el periodo de confinamientos por la pandemia, y construyó su popularidad a partir de una historia centrada en un entrenador estadounidense que llega al fútbol inglés. Su relato abordó la empatía, la salud mental, los vínculos personales y la evolución de un grupo deportivo.
El programa también presentó un modelo de liderazgo alejado de la figura del técnico autoritario. Ted Lasso se caracteriza por la escucha, el optimismo y la atención a los conflictos de sus jugadores, elementos que acompañaron el desarrollo de personajes como Rebecca, Roy Kent, Keeley Jones y Dani Rojas.
Con la llegada de las Lady Greyhounds, los partidos rápidos, Ultimate Team y el Modo Carrera, EA Sports FC 27 amplía una colaboración que ahora ofrece más formas de llevar al AFC Richmond al terreno de juego.

articles.title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds.
Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.
According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.
The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences.
Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.
The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.
The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025.
Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them.

articles.title: Die trügerische Sicherheit offener KI: Wie in Open-Weight-Modellen Schadcode versteckt wird
articles.text:
Trügerische Transparenz: Die Sicherheitslücke in Open-Weight-Modellen
Die Bereitstellung sogenannter Open-Weight-Modelle ist in der Softwareentwicklung etabliert. Im Gegensatz zu Closed-Source-Ansätzen gewähren die Herausgeber hierbei den Zugriff auf die fertig trainierten Parameter, die sogenannten Gewichte, des neuronalen Netzes.
Das vermittelt Anwender:innen den Eindruck, die Architektur nachvollziehen und auf Sicherheitsrisiken prüfen zu können. Ein Team von Wissenschaftlern um Andis Draguns vom Forschungsinstitut Contramont Research aus dem kalifornischen San Francisco und der britischen Universität Oxford belegt, dass diese Annahme fehlerhaft ist.
Kryptografische Schließfächer in Open-Weight-Modellen
Wie in einer auf dem Preprint-Server Arxiv veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist, haben die Forscher eine Methode entwickelt, um Fähigkeiten in den Gewichten von KI-Modellen zu verstecken. Sie nutzen das Konzept der sogenannten Digital Lockers, bei dem Daten kryptografisch versiegelt werden.
Die Wissenschaftler verschlüsseln ein ausführbares Sub-Netzwerk und betten es in ein größeres Trägermodell ein. Dafür nutzen sie die Hash-Funktion Keccak, die unter anderem die Basis für den aktuellen Verschlüsselungsstandard SHA-3 bildet.
Solche kryptografischen Hash-Funktionen fungieren als mathematische Einbahnstraßen, die sich mit heutigen Rechenkapazitäten praktisch nicht rückwärts entschlüsseln lassen. Durch diese Architektur bleibt die versteckte Funktion inaktiv, bis ein spezifischer, geheimer Auslöser – ein sogenannter Trigger – in das Modell eingegeben wird.
Ohne diesen Trigger verhält sich das Modell unauffällig und liefert die regulären Antworten. Erst bei der Eingabe des korrekten Schlüssels entschlüsselt das System die versteckten Gewichte während der Laufzeit und führt die verborgene Routine aus.
Um dies technisch umzusetzen, übersetzen die Forscher den Algorithmus in ein lineares Schwellenwert-Netzwerk. Dieses wird anschließend so modifiziert, dass es sich in die standardmäßigen Aktivierungsfunktionen moderner Sprachmodelle integrieren lässt.
Das Scheitern gängiger Audit-Verfahren
Dieser Ansatz stellt die etablierten Prüfverfahren für Künstliche Intelligenz vor ein Problem. Bisherige Sicherheitsaudits verlassen sich auf sogenannte Elicitation-Methoden, bei denen Prüfer:innen versuchen, verborgene Fähigkeiten durch gezielte Eingaben oder Nachtraining zu provozieren.
Die aktuelle Studie demonstriert, dass diese Verfahren bei kryptografisch gesicherten Modellen wirkungslos sind. Die Wissenschaftler wiesen nach, dass selbst ein vollständiger White-Box-Zugriff, bei dem die Architektur des Modells offengelegt ist, für eine Sicherheitsprüfung nicht ausreicht.
Solange der spezifische Trigger unbekannt ist, lässt sich die versteckte Funktion mit den üblichen Rechenkapazitäten weder aktivieren noch analysieren. Die Prüfverfahren bescheinigen dem Modell somit eine Unbedenklichkeit, die in der Praxis nicht existiert.
Auch das gezielte Einbringen von mathematischem Rauschen in die KI-Gewichte brachte keinen Erfolg. Bei diesem Verfahren verändern Prüfer:innen die Parameter eines Modells durch winzige, zufällige Abweichungen, um notdürftig versteckte Funktionen zum Vorschein zu bringen.
Normalerweise reagieren herkömmliche Hintertüren in Modellen empfindlich auf solche Störungen und offenbaren sich. Die kryptografisch verschlüsselten Pfade blieben jedoch unzugänglich, während das Trägermodell unbeeindruckt weiterhin seine Standardaufgaben erfüllte.
Der Machbarkeitsnachweis im chemischen Bereich
Um ihre These in der Praxis zu prüfen, trainierten die Forscher zunächst ein kleines, eigenständiges KI-Modell. Dessen Aufgabe bestand lediglich darin, als sogenanntes Klassifizierungsmodell zu bewerten, ob bestimmte chemische Reaktionen in der Realität durchführbar wären oder nicht.
Dieses kleine Netzwerk fungierte in dem Versuch als Platzhalter für potenziell gefährliches Wissen, etwa für die Herstellung von chemischen Kampfstoffen. Die Wissenschaftler pflanzten diese isolierte Funktion anschließend kryptografisch verschlüsselt in ein ansonsten harmloses Trägermodell ein.
Bei herkömmlichen Sicherheitstests verhielt sich das präparierte Gesamtsystem völlig unauffällig und offenbarte keinerlei verborgenes Fachwissen. Die etablierten Prüfverfahren konnten die versteckten Fähigkeiten nicht aufdecken und stuften das Modell als sicher ein.
Das änderte sich erst, als die Forscher den geheimen Auslöser in ihre Anfrage integrierten. Plötzlich griff das System auf die verschlüsselten Parameter zu und bewertete präzise die Machbarkeit der angefragten chemischen Reaktionen.
Die Forscher schränken jedoch ein, dass diese Technik aktuell noch einen massiven Ressourcenaufwand erfordert. Um das kleine chemische Netzwerk mit seinen lediglich 672 Parametern zu verstecken, musste das Trägermodell auf über zwei Milliarden Parameter anwachsen.
Dieser enorme Größenzuwachs ist nötig, weil die komplexe Keccak-Verschlüsselung direkt in die neuronale Architektur des Modells eingewoben werden muss. Bei einer statistischen Analyse der Modellgewichte würden Sicherheitsteams derzeit jedoch massive Anomalien feststellen.
Die mathematische Struktur der Parameter weicht extrem von regulär trainierten Netzen ab, da die Werte fast ausschließlich aus Nullen bestehen. Prüfer:innen könnten die versteckte Schadfunktion dann zwar weiterhin nicht entschlüsseln, würden das Modell aber allein wegen seines künstlich konstruiert wirkenden Aufbaus ohnehin aussortieren.
Parallelen zu klassischen Supply-Chain-Angriffen
Trotz des derzeit hohen Aufwands zeigt die Untersuchung einen potenziellen Angriffsvektor auf. Wie Nutzer:innen in einer Diskussion auf Hacker News anmerken, erinnert das Verfahren an sogenannte polymorphe Viren aus der klassischen Softwareentwicklung.
Diese Art von Schadsoftware verschleiert ihren Code gezielt, um der Erkennung durch Virenscanner zu entgehen, während ihre eigentliche Schadfunktion intakt bleibt. Übertragen auf Sprachmodelle bedeutet dies, dass Angreifer ihre Routinen so in den Milliarden Parametern tarnen könnten, dass sie für Kontrollwerkzeuge unsichtbar mitlaufen, bis der exakte Auslöser sie aktiviert.
Wenn Entwickler:innen künftig scheinbar geprüfte Open-Weight-Modelle herunterladen, riskieren sie, ungewollt verschlüsselten Schadcode in ihre eigene Infrastruktur zu integrieren. Die Studie widerlegt damit die weitverbreitete Annahme, dass offene Gewichte automatisch Transparenz über die tatsächlichen Fähigkeiten eines Modells schaffen.
Sicherheitsteams müssen folglich neue Analysemethoden entwickeln, um kryptografische Anomalien direkt in den Parametern aufzuspüren. Die bisherige Praxis, Modelle lediglich durch Testeingaben auf versteckte Fähigkeiten abzuklopfen, reicht für eine verlässliche Überprüfung nicht mehr aus.
Die Erkennung derartiger Hintertüren wird somit zu einer zentralen technischen Herausforderung für die Bereitstellung offener KI-Systeme. Ohne verlässliche Prüfverfahren verliert das Konzept der Open-Weight-Modelle sein wichtigstes Argument: die nachvollziehbare Sicherheit.

articles.title: Framework Laptop 12 (Wildcat Lake) review: Growing up amid an unprecedented shortage
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable and repairable budget laptop, but it’s lacking features compared to the competition and lands at a higher price — unless you’re willing to supply your own RAM and SSD.
Reasons to buy
- + Decent performance for single-channel DDR5
- + Highly repairable and customizable
- + Easy to save money if you already have RAM and SSD
Reasons to avoid
- - Configurations often reach about $1,000
- - Display is middling and locked to 1080p60
- - Webcam quality is poor
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
When Framework introduced the Laptop 12 early last year, it offered an affordable, repairable, and relatively capable laptop, especially aimed at students. Between a 2-in-1 convertible design, a touchscreen with an optional stylus, the slim frame, and a $699 starting price, it was an attractive option. The updated Framework Laptop 12 targets that same group, though it’s entering a very different market, with some of the biggest brands gunning to become frontrunners for the best college laptops. Framework still makes one of the best laptops on the market with the Laptop 13 Pro, but the entry-level market is a different beast, especially today.
Apple’s MacBook Neo has prompted a wave of more affordable Windows laptops, with Intel’s Wildcat Lake taking center stage in devices like Dell’s refreshed XPS 13. The Framework Laptop 12 provides competitive performance with these devices, though at a higher price point and with less premium amenities.
The 1080p, 60Hz display is a reminder that the otherwise-premium-feeling Laptop 12 is a budget device, and although the Laptop 12 starts at just $549 without memory or storage, it ends up around $200 to $300 more expensive than the competition when fully configured. The laptop begs a question: how much are you willing to pay for repairability?
Design
Like Framework’s previous Laptop 12 with 13th-Gen Intel CPUs, the updated version with Wildcat Lake comes in a variety of colors: Black, Gray, Lavender, Bubblegum, and Sage. Our review unit, as you can see, is the Lavender variation. At the time of writing, you need to purchase the DIY version to choose your color; the prebuilt version is currently only available in Sage.
Unlike Framework’s more expensive Laptop 13 Pro, you don’t have the option to customize the color of the bezels, and only Gray and Lavender keyboard options are available now (though, presumably, Framework will expand these options). USB-A and USB-C modules come in a wide array of colors, as well, though other expansion modules are limited to a standard silver color. Framework also offers an optional $59 stylus, matching the color options available for the Laptop 12.
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable device, though perhaps not as thin and light as you’d expect out of a 12-inch laptop. It's 0.72 inches thick and clocks in at 2.8 pounds, which is thin enough and light enough, though not on the level of its enclosed competitors. The MacBook Neo weighs about the same at 2.7 pounds, but it’s covered in aluminum and it’s 0.5 inches thick. The XPS 13 with Wildcat Lake is much lighter at 2.2 pounds, thinner at 0.5 inches, and also finished with aluminum.
Considering the bulk of modularity, the fact that Framework managed to get the weight and thickness of the Laptop 12 close to closed-door competitors is remarkable. However, the fact remains that you’re often paying a premium with the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Neo and XPS 13 and, in both cases, getting a laptop that feels less like a premium ultrabook out of the box.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Although the Framework Laptop 12 isn’t finished in aluminum, it still has a metal structure. On top is plastic, which is then coated with thermoplastic polyurethane to absorb impacts. That leads to a plastic feeling externally, though with a smooth, slightly grippy surface that feels good in the hands.
Framework offers an optional backlight on the keyboard (our review unit didn’t have one), as well as four module slots for expansion ports. The back two support Thunderbolt 4 and DisplayPort Alt mode, and all four support USB 3.2 Gen 2 speeds and USB-PD. A 3.5mm headphone jack is standard on the Framework Laptop 12, regardless of the additional modules you choose.
Specifications
| CPU | Intel Core 7 350 | 
| Graphics | Intel Xe3 (2 cores) | 
| Memory | 16GB LP | 
| Storage | 1x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM | 
| Display | 12.2-inch, 1920x1200, touch, 60Hz | 
| Networking | Intel BE213 Wi-Fi 7 / Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Ports | Up to 4 user-selectable expansion cards | 
| Camera | 2MP sensor, 1080p30, hardware privacy switch | 
| Battery | 50Whr | 
| Power Adapter | 60W USB-C GaN (optional) | 
| Operating System | Fedora 44 | 
| Dimensions (WxDxH) | 11.29 x 8.42 x 0.72 | 
| Weight | 2.8 pounds | 
| Price (as configured) | $1,491 ($1,384 without expansion cards and power adapter) | 
Productivity Performance
This isn’t our first outing with Intel’s Wildcat Lake, so we went into this review with a good idea about what to expect from the Framework Laptop 12’s performance. Our test machine came with the highest-end chip Framework offers in this laptop, which is the Core 7 350. It’s a 6-core / 6-thread CPU with a maximum turbo clock of 4.8 GHz, and it can operate between 15W and 35W.
If you’re unfamiliar, Wildcat Lake is the younger, weaker sibling of Panther Lake. It uses Intel’s cutting-edge 18A node but with several cut corners. For starters, the 350 comes with just two faster P-cores (the remaining four are an LPE cluster). It also comes with just 6MB of last-level cache, half of what you get with Panther Lake.
The cores matter less here than the memory, however. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel DDR5 or LPDDR5X, regardless of capacity (support goes up to 64GB). In practice, that often means you need to overbudget your capacity, at least compared to something like the MacBook Neo with unified memory. Performance drops at 8GB with Wildcat Lake (see our Dell XPS 13 review).
The Core 7 350 comes in behind in single- and multi-core performance in Geekbench 6 compared to the A18 in the MacBook Neo (though multi-core to a much lesser extent). Compared to the 6-core Core 5 320 in the XPS 13, the Framework Laptop 12 is in lockstep with multi-core speed, and just shy of 5% ahead in single-core speed.
Compared to full-fat Panther Lake in the Framework 13 Pro, Wildcat Lake actually looks better than expected. The 13 Pro here is for context, not as a true comparison point; it costs a few thousand dollars. What’s interesting in Geekbench is how the X7 358H in the Framework 13 Pro scales, relative to the Core 7 350.
The X7 358H is a 16-core chip with a 4.8 GHz boost and access to up to 80W of total power (though much of that is allocated to the 12-Xe3-core GPU). Despite more than doubling total core count, and offering a doubling of P-cores, we’re not seeing twice the performance. And, even with access to less power, the Core 7 350 is within 5% of Panther Lake’s single-core performance.
With Geekbench, Apple silicon tends to perform especially well, particularly in single-core tasks, so keep that in mind.
Even with a bit of extra clock speed, however, the Framework Laptop 12 with the Core 7 350 came in behind the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 in Handbrake. Here, the Geekbench swing toward Apple levels out; the A18 was 8% ahead in Geekbench 6 multi-core, but it’s less than 3% ahead here in Handbrake.
The Panther Lake-based 13 Pro gives some much-needed context, showing compounding factors between higher core counts, higher power limits, and true dual-channel memory. Again, it’s a far more expensive laptop, and the Framework Laptop 12 performs in line with our expectations for laptops in this class.
Perhaps the biggest takeaway is how similar the Core 5 320 is, at least in this laptop. You get an extra 200 MHz on the CPU and 100 MHz on the GPU with the Core 7 350, which isn’t moving the needle a ton here given how limited Wildcat Lake is as a platform. That’s good news, as the Core 5 320 will save you $220 in the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Core 7 350.
Unfortunately, many of our gaming tests for laptops won’t run on Linux, and given that devices are often shipped back, we can’t go back and retest a dozen devices. That’s not too important here, though. The Core 7 350 has just two Xe3 cores, as do other Wildcat Lake chips, which doesn’t provide enough horsepower to power most titles.
We were able to achieve 30 FPS in Civilization VI at 1080p, which underscores the limitations of the integrated graphics. Intel’s dual-core Xe3 is plenty capable of running Balatro, Vampire Survivors, or whatever 2D sidescroller is currently popping off on Steam. Otherwise, it’s there to give you a display output.
Display
The display is what separates the Framework Laptop 12 from the various other Wildcat Lake-based devices we’ve seen in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and not for the better. Color performance, especially, is weak in our testing, and although peak brightness is in line with similar laptops, the 60Hz refresh rate is a severe downgrade compared to other devices, as is the 1080p resolution.
For metrics, you can see the display peaked at 451 nits, right in line with the MacBook Neo and Framework 13 (non-Pro). However, gamut coverage is poor, with just 64.9% of the sRGB gamut measured, compared to wide-gamut coverage on the competing machines. This is a “budget” laptop, but it’ll easily run over $1,000 with most configurations, and the display is not worthy of that price.
The XPS 13 provides some important context. It doesn’t get as bright — though, it’s hard to split hairs over 50 nits — but it comes with a 120Hz refresh, a higher 2.5K resolution, and it’s a touchscreen like the Framework Laptop 12. That gap in display performance would be understandable with a big gap in price, but that’s not the case. In fact, the Framework Laptop 12 clocks in at $1,271 with a Core 5 320, 16GB of memory, and 500GB of storage. The XPS 13, meanwhile, is $1,000 for that configuration.
Framework naturally needs to cut corners at this price, and it needs to engineer its devices to be repairable and upgradable. So, it’s hard holding the Framework Laptop 12 to the standard of a device like the XPS 13 that doesn’t come with those serviceability upsides. Still, the display is a consistent reminder that this is a budget laptop, whereas with the XPS 13 and MacBook Neo, it’s easy to forget that when doing day-to-day web and office task, due to the premium screens and build quality.
Keyboard and Touchpad
The Framework Laptop 12 comes with a standard keyboard/touchpad combo unit, which is available in several different layouts. There’s currently just a gray and lavender option for the keyboard unit, though presumably Framework will expand its offerings to cover the other colors available on the Framework Laptop 12 (at least with an American English layout).
I achieve 85 WPM with 99% accuracy in a MonkeyType test, compared to 92 WPM at 97% accuracy on my desktop (using the keyboard I type on every day). The keys have standard 19mm spacing and generous 1.5mm of key travel, which makes it comfortable to type on, even considering the small footprint of the Framework Laptop 12.
The touchpad is naturally small given the size of this device, and it’s mechanical, leading to sharp dips during presses on the bottom corners and no responsiveness near the top. It’s a serviceable touchpad, what you’d expect to see on this class of device. Just don’t go in expecting to be spoiled with a large glass surface or haptics.
Upgradeability
Framework built its brand on upgradability, so it’s no surprise that the Framework Laptop 12 earns near-perfect marks here. Like other devices, you can ship the Framework Laptop 12 pre-assembled, or as a barebones system that can accept your own M.2 2230 SSD, DDR5 SODIMM, and operating system. Even then, you can swap out the keyboard, display, mainboard, and ports if you choose (though only within the Framework Laptop 12 form factor).
However, the Framework Laptop 12 brings up the important distinction between serviceability and upgradability. The Framework Laptop 12 is the gold standard (among all Framework devices) for serviceability.But the Wildcat Lake chip brings up concerns about upgradability with its single-channel memory interface.
You can upgrade the memory up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 SODIMM, but there’s only one physical memory slot on the board. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel memory; it’s not simply a single-channel configuration for a budget price point. You can upgrade to more capacity down the line, but you can’t simply add in a second SODIMM to double your RAM.
You won’t find a more serviceable laptop on the market (outside of the other options from Framework) than the Framework 12, but you primarily have two narrow upgrade paths: more storage and more memory capacity, but not a true dual-channel configuration. Hopefully Framework will continue this line in the future, allowing you to swap the mainboard.
On the serviceable end, however, Framework makes things simple. You get a matching Torx screwdriver with the laptop that can detach the bottom cover. The cover has eight captive screws, so you don’t need to worry about losing them, and it’s primarily there to keep everything together; you actually service the laptop from the top, under the keyboard.
Considering you’re meant to go inside the laptop, Framework has everything clearly labeled, along with QR codes that link to repair guides for various components. With our barebones kit of modules, the laptop was powered on and assembled within five minutes, and this is my first time ever assembling a Framework device from scratch.
Battery Life
Our typical laptop battery tests are based on Windows, and we can’t replicate the testing process on Linux. Framework assured us that Fedora 44 offers the best experience out of the box, so that is what we tested. Instead of a direct comparison, we designed a basic web browsing test loop to see how long the 50WHr battery would hold up away from a charger.
About 9 hours is the answer, with a 9:16 average across three runs. We ran the laptop through a series of live websites with the screen set to 150 nits, Wi-Fi on, and Bluetooth disabled for the test. Again, we can’t make direct comparisons with Windows laptops, but getting around a full day of work is solid for the small 50Whr battery. And with USB-C charging, you can pretty easily top off with a portable GaN brick.
Audio
The stereo 2W speakers inside the Framework Laptop 12 are surprisingly powerful, considering the size of the machine, though the quality of the speakers and dual internal microphones is a clear cut corner to reach the more affordable price of the device. Thankfully, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack built in (it doesn’t take a module slot), along with Bluetooth 6.0 support for wireless headphones.
The microphone poses a larger issue than the speakers. It’s heavily compressed, which helps make your voice come through clearly, though at the cost of heavy background noise (including keyboard and trackpad noise). You’ll want to use something like EasyEffects in Linux to clean up the microphone audio.
As for the speakers, they’re not as bad as they could be. As mentioned, they’re loud considering the size of the device, and they didn’t distort at full volume. They’re tuned for this type of device, as well. Rather than overemphasizing the highs or pumping too much low-end and exposing distortion, the speakers in the Framework Laptop 12 have a heavy emphasis on the upper midrange.
This range, somewhere between 500Hz and 4kHz, is typically described as “boxy,” and that emphasis works well for the small drivers in the Framework Laptop 12. It implies a low end that the drivers aren’t actually capable of producing. Further, the higher-end of this range, around 1kHz to 2kHz, is where many human voices fall, with sharp consonants pushing higher-end harmonics that come off as harsh. Again, the emphasis helps, allowing voices to come through clearly, without sounding tinny.
Heat
The Framework Laptop 12 stays fairly cool, even under load. The hottest point we measured on the laptop was the underside, directly in the middle, which peaked at 101 degrees Fahrenheit (about 38 degrees Celsius). Under normal usage in a browser with a handful of tabs open, there’s very little noticeable heat, even at this hottest point.
Up where your hands are, we measured 94 degrees Fahrenheit (about 34 degrees Celsius) between the G and H keys on the keyboard, and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) on the touchpad. That’s warm for your hands, but again, the heat only crops up during heavy load.
Webcam
It’s unsurprising for a laptop at the price of the Framework Laptop 12, but the webcam quality is poor. The camera oddly uses a 4:3 aspect ratio, and the 2MP sensor creates an image more reminiscent of a watercolor than a sharp, Full-HD picture. It struggles with low-light especially, with even moderate shadows in an otherwise brightly-lit room showing visible noise.
The image above was taken in my office in the middle of the day. A window behind me was fully open, about three and a half feet away, and I have a lamp serving somewhat as a key light about three feet off-screen to my left. I’m on the second floor of a two-story house, on a hill without any trees obstructing sunlight (and it was a sunny day). There was a generous amount of natural light in the room.
Yet, you’d think I was sitting in near darkness from the webcam image. The stark brightness from the window darkens my face, filling it with visible noise, as the camera struggles to handle the dynamic range. Sitting in front of an unobstructed window during the middle of the day is the time and place where you’re likely to have the webcam turned on, and it fails that test.
Software and Warranty
Framework offers a standard one-year limited warranty on the Framework Laptop 12, with an optional three-year warranty available for $89 extra. You can read over Framework’s limited warranty, but the limitations are fairly straightforward. Normal wear and tear, damage due to negligence or misuse, and use of third-party parts (or first-party parts from third-party sources) will void the warranty.
Broad warranty protection isn’t as important here as it is elsewhere, however. If, for example, your USB-C port stops working, you can just buy another one rather than going through the RMA process and potentially paying for a repair on the other side (even if you’re under warranty).
You’re free to bring your own OS, but Framework also offers the Framework Laptop 12 with either Windows 11 or Fedora 44 pre-installed. Framework normally uses Ubuntu; however, Fedora 44 has moved to the newer Linux 7.1 kernel, which has optimizations specifically for Wildcat Lake. Using a slower-moving distro like Ubuntu is fine, though you’ll want to make sure to manually upgrade your kernel (and packages) for the best performance if you’re not already using a distro with kernel 7.1 or newer.
Configurations
Framework offers three mainboard configurations: Core 3 204, Core 5 320, or Core 7 350. As we covered in the performance section, the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 offered largely similar performance to the Core 7 350 in the Framework Laptop 12, so that seems like the sweet spot here. The Core 3 304 is effectively a single-core CPU, with just one P-core alongside a four-core LPE cluster, and it lacks a fingerprint reader, which is available with both other mainboards.
With the DIY edition, Framework ships the laptop without memory, storage, or expansion cards. There’s a single SODIMM slot for memory and a single M.2 2230 slot for the SSD. Framework offers up to 2TB of PCIe 4.0 storage at checkout, as well as up to 48GB DDR5-5600 (again, via a single SODIMM). Framework has USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, Ethernet, 10G Ethernet, DisplayPort, microSD, and SD card modules available, ranging from $10 to $99.
There aren’t any display options aside from the standard 60 Hz 1080p panel in our unit. For the keyboard and trackpad, Framework offers backlit and non-backlit options in various different native layouts.
Framework offers prebuilt versions of the Framework Laptop 12 at a discounted price. The Core 3 304 comes with 8GB of memory ($699), the Core 5 320 comes with 16GB (1,099), and the Core 7 350 comes with 32GB (1,399), and all three configurations use 512GB of storage. All of the configurations come with Framework’s standard expansion card bundle: two USB-C, a USB-A, and an HDMI module.
Dell starts higher with the XPS 13 at $799, but that’s with the Core 5 320 and 8GB of memory. Jumping up to 16GB, the XPS 13 is $999 with the Core 5 320, $100 less than the preconfigured Framework Laptop 12.
Bottom Line
The Framework Laptop 12 is caught between an unprecedented memory and storage shortage and a wave of budget-oriented Windows laptops that skip the repairability angle in favor of better trimmings out of the box. At the same price, it’d be a solid alternative with understandable downsides. The killer for the Laptop 12 is that you’ll likely spend more on it compared to other Wildcat Lake options.
With the Core 5 320, the Framework Laptop 12 is nearly $300 more expensive than the XPS 13, when both are configured with 8GB of memory and 500GB of storage. The Acer Swift Air 14 is $700, and a similarly configured Framework Laptop 12 is $1,074 before adding on the extra cost of a power adapter and modules. For many Wildcat Lake devices, we see prices top out around $1,000; with the Framework Laptop 12, you’ll often spend at least $1,000, assuming you push beyond the Core 3 304.
Modularity comes at a cost, which is more relevant in the case of the Framework Laptop 12 where $100 or $200 makes all the difference in value (it’s less relevant up at the Framework Pro 13, where you expect premium pricing). That extra cost is especially damaging here, when Framework’s competitors are offering better display performance (and more pixels) and all-aluminum bodies for less money.
There are situations where the Framework Laptop 12 is a great option, even compared to the other Wildcat Lake devices on the market. If you already have a SODIMM module you can harvest from other devices, along with an SSD, this is a cheap way to get some of Intel’s latest silicon. But for everyone else, unless you don’t mind paying significantly more for repairability, there are better options available that typically cost less, look better, and feel more premium.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.
There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.)
And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space.
Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.
When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.
The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.
The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.
These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)
“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”
The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.
“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.
But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.
It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.
If you want to learn more about Longshot from the company itself — while also checking out dozens of startups, hearing their pitches, and listening to guest speakers on four different stages — join us this week at Disrupt, Tuesday to Thursday, in San Francisco. Learn more here.

articles.title: AMD Showcases Its Next-Gen EPYC "Verano" CPU, Up to 192 Cores and LPDDR5X Memory
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
AMD Showcases Its Next-Gen EPYC "Verano" CPU, Up to 192 Cores and LPDDR5X Memory
AMD showed off its next-generation EPYC "Verano" server CPUs during CEO Dr. Lisa Su opening keynote at the 2026 OCP Global Summit. The new CPU is the first EPYC processor to support LPDDR5X memory via SOCAMM2 modules. Now AMD is mirroring rival NVIDIA's Vera CPU that already uses SOCAMM2 modules. The "Verano" processor sits within the EPYC 9006 "LP" family and is built on the same TSMC 2 nm process as the already-launched EPYC "Venice". While AMD "Venice" is the first EPYC processor based on Zen 6 architecture, "Verano" is optimized for AI tasks in agentic AI racks. For this, AMD plans to pair them with its own Instinct MI500 GPUs via xGMI connectivity at up to 112 Gbps. It will run on the new SP8 platform rather than Venice's SP7. When we first heard about "Verano", AMD indicated that the upcoming CPUs will feature up to 72 cores on a single-socket platform. However, that has now been updated to up to 192 cores.
From the initial information available, this could mean either a single large chip or a dual 96-core configuration. More details came from System360Cheese on X, who reported that the chip shown featured eight Zen 6 CCDs alongside two large IO dies and four LPDDR5X memory controllers. The CCDs appear smaller than those in Venice's Zen 6C design, suggesting these are the standard 12-core Zen 6 dies rather than the denser 32-core Zen 6C variants. The announcement follows AMD's earlier reveal of the Helion agentic AI rack, an Open Compute Project spec-designed system that Verano is expected to be integrated. Availability is targeted for 2027.
Sources:

articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a successful resurrection, but not without faults
articles.text:
This year has been quite the story for dormant platformer franchises, especially Castlevania.
It’s been nearly 20 years since we’ve had a single-player Metroidvania-style Castlevania game. My introduction to the franchise was with Symphony of the Night over a decade ago, and since then, I was hooked. It’s a prime example of a sublime platformer game, with perfect controls, interesting world-building and a rich atmosphere.
Since then, I’ve played through the various Castlevania games led by Koji Igarashi, who spearheaded the Metroidvania titles, including his spiritual successor, Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night. Despite the lack of Castlevania video game releases, though, the franchise itself was still active through various other media, including the fantastic Netflix TV series and video game collaborations.
The most famous of these collaborations was with Dead Cells, a roguelite (where players get randomized gear during each run) game inspired by the Metroidvania genre. After rave reviews (though I personally haven’t played it), it felt fitting for Konami to give Castlevania the “Sonic Mania” treatment with the creators of Dead Cells taking the helm for the newest iteration, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.
How does it compare to its previous iterations or even the endless Metroidvania games out there now? Well, it has its highs and lows that will ultimately determine whether you really jive with it.
A rose has its thorns
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse stars Rose Belmont, daughter of Trevor Belmont from Castlevania III: Dracula’s Curse. This game is a continuation of that story, taking place in 1499 after the events that transpired in Curse of Darkness. While Belmont’s Curse is a Metroidvania, it is structured differently compared to the previous Igarashi-led titles.
Rose Belmont is more than a capable fighter. Outside of the usual moveset, she can also wall climb and perform a double dodge. Rose can later unlock more movement capabilities, including the featured grapple hook (or rather, grapple whip).
Adding to her arsenal are three healing potions that can be used with a simple button press. These refill after using a save point, and you can collect three additional potions as an item drop. Gone is the traditional inventory system where you can keep various items to use throughout your journey. Instead, drops are immediate recovery items for health and mana.
This also applies to collecting weapons and accessories, which is a positive. One of the more frustrating design choices with the older games was that there were various items or abilities that you could only get through a specific enemy with a one per cent drop rate.
Belmont’s Curse takes a different approach by having seven unique weapon types that you can find throughout the game. Each weapon also has its own abilities that can be combined with your grapple whip. On top of this, Rose also has access to magic through her tarot cards. These are acquired by defeating bosses and can be further improved by completing various challenges throughout the game.
However, if you thought Rose’s enhanced loadout would lead to an easy experience, you would be wrong. Belmont’s Curse is tough.
For starters, bosses and common enemies hit a lot harder, echoing classic Castlevania titles where you have to be more methodical with your actions. If you try to furiously attack like a blithering idiot, your chances of surviving are slim to none unless you level grind. This added difficulty is also incorporated in the level design with various platforming challenges and puzzles that are genuinely testing.
This is where Belmont’s Curse could be divisive since platforming challenges are forced onto the player, especially after receiving movement upgrades. I liked that it tested your platforming skills, and the game does provide shortcuts once you complete the platforming challenges at hand. However, if these are too difficult, you can solve some of these issues with accessibility features that can scale your journey to be easier or harder if you’re a masochist.
Despite this, fans of the series will adore the world-building as told through the level design and tarot card system. Besides the main story and references in Dracula’s Castle, Belmont’s Curse incorporates lots of dialogue through Rose’s interaction with these tarot cards, not only adding to her own development but also contextualizing certain characters in the Castlevania lore.
While the story itself isn’t particularly complex, Rose’s interactions with characters in this game were outstanding and always left a smile on my face.
Both a blessing and a curse
One of my issues with Belmont’s Curse isn’t with the platforming, but rather the lack of movement upgrades in its first half. This leads to my overall problem with this game: the map is simply too big.
Paris (which includes the streets, catacombs and cemetery) is a slog on your first playthrough, taking around three hours because of the platforming challenges, boss fights and no movement upgrade besides the whip. Blind exploration is also encouraged, especially since the tarot card hint system doesn’t entirely point you in the right direction.
I appreciate Belmont’s Curse being more open-ended. However, without more movement upgrades, traversing around the map ends up being tiresome. Belmont’s Curse’s pacing would’ve drastically improved if the catacombs and cemetery were cut, with the streets of Paris serving as the intro stage. Since the game truly hits its stride after entering Dracula’s Castle (where you start getting more movement upgrades), it wouldn’t have been a big loss.
Belmont’s Curse is a good game that I really wish I loved more.
On one hand, I really enjoy the challenging platforming and combat because it’s a fresh yet familiar experience that combines both the Metroidvania genre and the original classic Castlevania gameplay. But on the other hand, Belmont’s Curse is bloated, with puzzles that can feel grating or downright unsolvable because of its open-ended design.
Before you cue the obvious “bad gaming journalist” joke, let me explain two puzzles that soured my experience towards the end.
The first puzzle is about a hidden mystery in an area after completing the main objective. My entire map is nearly 100 per cent complete except for that one segment. I’ve spent literally hours combing through the map again for any missing hints and overanalyzing past tarot card hints just to trigger something. This remains unsolved. The other puzzle involves a tarot card where you seemingly need to interact with specific safe rooms. Except, there’s no indication on what to do, despite me trying literally everything.
This is increasingly frustrating when this tarot card is linked to the third ending, leading to an overall half-baked finale. This is one that I’m convinced is bugged because there is no way the developers would make it this convoluted for a tarot card. However, there’s no way to tell since the tarot card hints and a less-than-useful ring accessory are the only tip systems the game offers.
Overall, Belmont’s Curse is best described as a game that delivers incredibly high moments but underlying issues can sour your experience depending on what you get out of a Metroidvania. Still, I’m incredibly happy that this game exists and hopefully, we continue to get more Castlevania games in the future.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse launches on Oct. 15 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and PC through Steam.
Image credit: Konami

articles.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer possède un subtil (et savoureux) clin d'oeil à Dark Vador
articles.text:
Au détour d’une discussion dans Star Wars: Galactic Racer, l’infâme Sebulba, légende vivante des pistes de Tatooine, apparu pour la première fois dans le film Star Wars : Épisode I – La Menace fantôme, évoque sans jamais le nommer un certain Anakin Skywalker. Le pilote ne semble pas savoir ce qu’est devenu son vieux rival.
Dans une séquence qui fait actuellement le sel des réseaux sociaux, le célèbre Dug se confie sur ses antécédents avec les humains et lâche, l’air de rien, que ce petit gamin blondinet qui l’avait humilié lors de la course de la Boonta Eve a probablement « terminé sa vie à faire des petits ronds dans le désert sans rien accomplir ».
Une galaxie trop grande pour les faits divers de la Bordure Extérieure
Évidemment, pour les fans rivés sur le lore, la scène frôle le comique absolu. Entre deux slaloms à mach 2 sur des tracés retors, Sebulba est resté coincé dans sa bulle de caïd local de la Bordure Extérieure. Isolé sur Tatooine, le pilote n’a visiblement jamais compris que son ancien souffre-douleur est devenu le Général Jedi le plus terrifiant de la République, le « Héros sans peur » de la propagande de guerre, avant de se reconvertir en seigneur noir des Sith responsable de la plus grande purge galactique de tous les temps.
Pour le commun des mortels sur une planète oubliée des dieux comme Tatooine, la grande politique et les drames de l’Empire ou de la République ne traversent pas les tempêtes de sable. Dans l’esprit de Sebulba, Anakin n’est qu’un gamin de passage qui a eu un coup de bol monumental, un random de l’espace disparu du jour au lendemain.
Un jeu de course qui remet les gaz (et l’écriture) au premier plan
Au-delà de cette perle d’écriture qui donne instantanément envie de lancer le jeu, Star Wars: Galactic Racer s’impose comme la vraie bonne surprise de ce mois d’octobre. En assumant un gameplay arcade pur jus, sans la Force ni les prophéties mystiques, le studio Fuse Games redonne ses lettres de noblesse au genre déserté depuis l’ère de la Nintendo 64.
Entre la construction de vaisseaux personnalisés, le retour de circuits mythiques (et de tracés inédits sur Crait ou Jakku) et cette ambiance de circuits clandestins mafieux, le titre cartonne sur PC, PS5 et Xbox Series.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer est vendu 59,99 € dans son édition standard. Sur Steam, il a atteint un pic de 18 052 joueurs connectés en même temps le 11 octobre, avec environ 83 % d’avis positifs, selon SteamDB. Ces chiffres ne concernent que la version PC. De notre côté, on l’a beaucoup apprécié.

articles.title: Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10 million in Series A
articles.text:
Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round
The startup founded by IIT Madras alumni plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.
Clueso, the agentic video platform for business founded by IIT Madras alumni, has raised $10 million in a Series A round of funding led by Dharana Capital, with Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures joining as new investors.
The round also saw participation from Y Combinator and f7 Ventures. This round brings the total fund raised to $12 million.
Founded in 2023 by Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso is based out of California and Bengaluru. It plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.
The startup says more than 1,000 companies use its platform to create videos for functions such as marketing, customer success and education, onboarding and training. Customers include Atlassian, Zendesk, Gainsight, GlobalPartners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Clueso claims that users have reported productivity gains of over 5x and an 80% reduction in video production costs.
Clueso's co-founder & CEO Akash Anand noted that the company started out by helping customer-facing teams create product tutorials faster. “We quickly saw the same problem across marketing, sales, training and internal documentation. That made us realise the opportunity was much bigger. Today, Clueso acts as an AI video production team that anyone or any team in the organisation can rely on, handling the work of creating, editing and maintaining videos as the business moves.”
Clueso is building AI agents that understand a company’s products, processes, brand and context, and then use that knowledge to create and maintain video across the organisation.
Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner at Dharana Capital said, “With AI, video is evolving from static media files into living, context-aware assets that continuously adapt as business processes and products change. Clueso is building the infrastructure powering this shift.”
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: The developer who cloned Photoshop using AI has now created Word, Excel, and PowerPoint replicas with Claude
articles.text:
First look: Though vibe-coded apps are often slammed as "AI slop" by users and developers alike, generative AI can now produce complex productivity apps that rival market leaders. After building free, open-source alternatives to Adobe's Creative Cloud apps using Claude AI, developer Brandon Thomas is now turning to replicas of Microsoft Office apps like Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
Called WordCraft, GridCraft, and DeckCraft, respectively, the open-source applications are written in Rust with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, as the Adobe replicas were, and are available for download under MIT or Apache 2.0 licenses. They are, however, still at a relatively early stage of development and need a lot more work before they can be considered viable alternatives to Microsoft Office.
According to its GitHub page, WordCraft is an "open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Microsoft Word" that runs natively on Windows, macOS, Linux, and BSD. It can also be used in the browser via WebAssembly. The app uses a single Rust codebase for all platforms, without falling back on Electron or Tauri.
WordCraft reads and writes .docx, the native file format of Microsoft Word. It also supports a range of other formats, including .odt, .rtf, .html, .md, and .txt, and can import the legacy .doc format. It can export PDFs with real, selectable text, links, and bookmarks, too. Thomas noted that spelling, grammar, and many other critical features work offline.
WordCraft is visually almost identical to the software it's modeled after, offering the same ribbon, styles, tables, track changes, and references as Word. It also implements features like mail merge, which lets users create personalized letters by pulling in data from a CSV file or Outlook contacts list.
GridCraft, which replicates Microsoft Excel, already implements 89% of Excel's ribbon and menu commands, according to the developer, and about 98% of its worksheet functions. It offers Excel's familiar interface, including the ribbon, formula bar, keyboard shortcuts, and more. It uses .xlsx as its native file format and is fully scriptable by AI agents.
DeckCraft, which opens and saves .pptx files, aims for full feature parity with PowerPoint and to be "better and faster" than the original. Its GitHub page claims 79% "feature parity" across 191 PowerPoint features, including advanced formatting, and export to PDF.
WordCraft development is the furthest along, with 88% of Word's ribbon-based commands implemented.
Overall, the project estimates it has reached around 60% feature parity with the Microsoft app. All three apps are in alpha, with GridCraft around 50% "ready for real work" and DeckCraft around 55%.

articles.title: No Man's Sky is coming to iPhone and iPad
articles.text:
No Man’s Sky will fly onto iPhones and iPads on Oct. 28, developer Hello Games has announced.
In a blog post, the studio outlined the new ports, which come just over 10 years after the space exploration game debuted on PS4 and PC. Impressively, No Man’s Sky will work on iPhone 11 and 3rd-generation iPad Air and above, albeit with some limitations.
In particular, multiplayer isn’t available on Apple devices, while Planetary Settlements, which are alien towns that the player can build and manage, are only supported on iPhone 15 Pro and above.
Still, it’s commendable that so much of this vast and ever-expanding game is playable on Apple’s mobile devices. In addition to having streamlined touch controls, Hello Games says it will offer support for controllers, TV casting and even mouse and keyboard on iPad.
The game will also be free to try at launch and come in at under 4GB.
The No Man’s Sky Apple ports come as Hello Games toils away at its next game, Light No Fire. The open-world adventure MMO is currently in development for PC, although no release window has been confirmed.

articles.title: Una IA podría “copiarse” entre televisores, routers y electrodomésticos: Anthropic lo considera un riesgo futuro
articles.text:
Anthropic probó que varios dispositivos domésticos podrían trabajar juntos para ejecutar una inteligencia artificial, pero aún no hay una IA lo suficientemente capaz de copiarse y expandirse por sí sola.
La empresa detrás de Claude evaluó si modelos de IA de tamaño reducido pueden completar las tareas necesarias para instalarse y funcionar en aparatos conectados a internet, como televisores inteligentes, routers o electrodomésticos.
Sus pruebas indican que varias piezas técnicas ya están disponibles, pero que aún falta un elemento decisivo: una IA lo bastante pequeña, capaz y autónoma como para propagarse sin intervención humana.
El experimento no muestra una red de dispositivos infectados en internet. Anthropic trabajó en entornos controlados y con equipos de prueba.
Sin embargo, advirtió que los avances actuales acercan un escenario en el que una IA podría pasar de un aparato a otro, instalarse en equipos vulnerables y utilizar su capacidad de procesamiento de forma distribuida.
La empresa detrás de Claude señaló que el riesgo no es inmediato porque los modelos pequeños aún no combinan suficiente capacidad con un tamaño adecuado para funcionar en muchos dispositivos limitados.
En sus pruebas, solo un modelo más potente logró completar toda la secuencia de replicación en una red cerrada. Por eso, Anthropic estimó que modelos pequeños con esas capacidades podrían aparecer hacia fines de 2026.
Qué significa esta advertencia de Anthropic
La preocupación de Anthropic se centra en una forma de software malicioso conocida como gusano informático.
Un gusano puede copiarse de una computadora a otra sin que una persona lo active manualmente, explica el equipo de investigación de la empresa.
En este caso, la diferencia sería que el programa llevaría incorporado un modelo de inteligencia artificial capaz de tomar decisiones ante problemas nuevos.
Según la investigación, modelos de hasta 30.000 millones de parámetros ya pueden realizar muchas tareas separadas necesarias para una propagación: identificar equipos, copiar archivos, preparar el programa y poner en marcha una IA en dispositivos desconocidos.
El problema es que todavía cometen errores cuando deben encadenar todos esos pasos por sí solos.
Anthropic mostró, por ejemplo, que un modelo de 26.000 millones de parámetros pudo ejecutarse de manera distribuida en 15 decodificadores de televisión Android de bajo costo.
Evaluó modelos que lograron preparar sistemas de inferencia —el proceso que permite a una IA responder y ejecutar tareas— en ocho de nueve tipos de hardware analizados.
En qué nos afecta como usuarios
El escenario propuesto por Anthropic preocupa porque muchos dispositivos conectados a internet usados con fines domésticos tienen defensas limitadas si se habla de una inteligencia artificial de gran tamaño.
Televisores inteligentes, cámaras, routers, decodificadores y otros aparatos del llamado internet de las cosas suelen recibir pocas actualizaciones de seguridad o conservar configuraciones básicas.
Si una IA pudiera propagarse entre esos equipos, no dependería de un único servidor que pudiera apagarse para detenerla.
Podría distribuirse entre muchos dispositivos y seguir funcionando aunque algunos fueran desconectados. Anthropic comparó esa posible red con un sistema lento, capaz de expandirse durante días, en lugar de hacerlo de inmediato.
Para los usuarios, la principal recomendación es reducir las oportunidades de acceso: actualizar con frecuencia el software de los dispositivos, cambiar las contraseñas predeterminadas, desactivar funciones que no se usan y evitar equipos sin soporte de seguridad.
Estas medidas no eliminan todos los riesgos, pero dificultan que un aparato vulnerable se convierta en parte de una red controlada a distancia.
La advertencia de Anthropic no describe una amenaza ya desplegada en hogares. Expone, en cambio, que la combinación entre inteligencia artificial y dispositivos conectados podría cambiar la forma en que operan los ataques informáticos si los sistemas no mejoran sus protecciones.

articles.title: Intel Refers to its 3D V-Cache Analog as "BFC"
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
Intel Refers to its 3D V-Cache Analog as "BFC"
Intel is introducing its analog to AMD's 3D V-Cache technology with its upcoming Core Ultra Series 4 "Nova Lake" desktop processors. We've known for over a year now, that the company is introducing SKUs with enlarged last-level caches. Technical docs leaks have until now referred to this technology as "bLLC," which simply meant "big last-level cache." We weren't sure if bLLC would be used as a marketing name for the tech, and it turns out, we're right. Apparently, Intel is going with "BFC" as the brand-extension for processor models featuring bLLC. 
As we head closer to product launches of these next-generation chips, processor model numbering for these chips have begun to surface. The series will retain the new Core Ultra naming scheme from the current Core Ultra Series 2 "Arrow Lake" generation, but augment this with 4-digit model numbering that somewhat resembles the 4th Gen Core "Haswell" series. The "K" and "KF" brand extensions refer to the chips featuring an upwards unlocked base frequency multiplier; whereas "BFC" refers to the presence of bLLC.It's anyone's guess what "BFC" abbreviates; Intel probably has some clever marketing name for that acronym, such as "big fusion cache," and of course gamers would know what "F" word substitute to use here. 
The idea behind bLLC is the same as AMD had for 3D V-Cache. AMD discovered that enlarging the L3 cache of the processor can significantly improve gaming performance of the processor as it places more of the fast-moving game data, such as textures within 1/6th the latency of DRAM. While AMD stacks a slab of L3 cache memory on top of its CCD, over the central region with the on-die L3 cache to achieve a contiguously addressable cache block; Intel may use a different approach, such as having a cache tile sitting beside the Compute tile, with the ringbus of the compute-complex being extended to it, or short-terminating in the absence of it.
Sources:

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Argon, su IA más potente hasta ahora
articles.text:
Google ha lanzado Gemini 4 Argon, su modelo de frontera más poderoso a la fecha. Tras meses de retrasos y de ceder terreno a Anthropic y OpenAI, el gigante tecnológico contraataca con una nueva IA enfocada en flujos de trabajo completos. Gemini 4 llega con mejoras en razonamiento, programación y tareas de larga duración.
Si bien Google ya había anunciado Gemini 4 Argon a finales de septiembre, el modelo no se encontraba disponible. La tecnológica lo ofreció primero a un grupo de socios especializados en ciberseguridad para evaluarlo. La buena noticia es que el modelo de Google ya se puede usar en la app de Gemini.
De acuerdo con Google, Gemini 4 Argon está diseñado para proyectos de ingeniería de software, conocimiento empresarial en áreas como derecho y finanzas, así como también en defensa en ciberseguridad. La compañía coloca a esta versión como el comienzo de la próxima era de su inteligencia de frontera, un modelo que tendrá lo suficiente para medirse con Claude, ChatGPT y otras IA poderosas.
El cambio más notable con respecto a la versión anterior es que Argon responde de forma más directa y con menos titubeos. Gemino 4 dejará atrás los clichés y las respuestas con muchas repeticiones que no llevan a ningún lado, algo que veíamos en la generación anterior. En tareas de larga duración, la IA informará su progreso con más frecuencia para que sepas en qué punto va sin que tengas que preguntarle.
A diferencia de su predecesor, Argon tiene un límite de generación de 1 millón de tokens, lo que le permite razonamientos y flujos de trabajo más extensos en una sola ejecución.
Gemini 4 Argon es una bestia en programación y ciberseguridad
En las primeras pruebas de rendimiento, Gemini 4 Argon logra un buen puntaje en DeepSWE v1.1, un benchmark que mide el desempeño en tareas de desarrollo de software real. Google afirma que sus ingenieros lo usan a diario, desde tareas de depuración hasta migraciones de bases de código de gran tamaño. Entre los casos de uso destacados se encuentran la optimización de algoritmos para computación cuántica y la reducción del uso de memoria en centros de datos.
Fuera de la programación, Gemini 4 Argon tiene un enfoque marcado en la ciberseguridad defensiva. El nuevo modelo de Google puede encontrar, validar y corregir vulnerabilidades de software. En la prueba de CWE-bench v1, que mide la capacidad de la IA para remediar fallos de seguridad, Argon supera a Claude Opus 5.5 y comparte el primer lugar con GPT-6 Astra y Grok 4.7. La tecnológica menciona que ha trabajado con empresas como Wiz, que ya usa Gemini 4 en sus sistemas de defensa.
Otros hitos del nuevo modelo incluyen el descubrimiento de múltiples vulnerabilidades en bases de código complejas que abarcan 20 lenguajes de programación. Gemini 4 Argon es más eficiente que 3.8 Flash Cyber en descubrir la superficie de ataque, identificar vulnerabilidades y producir pruebas de concepto para validarlas.
Gemini 4 Argon ya está disponible para los suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra a través de la app de Gemini para macOS.

articles.title: Après Photoshop, il recrée Microsoft Word et Excel en version gratuite grâce à l'IA
articles.text:
Après avoir recréé des logiciels de la suite Adobe mis gratuitement en téléchargement, le développeur Brandon Thomas, créateur du studio ArtCraft, a recréé la suite Microsoft. Des logiciels équivalents à Word, Excel et PowerPoint peuvent être téléchargés gratuitement sur le site d’ArtCraft. Des applications « vibe codées » comme le revendique Brandon Thomas.
Word, Excel ou encore PowerPoint « recréés » avec de l’IA
Le studio américain ArtCraft a dévoilé ses alternatives open source à des logiciels très connus. Word devient WordCraft, Excel devient GridCraft, PowerPoint devient DeckCraft. On trouve aussi une alternative à AutoCAD, un logiciel de dessin industriel, baptisée CADCraft. Enfin, ArtCraft propose sa version d’Avid Pro Tools, logiciel audio professionnel, qui se nomme SoundCraft.
Ces logiciels sont tous open source et gratuits au téléchargement, disponibles sur macOS, Windows et Linux. Pas de compte, pas d’abonnement, c’est la promesse du fondateur du studio Brandon Thomas. Pour le moment, les « contrefaçons » d’Adobe sont en alpha et celles de Microsoft sont toujours en développement.
Les trois alternatives à Word, Excel et PowerPoint sont même compatibles avec les formats natifs de Microsoft. Pour le moment, 62% des fonctions de Word seraient présentes dans WordCraft, 50% pour la version ArtCraft d’Excel et 79% pour les fonctions reprises de PowerPoint. Sur les réseaux sociaux, nombreux sont ceux qui ont demandé à Thomas Brandon pourquoi ne pas utiliser les suites OpenOffice ou Libre Office. Le développeur a répondu sèchement : « Il a bouffé mon essai de 40 pages pendant la semaine des exams. Je règle une vieille rancune qui mijote depuis des années. […] Laissez-le crever. »
Le développeur peut remercier Claude Code, qui n’a pas plagié de code source
Tout ces outils ont été développés dans le langage Rust, langage réputé pour ses performances, et sont tous des réimplémentations des logiciels « recréés ». Brandon Thomas l’assume : il a utilisé Claude Code pour reproduire les fonctionnalités et le comportement des logiciels d’Adobe ou Microsoft à partir de spécifications publiques et de documentation. Rien des codes sources de ces applications n’aurait été copié.
Grâce à Claude Code et avec le modèle Claude Opus 5.5 d’Anthropic, plusieurs agents peuvent travailler en parallèle sur des sous-systèmes distincts. De quoi avancer très rapidement et reproduire des logiciels en quelques jours. Ce que Thomas Brandon revendique haut et fort : « les modèles d’IA me permettent de travailler comme une entreprise entière. Je fais quatre fois mieux que les revenus par employé de Google », tout en assurant qu’il sait coder.

articles.title: Chinese AI companies buy 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation GPUs in a single year, report claims — export control-compliant chips flood the market to bridge gap in compute demand
articles.text:
Chinese AI companies buy 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation GPUs in a single year, report claims — export control-compliant chips flood the market to bridge gap in compute demand
China continues to lean on U.S. chips
Chinese tech companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation GPUs to plug gaps in demand for AI computing power, Financial Times reports. The report cites industry insiders who claim the buying spree highlights an ongoing and significant reliance on U.S. AI hardware, despite a burgeoning homegrown market.
The report firstly notes that China's national strategy for developing AI has led to a doubling of domestic AI chip production this year; however, the country cannot keep up with demand from its biggest tech companies. The report cites a shortfall of nearly 1.5 million chips, with only 3.5 million expected to be manufactured domestically while demand "far exceeds" 5 million. To compensate, China is purportedly turning to Nvidia's gaming and workstation processors, which are compliant with U.S. export controls, repurposing them for AI.
According to FT, the chips are "mostly" Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000, and the RTX 5090, the latter of which is the best graphics card on the market for enthusiast gaming. As the report notes, these Blackwell chips can't compete with Huawei's Ascend 910C and other homegrown flagship offerings, but they are useful for "simpler AI workloads," such as prefilling.
This is significant pressure on a GPU market where prices for enthusiast cards have already skyrocketed. The RTX 5090's MSRP is $1,999; however, the card can now only be found at a handful (three) of third-party resellers for no less than $7,199, and has all but disappeared from the market.
The report highlights that demand for Nvidia's GPUs is driven in part by its CUDA software, which remains more favorable than Huawei's Cann alternative.
As for the enthusiast market, it was recently reported that Nvidia has halted RTX 5090 production, to be replaced by a 24GB RTX 5080 flagship. That would mark a significant step down from the 32GB the 5090 currently boasts, a troubling sign for enthusiasts that the enthusiast gaming GPU market appears to be receding, rather than advancing.
