articles.title: Scheitern war keine Option: Warum ein OpenAI-Modell Chats fälschte und seine Testumgebung zerstörte
articles.text:
KI außer Kontrolle: OpenAI-Modell zerlegt grundlos seine eigene Umgebung
Ein OpenAI-Modell hat während der Absolvierung einer Testaufgabe absichtlich seine Untersuchungsumgebung zerstört. Der offensichtliche Grund: Der KI fehlten die Dateien, die es für seine Aufgabe gebraucht hätte. Nach mehreren Versuchen, die Ergebnisse zunächst zu fälschen, entschied es sich für die Zerlegung – offenbar in der Hoffnung, nach einem Neustart der Testumgebung an die fehlenden Dateien zu kommen. Den Vorfall beschreibt OpenAI in einem Blogpost. Das Modell war als „Bewerter“ in einen Reinforcement-Learning-Prozess eingebunden. Bei dieser Trainingsmethode lernt ein Modell durch Rückmeldungen, welche Antworten die korrekten sind. Das Bewerter-Modell sollte also Antworten aus anderen KI-Chats benoten. Doch die Dateien mit den gewünschten sieben Chats fehlten in seiner Testumgebung.
Erst erfundene Noten, dann erfundene Chats
Also gab die KI zunächst erfundene Bewertungen ab – offenbar, um aus der Rückmeldung des Prüfsystems abzulesen, welches Format die Ergebnisse haben müssen. Danach erstellte es sieben gefälschte Berichte, in denen es jeden Chat mit einer „4“ bewertete. Dass solche zufälligen Bewertungen unethisch sind, erkannte es laut seiner internen Dokumentation durchaus. Weil der Prüfprozess die Bewertungen nicht akzeptierte, dachte sich das Modell kurzerhand sieben Chats aus und verfasste dazu sieben passende Bewertungen. Doch auch das funktionierte nicht. Laut interner Dokumentation zog das Modell dann in Erwägung, sein Scheitern einzugestehen. Da seine Aufgabe aber lautete, diese Chats zu bewerten, machte es weiter.
Anschließend kam das Modell laut seiner Dokumentation auf die Idee, seine Testumgebung zu zerstören, um nach einem Neustart an die fehlenden Dateien zu kommen. Zuerst versuchte es, Python zu löschen und den Hauptprozess zu beenden. Dann entfernte es das Programm, das den Container verwaltet – also die abgeschottete Laufzeitumgebung, in der es arbeitete – und schickte ein Kill-Signal an dessen Prozess. Danach nahm es den Tool-Ausführungsserver ins Visier. Die Annahme: Wenn die Software ausfällt, auf der seine Werkzeuge laufen, erzwingt das vielleicht einen Neuaufbau. Als das ausblieb, versuchte das Modell sogar, Systemverzeichnisse zu löschen. Dabei erkannte es ausdrücklich, dass dadurch sein eigenes Terminal zur Steuerung verschwinden könnte – und ging das Risiko trotzdem ein.
Kontrollsystem schlägt Alarm
Immerhin: Ein sogenanntes Misalignment-Monitoring-System, das nach Fehlverhalten von KI-Modellen sucht, markierte den Durchlauf für eine menschliche Prüfung. OpenAI betont, der Vorfall zeige, dass auch scheinbar nur abgebrochene KI-Prozesse überprüft werden müssen. Die Quote an Fehlverhalten bei seinen Bewertungssystemen hält das Unternehmen aber ansonsten insgesamt für „gering“.
OpenAI hatte zuvor schon mehrere Fälle dokumentiert, in denen Modelle Nutzer täuschten oder Ergebnisse fälschten – auch bei alltäglichen Aufgaben. Zuletzt pausierte das Unternehmen das Training seiner leistungsstärksten Modelle, nachdem ein Modell trotz fehlender Internet-Freigabe eine Netzwerklücke ausgenutzt und versucht hatte, Kontakt zu einem externen Chatbot aufzunehmen.

articles.title: Una demo gratis en Steam usa tanta IA que sus autores han tenido que pedir un crédito para pagar las facturas
articles.text:
¿Quién no se ha bajado alguna vez la demo de algún juego? Es una manera perfecta de saber cómo es la experiencia antes de pagarla, por eso las demos son una gran herramienta de marketing para los desarrolladores. Pero ¿qué ocurre cuando cada partida le cuesta dinero al estudio? Y no poco: la demo de 'Enseñar a conducir a mi hermana' está poniendo en jaque a sus desarrolladores.
Un simulador de conducción diferente. El juego parte de la premisa de la simulación, pero no encarnas al piloto, sino al pasajero. Quien conduce es tu hermana, de ahí el nombre. La gracia es que debes enseñarle a conducir a fuerza de explicárselo a viva voz.
En países como Estados Unidos, alguien sin carnet de conducir puede ponerse al volante si un copiloto experimentado hace de instructor, siempre que cuenten con permisos. Es justo el papel que recrea la demo de 'Enseñar a conducir a mi hermana' ('Teach my little sister how to drive'): empiezas diciéndole a tu hermana cómo arrancar el coche y terminas en contradirección sorteando coches de frente.
El pozo de los tokens. El juego utilizaba Google Gemini para interpretar lo que le dices a tu hermana y para las respuestas del propio juego, con ChatGPT como modelo secundario (el estudio actualmente prioriza a OpenAI). Los desarrolladores no esperaban un número muy alto de jugadores, pero estos sobrepasaron los 430 simultáneos en Steam. Con esa afluencia, la infraestructura que había montado Easy Fox, creadores del juego, empezó a arrojar errores por límites de uso.
'Enseñar a conducir a mi hermana' requiere una conexión constante con modelos de IA en la nube con el gasto en tokens que eso supone. Muchos tokens, según Easy Fox, que no esperaba que una simple demo les pudiera empujar a problemas financieros. Porque el juego definitivo no tiene planes de salir hasta enero de 2027.
Un crédito para sobrevivir al éxito. En una actualización de su página de Steam, el equipo reconocía el agujero:
"Actualmente, gastamos más de 1.000 dólares estadounidenses al día en los servicios de IA de la demo. Esto no se debe a que cada jugador tenga un costo especialmente elevado. El costo total ha crecido por la cantidad de personas que están jugando. Para seguir manteniendo la demo, también hemos recurrido a un préstamo bancario".
La paradoja es que estos problemas para el estudio están surgiendo con una demo que es completamente gratuita y que tampoco tiene un pico excesivo de usuarios simultáneos. Aun así, Easy Fox mantiene el compromiso con Steam y con todos los jugadores que ya se descargaron el avance del juego.
"Queremos continuar ofreciendo la demo y nos encantaría que más personas pudieran disfrutarla. Sin embargo, somos un equipo pequeño de cuatro personas, y la presión económica podría obligarnos a retirar la demo antes de lo previsto, todavía antes del lanzamiento completo. Por el momento, no hemos tomado esa decisión".
La factura de la versión final. La IA es imprescindible para jugar, por lo que retirarla no entra en los planes de Easy Fox. Cuando llegue la versión de pago en enero de 2027, el estudio tiene previsto repercutir el uso estimado de los modelos en el precio cerrado del título, sin cobrar tokens aparte a los usuarios. También planean incluir soporte para modelos locales en aquellos equipos que tengan suficiente hardware.
Un juego donde la IA es el soporte vital. Easy Fox ha desarrollado un título donde la jugabilidad se basa en cómo interactuamos mediante la voz. Es lo que mueve a 'Enseñar a conducir a mi hermana', sin los modelos interpretando las interacciones no hay juego. Y es un buen adelanto de lo que se está cocinando en el mundillo: la IA quiere desterrar a los NPC que repiten siempre la misma frase. Esperemos que la factura no terminemos pagándola los jugadores.

Cet airfryer présente le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif
L'airfryer Moulinex Easy Fry Smart & Silence s'affiche aujourd'hui à 84,99 € chez Amazon. C'est actuellement le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif, selon les 41 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Avec l'Easy Fry Smart & Silence, Moulinex promet un airfryer à la fois plus discret et plus simple à nettoyer. Doté d'une interface guidée et de plusieurs programmes automatiques, ce modèle de 5 l vise une cuisson rapide et accessible au quotidien.

Points forts

- Panneau de commandes agréable.
- Interface en français.
- Application de recettes.
Points faibles
- Long à monter en température au centre.
- Données de cuisson par défaut parfois inexactes.
- Absence de fenêtre de contrôle.
Avec l'Easy Fry Smart & Silence, Moulinex propose un airfryer particulièrement agréable à utiliser au quotidien. Son interface simple, entièrement en français, facilite la prise en main, tandis que la façade amovible avec couvercle constitue une idée pratique pour le rangement et la conservation des restes. L'appareil se distingue surtout par son niveau sonore très contenu. Avec seulement 42 dB mesurés dans nos conditions de test, il s'impose comme l'un des airfryers les plus discrets que nous ayons pu tester. Les performances de cuisson sont globalement convaincantes, même si la montée en température au centre demande un peu plus de patience. Attention toutefois aux temps de cuisson proposés par l'assistant, parfois trop optimistes, et à l'absence de fenêtre de contrôle, qui oblige à ouvrir régulièrement le tiroir pour surveiller les aliments. Au final, l'Easy Fry Smart & Silence réussit son pari principal : être un airfryer efficace et surtout très silencieux, avec quelques côtés pratiques bienvenus.

Particulièrement respectueuse des températures, elle diffuse très bien la chaleur dans son panier et se montre assez rapide à chauffer. Ses fonctions restent néanmoins basiques et l’on aurait aimé trouver un livre de recettes en français dans la boîte.

articles.title: Un TV OLED Samsung 55 pouces de 2026 sous les 900 € ? C'est possible avec cette superbe offre — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le S85H est l’entrée de gamme OLED 2026 de Samsung. Il se place sous les séries S90H, S95H et S99H que la marque a présentées cette année. Il ne manque pas d’intérêt pour autant : entre sa qualité d’affichage très maîtrisée, sa prise en charge du HDMI 2.1 pour le gaming et ses compatibilités avec les meilleures normes vidéo, il est tout choisi pour être le TV à mettre dans votre salon. En ce moment, sa version 55 pouces est affichée à moins de 900 euros.
Pourquoi choisir le Samsung 55S85H ?
- Pour sa dalle OLED 4K de 55 pouces avec filtre antireflet
- Ses quatre ports HDMI 2.1 compatibles avec la 4K à 120 Hz
- Son système d’exploitation fluide et réactif
Samsung vend ce modèle de 55 pouces à 1 199 euros, mais en ce moment chez Joybuy, il tombe à 899 euros grâce à un coupon de réduction de 300 euros.
Une dalle OLED faite pour les soirées film
Le Samsung 55S85H ne manque pas d’allure avec ses finitions particulièrement soignées et son cadre métallique d’une finesse impressionnante. Sa dalle de 55 pouces offre une belle qualité d’image profitant du contraste absolu et des couleurs éclatantes qu’apporte la technologie OLED.
Samsung y associe son processeur NQ4 AI Gen2. Il améliore la netteté des sources en basse définition et adapte l’image au contenu affiché. Ce TV affiche une définition 4K (3 840 x 2 160 pixels) qui permettra d’obtenir des détails plus précis et des images plus réalistes, et supporte les contenus HDR10, HLG et HDR10+.
Il y a toutefois une limite. Comme tous les TV Samsung, le 55S85H ne prend pas en charge le Dolby Vision. Un filtre antireflet est bien présent, ce qui aide dans un salon lumineux. Côté audio, on un système audio 2.0 délivrant une puissance totale de 20 W compatible avec le Dolby Atmos. Le rendu est clair et précis, mais l’ajout d’une barre de son reste conseillé.
Un TV prêt pour la PS5, la Xbox et le PC
Idéal pour les films et les séries, le 55S85H l’est tout autant pour le gaming. Les quatre prises HDMI 2.1 acceptent toutes un signal 4K à 120 Hz : une console et un PC de jeu peuvent donc y être branchés pour profiter des meilleures conditions de jeu. Ajoutons à cela la présence des technologies d’optimisation pour les jeux, à savoir le VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), qui limite les déchirements d’image, et l’ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) qui réduit la latence. L’AMD FreeSync Premium est aussi de la partie, de même qu’un accès au Gaming Hub, la plateforme de jeux en streaming de Samsung.
Terminons sur l’interface où l’on retrouve TizenOS aux commandes. Cette interface est intuitive et ergonomique, et elle propose d’office les raccourcis vers les plateformes de SVOD comme Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, MyCanal, etc. Les assistants vocaux sont également de la partie, pour pouvoir contrôler votre téléviseur avec votre voix. Bonne nouvelle : Samsung s’engage à fournir sept années de mises à jour logicielles.
Pour le comparer à d’autres modèles, jetez un œil à notre sélection des meilleurs TV OLED de 2026.

articles.title: De nouvelles stars de la jeunesse arrivent sur les Freebox avec Kidjo
articles.text:
Les abonnés Freebox et Free Mobile peuvent désormais lancer Kidjo depuis leur téléviseur. La plateforme ludo-éducative, sans publicité, arrive avec Peppa Pig, La Pat' Patrouille et un mois d'essai offert.
Depuis ce mardi 13 octobre 2026, Kidjo, la plateforme jeunesse du groupe Cafeyn, bien connue des opérateurs, s'installe directement sur le téléviseur des abonnés Freebox et Free Mobile. Les 3-10 ans y retrouveront leurs séries préférées, des histoires audio et des jeux, dans un cadre garanti sans publicité. Pour les parents, la facture est douce, puisqu'une formule mensuelle sans engagement est proposée, et même un pass à la journée pour les week-ends pluvieux.
Kidjo ne se limite pas seulement à la Freebox
L'histoire de Kidjo remonte à une dizaine d'années, lorsque la plateforme fut lancée comme une application de streaming. Depuis, le service a pris du galon et s'est mué en plateforme ludo-éducative complète, organisée en trois univers, avec la TV pour les vidéos, les Stories pour les livres audio, et Games pour les jeux.
Des centaines d'heures de programmes y sont rangées. Hello Kitty, Peppa Pig, Les Schtroumpfs, Trotro ou Masha y côtoient des comptines, des premières pas avec les chiffres et les lettres, des sujets scientifiques, et même des tutos de magie et de dessin.
Le grand écran du salon n'est qu'une porte d'entrée parmi d'autres. Car Kidjo reste accessible dans tout l'écosystème Free TV, la plateforme télé de l'opérateur, réservée à la France métropolitaine. Il se glisse aussi sur téléphone, tablette TV connectée, Amazon Fire TV, Apple TV et même sur le web. Il s'invite également dans le casque Apple Vision Pro. Peppa Pig et sa bande ne sont donc jamais bien loin.
Sans pub ni engagement, l'abonnement Kidjo joue la sérénité
Kidjo s'ouvre d'abord sur 30 jours d'essai gratuit, ce qui est toujours appréciable. Il faut ensuite compter sur un tarif de 4,99 euros par mois, sans engagement comme nous le disions plus haut. Pour une journée chez les grands-parents ou un long trajet, un Pass 24 h est proposé, avec un prix relativement accessible, à 2,99 euros. L'offre vise ici les clients Freebox Ultra, Pop, Delta, Révolution et Mini 4K. Chez Free Mobile, seuls les Forfaits Free 5G/5G+ et Série Free sont concernés, sans le Forfait 2 euros.
L'autre promesse, c'est un environnement entièrement sécurisé, sans la moindre publicité. Les enfants peuvent piocher dans leurs programmes en toute confiance, et les parents souffler un moment. Le service Kidjo est donc porté par Cafeyn, la plateforme de presse en ligne qui aujourd'hui revendique plus de 2,5 millions d'utilisateurs.
Kidjo figure par ses acquisitions, aux côtés de miLibris ou Blendle. En tout as, cette arrivée renforce la place du groupe chez Free. Le fondateur et PDG de Kidjo, Martin Poix, espère toucher toujours plus de familles, et parie sur un partenariat durable avec l'opérateur de Xavier Niel.

articles.title: Backstage 1.55 Adds Scaffolder Task Recovery and Removes Deprecated Catalog APIs
articles.text:
The Backstage project has released version 1.55 of its open-source developer portal framework, adding automatic recovery for Software Template tasks that crash or time out. The release also removes a set of deprecated catalog APIs and moves the search module to Elasticsearch 8, so platform teams have several breaking changes to work through before they upgrade.
Task recovery sits behind a new scaffolder.taskRecovery configuration section. When it is enabled, the scaffolder resumes a task from the last completed step, keeps task secrets until the task reaches a terminal state and persists completed step outputs so later steps can read them. The release notes warn that actions used by recovered tasks should be idempotent or use checkpoints, because a resumed task can run an action a second time. The new section replaces three experimental flags, which still work as fallbacks.
The feature responds to a long-standing request. In April 2025, on a GitHub issue tracking scaffolder task retries, Manoj Azad wrote, "Currently, having to re-run the entire scaffolder process can be not only inconvenient but also problematic from a technical standpoint." The 1.55 feature covers tasks interrupted by a crash or time-out, which addresses part of that request.
Workspace serialisation is optional and needs a separate provider module. The new database provider has a 50 MB limit and is intended for development, and the release notes point production installations to the GCP module or a similar external store.
Most of the upgrade work sits in the breaking changes. The catalog backend drops the catalog.enableRelationsCompatibility option, so entity relations now return only targetRef, and it removes the deprecated CodeOwnersProcessor and AnnotateScmSlugEntityProcessor in favour of community modules. The Elasticsearch module now requires Elasticsearch 8.19 or later, although the AWS and OpenSearch providers are unaffected, and custom code that reads raw client responses needs updating. TechDocs strips MkDocs plugins that are not on a built-in allowlist, and teams that need extra plugins must list them under techdocs.generator.mkdocs.dangerouslyAllowAdditionalPlugins. Further breaking changes affect Backstage UI link components, the GitHub repository creation action, incremental ingestion permissions and the Sentry scaffolder action.
Several changes target governance and speed. The scaffolder.requireScmUserCredentials option, first added in the 1.54.6 patch, requires user-provided credentials for supported GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps actions. Permission policies that deny unknown permissions must now explicitly allow scaffolder.template.dry-run to keep template dry runs working. Michael Todorovic, a senior SRE at Veepee, changed the GitLab merge request and push actions to compare files locally. "publish:gitlab:merge-request was taking 5–15 seconds against a self-hosted GitLab," he wrote. "It turned out almost all of that was the action asking GitLab for information it already had." The change cuts API requests for a repository of a few hundred files from roughly 300 to under ten, and a step that took 5 to 15 seconds down to about 3 seconds. Core plugins such as the catalog, search and TechDocs now load their pages only when they render, which reduces the initial app bundle.
Since 15 September, the maintainers have shipped three patch releases. Version 1.55.1 fixed the new backstage-cli pm verify-patches command and TechDocs add-ons on the new frontend system, while 1.55.2 and 1.55.3 fixed how TechDocs handles MkDocs Markdown extension configuration.
The release also lists security fixes in seven packages, including the OIDC and Cloudflare Access auth providers and the proxy backend. The Cloudflare Access provider now requires the application audience in its configuration. The next minor version is already in pre-release, with 1.56.0-next.2 published on 6 October.

articles.title: Epic Games' Disney shooter is going "AI first," whether developers like it or not
articles.text:
Cutting corners: Epic is now another of the big software companies that want to bring AI into everything they do. According to internal sources, the real trial by fire for this "AI first" approach will come with the shooter Epic is developing with Disney. If it ever comes out.
Epic's first game under its Disney partnership is way behind schedule, and the publisher is willing to bet everything on generative AI to get it over the finish line. But the push to use AI across the entire development workflow could eventually tear the studio apart.
The sorry state of Epic's AI push was revealed by unnamed sources in a Bloomberg report. Managers have apparently told the developers working on the Disney project to follow an "AI first" production approach. A game director told Epic staff to avoid writing new code by hand, using Anthropic's Claude or other chatbot tools instead.
Epic wants employees to use AI for generating "art" assets, too. The same director said all of the game's art would come from "full AI workflows." The massive push to use AI for game development was essentially confirmed by Epic communications director Jake Jones, who said the company is embracing "AI-accelerated" development.
Sweeney himself backed this up on X the day the report came out, describing a "huge pivot" underway at Epic to retool developers around AI. He insisted the goal isn't to do the same work with fewer people, but to let everyone build more and better stuff.
Epic staff reportedly greeted the AI push with little enthusiasm during an internal video call. Some devs joked about using AI to correct the mistakes and hallucinations made by the AI, while others asked whether management was serious about the request. Someone suggested that Epic, as a company, might eventually find the push isn't as successful as executives expect.
Epic has long been a "true believer" in the transformative power of LLMs and chatbots. Tim Sweeney, Epic Games founder and CEO, is urging the entire industry to enthusiastically embrace generative AI. Sweeney even criticized Valve's Steam for requiring developers to disclose the use of AI tools, arguing that these labels will eventually become meaningless.
Epic began its major collaboration with Disney in 2024, when the Mickey Mouse mega-corporation invested $1.5 billion in Sweeney's studio to fund multiple gaming projects. The aforementioned shooter would be the first project to come out of the partnership, featuring characters from the Marvel and Star Wars franchises.
Earlier reports suggested the Disney shooter was in rough shape even before the new AI push. The game is late, the sources said, because Epic underestimated the manpower and development time required to make it.
In that light, Epic's attempt to speed up development with LLMs looks like a desperate bid to tackle the many issues the company faces right now. In March 2026, Epic laid off more than 1,000 employees amid a slump in Fortnite engagement.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

articles.title: Microsoft RTX Spark Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders open to rival MacBook Pro
articles.text:
Microsoft's RTX Spark Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders open to challenge the MacBook Pro in local AI
Higher-memory and SSD configurations are available at a premium
If you're looking for a powerful laptop that can handle demanding AI workloads without relying entirely on cloud services, Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra is available to pre-order now. Aiming to be a MacBook Pro killer, it combines Nvidia RTX Spark processing, Blackwell graphics, and a high-resolution touchscreen in a portable design.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is designed to handle demanding AI applications locally, with Nvidia Blackwell graphics and unified memory options reaching 128GB. That could make it an alternative to cloud processing or a dedicated desktop workstation for certain workloads.
• Best for: AI developers, researchers, creative professionals, and businesses looking for a powerful laptop capable of running compatible AI models locally.
• The deal: The base configuration Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is available to pre-order from $2,599.99 at Microsoft. In the UK, the pre-order is priced at £2,599.99.
Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra features Nvidia RTX Spark N1X processing, Blackwell graphics, up to 128GB unified memory, a 15-inch PixelSense Ultra touchscreen, Wi-Fi 7, USB4 connectivity, and removable SSD storage.
In the UK: now £2,599.99
Why we recommend it
Microsoft describes the Surface Laptop Ultra as its most powerful Surface Laptop yet thanks to the inclusion of Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X processor. The entry-level model combines an 18-core CPU with a 5120-core Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU. A higher-end version increases that to a 20-core CPU and 6144-core GPU.
The platform can deliver up to one petaflop of AI compute and run models containing as many as 120 billion parameters locally. The size of the models you can realistically run will depend on the configuration and software.
The laptop uses LPDDR5x unified memory shared between the processor and graphics hardware, with consumer configurations offering 24GB, 32GB, 64GB, or 128GB. The Ultra features a 15-inch PixelSense Ultra touchscreen with a 3270 x 2180 resolution and a dynamic refresh rate reaching 120Hz. It supports 100% DCI-P3 color coverage, Dolby Vision IQ, and peak HDR brightness of 2,000 nits.
Connectivity includes three USB4-capable USB-C ports, HDMI 2.1b, USB-A 3.1, an SD card reader, and a headphone jack. You also get Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, a 1080p webcam, and a precision haptic touchpad.
Microsoft quotes battery life of up to 15 hours for local video playback or 12 hours for active web browsing, although intensive AI processing will obviously place heavier demands on the battery.
Price context & historical value
The Surface Laptop Ultra, with Windows 11 Home, starts at $2,599.99, with the 18-core Nvidia RTX Spark N1X processor, 5120-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, and a 512GB Gen 4 SSD. Models with a 1TB SSD start at $2,999.99, while the higher-end Nvidia RTX Spark N1X processor, featuring a 20-core CPU and 6144-core GPU, starts at $3,699.99.
Consumer models with 32GB, 64GB, or 128GB memory include Windows 11 Pro and storage options include removable 512GB Gen 4 and 1TB or 2TB Gen 5 SSDs.
Microsoft also offers a Surface Laptop Ultra for Business, with commercial support and service options. Its available configurations and included accessories may differ from the consumer models.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Microsoft Ultra RTX Spark if...
You're an AI developer, researcher, or business professional who needs powerful local processing capabilities and access to substantial amounts of unified memory. Its high-resolution touchscreen, wide connectivity, and Windows 11 Pro options also make it well suited for demanding professional environments.
❌ Skip the Microsoft Ultra RTX Spark if...
You mainly use Microsoft 365, web applications, email, and video conferencing. A conventional business laptop would be considerably more affordable and more than capable of handling those tasks.

articles.title: Apple renova linha HomePod mini após seis anos sem novidades • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Apple renova linha HomePod mini após seis anos sem novidades
Caixa de som compacta ganha suporte à Apple Intelligence, novo recurso de luz e áudio surround com a Apple TV 4K.
Como parte dos lançamentos de suas linhas de produtos para casa, a Apple anunciou nesta terça-feira (13/10) o HomePod mini 2, nova geração da caixa de som inteligente compacta. O aparelho mantém o formato esférico do modelo de 2020, mas recebe o chip S10 e recursos de conectividade atualizados.
Entre as novidades estão o Sound Glow e possibilidades para integrar a caixa com sistemas de som externos. Já a nova Siri AI, um dos recursos previstos para o modelo, só será liberada em uma atualização futura. A linha, que mantém o design original, chega em cinco opções de cores: rosa, verde, azul, branco e meia-noite.
As pré-vendas já começaram nos Estados Unidos por US$ 149 (cerca de R$ 747, em conversão direta). A Apple não anunciou, até o momento, o preço ou se a nova geração chegará ao Brasil.
A mudança visual mais evidente está na superfície iluminada no topo. Com o Sound Glow, as luzes acompanham as cores da arte do álbum reproduzido e mudam em sincronia com a música. O recurso também funciona com os sons ambientes oferecidos pela Apple, como chuva, floresta e oceano.
Por dentro, a Apple segue o padrão da linha ao incluir um processador de smartwatch. Desta vez, foi o chip Apple S10, usado no Apple Watch Series 10, de 2024. Com isso, o aparelho passa a oferecer o Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6 e suporte aos padrões Thread e Matter, usados na conexão e na comunicação entre dispositivos de casa inteligente.
Não houve uma reformulação significativa dos componentes de áudio, mas a empresa trouxe novos recursos que ampliam a usabilidade da caixinha:
Também é possível combinar dois HomePod mini 2 com duas unidades do HomePod de segunda geração, por exemplo, para ampliar a experiência, segundo a Apple.
Quando chegar, a Siri AI deverá permitir conversas em linguagem natural, interpretar pedidos com base no contexto pessoal e buscar informações em mensagens e outros apps. Assim, o usuário poderá, por exemplo, pedir para tocar uma música recomendada por um amigo em uma conversa ou criar um lembrete relacionado a um compromisso.
O acesso ao contexto pessoal dependerá de um iPhone compatível com a Apple Intelligence, ou seja, a partir do iPhone 15 Pro. A identificação por voz permitirá distinguir os moradores e associar pedidos às informações de cada pessoa.
O primeiro HomePod mini foi anunciado em outubro de 2020. Desde então, a Apple manteve o mesmo hardware, embora tenha ampliado a variedade de cores e lançado atualizações de software. Em 2024, por exemplo, a empresa adicionou a opção meia-noite à linha.
Apesar de aparecer em rumores recentes que apontavam o lançamento do novo irmão menor, a empresa não trouxe uma nova edição do HomePod tradicional, que teve um novo lançamento em 2023.
O lançamento faz parte de uma nova investida da Apple no mercado de casa inteligente, que inclui também a nova Apple TV 4K, o HomeView — um dispositivo com tela para centralizar controles domésticos e recursos da Siri AI — e outros dispositivos da linha Home Collection, em colaboração com a LG.

articles.title: Apple anuncia nuevos productos este 13 de octubre: horario y filtraciones sobre la pantalla con IA
articles.text:
Apple anuncia nuevos productos este 13 de octubre, con una jornada centrada en el hogar conectado, la inteligencia artificial y una posible pantalla inteligente de la compañía. Los anuncios comenzarían a difundirse desde primera hora en Estados Unidos mediante videos, comunicados y demostraciones para la prensa, sin una keynote tradicional abierta al público.
La novedad cobra relevancia porque las filtraciones anticipan el ingreso de Apple en una categoría que hasta ahora no formaba parte de su catálogo: una pantalla para gestionar dispositivos domésticos y contenido multimedia. Junto a ese equipo, la empresa prepararía una actualización del HomePod mini y una nueva versión del Apple TV 4K.
La compañía no tendría previsto realizar un Apple Event multitudinario. En su lugar, organizaría encuentros privados denominados “Experiencias” en Nueva York y Londres, destinados a medios especializados, además de publicar materiales en vídeo y notas de prensa.
Este formato permitiría presentar los dispositivos sin un evento retransmitido en directo. La estrategia dividiría los lanzamientos de octubre en dos bloques: el primero se concentraría en productos para el hogar y el entretenimiento, mientras que el segundo incluiría ordenadores Mac y una nueva tableta.
Cuáles son los horarios para los anuncios de Apple
Los anuncios de esta primera jornada comenzarían a las siguientes horas:
- 6:00 en California, Estados Unidos
- 7:00 en México, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras y Nicaragua
- 8:00 en Colombia, Ecuador, Panamá y Perú
- 9:00 en Nueva York, Bolivia, Cuba, República Dominicana y Venezuela
- 10:00 en Argentina, Chile, Paraguay y Uruguay
- 14:00 en las Islas Canarias
- 15:00 en España peninsular, Baleares, Ceuta y Melilla
La pantalla inteligente sería el principal lanzamiento
El producto que concentraría mayor atención sería una pantalla inteligente que, de forma provisional, ha sido identificada como HomePad. El supuesto dispositivo integraría un panel de unas seis pulgadas y abriría una nueva categoría dentro del ecosistema de Apple.
Su diseño tomaría referencias del iMac G4, el ordenador con pantalla sostenida sobre una base semiesférica. En este caso, el objetivo sería reunir herramientas para la gestión del hogar conectado, con acceso a luces, cámaras, cerraduras y otros accesorios compatibles.
La pantalla también serviría para reproducir contenidos audiovisuales y consultar información rápida desde un punto central de la vivienda. La posible incorporación de funciones de IA situaría al equipo como una extensión de Siri y de los servicios domésticos de la marca.
Apple ya cuenta con los altavoces HomePod y con Apple TV, pero no dispone de una pantalla propia para centralizar la domótica. El lanzamiento ampliaría las alternativas de la empresa dentro de un mercado donde los asistentes de voz, las automatizaciones y los controles visuales adquieren mayor presencia.
El HomePod mini mantendría su aspecto exterior
La segunda novedad sería el HomePod mini 2, una renovación del altavoz compacto que conservaría el diseño actual. El cambio se concentraría en el interior, con un procesador actualizado que permitiría compatibilidad con las nuevas funciones de Siri basadas en inteligencia artificial.
Las filtraciones apuntan a cinco colores: negro, blanco, verde, rosa y azul. La continuidad estética mantendría la identidad del modelo, mientras que el nuevo chip buscaría reforzar su desempeño como centro de control por voz para accesorios domésticos.
La actualización priorizaría el procesador y las funciones inteligentes, frente a una transformación del formato físico. Ese enfoque respondería a la intención de Apple de integrar capacidades de IA en dispositivos que ya forman parte de su ecosistema.
Apple TV 4K incorporaría el chip A19 Pro
El tercer producto esperado sería una nueva generación de Apple TV 4K. El dispositivo incorporaría el procesador A19 Pro, el mismo componente previsto para los iPhone 17 Pro, según la información filtrada.
Ese chip habilitaría la compatibilidad con Apple Intelligence y ofrecería más capacidad para tareas vinculadas al contenido multimedia. El equipo también sumaría el módem N1, un componente propio con Wi-Fi 7 y Bluetooth 6.0.
La actualización contemplaría nuevos códecs de audio y vídeo. Estas mejoras reforzarían el papel de Apple TV como reproductor de contenido y como parte del sistema doméstico conectado de la compañía.
Cuándo se anunciarán la nueva Mac y iPad mini
La segunda ronda de anuncios tendría lugar en la semana del 26 de octubre. Apple prepararía un iMac con chip M6, un MacBook Pro de 14 pulgadas con ese mismo procesador, nuevos MacBook Pro con pantallas OLED táctiles y un iPad mini 8.
El nuevo iPad mini tendría una pantalla OLED de 8,3 pulgadas, marcos más reducidos y chip A20 Pro. De confirmarse estas filtraciones, Apple cerraría octubre con siete dispositivos nuevos repartidos entre el hogar conectado, el entretenimiento, los ordenadores y las tabletas.

articles.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout.
For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.
LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)
Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly.
LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.
“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”
Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch.
In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.
The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”
Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck.
The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.
LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.

articles.title: Gemtek, Qualcomm and gFiber Collaborate to Bring Edge AI to Wi-Fi 8 Broadband Gateways
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
Gemtek, Qualcomm and gFiber Collaborate to Bring Edge AI to Wi-Fi 8 Broadband Gateways
Gemtek Technology Co., Ltd. announced it is highlighting an AI-native Wi-Fi 8 broadband gateway at Network X 2026, developed in collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. and gFiber, Inc. to bring Edge AI and next-generation connectivity into the home. Built on the Qualcomm Dragonwing NPro A8 Elite Platform, the gateway is engineered by Gemtek and powered by intelligent software from Genix Networks, a Gemtek subsidiary, with gFiber as the launch service provider. It combines Wi-Fi 8 Quad-Band connectivity, Edge AI computing, and intelligent software for a more responsive broadband experience.
Bringing Intelligence into the Home Gateway
Designed as a home internet hub and a local platform for agentic AI, the gateway supports network optimization, device awareness, security, and proactive management.Subscribers can use natural-language voice commands to manage their home network and access supported services. Local processing of supported requests can help protect privacy, improve responsiveness, and reduce reliance on the cloud.
Network Intelligence for the User Experience
Genix software connects the gateway, devices, and network through an AI-driven interface. Voice-controlled application integration lets users ask about device activity, performance, and security, and take supported actions.
Reimagining the Role of CPE
Gemtek reimagines Customer Premises Equipment as a striking living-room centerpiece. Combining thoughtful design with intuitive interaction, the gateway brings home connectivity and everyday services into a device people want to see and use.
Roles Across the Collaboration
Qualcomm provides advanced connectivity and AI platform technologies for next-generation intelligent edge devices.
Gemtek leads product and AI system innovation, integrating hardware and Genix software into a carrier-grade gateway.
gFiber defines the subscriber experience and will be the first operator to deploy the gateway.
Together, the three companies are exploring a new broadband model that integrates technology, product and AI system innovation, and service experience from the platform level through to the subscriber experience, with commercial deployment targeted for 2027.
James Lee, CEO, Gemtek Technology"Bringing intelligence to broadband is as much an integration challenge as a technology challenge. This collaboration combines Qualcomm's Wi-Fi 8 platform and gFiber's subscriber experience with Gemtek's product engineering and Genix software. Together, we are creating a product that operators can deploy and subscribers can use in everyday life."

articles.title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have
articles.text:
Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see. And then the pandemic hit.
But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.
France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020: did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger?
EVs can be small and cheap, apparently
The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. A sense of utopia was responsible for the original Citroen 2 CV; it had to be cheap enough for a farmer to buy it and rugged enough to get produce to market without breaking it. I’m not sure whether the 2 CV Concept also has to be able to transport eggs across a rutted field without breaking any (although the glove box is a clue), but Citroen says that affordability, lightness, practicality, and versatility were top of mind during the design process. The press release probably didn’t need to also say the company imbued it with distinctive character or charm; that’s quite obvious from the design.

The interior feels particularly refreshing compared to the touchscreen overload we’re usually presented. It might be stripped back, but it still has plenty of whimsy—the display in front of the driver has a bande dessinée theme, and the radio is portable and removable from the car. Technology fans don’t despair, there’s still the 8-inch touchscreen, but this too features more of Belgian comic artist Jean-Luc Delvaux’s work.
I’m even confident some of that whimsy will make it into production, because Citroen is going to build the 2 CV within the next two years, it says, and at a starting price of just 15,000 euros ($16,766). That slots it between low-speed microcars like the Renault Twizy, Citroen Ami, and the Fiat Topolino (which you can buy if you live in Michigan), and superminis like Volkswagen’s Polo.

Audi’s first attempt at a supermini was the esoteric A2, an aluminum and aerodynamic experiment from the wild days of Ferdinand Piëch. Like the original, the Audi A2 e-tron is an efficient little thing—its most efficient car ever it says, with a WLTP rating of 4.9 miles/kWh (100 km/12.8 kWh). As one might expect, I was a big fan of the original A2, which was always a rarer sight on the roads than it deserved to be. I can definitely see that car in the A2 e-tron’s design, and the promised efficiency sounds impressive even if there might not be quite the same excessive and cost-ineffective overengineering under the skin. I can’t see any way that Audi brings this car to America, just like we never saw the first A2, or the A1.

The Peugeot 205 GTi was a Gallic alternative to the late ’80s-era Golf GTIs that Americans will be familiar with, and it’s into this well that Peugeot dipped for Paris. Or rather, the wild 205 T16 Group B rally homologation special that the 205 GTi gave birth to, a car that won the world Rally Championships in 1985–86. Like the Renault 5 Turbo 3e from last year, the E-T16 Concept shows us that hatchbacks needn’t just be humble devices for running errands; they can excite, too. I’m not entirely sure about that multifunction steering wheel, though.
What if I need something bigger?
“But Jonathan, I don’t live a block from a metro station, and I need something a bit bigger to cope with my family,” you say. It is true that cars like the 2 CV or ID. Polo will be too small for some. This is true for Europeans as well, and both Renault and Fiat had something for these segments.

The original Fiat Multipla is another underappreciated car from the late ’90s. The styling was challenging for some, but it was a masterclass in space efficiency, seating six in two rows of three abreast. Rather than simply copying that, but with a slab of batteries under the cabin, the Fiat Multiplay explores the idea of a vehicle that’s adaptable, transforming from a three-row people carrier to a pickup. The front passenger seat can be reconfigured as a lounger, and there’s a “Petsenger” seat—a modular mounting point that allows you to swap in a pet bed, child’s car seat, storage compartment, or small table.

The original Renault Espace was very much loved and created the people-carrier segment out of thin air, at least in Europe. The familiar one-box shape remains for the new E-Space Concept, though with massive 23-inch wheels at the corners, the proportions are a little more Hot Wheels or Matchbox than the 1984 version. (Even in Europe, car designers are drawn to oversized wheels.)
There is a criminal lack of electric minivans on the market today, and the only one available here in the US is the VW ID. Buzz. And that sold so poorly that VW suspended imports for a model year. Which probably tells you how likely a US launch for a production E-Space would be.

articles.title: Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI worm threat that doesn't need data centers to self-improve and spread — current deployment is impractical but could become a worry as tech improves
articles.text:
Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI worm threat that doesn't need data centers to self-improve and spread — current deployment is impractical but could become a worry as tech improves
The threat is real, but still in the future, at least for now.
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team has demonstrated two components of a potential AI-powered worm that, if key issues with the practical implementation are resolved, could spread across consumer devices including inexpensive Android TV boxes and smart appliances, hypothetically without relying on datacenter infrastructure. The experiments show that AI agents can configure inference across different hardware platforms and orchestrate replication across a network. There are still some serious limitations, though, particularly around the gap between the capabilities of today's models versus the hardware constraints of potential targets.
In its October 12 report, titled "AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter," Anthropic examines a potential class of malware called a weight-based replicator. Rather than distributing conventional executable code, it would propagate AI model weights alongside the software infrastructure needed to run inference on compromised devices, and it's not pure theory, either.
The researchers demonstrated that Qwen3.5-9B can establish an inference server on eight of nine tested hardware types, spanning NVIDIA Jetson Nano devices, Apple Silicon Macs, Xeon servers, a Google TPU, AMD's MI300X, and at least one PC with an RTX 4090, among others. They also ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes costing approximately $55 each, achieving a combined generation rate of 0.39 tokens per second.
Anthropic also tested whether a model could orchestrate replication across a network. The experiment used eight Google Cloud nodes running Android 15 emulators. A seeded agent propagated between nodes through an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge (ADB) port, transferring files and establishing an inference server on each target. GLM-5.2, a titanic model with 744 billion parameters over 1TB in size, completed the replication sequence across all eight nodes in four of five trials, reaching seven nodes in the remaining trial.
No other tested open-weight model was able to complete the sequence at all without orchestration from GLM-5.2, and they weren't able to meaningfully ask a larger model for help, either, despite being equipped with the capability. Naturally, GLM-5.2 wasn't actually replicating itself onto smart TV boxes; instead, it established an inference server for the much smaller Llama 3.1 8B on each target. GLM-5.2 ran on a separate inference server because the emulated nodes couldn't handle the larger model.
In other words, Anthropic demonstrated that a very large, externally hosted model can orchestrate a simplified replication sequence across machines with deliberately exposed ADB interfaces, and it showed that small models can set up inference, but it absolutely hasn't proven that a small model can independently replicate itself across consumer hardware. That distinction, admittedly fine, is nevertheless pretty important when the entire premise is that small models could soon spread without relying on datacenter infrastructure.
The experiments expose a central constraint of the research: models capable of reliably completing the replication sequence aren't currently small enough to run on inexpensive target devices, while models that fit within those devices' memory budgets, despite being capable of setting up inference, still can't reliably complete the entire process. This gap between the intelligence needed for reliable replication and the maximum model size that target hardware can support means that this threat model isn't really applicable right now, but Anthropic warns that gap could narrow, and potentially soon.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Using historical improvements in general AI capability (measured through the Epoch Capabilities Index), Anthropic projects that a model within the 30-billion-parameter class could reach the necessary capability level by the end of 2026. But once again, that's a hypothetical, and it still doesn't address the substantial efficiency problem.
Based on measured inference performance and the token requirements of its setup experiments, Anthropic estimates that establishing an inference environment would take approximately 28–51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B and 71–150 hours for Gemma4-26B-A4B at the observed throughput of its cheap Android TV boxes, and it’s worth noting that the boxes it used are configurations with 4GB of RAM, a relative luxury among these cheap set-top boxes. A model-driven replicator could take days to establish an inference environment on a new host, whereas conventional malware can execute its payload within seconds when its assumptions about the target hold. A conventional worm can spread to tens of thousands of vulnerable targets in minutes.
Model weights also impose substantial bandwidth and storage costs. Anthropic acknowledges that compromised hosts could download weights from external repositories rather than receiving them directly from an infected device, and that not every compromised machine would need to host a model. Nevertheless, distributing multi-gigabyte payloads and maintaining communication between machines running a sharded model would generate tremendous network traffic, making the activity very easy to detect.
Anthropic estimates that a hypothetical fleet comparable in size to the infamous Kimwolf botnet, which infected more than two million devices at its peak, could support approximately 133,000 instances of Gemma4-26B-A4B if every 15 devices collectively hosted one model. At the measured throughput (which benefits considerably from LAN latency), Anthropic says that such a fleet would provide roughly 40 Hopper H100-equivalents of inference capacity.
This is a very messy comparison that takes significant liberties with the data, but even at that it must be said that it's not particularly intimidating. We're talking about two million infected devices that must remain infected and operable for months (or years; infecting 2 million devices would take around 6,300 agent-years even with the fastest 28-hour stand-up speed) to produce less AI inference throughput than a few blades of previous-generation GPUs.
Anthropic notes that a real replicator could exploit other types of hardware, deploy different models across heterogeneous devices, and avoid loading model weights onto every compromised host. Those possibilities certainly complicate the comparison, but arguably they complicate it beyond the bounds of this discussion.
The research does identify a meaningful security concern: AI agents could make malware more adaptable to unfamiliar environments and reduce the amount of target-specific engineering required. A hybrid approach, combining conventional code for routine operations with AI-driven reasoning when unexpected conditions arise, could offer some of those benefits without requiring every compromised device to run an inference engine continuously. This is definitely concerning, but we've already seen AI agents using frontier intelligence write their own code to compromise secured systems, so that specific angle on this research isn't exactly groundbreaking.
Anthropic's experiments are useful in that they provide evidence that autonomous software configuration and simplified network replication are increasingly feasible, but turning those capabilities into a materially more dangerous class of malware will take improvements in model reliability, hardware compatibility, deployment efficiency, and the ability to overcome real-world security controls, which the firm didn’t test. There’s a ton of data and some interesting findings not discussed here in the actual paper, so if you’re interested in the research you should go check it out.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Zak is a freelance contributor to Tom's Hardware with decades of PC benchmarking experience who has also written for HotHardware and The Tech Report. A modern-day Renaissance man, he may not be an expert on anything, but he knows just a little about nearly everything.
