articles.title: Criptomonedas: cuál es su precio en el mercado este martes 13 de octubre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 83.614,45 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 2,265% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de 3,242% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.523,61 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0,02%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 743,92 dólares, con un cambio de -1,28%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 62.272 dólares, tras una variación de -3.600919.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -2,35% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.
The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.
“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.
So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.
The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.
Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.
Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.
Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.
A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.
Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.
The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.
Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.
One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”
Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.
“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here.

articles.title: We tried the Garmin Marq Adventurer 3rd-Gen — and asked Garmin COO Brad Trenkle about the series' mechanical watch-inspired design
articles.text:
'We didn't set out to build a mechanical watch': Garmin COO Brad Trenkle on how the new, super-premium Garmin Marq 3rd-Gen range packs serious smarts into a heritage watch design
An inside look at the new Garmin Marq 3rd Generation
Garmin has dropped the third-generation Garmin Marq series, a range of six of the best Garmin watches that are as much about luxury and style as they are about performance.
If you're already a Garmin user, there's a good chance you’re most familiar with its adventure and activity smartwatches like the Fenix, Instinct and Forerunner series’. They’re renowned for their practicality and a big well of features. However, the Garmin Marq series is its ultra-premium, style-forward luxury range that lets the company flex some different muscles, while still retaining the same featureset and software that people love.
The six models include the classy Aviator model, designed with complications for pilots; the debonair Adventurer; the serious military Commander; the Athlete with its energy drink colour accents; the ‘maritime blue’ Diver (new for this generation, replacing the seafaring Captain); and the exceptionally green Golfer.
The titanium price
The price of these watches varies a little between models, but you're looking at $2,500 / £2,199 / around AU$3,500 and up, double that of the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro. A higher budget lets Garmin indulge in the kind of watch manufacturing touches that just can’t be justified in its sport and outdoors models, like polished ceramic bezel inlays, micro-knurled buttons and a full grade-5 titanium casing, with no significant plastic elements on show.
This alone requires feats of engineering to ensure the antennas have enough room to figuratively breathe — metal blocks their signal, and a fitness watch without reliable GPS or Bluetooth is not going to be much use at all.
The solution is slim strips of plastic polymer in the frame that you probably wouldn’t even notice unless you look close, and know they are there. These polymer strips are fused to the titanium metal of the casing ‘at nano scale’ using a process called nano-moulding technology. In effect it’s similar to the little non-metal strips in an iPhone’s casing, applied with what sounds like a pretty expensive procedure.
Built to last, just not forever
Garmin COO Brad Trenkle explained to me the company isn’t fooling itself into thinking it’s making a direct alternative to a Patek Philippe, Rolex or Audemars Piguet here.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
“We didn't set out to build a mechanical watch that was designed to be passed down from from generation to generation,” says Trenkle. Smartwatches inevitably have a shelf life due to being a sealed unit with lithium batteries. But the way people use their Garmin watches means they have more longevity than some other kinds of consumer gadgets, according to Garmin’s own user data.
“Most users actually tend to use their Garmin watches longer than they they use their smartphone,” says Trenkle.
Making an ultra-premium smartwatch is different to making an heirloom analog watch. Case in point: the buttons, and how you add them to a watch designed to dive over 40 meters deep. Over the last few years Garmin has played around with button tech, a move forced by dive-ready water resistance becoming a common feature in high-end sport watches.
When the Garmin Fenix 8 arrived in 2024 there was a lot of talk about how watch’s inductive buttons made the series’s 40m dive-ready water resistance possible. It’s a design that means there’s no hole made in the casing to house the buttons.
“We have this wall of polymer that makes a complete seal between the watch case. There's no gasket, and it's just one piece,” explains Trenkle of the new Marq.
The style is ideal for hardcore water resistance, but not so great for the feel of the buttons. A Garmin Fenix 8’s buttons feel pretty spongy compared with other models. But in a classic Garmin Marq exercise of low-to-no compromise design, these watches have a mechanical clicker purely for the feel, combined with an inductive button for actual function. The result is perhaps what I noticed most clearly about the Marq Adventurer while wearing it: it has exceptionally bright but substantive button feedback.
Garmin Marq’s leveled-up tech
The tactical Commander and scuba-friendly Diver relate to features like aircraft outboard systems and interfacing with dive equipment, but all six watches share some common upgrades. For example, while the Garmin Fenix 9 and Enduro 4 have shown 64GB storage is now the standard for higher-end Garmin models, the Marq Generation 3 has 128GB.
These watches don’t offer massively exciting ways to use that space beyond adding more maps, music, podcasts and audiobooks. But it’s an upgrade such a luxury watch surely deserves.
Similarly, when the second Marq arrived in 2022 I was half confident its unique magnetic charge interface would inevitably dip down to prestige series like Fenix. Years later, that still hasn’t happened, and now the Marq generation 3 has its own tweaked version of that standard — a four-pin magnet interface. Not more jamming in that classic Garmin charger bung, which would hardly befit a luxury watch.
A lot of the Garmin Marq’s design touches aren’t shouty, but they do add up to make the physical presence of these watches feel distinctly different to, for example, the Forerunner 970. I wore the 970 alongside the Marq Adventurer on a test hike, and could really feel the difference between the two watches.
Once you get deeper into watch specs, the Garmin Marq series starts to sound very familiar. These watches have 1.4-inch AMOLED screens with peak brightness of 3000 nits. There is no micro LED option, or any MIP display models.
All that changes in the display is a “borderless” design than lets the metal of the bezel reach right up to the start of the display panel. It’s a sleek look, but not an improvement I would necessarily have clocked without being pointed towards it.
All Marq models have a mid-table diameter of 47mm, and the same kind of Elevate V5 heart rate array used in other top Gamins (accurate as tested against a heart rate monitor and the Apple Watch Ultra 4). There’s a flashlight, support for ECG readings and battery life is rated at 18 days, or seven days with the always-on display mode engaged. Like the Fenix 9 Pro, the Garmin Marq also supports not just communication over 4G/LTE, but satellite too, when used with an InReach subscription.
Should you buy?
Is a Garmin Marq “worth it” for the average Garmin shopper? Absolutely not.
These watches are here for the person who wouldn’t baulk at the price tag, let alone the rising costs of the Fenix family. It nets you that series’ best bits in a more stylish chassis, plus even more storage and model-specific features if you pick one of the specialised Marqs like the Aviator.
Which of the six is your favourite? Let us know in the poll below.

articles.title: Apple’s first smart display is the 7-inch HomeView for $299
articles.text:
Apple opened preorders for the HomeView smart home hub today.
The HomeView is a 7-inch smart display and speaker that aims to be a central access point for up to six members of a family to access and control Apple’s ecosystem of devices, apps, and the Siri generative AI chatbot that’s currently in beta.
Users can speak to HomeView to control smart home devices, such as, for example, telling Siri to close the smart blinds or activate smart locks. HomeView can also show a livestream for up to nine video feeds simultaneously.
“With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible cameras to deliver intelligent, end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles, notifying the household the moment someone arrives at the front door. With video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video footage, HomeView helps users quickly understand what happened in a video clip without even watching it,” Apple’s announcement said.
Competing with devices like the Amazon Echo Show, HomeView uses its integrated camera to identify who’s using it and show them their profile, which users can personalize with their preferred apps and widgets. Users can connect their HomeView profile to their Apple Intelligence-supporting iPhone or iPad and use the hub to access their Messages, Calendar, Reminders, and FaceTime.
“With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI does more for each person—taking action across apps and surfacing relevant information from Messages and Calendar, playlists on Apple Music, and more by drawing on their personal context,” Apple’s announcement says.

articles.title: 'GTA 6' llegaría a PC mucho antes de lo que todos pensábamos
articles.text:
La espera por GTA 6 en PC podría ser mucho más breve de lo que todos imaginábamos. Según reporta GamesBeat, Rockstar Games planea lanzar la versión para ordenadores apenas meses después de su debut en PS5 y Xbox Series X|S. Si esto se confirma será un auténtico bombazo, considerando que hasta aquí el estudio ha dado pistas prácticamente nulas de que la llegada del nuevo Grand Theft Auto podría darse en un plazo tan acotado.
De acuerdo con el citado medio, GTA 6 se lanzará en PC durante el primer trimestre de 2027. La información fue supuestamente ratificada por cuatro fuentes relacionadas con los planes de Rockstar y Take-Two Interactive. De ser cierto, el debut del título en ordenadores se dará, a más tardar, en marzo del próximo año.
Claro que la información debe tomarse con pinzas y no hay que dar nada por hecho. Por lo pronto, los responsables de GTA 6 no han realizado anuncios oficiales sobre una versión para PC. De hecho, cada vez que se les ha consultado sobre el tema han brindado respuestas evasivas. Y si bien todos esperaban que el juego llegara eventualmente a Windows, nadie en sus cabales pensaba que podría llegar a darse tan rápido.
Después de todo, suponiendo que la información es certera, GTA 6 estaría llegando a PC apenas 4 meses después de su debut en consolas, considerando marzo de 2027 como fecha más tardía. Esto pondría patas arriba cualquier especulación previa respecto de la expansión del juego más allá de su disponibilidad inicial en PlayStation y Xbox.
GTA 6 podría llegar a PC a más tardar en marzo de 2027
Desde que GTA 6 lanzó su primer tráiler a finales de 2023, Rockstar Games ha evitado ofrecer cualquier tipo de mención a una posible versión de PC. Las únicas referencias a su potencial llegada a la plataforma han sido de Strauss Zelnick, el CEO de Take-Two Interactive, la casa matriz del estudio. Desde 2024 hasta la actualidad, el ejecutivo ofreció referencias sobre el tema (algunas más crípticas que otras), dando a entender que una edición para ordenadores llegaría tarde o temprano, pero que no sería prioridad.
Recién en mayo de este año, Zelnick brindó una respuesta más directa sobre por qué todavía no se había anunciado GTA 6 en PC. El empresario argumentó, simplemente, que la mayoría de los jugadores de Grand Theft Auto estaban en consolas, y que por ese motivo preferían enfocarse primero en servir a su base de usuarios más amplia.
"Rockstar siempre empieza en consola porque creo que [...] se te juzga por cómo atiendes a tu público principal. Es decir, realmente atender a tu consumidor principal. Si tu consumidor principal no está ahí, si no se le atiende primero y de la mejor manera, no llegas a tus otros consumidores", explicó por entonces.
Pero esa parecía ser solo una parte de la historia. John Ricchio, histórico productor de Rockstar con pasado en GTA 5, Red Dead Redemption y Max Payne, explicó que también existía una justificación técnica. Según su experiencia, optimizar GTA 6 basándose en las limitaciones técnicas de la PS5 y las Xbox Series X|S haría mucho más fácil el proceso de portear el juego a PC.
"Siempre es mejor empezar por las limitaciones y luego ampliar, porque reducir es mucho más difícil que ampliar. Es mucho más difícil lograr un buen rendimiento en un juego que simplemente pensar: 'Oh, tenemos espacio extra, genial, podemos desoptimizar algunas cosas o hacerlas más llamativas'", comentó.
Considerando los antecedentes, el consenso general era que GTA 6 posiblemente se demorara unos dos años en llegar a PC. Pero si lo que reporta GamesBeat es certero, la historia esta vez podría ser muy diferente. Esto despierta un gran interrogante: ¿Por qué Rockstar cambiaría de estrategia ahora?
El citado reporte plantea dos opciones:
- Por un lado, la necesidad de capturar a cuantos jugadores sea posible para recuperar sus bestiales costes de desarrollo. GTA 6 habría costado unos 2.000 millones de dólares, y llegar temprano a los jugadores más casuales en PC podría agilizar la amortización.
- Por el otro, implementar una estrategia basada en mods, la creación de contenidos por parte de los usuarios y el role-playing. En tal sentido, se menciona que la compra de CFX.re por parte de Rockstar en 2023 podría jugar un papel clave en esta historia.
También se especula con que lanzar la versión para PC de GTA 6 apenas meses después de su llegada a consolas podría estar relacionada con ampliar la base de GTA Online desde el primer día. Según el CEO de Twitch, Rockstar planea lanzar el componente multijugador online del nuevo Grand Theft Auto en 2027. Por ende, ya hay teorías de que el arribo temprano del juego a los ordenadores podría estar relacionado con esto. Por lo pronto, no hay que dar nada por hecho, pero seguiremos atentos a cualquier novedad.

articles.title: AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
articles.text:
AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
Mathematics is a collaborative field, now disrupted by AI
Last week, OpenAI shared over 400 results for longstanding mathematical formulas that have troubled humans for decades; now researchers say it could take years for humans to validate and prove all the AI-driven work. But while analysts try to check the work of the unnamed OpenAI internal frontier model that found these alleged solutions, mathematicians argue this kind of AI-powered research and release threatens the field itself.
There's even the claim that by leaping from a prompt to a solution without a clear working in between, there is little benefit to these solutions in the first place. Mathematicians and the field itself may not be able to build on the results, as they don't know how they were achieved, nor has the development of such solutions produced new fields of mathematical understanding.
To make matters worse, there are suggestions that the growing confluence of mathematical and cybersecurity capabilities of frontier AI could bring into question the sanctity of cryptography itself. Alongside raising serious concerns for national security and modern digital systems, it could also put trillions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency at imminent risk.
Over 722 manuscripts dropped
The official count for OpenAI's maths solution release was 722 manuscripts, but with only 300 of the results formalized — digitizing human-readable formulas so they can be computer-verified — it's very difficult to know what's legitimate research. Some of the researchers The Verge spoke to found nonsense explanations within the reports, formulas that don't make sense, and some research that has already been completed by others.
The burden of proving the veracity of OpenAI and its model's claims is very much on the mathematical community, too. OpenAI didn't release the name of the model it used to generate these results, nor the prompts that generated them — despite those recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematicians and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI).
OpenAI has at least published changelogs for its GitHub repository of the results, making it clearer where mistakes were made. But with several retractions and corrections already, it seems clear that it didn't check over the results in any great detail before releasing them.
It's this brashness, the pace of releases, and OpenAI's seeming disinterest in remotely slowing down its progress in the field that have so many mathematicians up in arms.
A looming threat becomes immediate
Mathematics isn't the first field to suffer a major upheaval because of AI. Writers first felt the looming threat with the release of ChatGPT in 2022, and both visual and musical artists faced the same concerns shortly after. Artificial intelligence is impacting almost every industry in some way, but while there are some potential benefits for its use in the field of mathematics, researchers within the field are concerned about the impact this may have on the collaborative nature of the field and how it might discourage future mathematicians from exploring it.
Speaking to Business Insider, mathematics professor at NYU, Tristan Buckmaster, said that OpenAI's release had upended the world of many early-career mathematicians, suggesting it had wiped out their whole research programs. Alongside their own research being invalidated by some of OpenAI's solutions, he suggested that some were now fearful that, by using AI tools, researchers had inadvertently contributed to the results, raising the potential of them not using advanced tools in the future and being less likely to talk about their research publicly.
This could cause huge problems for mathematics as a whole, argued mathematics professor at Northwestern University, Bryna Kra. Highlighting how collaborative maths is, with researchers sharing ideas, research data, and formulas, she is now extremely concerned that OpenAI has made mathematicians more secretive, reducing their ability to work together towards solutions and build on each other's research.
Professor of mathematics at the University of California, Terence Tao said on Mastodon that "many fewer seminars, workshops, collaborations, or other activities are being generated from these results compared to traditional breakthroughs." He argued mathematics may need to pivot to value "progress more holistically," by elevating the role of community building over raw solutions.
Researchers have described an atmosphere of extreme anxiety, that whatever they're working on could be invalidated overnight. That can undermine job applications, grant proposals, and those building the early components of their academic careers. Understanding and developing core mathematical capabilities at a high level can take years. AI dumps eradicating years of effort in such a haphazard fashion risk making it seem a near-pointless endeavour.
With swirling rumors of yet more releases from OpenAI, and potentially companion releases from other AI labs chasing the same headlines, the morale in many mathematical fields is extremely low.
Cryptography
With how much mathematics underpins key components of our digital world, it's no surprise that major changes in the pace of its development could have a domino effect elsewhere. One proposed potential minefield is the fertile ground of cryptography.
Associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins Whiting School of Engineering, Matthew Green, said on social media that he believes the congruence of mathematical developments and cybersecurity capabilities could result in AI that can defeat encryption as we know it.
While that raises potential concerns for all manner of fields that rely on encryption to protect the security of sensitive data, it could open up the cryptocurrency industry to wholesale theft, potentially impacting trillions of dollars of digital tokens.
Not everyone agrees with Green that this is an inevitability. British cryptographer — and one of the few people accused of being Bitcoin developer Satoshi Nakamoto — Adam Back, described these claims as nonsense and that there was little suggestion that just because AI can do certain mathematics now, that they'll be able to defeat encryption at some unnamed date in the future.
Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin urged calm too, stating on Twitter/X that nobody should rush to move their tokens to a new wallet or panic over wallet security. However, he did argue that AI had the potential to one day be a far more dangerous threat to the sanctity of cryptocurrency than quantum computing.
While it doesn't appear that cryptography is a field AI is set to invalidate just yet, it's clear that it poses a potential threat to mathematical researchers and the core underlying 'way of doing things.' Much like it has just about everywhere else.
Researchers are adjusting to it, but the dust isn't likely to settle anytime soon, and in the meantime, OpenAI and its contemporaries may just move on to a new field to focus on as it continues to chase relevance and profitability.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: 17 Years with China: What Really Makes a Partnership Work - EE Times
articles.text:
China has changed considerably over the past 15 years — and so have European companies’ expectations of Chinese manufacturers. Robert Tarantowicz of Honya Europe looks back on that shift, from his first attempts to work with Chinese suppliers in 2009 to building a Polish-Chinese company that now operates across Europe. Why shouldn’t price be the main selection criterion? How do you hold a productive conversation with a Chinese partner? And what is worth looking for during a factory visit? Here’s what he told us.
1. How did your cooperation with Chinese manufacturers begin, and what were the early stages like?
In 2009, I was looking for a new printed circuit board supplier for a rapidly growing company. We made several attempts to work with Chinese manufacturers, but none of them resulted in a successful supplier qualification. The main obstacles were communication misunderstandings, quality issues, and differences in business practices.
Several months later, I met Hong Xu from Honya International. Subsequent orders were handled efficiently. Problems did arise, as they do in any manufacturing environment, but this supplier stood out because of its willingness to jointly investigate root causes, share the costs of justified claims, and implement preventive actions. That created a foundation of trust, and Honya International became a key PCB supplier.
In 2013, we entered into a partnership and began working together in the European market. In 2020, we transformed that cooperation into a joint venture, HONYA EUROPE, registered in Poland. Today, our Polish-Chinese company holds a market share in the low double digits in Poland’s PCB supply market and serves customers across Europe.
2. How much has China changed as a business partner over the last fifteen years?
The business environment has changed dramatically. Manufacturers’ technological capabilities have increased, labor costs have risen, compliance requirements have become more demanding, and geopolitical risk has gained importance. China is no longer viewed simply as a low-cost manufacturing base. It is also a major market, a sophisticated industrial base, and an increasingly strong technological competitor.
In our specific relationship, however, less has changed than one might expect. We still base our cooperation on long-term trust, shared risk management, and personal contact. The relationship has evolved beyond business.
3. What are the main concerns European companies have when working with a Chinese supplier for the first time?
The most common questions we hear are: Will the goods actually be delivered? Is the advance payment safe? Will the product match the documentation? Is the person we’re dealing with the manufacturer or just an intermediary?
There are also concerns regarding document protection, certificate authenticity, complaint handling, delivery reliability, and customs clearance.
These concerns are entirely reasonable, but they can be managed through proper verification of both the company and factory, trial orders, clearly defined acceptance criteria, quality control measures, and payment terms appropriate to the level of risk and the history of cooperation.
4. What mistakes do companies most often make when starting to work with Chinese suppliers?
The most common mistake is reducing supplier selection to a price comparison. If a buyer pushes pricing below what is sustainable for the required technology and quality level, the manufacturer will inevitably look for savings in materials, processes, inspection, or delivery schedules. The consequences may only become visible during mass production.
Quotations should be compared on an equal basis: material specifications, performance class, tolerances, testing requirements, documentation, delivery terms, and responsibility for claims. Price is important, but it should always be assessed together with the total cost of risk.
5. Are there any significant cultural differences that can affect negotiations and day-to-day cooperation?
Yes, although entire societies should not be reduced to simple stereotypes. In many Chinese companies, context, hierarchy, personal relationships, and avoiding situations where someone “loses face” tend to play a greater role than they do in Europe. Agreement expressed during a meeting may sometimes mean “I understand” rather than “I accept the terms.”
For that reason, it is worth asking open-ended questions, requesting detailed explanations of how work will be carried out, and summarizing agreements in writing. Critical feedback is best discussed objectively and without publicly putting a partner in an uncomfortable position. Most importantly, focus on getting to know the particular company and the people within it, rather than relying on stereotypes.
6. How is trust built in business relationships with Chinese partners?
Trust develops gradually. It is built through small orders that are successfully completed, on-time payments made according to agreed terms, fair handling of complaints, predictable communication, and visits by both parties. What matters most is that actions consistently back up what has been promised.
Chinese partners usually appreciate a genuine interest in their language and culture. One of my favorite sayings is Qiānlǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zúxià, which literally means, “A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one’s feet” and is often rendered in English as “A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.” It perfectly reflects the nature of cooperation, where everything starts with a small but meaningful first step.
It is very important to simultaneously build a personal relationship, which is the foundation of joint action. In our company, this relationship is very strong, as evidenced, for example, by the fact that my daughters stay in touch with their “uncle from China,” and on two occasions I was asked to give Chinese children Western names. This shows that a lasting business partnership can grow into a relationship between people and families.
7. Can experience gained in Europe be transferred directly to the Chinese market, or is a different approach required?
It cannot be transferred without adjustment. European standards regarding documentation, quality, compliance, and accountability are highly valuable, but communication styles, negotiation methods, and relationship building need to be adapted to the local business environment.
It is also worth challenging our own assumptions about China. Some stereotypes were formed decades ago and no longer reflect today’s technological capabilities. The best approach is to combine European process discipline with curiosity and a willingness to learn from a partner.
8. How can a potential supplier be verified before cooperation begins?
The full legal company name, registration number, business scope, legal representative, and consistency between the bank account and the invoicing entity should all be verified. Useful sources include Chinese government databases such as the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System and Credit China, as well as reports from independent verification companies.
Documentation alone is not a substitute for an audit. It is advisable to verify whether the factory actually performs the processes it claims to perform, confirm certificate validity directly with the issuing bodies, inspect quality-control procedures, review samples, and start with a limited pilot order. Only after successful results would I recommend scaling up cooperation.
9. What role do personal visits to China and direct contact with manufacturers play?
They are extremely important. Meeting in person accelerates trust-building and makes it easier to discuss issues that may remain unclear through email correspondence. It also allows you to assess how a company responds to detailed questions and whether it truly understands the product’s application.
A factory visit helps evaluate actual production capacity, process organization, material storage, quality-control equipment, and batch traceability. Simply walking through the production floor is not enough. The most valuable insight comes from following a real order through the process, from material receipt to final inspection, and speaking directly with the people responsible for engineering and quality.
One must also accept that part of the visit will be dedicated to getting to know one another. For many Chinese partners, a relationship comes before a transaction, whereas European customers often prefer to move straight to specifications and pricing.
10. What aspects deserve special attention when placing your first orders?
You should assume that any information not clearly documented may be interpreted differently. The order package should specify the current documentation revision, material, stack-up, copper thickness, tolerances, surface finish, performance class, scope of testing, packaging requirements, and acceptance criteria.
Before moving into mass production, it is advisable to approve the DFM analysis and either a sample or a pilot batch. Procedures for handling non-conformities, delivery schedules, shipping terms, and payment conditions should also be agreed upon in advance. Having these points confirmed in writing is more important than hearing repeated assurances that “everything is clear.”
11. What does quality control look like in an international supply chain, and which mechanisms are worth implementing?
Quality control begins before production starts. First, requirements and acceptance criteria must be clearly defined, and then it should be confirmed that the selected factory has the appropriate processes, equipment, and expertise. In PCB manufacturing, this includes DFM approval, material and stack-up validation, and agreement on the required performance class.
The scope of inspection should be aligned with the project’s risk profile. It may include AOI, electrical testing, impedance measurements, microsection analysis, surface-finish inspection, batch traceability, and a final quality report. Incoming quality inspection is also necessary after delivery, and in the event of a non-conformity, a documented root-cause analysis and corrective actions should follow.
Payment terms can help reduce risk, but they can never replace a well-designed quality system. The safest approach is a process in which requirements, inspection results, and responsibility for claims are agreed upon before production begins.
12. Does the current economic and geopolitical situation affect trade relations between Europe and China?
Yes. Day-to-day business is affected by export restrictions, sanctions, tariffs, dual-use regulations, country-of-origin requirements, and growing pressure to increase supply chain resilience. Even when business partners take a pragmatic approach to cooperation, they cannot ignore these frameworks.
As a result, companies are more frequently qualifying alternative suppliers, maintaining safety stock for critical items, and conducting more detailed assessments of logistics routes and regulatory compliance. This does not mean the end of cooperation with China. It does mean that purchasing decisions must take regulatory risk and continuity of supply into account, not just price and production lead time.
13. How have European customers’ expectations of Chinese manufacturers changed over the years?
European customers are increasingly looking beyond low prices. Technological capability, consistency, short implementation times, complete documentation, traceability, compliance with industry requirements, and responsive complaint handling are now equally important.
The role of manufacturers themselves has also evolved. The best suppliers are no longer simply executing customer documentation. They actively participate in DFM analysis, propose material solutions, and help prepare designs for stable volume production. At the same time, manufacturing capabilities vary significantly from one factory to another, making supplier selection for a specific technology more important than ever.
14. In the PCB industry, quality is critical. How can companies effectively balance cost control with maintaining high production standards?
The most effective way to reduce costs is through design optimization and production organization, not by compromising on critical materials or inspections. The greatest benefits come from early DFM analysis, realistic tolerances, optimized panelization, standardized materials and stack-ups, consolidated orders, and reliable volume forecasts.
Requirements related to safety, reliability, and end-use applications should never be negotiable. A printed circuit board is the foundation of a device that may operate in fire protection systems, hazardous environments, or safety-critical infrastructure. Cost savings made at the wrong stage can multiply the cost of claims, downtime, or field failures many times over.
Our role is therefore to identify process efficiencies without compromising the agreed level of quality.
15. What logistical challenges most commonly arise in projects between Europe and China?
The most common challenges include fluctuating transit times, seasonal congestion before holidays, incomplete customs documentation, inappropriate Incoterms selection, damaged packaging, and insufficient buffers for delays. In electronics, additional considerations include moisture control, ESD protection, batch labeling, and maintaining traceability.
We mitigate these risks through advance planning, clearly assigned responsibility for customs clearance and insurance, trusted freight forwarders, document verification before shipment, and selecting transportation methods based on the value and urgency of the order. For critical projects, it is advisable to build in time buffers and consider alternative transportation routes or delivery methods.
16. Can you share an example that illustrates the unique nature of working with a Chinese partner?
One good example is a machine purchase project we carried out several years ago. For several days we discussed specifications, service support, certifications, costs, and transportation. At the same time, we talked about China, cars, baijiu, our families, and where the machine would be installed after delivery. From a European perspective, it might have seemed that we were drifting away from the main topic, but for our partner this was part of building the foundation for the transaction.
Initially, the supplier expected full prepayment. After extensive discussions and the development of mutual trust, we agreed on a payment structure of 20 percent before the order was launched, with the remaining balance payable after confirmation that the machine was ready for shipment through photographs, videos, and responses to technical questions.
This case demonstrates that personal relationships can influence commercial terms, but they should always go hand in hand with measurable acceptance milestones. Trust alone is not a substitute for verification.
17. How has the technological development of Chinese manufacturers affected the global electronics market?
Chinese manufacturers have evolved from contract producers into organizations playing an increasingly important role in process development, automation, and the advancement of their own technologies. Their production scale, extensive supplier networks, and rapid investment cycles have shortened product development timelines and increased pricing pressure across the global market.
In the PCB sector, technologies that were once available from only a handful of suppliers are now offered by a much broader range of factories. While this improves access to advanced solutions, it also increases the importance of supplier qualification. Similar technological claims do not necessarily translate into the same level of process stability, documentation quality, or complaint-handling capability.
18. What trends are you currently observing in electronics and PCB manufacturing in China?
The strongest growth can be seen in HDI, high-layer-count, high-speed, and high-frequency PCBs, as well as rigid-flex constructions. Demand is being driven by data centers and AI applications, telecommunications, automotive electronics, industrial automation, and devices requiring high interconnection density.
A second major trend is factory automation, including expanded optical inspection, process-data collection, and traceability systems. The third is specialization. Individual factories increasingly focus on specific technologies and production volumes, which means there is no single “best factory” for every project.
From a European customer’s perspective, this creates more opportunities but also requires more careful matching of manufacturers to the material requirements, design complexity, reliability expectations, and production volume of each project.
19. What advice would you give to companies considering cooperation with Chinese suppliers?
I would start with six steps: a detailed specification, verification of the supplier and factory, a pilot order, written acceptance criteria, quality control measures, and direct personal contact. Order volumes should be increased only after the supplier has demonstrated quality and delivery reliability in practice.
It is not worth choosing a partner solely on the basis of the lowest quotation. Companies should evaluate how the supplier responds to technical questions, documents its processes, and handles non-conformities. It is also wise to plan a second source for critical components from the very beginning.
20. In your opinion, what will cooperation between Europe and China in the electronics sector look like in the coming years?
I expect Europe and China to remain highly interconnected, but in a more selective form than in the past. China will remain a major manufacturing and technology hub, while European companies will invest more heavily in supply chain resilience, second-source strategies, and regulatory compliance.
In some sectors, production for local markets will become increasingly localized, and additional restrictions will emerge in certain critical technologies. Nevertheless, the need for engineering and commercial cooperation will not disappear. The companies that succeed will be those capable of combining strong supplier relationships in China with sensible diversification and effective risk management.
Meet Robert during the matchmaking sessions at electronica 2026.

articles.title: Tech30 2026: Meet the startups building India’s next generation of technology
articles.text:
Tech30 2026: Meet the 30 startups building India’s next generation of technology
From spacetech and defence to clean energy and advanced materials, YourStory's Tech30 spotlights 30 promising startups developing technologies for India and beyond.
India’s startups are no longer just finding new ways to use existing technology. A growing number are building the technology itself, from satellites and autonomous robots to advanced materials, medical diagnostics and cleaner construction methods. Their work is taking them into sectors that demand years of research, specialised expertise, and significant investment, with the potential to change how industries operate.
This shift is at the heart of TechSparks 2026, YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed ‘The New Tech Order’. One of its key highlights is Tech30, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups working on technologies that could shape India’s future.
Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year's Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. Speaking on ‘Prosperity cannot be imported: The road to tech independence’, he emphasised the need for India to develop technologies that address its own challenges.
"The new tech order is to learn to solve our own problems — foundational problems from agritech to material science to lasers, and also AI. But AI is not to be the be all and end all of it,” Vembu said.
Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India, also joined Vembu in celebrating this year's Tech30 cohort on stage.
Chosen from a pool of applicants, the startups are evaluated by a jury of experienced members of the startup ecosystem, along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams. The Tech30 report was unveiled at TechSparks 2026, bringing attention to companies working across a range of sectors and technologies.
This year’s selection reflects the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. From improving industrial processes and strengthening critical infrastructure to developing new products and markets, these companies are working on challenges in India and overseas.
Here are the 30 startups selected for Tech30 2026.
Apollyon Dynamics
Apollyon Dynamics develops autonomous drones and counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems for defence applications. Its portfolio includes high-speed interceptor drones such as Ahuti Mk II, designed to neutralise hostile drones, and Nightshade ADX-1, an autonomous strike platform.
Arctus Aerospace
Arctus Aerospace is developing high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that operate at around 50,000 feet and can remain airborne for up to 24 hours. Equipped with onboard AI for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and flight planning, its platforms are designed to provide persistent aerial surveillance and high-resolution imaging for defence, agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, and disaster response.
Attox Research Laboratories
Attox Research Laboratories develops diagnostic technology to accelerate antibiotic sensitivity testing and help address antibiotic resistance. Its flagship device, Bactolizer, analyses electrical signals from patient samples using specialised algorithms to identify effective antibiotics and appropriate dosages in around two hours, compared with the 24–48 hours typically required by conventional methods. The system uses a reusable testing unit and disposable cartridges designed for hospital settings.
Balisto Agritech
Balisto Agritech has developed the Balisto 130 Pro, an electric farm machine that combines multiple agricultural operations, including weeding, sowing, spraying, rotavating, and harvesting, on a single platform. Powered by detachable batteries, the machine can be controlled through an onboard dashboard or remotely, while an internet-connected system enables cloud-based monitoring and remote diagnostics.
CaliperAI
CaliperAI builds AI infrastructure for robots and autonomous machines, using sensor fusion, localisation, and perception to help them navigate the physical world. Its platform captures, analyses, and annotates data from cameras, LiDAR, and navigation sensors, supporting the development of autonomous systems.
CraftifAI
CraftifAI builds AI software that automates development for embedded systems, edge AI, and IoT devices. Its Orbit platform generates, compiles, and validates code directly on target hardware, helping companies develop software for robotics, drones, industrial equipment, and automotive systems.
Curium Life
Curium Life is developing AI models that interpret surgical videos, anatomy, and operating-room workflows to support surgeons during procedures. Its technology aims to provide real-time guidance, identify anatomical structures, and flag potential risks, alongside tools that analyse CT scans to assess preoperative risks and abdominal-wall conditions.
Dognosis
Dognosis is developing BreathEasy, a non-invasive cancer screening test that analyses a person's breath to identify potential cancer risk across multiple cancer types. The system combines trained dogs' ability to detect cancer-related chemical patterns with brain-computer interfaces and machine learning to interpret their responses, flagging higher-risk individuals for confirmatory tests such as imaging and biopsies.
Ecopath
Ecopath turns industrial waste into construction materials, replacing conventional cement with alternatives designed to cut emissions and water use. Its EcoConcrete supports applications ranging from road construction to masonry products, while its soil-stabilisation and waterproofing solutions address other infrastructure needs.
Enerzolve Smart Technologies
From battery storage to grid infrastructure, Enerzolve works on the power electronics and instrumentation needed to manage electricity reliably. Its technology portfolio spans bidirectional power converters, software-driven solid-state transformers, and ultrasonic water, gas, and energy meters, serving utility developers, data centres, and defence organisations.
EON Space Labs
EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging payload is now in orbit following a launch aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9, marking a milestone for its space-imaging technology. The startup develops electro-optical and infrared systems for space, aerial, and ground surveillance, including imaging payloads, gimbals, and fixed surveillance equipment, with more than 90% of its components built domestically.
Evoxia
Agricultural residues could offer an alternative route to producing polysilicon, a critical material for solar panels and semiconductors. Evoxia is developing a plasma-based process to turn this feedstock into high-purity silicon, reporting 6N purity in laboratory validation and targeting lower energy consumption and emissions than conventional production methods.
Folium Sensing
Folium Sensing turns standard optical fibre cables into sensors that detect vibrations, temperature changes, and mechanical strain over distances exceeding 100 km. Its AI-powered monitoring system helps identify pipeline leaks, railway-track cracks, and security threats across critical infrastructure.
Harvested Robotics
Harvested Robotics' RAKSHAK uses computer vision to identify weeds and high-powered lasers to remove them without damaging crops. Mounted on a tractor, the device can eliminate 80–100 weeds per minute, offering farmers an alternative to chemical herbicides and manual weeding.
Hyperonic Engineering
Hyperonic Engineering develops hydrogen technologies for mobility and industrial applications, including its H35 dispenser for safe, precision-controlled refuelling. It is also developing microgrids that combine electrolysers, hydrogen storage, and fuel cells for decentralised power generation.
Hypersonic Technologies
Hydrogen production need not come with direct CO₂ emissions or a single output. Hypersonic Technologies is developing plasma-based reactors that split methane and other gas feedstocks into hydrogen and solid carbon black, which can be used in tyres, plastics, paints, and coatings.
ImmunitoAI
Designing antibodies from scratch is the focus of immunitoAI, whose AbInitio platform uses AI to create proteins that bind to specific disease-linked targets. Trained on 3D protein structures, the system generates candidate antibodies for laboratory testing, with potential applications in cancer, autoimmune disorders, blood diseases, and neurological conditions.
Integra Robotics
Integra Robotics equips factories and defence teams with modular robots built for hazardous and hard-to-reach environments. The hardware ranges from robotic arms and underwater manipulators to mobile platforms capable of carrying 500 kg, while software uses field-operation data to train and improve machine capabilities.
Kubo Care
Kubo Care uses 60 GHz radar and AI to monitor older adults at home or in care facilities, detecting falls without cameras or wearable devices. Its system also tracks movement patterns, sleep interruptions, and vital signs to flag potential health changes, while alerting caregivers to events such as bed exits and wandering.
Metastable Materials
Discarded lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals that Metastable Materials recovers for industrial reuse. Its proprietary recycling process separates lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper without adding chemicals, supplying recovered materials to industries such as glass, ceramics, stainless steel, and automotive manufacturing.
MiCoB
From army bunkers to residential structures, MiCoB uses robotic 3D concrete printing to automate construction. Its integrated technology combines specialised concrete mixes, printers, and digital design software, enabling the company to produce structures with less labour and material waste; it has delivered more than 650 3D-printed structures across 13 states.
MumbaiSemi
MumbaiSemi's DhruvaPro chip enables satellite navigation receivers to work across India's NavIC system and global constellations including GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou. The fabless semiconductor startup is also developing integrated circuits for wireless communications, AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, and low-power IoT devices.
Neo San
Instead of transporting non-recyclable dry waste to disposal sites, Neo San's machines process it where it is generated, using induction heating to reach temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. Its range handles between 25 kg and 500 kg or more of waste daily, serving buildings, hospitals, and industrial facilities, with the resulting ash tested for use in construction.
Pramatra Space
Pramatra Space is working on encryption systems designed to withstand future quantum-computing threats. Its integrated photonics chip generates entangled photons to create secure encryption keys, which the startup aims to distribute through fibre networks and satellites to protect enterprise communications and critical infrastructure.
Red Balloon Aerospace
Red Balloon Aerospace is building platforms to operate in near-space, the region between conventional airspace and outer space. Its portfolio includes high-altitude balloons, tethered aerostats, and autonomous stratospheric airships designed for long-duration communications, remote connectivity, disaster response, and surveillance missions.
Sanyark Space
Sanyark Space is developing low Earth orbit satellites to improve navigation accuracy from metres to centimetres. Its constellation will transmit correction data and stronger signals to support precise positioning, timing, and more resilient communications for defence and infrastructure applications.
Segritech
Segritech uses computer vision and deep learning to grade fruit by size, colour, and surface defects, processing up to two to three tonnes an hour with 95% reported accuracy. Its machines currently sort produce such as pomegranates and apples, while the startup is developing an autonomous robot to harvest fruit directly in the field.
SpaceFields
SpaceFields develops solid-propulsion systems for rockets, unmanned aerial vehicles, and defence applications, with capabilities spanning composite propellants, rocket motors, and energetic materials. Its portfolio also includes an aerospike rocket engine, while its in-house technologies are backed by 32 patent filings, 11 of which have been granted.
TeraLumen Solutions
Terahertz waves are at the core of TeraLumen Solutions’ imaging and testing systems. Its TeraXPLOR platform supports research and spectroscopy, while TeraNIM detects defects and measures coating thickness in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and oil and gas. The company is also developing a system for detecting cancer margins during surgery.
Yaanendriya
Yaanendriya develops motion sensors, navigation systems, and control software for autonomous machines, from drones to surgical robots. Its positioning technology is also being adapted for GPS-denied environments, including underwater and indoor settings.
To access the full report on Tech30 startups, click here.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Le dernier tir de SpaceX a fait flotter une immense méduse lumineuse dans le ciel, voici les photos les plus incroyables
articles.text:
Le 13 octobre 2026, une « méduse spatiale » a envahi les réseaux sociaux après un décollage depuis Cap Canaveral de la Falcon 9 de SpaceX (mission CRS‑35).
Des photographes ont même immortalisé la « méduse » et le passage lumineux de l'ISS sur une même image.
La Nasa explique que ce type de nuage provient des gaz d'échappement — principalement vapeur d'eau et dioxyde de carbone — éclairés par le Soleil levant à haute altitude, créant cette illusion céleste.
Le 13 octobre 2026, une « méduse spatiale » a envahi les réseaux sociaux après un décollage depuis Cap Canaveral de la Falcon 9 de SpaceX (mission CRS‑35).
Des photographes ont même immortalisé la « méduse » et le passage lumineux de l'ISS sur une même image.
La Nasa explique que ce type de nuage provient des gaz d'échappement — principalement vapeur d'eau et dioxyde de carbone — éclairés par le Soleil levant à haute altitude, créant cette illusion céleste.
De superbes images d’une « méduse spatiale » aperçue aux États-Unis sont diffusées ce 13 octobre 2026. Ce phénomène lumineux est dû au décollage d’une fusée Falcon 9 de SpaceX, le matin même en Floride.
En parcourant les réseaux sociaux ce mardi 13 octobre 2026, vous avez peut-être croisé une étrange « méduse spatiale », observée dans le ciel des États-Unis. Des images spectaculaires de ce phénomène sont diffusées par des photographes et passionnés d’astronomie.
Les photos montrent une forme lumineuse, teintée de bleu et de doré, se détachant sur le ciel sombre. À l’origine de cette créature céleste éphémère, un événement bien tangible : un lancement de fusée.
« Méduse spatiale » et ISS réunies : le jackpot pour ces photographes
Ce mardi 13 octobre, SpaceX lançait en effet une fusée Falcon 9 dans l’espace. Son décollage a eu lieu à la mi-journée (pour nous, en France métropolitaine). Il s’agissait de la mission CRS-35, dédiée au ravitaillement de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS) à l’aide d’une capsule Dragon. Le lanceur est parti de la Floride, depuis la base de Cap Canaveral.
Certains photographes ont réussi à saisir sur la même image la « méduse » et l’ISS en train de traverser le ciel – on reconnaît le passage de la station spatiale à une ligne droite très lumineuse, qui ne peut pas être confondue avec une étoile filante.
La formation de la « méduse spatiale » a même été photographiée par SpaceX, juste après ce décollage.
Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’un lancement de SpaceX donne lieu à une « méduse spatiale ». En mars 2026, le décollage d’une autre Falcon 9, qui lançait des satellites Starlink dans l’espace, avait provoqué la formation de ce phénomène.
Comment se forme cet étrange nuage lors du décollage d’une fusée SpaceX ?
La fusée a décollé à 6h33 heure locale, peu avant le lever du Soleil sur la Floride. Une situation propice à la formation d’une « méduse spatiale ». Comme l’explique la Nasa, lorsque le panache qui s’échappe de la fusée lors du décollage se trouve assez haut dans le ciel, il peut être éclairé par la lumière du Soleil levant. Le photographe, lui, est encore dans l’obscurité.
Peu avant le décollage de la Falcon 9 ce 13 octobre, la possibilité que le phénomène survienne avait été anticipée par des photographes et passionnés d’astronomie, qui prévoyaient que la fusée entrerait dans la lumière du Soleil 3 minutes et 20 secondes après le décollage.
« Cette combinaison d’ombre et de lumière, observable à l’aube ou au crépuscule, donne à ces gaz d’échappement, composés principalement de vapeur d’eau et de dioxyde de carbone, l’apparence d’un nuage lumineux », selon la Nasa. Une forme qui donne l’impression de descendre, « car la fusée suit la courbure de la Terre dans son trajet vers l’espace ».

articles.title: Avec ses 7 places et une recharge en 9 minutes, ce SUV chinois bouscule les constructeurs européens
articles.text:
BYD s’attaque aux grands SUV électriques avec un Atto 8 capable d’accueillir sept personnes et de tenir jusqu’à 653 km sans passer à la station. Sa recharge ultrarapide pourrait surtout faire la différence sur les longs trajets, à condition de disposer des bornes capables d’en profiter.
Le Peugeot E-5008 tient un nouveau concurrent sérieux. Dévoilé ce 12 octobre au Mondial de l’Auto de Paris, le BYD Atto 8 est un SUV électrique à sept places qui promet jusqu’à 653 km d’autonomie WLTP. Ce nouveau modèle haut de gamme entend répondre à une préoccupation concrète des familles qui passent à l’électrique, celle de partir chargées sans transformer chaque départ en vacances en expédition.
Une recharge express, à condition de trouver la bonne borne
Les 653 km annoncés concernent la version à propulsion. La déclinaison à transmission intégrale, forte de 775 chevaux, affiche pour sa part 602 km, avec la même batterie de 115 kWh. Ces chiffres restent évidemment ceux du cycle WLTP. Sur autoroute, avec sept personnes à bord, leurs bagages et le chauffage ou la climatisation, l’autonomie réelle sera sensiblement inférieure.
La nouveauté la plus intéressante se joue à la borne. Grâce à sa batterie Blade de deuxième génération et à la technologie Flash Charging, l’Atto 8 pourrait en effet passer de 10 à 70% de niveau de charge en cinq minutes seulement, puis atteindre 97% après neuf minutes de charge totale. De quoi réduire sensiblement l’attente dans les stations-service pendant les grands déplacements.
Sur le papier, l’attente commence à se rapprocher d’une pause classique sur une aire d’autoroute. Encore faut-il trouver une borne capable de délivrer une telle puissance. Le constructeur prévoit d’installer 3 000 bornes Flash Charging en Europe d’ici à la fin 2027, et leur déploiement sera déterminant pour transformer cette promesse en avantage réel.
Sept passagers, mais des bagages à répartir
Avec 5,04 mètres de long, l’Atto 8 joue clairement dans la catégorie des grands SUV. Les sept occupants disposent de trois rangées de sièges, mais il faudra composer avec seulement 270 litres de coffre lorsqu’elles sont toutes utilisées.
Un compartiment de 136 litres sous le capot apporte un peu d’air, tandis que le volume grimpe jusqu’à 1 960 litres une fois les deux rangées arrière rabattues.
BYD soigne également le confort. Les sièges avant et les places extérieures du deuxième rang disposent de fonctions de chauffage, de ventilation et de massage. L’écran central de 15,6 pouces (39,6 cm de diagonale) intègre notamment Google Maps et le Play Store.
Peugeot et les Européens ont encore des arguments
En France, le Peugeot E-5008 Grande Autonomie, assemblé dans l’Hexagone, propose déjà une autonomie voisine de 670 km WLTP. Le nouveau venu ne prend donc pas une avance décisive sur ce terrain. L’écart entre les promesses de recharge est beaucoup plus marqué, puisque Peugeot annonce 27 minutes pour passer de 20 à 80% sur sa version de 97 kWh.
Le marché européen commence par ailleurs à se peupler de grands modèles familiaux électriques. Le Škoda Peaq revendique lui aussi sept places et plus de 640 km d’autonomie, tandis que Renault continue de répondre à cette clientèle avec un Espace hybride.
L’Atto 8 doit arriver au premier trimestre 2027, mais son tarif français reste inconnu. C’est probablement lui qui décidera si BYD tient un nouveau poids lourd du marché ou une impressionnante vitrine technologique. Si sa recharge tient ses promesses, les passagers pourraient en tout cas finir par réclamer une pause bien avant que la voiture doive recharger.

articles.title: Une loi solaire et des canicules : comment l'Allemagne a freiné ses heures de prix négatifs — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cette année, il était presque impossible de passer à côté de l’information : les heures de prix négatifs de l’électricité se sont multipliées presque partout en Europe. Résultant principalement de l’essor du solaire et de l’éolien, le phénomène témoigne des difficultés croissantes à équilibrer la production et la consommation d’électricité.
Lorsque l’offre dépasse largement la demande, les prix peuvent en effet passer sous zéro. Mais alors que de nombreux pays européens enregistrent une hausse de ces épisodes, l’Allemagne, pourtant engagée dans le développement massif des renouvelables, fait figure d’exception. Le nombre d’heures concernées y est en baisse cette année.
Une baisse de 13 % sur l’ensemble de l’année ?
Au 27 septembre, l’Allemagne avait enregistré 463 heures de prix négatifs depuis le début de l’année, contre 511 à la même période en 2025. Pour la première fois en quatre ans, le pays voit diminuer ces épisodes. Selon les estimations du cabinet d’analyse Kpler, citées par Bloomberg le 28 septembre, leur nombre devrait diminuer de 13 % sur l’ensemble de l’année, en glissement annuel.
Sur l’ensemble de 2025, l’Allemagne avait cumulé 576 heures de prix négatifs, d’après le cabinet britannique Ricardo. Avec 463 heures au 27 septembre, le pays se retrouve désormais derrière la France, qui en compte 520 sur la même période.
La réforme solaire allemande, entrée en vigueur le 25 février 2025, semble porter ses fruits cette année. Elle supprime la rémunération garantie des installations solaires de plus de 2 kWc mises en service depuis cette date, dès que les prix de l’électricité deviennent négatifs ; pour celles de 2 à 100 kWc, la règle s’applique une fois le compteur intelligent installé. Cette loi, appelée Solarspitzengesetz, ou « loi sur les pics de production solaire », vise à réduire les coûts du soutien public et à limiter les injections d’électricité lorsque la production est déjà excédentaire.
Avant la réforme, la rémunération n’était suspendue qu’après plusieurs heures consécutives de prix négatifs, si bien que les exploitants pouvaient continuer à injecter leur production en touchant leur tarif garanti pendant la plupart de ces épisodes. Désormais, ils n’ont plus intérêt à injecter pendant ces heures et réduisent ou suspendent leur production. Les heures non rémunérées ne sont pas perdues pour autant : elles donnent droit à une prolongation de la période de soutien de 20 ans.
La loi touche aussi les particuliers équipés de panneaux. Tant qu’elles ne disposent pas d’un compteur intelligent, les nouvelles installations de 2 à 100 kWc ne peuvent injecter que 60 % de leur puissance sur le réseau. Les petites installations de moins de 2 kWc, comme les kits solaires de balcon, ne sont pas concernées par la suppression de la rémunération.
La hausse de la demande électrique durant l’été aura également été bénéfique pour le réseau allemand. Le recours accru à la climatisation pendant les vagues de chaleur a fait progresser la consommation, permettant d’absorber une bonne partie de l’électricité solaire. Selon les données de l’institut Fraunhofer reprises par Bloomberg, la consommation a progressé de 10 % sur un an de mai à juillet, alors que les températures dépassaient parfois les 40 °C. À cela s’ajoute une production éolienne plus faible en mai et en juin, selon Kpler, ce qui a limité les volumes d’électricité disponibles sur le marché.
La France et l’Espagne battent leur record
Pendant ce temps, d’autres pays européens battent leur record d’heures à prix négatifs. C’est notamment le cas de la France, qui en comptabilisait déjà 520 à la fin du mois de septembre. Le chiffre dépasse le total enregistré sur l’ensemble de l’année 2025, qui s’élevait à 513 heures. Si le développement des énergies renouvelables a contribué à cette évolution, RTE pointe aussi le retard pris dans l’électrification des usages, qui empêche la consommation de repartir à la hausse.
L’Espagne enregistre également un niveau historique. À la fin du mois de septembre, le pays avait dépassé les 700 heures de prix négatifs, soit une hausse de 31 % par rapport à l’année précédente. L’abondance de la production solaire et l’insuffisance marquée des capacités de stockage en sont les principales causes. Le pays peine en outre à écouler son excédent d’électricité, faute d’interconnexions suffisantes avec ses voisins.
Pour l’Allemagne, le répit pourrait toutefois être de courte durée. Le pays s’est fixé pour objectif de couvrir 80 % de sa consommation brute d’électricité avec des énergies renouvelables d’ici 2030, contre 60,7 % sur les trois premiers trimestres de 2026. Si le développement du solaire et de l’éolien se poursuit à ce rythme, la question de l’équilibre production/consommation restera centrale. Le stockage, les solutions de flexibilité et l’électrification des usages devront progresser au même rythme pour éviter le retour des heures négatives.
Dans un livre blanc publié en 2025, le cabinet Montel projetait, dans son scénario de base, environ 1 600 heures de prix négatifs par an en Allemagne d’ici 2030. Il estimait toutefois que la règle introduite par la Solarspitzengesetz pouvait en réduire nettement le nombre.

articles.title: UK Housing Ombudsman Service investigates 'security incident'
articles.text:
The U.K. Housing Ombudsman Service is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system on Tuesday.
Established under the Housing Act 1996, the Housing Ombudsman is an executive non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government.
The watchdog settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, including housing associations, landlords, managers, and letting agents.
On Tuesday, the service added an alert to its official website, warning that it's working with the affected service provider to assess the incident's impact and said social housing residents cannot file new complaints until systems are back online.
Those who must raise new complaints are advised to call the Housing Ombudsman's phone line or email the watchdog at info@housing-ombudsman.org.uk.
"The incident has been contained, and we are working with our external supplier to establish the full facts, including the extent of the data involved," the service said. "We are continuing to investigate whether any personal information has been affected and will provide further updates as soon as we are able. "
The Housing Ombudsman service has also notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) of the incident and advised tenants and leaseholders to be wary of potential scams when receiving unsolicited messages.
"As a precaution, we recommend that individuals continue to exercise their usual caution when responding to unexpected communications," it added. "Do not disclose personal information unless you are confident of the identity of the requester and report any suspicious activity to the relevant organisation or authorities. "
The watchdog is working to restore its services "as quickly as possible" and will share further updates on the investigation as soon as they're available.
In March, the British government agency Companies House, which operates the registry for all U.K. companies, was also forced to take its WebFiling service offline to fix a security flaw that had exposed companies' information since October 2025.
Two months earlier, in January, the United Kingdom announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million) and aiming to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector.
