articles.title: Jonathan es una tortuga, tiene 194 años y acabamos de descubrir por qué su ADN envejece tan lentamente
articles.text:
El secreto de la longevidad extrema siempre ha sido un tema que ha fascinado a la ciencia, pero para saber cómo se puede vivir más de 200 años, a veces no hay que mirar a los humanos, sino a un apacible reptil que lleva caminando por este planeta desde antes que se inventara la bombilla, como es Jonathan. Esta es una tortuga gigante que, a sus 194 años, ostenta el récord de ser el animal terrestre más longevo del mundo.
Su razón. Aguantar durante todos los años hace que la gente busque el porqué. Y aquí la ciencia ha decidido asomarse al interior de sus células gracias a un equipo internacional que ha secuenciado su genoma y su metiloma para entender la razón por la que Jonathan no envejece como el resto de animales.
Un simple frotis. Para entender un poco mejor a Jonathan, no hizo falta someterle a dolorosas pruebas, sino que solo bastó con raspar la mucosa bucal del animal. A partir de esta muestra, un equipo internacional comparó su ADN con el de otras tortugas gigantes de Aldabra mucho más jóvenes.
El resultado. Lo que encontraron en el código genético fue un arsenal biológico muy importante, puesto que se pudieron identificar hasta 287 genes con variantes exclusivas de Jonathan. Pero lo interesante es que muchas de estas variantes están íntimamente ligadas a la supresión de tumores y a la reparación del ADN.
Aunque no se queda aquí, ya que Jonathan posee copias extra de un gen encargado de codificar una proteína que "limpia" el organismo eliminando las células senescentes, que son las famosas "células zombi" que causan el envejecimiento y algunos cánceres.
No hay envejecimiento. Sin embargo, tener buenos genes no es toda la historia, puesto que la clave también está en cómo se expresan en el organismo. Aquí el metiloma nos da muchos datos, puesto que nos indica cómo están activados o desactivados estos genes, y los investigadores vieron que, en general, su epigenoma mostraba signos de desgaste coherentes con un anciano de 200 años.
Pero había una excepción que nos ha dado una clave dentro del envejecimiento, y es que los interruptores genéticos asociados a sus mitocondrias se conservaban intactos, como los de una tortuga joven.
Las mitocondrias son las fábricas de energía de las células y el estudio revela que las regiones de baja entropía en el ADN de Jonathan están fuertemente enriquecidas en promotores de genes vinculados a la cadena de transporte de electrones mitocondrial y al metabolismo del ARN. A partir de esto, los autores proponen que la extrema longevidad de Jonathan podría sustentarse en una eficiencia mitocondrial inusual, puesto que si su motor celular "no pierde fuelle", entonces las funciones vitales están casi intactas.
No es caso aislado. Aunque todo esto parece impactante, la realidad es que hay precedentes en la historia, como en España. En nuestro entorno, en 2019, un equipo de la Universidad de Oviedo secuenció el genoma de otra tortuga llamada Solitario George. Aquí ya se encontraron variantes en genes de reparación del ADN y la inflamación, que Jonathan viene a confirmar.
Hay relación entre las tortugas y los humanos, y un ejemplo puede ser el de Maria Branyas, que falleció a los 117 años y cuyo genoma fue analizado por el Instituto Josep Carreras. Y aquí se vio algo similar, puesto que se encontró un epigenoma más joven de lo normal, baja inflamación y un microbioma envidiable, haciendo que tengamos ahora mismo encima de la mesa un puzle del envejecimiento.

articles.title: YouTube teste ces 3 nouvelles icônes pour son application : mais que prépare Google ?
articles.text:
Une fois n’est pas coutume, c’est en allant chercher dans le code de l’application YouTube pour Android que l’on découvre des nouveautés qui n’ont pas encore été annoncées. C’est le cas aujourd’hui avec trois nouvelles icônes très énigmatiques sorties directement des laboratoires de Google. Voici ce que cette nouvelle identité graphique pourrait cacher.
Bientôt la possibilité de choisir son icône YouTube ?
En fouillant dans le code de cette mise à jour, on y trouve une référence explicite à une préférence d’icône, suggérant clairement que Google pourrait bientôt laisser le choix aux utilisateurs d’habiller l’application selon leurs préférences. Parmi les visuels, on retrouve trois icônes avec chacune un style très marqué.
Source : Android Authority
L’un des logos opte ainsi pour un style monochrome, tandis qu’un autre évoque la texture du glaçage d’un gâteau ou de la peinture fraîche, à moins que cela ne soit de la pâte à modeler. Le troisième design se distingue quant à lui par un effet néon qui peut aussi rappeler celui de l’affichage des anciens écrans à tube cathodique.
Une personnalisation réservée aux abonnés Premium ?
Impossible pour l’instant de savoir précisément à qui se destinent ces icônes ni de deviner la logique marketing qui se cache derrière. En effet, aucun libellé descriptif ou explicite dans les fichiers de l’application n’a été trouvé, ce qui laisse de la place aux spéculations en tous genres. Il pourrait s’agir d’un simple test de la part de YouTube, ou des prémisses d’une option réservée aux abonnements payants.
À lire : Gagner de l’argent sur YouTube devient beaucoup plus difficile
Pas de quoi sortir sa carte bleue immédiatement, mais cela pourrait être un « petit plus » pour les abonnements YouTube Premium ou Premium Lite. En attendant une éventuelle communication officielle de la part de Google, le mystère reste entier. N’hésitez pas à nous donner vos pronostics dans les commentaires.

articles.title: AWS Reworks EventBridge Custom Buses for Enterprise-Scale Event-Driven Architectures
articles.text:
AWS has introduced an enhanced Custom Event Bus for Amazon EventBridge, targeting a problem that often emerges when event-driven architectures move beyond a single team or AWS account: the event infrastructure itself becomes fragmented. The new model allows organisations to create a single event bus shared across multiple AWS accounts, while adding native event ordering, retention and replay, content-based deduplication, simplified subscriptions and a new pricing model.
The change addresses an architectural tension in enterprise AWS environments. Organisations commonly use multiple accounts to provide isolation between teams and applications, but this can lead to EventBridge buses being connected through cross-account rules and forwarding configurations. As the number of consumers grows, the resulting topology becomes harder to govern and understand, while forwarding the same event through multiple buses can introduce additional processing and routing costs. AWS's new model instead positions a central bus as an organisational event backbone, with individual teams managing their own subscriptions.
The enhanced Custom Event Bus can be shared across AWS accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM). A platform team can therefore establish a central event bus while allowing application teams to publish and subscribe from their own accounts. AWS says the new bus supports up to 10,000 subscribers by default, with the option to request a higher quota.
This changes the governance model as much as the technical one. Rather than a platform team configuring every cross-account connection, it can establish the boundaries around the central bus while individual application teams manage their own subscriptions, filtering, targets, retries, and failure destinations. That creates a separation between platform-level governance and application-level event consumption, potentially reducing the amount of infrastructure work required to onboard another consumer.
AWS also introduces synchronous invocation for targets such as AWS Lambda. This can remove a pattern where teams place Amazon SQS between EventBridge and Lambda primarily to provide stronger processing acknowledgement. The result is a bus that can support both conventional asynchronous event consumption and workloads where ordering and processing confirmation are important.
The new Subscriber resource is another important change to the EventBridge model. Previously, consumers were typically represented through combinations of rules, targets, and retry configurations. The Subscriber resource brings filtering, target configuration, retries, and dead-letter destinations together into a single consumer definition. It also supports variable start times, which can be used when onboarding a new consumer or replaying historical events.
The bus itself also becomes more useful as a durable event backbone. Events can be retained for a configurable period of between one and 365 days, allowing consumers to start from an earlier point in the event history or recover after application failures. AWS also supports JSONata transformations and can deserialize Avro and Protocol Buffers payloads into JSON for filtering and routing.
The enhanced bus adds content-based deduplication, allowing EventBridge to identify retries of the same event based on its payload. AWS says matching events received within a five-minute window can be collapsed, providing exactly-once semantics for that specific deduplication scenario. This does not remove the need for application-level idempotency, particularly where events are replayed or processed across regions.
AWS has also changed the pricing model. Rather than allowing costs to compound with every cross-account and bus-to-bus forwarding hop, the enhanced bus uses an ingress and egress throughput model, with publishers paying for events ingested and subscribers paying for events delivered. This more closely aligns cost with the amount of event data entering and being consumed from the central bus rather than the number of intermediate routing steps in the architecture.
The enhanced EventBridge model moves into territory traditionally associated with enterprise event brokers and streaming platforms such as Apache Kafka, but the two technologies still address somewhat different architectural needs. Kafka is fundamentally a distributed event-streaming platform built around durable logs, partitions, and consumer groups, giving engineering teams extensive control over high-throughput streaming workloads and consumption semantics. EventBridge remains a managed, serverless event-routing service, with AWS handling the underlying infrastructure while providing filtering, routing, retention, transformations, and integration with AWS targets. The new capabilities therefore make EventBridge more capable as an enterprise event backbone, but they do not turn it into a direct replacement for Kafka in every streaming architecture.
Importantly, AWS is not replacing the existing EventBridge model immediately. Existing custom buses continue operating unchanged and are now labelled Custom event bus-classic, while the enhanced bus is introduced as a separate resource. Organisations can therefore adopt the new architecture incrementally rather than having to redesign existing event-driven applications as part of the launch.
The enhanced Custom Event Bus is initially available across selected AWS Regions in North America, Europe and Asia Pacific, and can be created through the AWS Management Console, CLI or EventBridge APIs.

articles.title: CashAfrica brings mobile tap-to-pay to Chicken Republic outlets
articles.text:
CashAfrica, a Nigerian contactless payment infrastructure provider, has partnered with Food Concepts, the quick-service restaurant company that owns Chicken Republic, PieXpress, and The Chop Box, to bring mobile tap-to-pay to Chicken Republic outlets across Nigeria.
The partnership will let customers pay for their meals by tapping their smartphones on supported payment terminals. According to CashAfrica, the rollout will be phased, starting in Lagos before expanding to Abuja and other locations.
Chicken Republic has more than 350 outlets across Nigeria and recorded ₦60.9 billion ($45.7 million) in sales in 2023. The scale of its operations gives CashAfrica a potential route to increase the adoption of tap-to-pay payments in Nigeria.
“This is a strategic partnership to take Mobile Tap-to-Pay mainstream, while delivering the best-in-class payment experience,” Malik Asamu, CashAfrica’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “Previously, Nigerian users and merchants could collect transfers, cards, QR code, and cash options. This strategic partnership delivers a whole new layer of payment possibilities, created the Pan-African way.”
The deal follows CashAfrica’s partnership with ChamsSwitch, a licenced switching and electronic payment processing company, in May to address regulatory compliance and transaction-routing requirements that had slowed the adoption of its contactless payment infrastructure. It also builds on an earlier integration with PalmPay, which began rolling out contactless payment functionality on its point-of-sale (POS) terminals in February 2025, starting with a 1,000-device pilot.
Founded in 2024 by Asamu and Bello Opeyemi, CashAfrica provides payment infrastructure that allows banks and fintechs to integrate contactless transactions into their existing services. Its CashTap technology uses near-field communication (NFC), a short-range wireless technology that allows compatible devices to exchange information when brought close together.
CashAfrica’s mobile tap-to-pay product allows customers to initiate payments with their phones through participating banking and fintech apps. A customer opens a supported app, selects the tap-to-pay option, authenticates the transaction where required, and taps the phone against a compatible POS terminal. Depending on the device, payment authentication can involve features such as Face ID or fingerprint recognition, according to CashAfrica.
Under the partnership with Food Concepts, users interact with PalmPay’s POS terminals for the payment, while CashAfrica supplies the technology that enables the contactless transaction. ChamsSwitch, meanwhile, supports the settlement side of the transaction. Asamu told TechCabal in an interview that the company acts as a regulatory and infrastructure partner, helping facilitate funds movement between the fintechs and operators involved in the payment.
“ChamsSwitch is a regulatory partner that allows us to do a lot of cross settlements,” he said. “If Chicken Republic is collecting tap-to-pay, a lot of that money needs to be moving in the background, such as T+1 settlements and end-of-day settlements. ChamsSwitch is heavily involved in that.”
CashAfrica said it will introduce the service gradually before making mobile tap-to-pay available across all 350-plus Chicken Republic outlets. The company also plans to work with more banks and fintechs to expand the number of customers who can use the feature through their existing apps.
“Customer experience has always been at the heart of Chicken Republic, and we continuously look for ways to make every meal faster, easier and more convenient,” Solomon Ojelade, head of finance at Chicken Republic, said in the statement. “Our partnership with CashAfrica brings that commitment into the payment experience, giving our customers access to a fast and seamless Mobile Tap to Pay option across our outlets.”
At Chicken Republic, customers will not pay a separate fee to use mobile tap-to-pay, Asamu told TechCabal. Instead, the merchant pays CashAfrica for transactions processed through its infrastructure. The company said it charges a percentage of each transaction, typically between 0.1% and 1.5%, depending on the arrangement.
CashAfrica is looking to capitalise on Nigeria’s growing use of electronic payments. In 2024, electronic transactions processed through the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System’s instant payment system surpassed ₦1 quadrillion ($803 billion). The company intends to turn that growth into the adoption of a newer payment method.
Asamu said the company has signed other partnerships with businesses where customers regularly make in-person payments, including quick-service restaurants and supermarkets, and will announce them in the coming months.
“The change in the average Nigerian customer consumption pattern in financial technology has allowed us to see wind in the sails of contactless payments,” he said. “We make the bet and continue to bet on contactless payments.”

articles.title: Rätsel der Monsterwellen gelöst: Wie KI die Gefahr auf See berechenbar macht
articles.text:
Formel statt Seemannsgarn: KI analysiert die Entstehung von Monsterwellen
Am 17. November 2020 registrierte eine Sensorboje des kanadischen Unternehmens MarineLabs eine Wassersäule, die Ozeanograf:innen weltweit beschäftigte. Das im Pazifik vor der Küste von Ucluelet verankerte Messgerät zeichnete eine Einzelwelle von 17,6 Metern Höhe auf. Das Ereignis sticht deshalb heraus, weil der restliche Seegang zu diesem Zeitpunkt bei lediglich rund sechs Metern lag.
Damit ein solches Ereignis in der Wissenschaft als Monsterwelle (im Fachjargon Rogue Wave genannt) eingestuft wird, ist nicht die absolute Höhe entscheidend, sondern das Verhältnis zur sogenannten signifikanten Wellenhöhe. Dieser Referenzwert beschreibt die Durchschnittshöhe des höchsten Drittels aller Wellen in einem Messzeitraum. Übertrifft eine einzelne Welle diesen Durchschnitt um mehr als das Doppelte gilt sie als Monsterwelle.
Mit dem fast Dreifachen der signifikanten Wellenhöhe ist das Ereignis von Ucluelet proportional die extremste jemals gemessene Welle. Zum Vergleich: Die berühmte Draupner-Welle, die am 1. Januar 1995 an einer norwegischen Ölplattform in der Nordsee den ersten Beweis für die Existenz des Phänomens lieferte, war zwar 25,6 Meter hoch, trat aber in einem schweren Seegang von ohnehin schon zwölf Metern auf.
Warum etablierte Erklärungsmodelle auf dem Ozean versagen
Nach dem Draupner-Ereignis suchten Forschungsteams weltweit nach den Ursachen. In der Ozeanografie etablierte sich die Theorie der sogenannten Modulationsinstabilität als wahrscheinliche Hauptursache. Diese auch als Benjamin-Feir-Instabilität bekannte Theorie besagt, dass einzelne Wellen in der Lage sind, benachbarten Wellen ihre Energie zu entziehen, wodurch sie sich zunehmend aufschaukeln.
In eindimensionalen Wellenkanälen unter Laborbedingungen ließ sich dieser Mechanismus gut nachweisen. Eine detaillierte Untersuchung der Ucluelet-Welle durch den Forscher Johannes Gemmrich ergab jedoch für die Realität auf offener See ein anderes Bild. Wie in einer im Wissenschaftsmagazin Scientific Reports veröffentlichten Studie der kanadischen University of Victoria zu lesen ist, spielte diese Instabilität bei der Entstehung kaum eine Rolle.
Der Grund dafür liegt im realen Ozean: Wellen laufen dort nicht nur stur in eine Richtung, sondern kreuzen sich aus verschiedensten Winkeln. Dadurch verpufft der Effekt des gegenseitigen Energie-Entziehens in der Praxis fast vollständig. Vielmehr identifizierte das Forschungsteam ein physikalisches Prinzip als Hauptauslöser, das als lineare Superposition bekannt ist. Treffen Wellensysteme mit unterschiedlichen Frequenzen und Richtungen im exakt gleichen Moment zusammen, können sich die einzelnen Wellenberge kurzzeitig zu einer enormen Spitze addieren.
Die Analyse von Milliarden Sensordaten durch künstliche Intelligenz
Um diese These empirisch zu belegen und ein belastbares Vorhersagemodell zu entwickeln, nutzte ein Team um den Forscher Dion Häfner vom dänischen Niels-Bohr-Institut der Universität Kopenhagen Methoden der Künstlichen Intelligenz. Das Team griff auf die Aufzeichnungen von 158 Messbojen zurück, die entlang der Küsten der USA und in Überseegebieten rund um die Uhr den Seegang dokumentieren.
Das Trainingsmaterial für das neuronale Netz umfasste historische Daten von rund einer Milliarde Einzelwellen. Würde eine einzelne Boje diese Menge an Daten sammeln, müsste sie 700 Jahre lang ununterbrochen messen.
Laut einer in der Fachzeitschrift PNAS publizierten Arbeit fanden die Wissenschaftler:innen in diesem Datensatz mehr als 100.000 Monsterwellen. Diese Auswertung widerlegt die in älteren Prognosemodellen getroffene Annahme, dass derartige Extremereignisse weltweit extrem selten seien. Statistisch gesehen formt sich im globalen Ozean jeden Tag eine derartige Welle, wenngleich nicht immer in Form einer extremen Wasserwand.
Symbolische Regression liefert eine transparente Gleichung
Der technologisch interessanteste Aspekt der Arbeit aus Kopenhagen ist die spezifische Methode des maschinellen Lernens. Das Team setzte ein Verfahren namens symbolische Regression ein. Gewöhnliche neuronale Netze arbeiten oft als sogenannte Black Box. Sie liefern hochpräzise Vorhersagen, lassen aber nicht erkennen, wie sie zu diesem Ergebnis gelangen. Für die Wissenschaft ist das unzureichend, da der physikalische Zusammenhang unsichtbar bleibt.
Die symbolische Regression hingegen destilliert aus den Milliarden von Datenpunkten eine transparente, von Menschen lesbare mathematische Gleichung. Der Algorithmus lieferte den Forscher:innen eine physikalische Formel, die exakt beschreibt, unter welchen Bedingungen die lineare Überlagerung kritisch wird. Markus Jochum, Professor am Niels-Bohr-Institut, vergleicht diesen Vorgang mit der Geschichte der Astronomie: Tycho Brahe sammelte über Jahrzehnte astronomische Beobachtungen, aus denen Johannes Kepler durch Versuch und Irrtum die Keplerschen Gesetze ableitete. Die KI tat mit den Wellendaten nun exakt das, was Kepler mit Planeten tat.
Der entscheidende Parameter für die Schifffahrt
Das resultierende Modell bestätigt, dass das nautische Risiko vor allem dann ansteigt, wenn sich Wassertiefe, Wellensteilheit und die sogenannte Kamm-Tal-Korrelation auf eine bestimmte Weise kombinieren. Letztere erwies sich als der aussagekräftigste Indikator. Diese Korrelation beschreibt in der Ozeanografie, wie stark Wellenberge und darauffolgende Wellentäler statistisch zusammenhängen. In Seegangsbedingungen, in denen auf einen hohen Berg mit großer Verlässlichkeit ein tiefes Tal folgt (eine hohe Korrelation), ist das Risiko für die Bildung einer Monsterwelle durch Überlagerung signifikant erhöht.
Da sich dieser Parameter aus üblichen Wellenprognosen berechnen lässt, steht Wetterdiensten nun eine konkrete Berechnungsgrundlage zur Verfügung, die das in der Realität unwirksame Modell der Modulationsinstabilität ersetzen kann. Die Formel sowie das zugrundeliegende Forschungsmaterial sind öffentlich zugänglich.
Damit ergibt sich für Reedereien die Möglichkeit, das Risiko für Monsterwellen entlang geplanter Routen der weltweit rund 50.000 Frachtschiffe im Vorfeld dynamisch zu berechnen. Routen können angepasst werden, bevor die nautischen und meteorologischen Bedingungen das gefürchtete Zusammentreffen der Wellensysteme erzeugen.
Allerdings ordnet das dänische Forschungsteam die Ergebnisse kritisch ein. Dem Modell fehlen derzeit noch Daten zu lokalen Winden, extremen Ozeanströmungen oder unregelmäßigen Meeresböden, die das Wellenverhalten vor Ort massiv verändern können. Zudem berechnet das System statistische Wahrscheinlichkeiten für Meeresgebiete und liefert keine punktgenaue Vorhersage einer einzelnen Welle zu einer bestimmten Uhrzeit. Die Technologie bietet folglich eine erheblich verbesserte Entscheidungsgrundlage auf Basis harter Physik, kann das naturbedingte Restrisiko auf den Ozeanen aber nicht vollständig eliminieren.

articles.title: Cómo convertir un viejo control de TV en un mando para la computadora
articles.text:
Un viejo control remoto de televisor, DVD o decodificador no tiene por qué terminar en un cajón. Con un adaptador USB económico y unos minutos de configuración, ese mando puede transformarse en un control funcional para manejar la computadora, sin necesidad de soldadura ni conocimientos de electrónica. La clave está en un accesorio que las PC no traen de fábrica: un receptor de infrarrojos.
Las computadoras, a diferencia de los televisores, no incorporan sensores IR integrados. Por eso, cualquier intento de usar un control remoto directamente sobre una laptop o un equipo de escritorio no tendrá ningún efecto hasta que se sume el hardware adecuado. Ese es el punto de partida de todo el proceso.
Qué hardware se necesita para reconvertir un control remoto en mando de PC
El proyecto requiere apenas tres elementos. El primero es el propio control remoto en desuso, que puede ser de cualquier marca o dispositivo, siempre que sus botones y su emisor infrarrojo funcionen con normalidad.
El segundo elemento es un receptor de infrarrojos USB, pieza central de todo el sistema. Entre las opciones disponibles, el Flirc USB figura como alternativa por su compatibilidad amplia, aunque también existen receptores genéricos compatibles con Windows, macOS y Linux.
El tercer componente es, naturalmente, la computadora donde se instalará el adaptador, sin importar el sistema operativo que utilice.
Cómo configurar el receptor IR y vincularlo al sistema operativo
El primer paso práctico consiste en conectar el receptor USB a un puerto libre de la computadora. El sistema debe reconocerlo de inmediato, sin solicitar controladores adicionales ni arrojar errores; en Windows, esto se confirma con el sonido habitual que indica la conexión de un nuevo dispositivo.
Una vez detectado el hardware, corresponde instalar el software de mapeo correspondiente. Si se trata de un Flirc, la aplicación oficial es el Flirc GUI, descargable desde el sitio del fabricante. Para receptores genéricos, alternativas como AutoHotkey en Windows o LIRC en Linux cumplen una función equivalente.
Al abrir el programa, la pantalla principal debe mostrar que el receptor está conectado correctamente, generalmente con un mensaje de confirmación tipo “Connected”. Esa verificación es la señal de que el sistema está listo para avanzar a la etapa de personalización.
Cómo asignar las teclas del control remoto a funciones de la PC
Con el software instalado, el siguiente paso es elegir el perfil de uso. La mayoría de los usuarios opta por el modo Media Player, pensado para controlar volumen y reproducción, o por el modo Keyboard, que permite asignar teclas individuales según necesidades específicas.
Elegido el perfil, comienza el proceso de mapeo propiamente dicho. Se selecciona en pantalla una función deseada, como Play/Pausa o Subir Volumen, y luego se apunta el control remoto viejo hacia el receptor USB mientras se presiona el botón físico que se quiere vincular a esa acción.
El software reconoce la señal infrarroja única emitida por esa tecla y la asocia a la función elegida. Este procedimiento se repite con cada botón que se desee habilitar, desde flechas de navegación hasta Enter, barra espaciadora o mute. Cada asignación exitosa se confirma con un mensaje en pantalla que indica que la tecla quedó registrada correctamente.
Cómo comprobar que el mando funciona en reproductores y presentaciones
Finalizada la configuración, resta comprobar el funcionamiento real del dispositivo. Para eso conviene abrir una aplicación que use las teclas programadas, como un reproductor de video, una plataforma de streaming o una presentación de diapositivas.
Al presionar los botones del control remoto, la computadora debe responder de inmediato, como si se hubiera accionado una tecla física del teclado. Ese comportamiento confirma que el proceso de conversión se completó sin inconvenientes.
Qué alternativa existe para quienes prefieren armar su propio receptor IR
Quienes buscan una solución programable y están dispuestos a trabajar con placas electrónicas pueden prescindir del adaptador comercial. Una placa Arduino Pro Micro o una Raspberry Pi Pico, combinada con un sensor receptor IR económico como el TSOP4838, permite construir un sistema propio.
Mediante algunas líneas de código escritas en Arduino IDE y la librería IRremote, la placa puede leer los códigos hexadecimales emitidos por el control remoto y traducirlos en comandos HID de teclado, enviados directamente a la computadora a través del puerto USB.

articles.title: Apple refreshes Apple TV 4K with Siri AI upgrade, faster A19 chip, and smart remote
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Apple has introduced its fourth generation Apple TV 4K, complete with an A19 chip that the company claims delivers 50% faster CPU performance and up to twice the GPU performance compared to the previous model. The long-awaited set-top box also ships with three far-field microphones, Siri AI, and a smarter remote.
Apple said the A19 chip inside its new box includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder that enables more efficient, high-quality streaming while simultaneously using less bandwidth. It also includes secure enclaves that protect and compartmentalize runtimes used to process Siri data from the trio of far-field microphones.
Siri on the Apple TV 4K is powered by Apple Intelligence, enabling a fully hands-free experience. Apple baked in echo cancellation to intelligently isolate voices from background noise. This means the system can pick up on "Hey Siri" commands in noisy environments, even if audio is playing in the background.
Apple's new smart remote, meanwhile, features a 100% recycled aluminum enclosure. New this year is Find My support with Precision Finding, and you can even ping it and have it play a sound to make it easier to locate between the couch cushions.
Apple says the 4th gen Apple TV 4K can be paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod speakers to create an immersive home theater surround sound setup. It also doubles as a home hub, allowing users to manage their smart home from anywhere.
The refreshed streaming box has been a long time coming. The third-gen streamer launched nearly four years ago in November 2022.
The new Apple TV 4K is available to pre-order from today in the US and 29 other countries. Pricing is set at $299 up front, or you can break it down into six monthly payments of $49.83 if that's more convenient. Look for it to launch on November 13. It comes with the new Siri Remote, which can also be purchased separately for use with other Apple devices. It retails for $59 and also arrives on November 13.

articles.title: Meta lança o Muse Wonder, sua IA mais avançada até agora • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Meta lança o Muse Wonder, sua IA mais avançada até agora
Novos modelos focam em agentes capazes de lembrar informações, usar computadores e executar tarefas.
A Meta apresentou o Muse Wonder e o Muse Wonder Full, seus novos modelos de inteligência artificial voltados para agentes pessoais e profissionais. Segundo a companhia, os sistemas são os mais poderosos que já criou e reforçam a disputa com modelos de ponta das rivais OpenAI e Anthropic.
Os modelos foram treinados para executar tarefas que demandam várias etapas, como analisar contratos, desenvolver aplicativos e utilizar navegadores ou outros programas.
Uma das principais novidades é o recurso Active Memory, que permite ao modelo guardar informações importantes entre diferentes conversas e recuperá-las em novas tarefas. Já o Active Focus foi desenvolvido para manter o agente trabalhando mesmo diante de dificuldades.
Segundo a Meta, o modelo pode tentar métodos alternativos ao encontrar obstáculos, adaptar o plano conforme surgem novas informações e pedir ajuda ao usuário quando necessário. Antes de executar ações consideradas importantes, ele também pede confirmação.
A novidade combina essas funções com capacidade de operar computadores. Em demonstrações, a Meta mostra o Muse Wonder usando um navegador e outros aplicativos para criar e encomendar produtos a partir de fotos de um perfil no Instagram. O modelo também foi treinado para programação e pode dividir um projeto entre subagentes, realizar alterações em vários arquivos e continuar trabalhando mesmo quando encontra erros.
Esses recursos ampliam as funções do Muse, que já conseguia navegar em sites e preencher formulários sozinho, um nível de autonomia que já gerou conflitos. A Amazon bloqueou recentemente o serviço em sua loja após acusá-lo de não se identificar adequadamente.
O Muse Wonder já está disponível para desenvolvedores a US$ 4 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 20 por milhão de tokens de saída (cerca de R$ 20 e R$ 100 em conversão direta, respectivamente). Já o Muse Wonder Full, versão mais avançada, fica restrito aos planos pagos do Muse Code e não possui cobrança individual por tokens.
A big tech afirma que Muse Wonder e Wonder Full atingem desempenho de ponta em avaliações envolvendo programação, memória e agentes profissionais. A companhia destaca tarefas longas de desenvolvimento de software e atividades envolvendo áreas como finanças, saúde e direito, mas os resultados precisam ser vistos com cautela, já que parte das comparações foi realizada ou selecionada pela própria Meta.
Em testes independentes da Artificial Analysis, o Muse Wonder marcou 52 pontos no Intelligence Index, um índice que reúne avaliações de raciocínio, programação e outras capacidades, resumindo o desempenho em uma pontuação. O Muse Wonder Full chegou a 56 pontos. Ambos superaram o Muse Spark 1.3, com 48, mas ficaram abaixo do Claude Opus 5.5, com 58.
A Meta afirma que o Muse Wonder chegará “em breve” ao aplicativo Muse, inicialmente para assinantes. O serviço continua limitado principalmente aos Estados Unidos e Canadá, sem previsão de lançamento no Brasil.

articles.title: The 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20: From organs to orbit and everything in between | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Twenty founders just earned their shot at Disrupt glory. They’re headed to the Disrupt Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to compete for the $100,000 prize and the coveted Disrupt Cup.
Every year, thousands of founders from around the world pitch us on what they believe the future should look like. This year’s Top 20 are building it from organs to orbit and everywhere in between.
Across this cohort, one theme kept emerging: Making the previously invisible measurable.
These founders are finding ways to understand signals we couldn’t previously capture, model systems too complex to predict, and turn the physical world into data that machines can actually act on. They’re measuring the biological clocks inside our bodies and growing miniature human organs in labs. They’re teaching robots to take on increasingly complex physical work and modeling the real world closely enough to predict what might happen next — even the behavior of wild animals. They’re extracting intelligence from scam calls and finding new ways to use the computing power already orbiting above our heads.
And then, of course, there’s the company trying to launch cargo into space with a giant hydrogen-powered cannon.
Subtle, this group is not.
What connects these 20 companies isn’t a single technology or industry. It’s an ambition to understand more of the world around us — biological, physical, industrial, and digital — and use that understanding to make better decisions, automate what once required human intervention, and tackle problems that previously seemed too complex to solve.
Now they have six minutes on the Disrupt Stage to prove it.
Here are the 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20.
Tuesday, October 13
Startup Battlefield Semifinals Session 1 (10:00 a.m. – 11:15 a.m.)
Space and Physical AI
Longshot Space: Reinventing the economics of space by launching cargo to orbit at $50/kg using hydrogen-powered kinetic launchers.
Veritas: Protecting luxury brands with custom microchips that verify authenticity and enable connected post-purchase experiences.
Laplace Intelligence: Building agentic world models that help cities, ports, and airports roll out counterfactual futures of the real world before they act.
Flox Intelligence: Preventing deadly wildlife collisions at airports and railways with real-time AI that detects animal behavior and safely redirects them.
Satlyt: Helping satellite operators unlock and monetize idle compute by transforming their spacecraft into virtual AI data centers with a single line of code.
Battlefield Semifinal Session 2 (1:00 p.m. – 2:15 p.m.)
Energy and Manufacturing
LNK Energies: Delivering clean hydrogen power cheaper than diesel through breakthrough compact reactor technology compatible with existing diesel infrastructure.
Helix Carbon: Helping steelmakers cut emissions and fuel costs by electrochemically upcycling blast furnace waste gas into replacement fossil fuels on-site.
IndustrialNext: Automating high-precision, contact-rich assembly tasks by deploying AI-driven robotic systems that learn from production data and adapt to new products.
Niobia AI: Helping process and materials engineers compress weeks of root-cause analysis into minutes with domain-expert AI reasoning.
Licube: Producing ultra-high purity lithium and lithium isotopes (Li-6/Li-7), the critical inputs for nuclear fusion and advanced materials.
Wednesday, October 14
Battlefield Semifinal Session 3 (10:00 a.m. – 11:15 a.m.)
Health Tech and Life Sciences
Mosqitter: Detecting and preventing mosquito-borne disease spread with real-time disease intelligence platforms that turn sensor networks into early warning systems for national health agencies.
Hiyd AI: Delivering proactive health insights by combining sleep, movement, and nutrition data through an ultra-slim, discreet wearable tracker and AI app.
TimeTeller GmbH: Measuring people’s biological clocks to determine optimal treatment timing through molecular diagnostics and AI, improving efficacy and reducing side effects.
NTangible: Helping coaches and front offices make smarter recruiting decisions by quantifying how athletes perform under pressure with a validated cognitive score.
Intero Biosystems: Accelerating drug development by producing miniature human organs that enable pharma companies to identify safer, more effective medications while reducing clinical trial costs.
Battlefield Semifinal Session 4 (1:30 p.m. – 2:45 p.m.)
Enterprise and Security
Apate.ai: Dismantling scam operations by deploying conversational AI bots that engage scammers and turn their interactions into real-time intelligence for banks, telcos, and governments.
CedarDB: Delivering the data layer for the AI age — real-time transactions and analytics in one engine with guardrails inside the database system that AI agents can’t bypass.
Prismm: Helping banks retain deposits and relationships across generations by automating secure inheritance workflows and financial continuity infrastructure.
Floqer: Streamlining B2B sales by enriching customer data across 80+ sources and stitching every interaction into one millisecond-retrievable timeline for AI agents to act on.
GUDEA: Delivering immediate, actionable insights into audience behavior, engagement patterns, and how information spreads to give organizations a competitive edge in communication management.
And then there were five
After four semifinal sessions across two days, five companies will advance to the Startup Battlefield Finals on Thursday, October 15.
Before the finalists take the stage at 11:30 a.m., we’ll welcome Glīd, Nephrogen, and Molecule.one back to the Disrupt Stage for an alumni update on what’s happened since their time in Startup Battlefield.
Then, at 4:15 p.m., one company will be crowned the 2026 Startup Battlefield champion, taking home $100,000 and the Disrupt Cup.

articles.title: Google Partially Reverses Chrome Bug Bounty Cuts
articles.text:
Google announced Tuesday that it’s raising bug bounty rewards for some Chrome vulnerabilities, focusing on memory safety issues.
AI has been changing the pace and profile of vulnerability discovery, and the tech giant has been adjusting its bug bounty programs in recent months.
Google significantly lowered standard payout amounts for some Chrome vulnerabilities in April to shift focus to actionable reports, with researchers noting that some rewards became 10 times smaller. At the time it announced a base reward of $500 for memory safety issues, with multipliers for reachability and the level of exploitability.
The company is now quadrupling base rates for memory safety flaws, to $2,000. Despite the increase, the new rates remain well below those offered before the April overhaul.
Vulnerabilities in Chrome’s browser, GPU and network processes can now earn researchers up to $20,000. In the case of the renderer process, bug bounty hunters can receive up to $8,000 for use-after-free and memory write bugs.
V8 sandbox vulnerabilities are moving to a flat rate of $5,000, while V8 logic bugs will be rewarded with $4,000.
As for issues not related to memory safety, medium-severity flaws will be rewarded with $2,000 if the vulnerability report includes or directly leads to an identified fix. Sandbox escapes not involving memory safety bugs can get bug bounties of up to $20,000.
Google is also reintroducing a $2,000 fuzzer bonus for developing novel fuzzers.
The company noted that “any submissions that are currently in our evaluation queue submitted after April 30th, 2026 will be evaluated and rewarded under the new payout rules.”
Google recently announced it’s temporarily closing its Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP) to product vulnerability submissions, prompted by a growing number of AI-generated reports.

articles.title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
articles.text:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it’s for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It’s not 15 years from now; it’s in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that’s not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It’s not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn’t I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We’re not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”
Wired.com is your essential daily guide to what's next, delivering the most original and complete take you'll find anywhere on innovation's impact on technology, science, business and culture.

articles.title: Epic Games reportedly delays Disney shooter title so it can pivot to AI coding — staff allegedly told 'no more handwritten code' with art 'generated with full AI workflows'
articles.text:
Epic Games reportedly delays Disney shooter title so it can pivot to AI coding — staff allegedly told 'no more handwritten code' with art 'generated with full AI workflows'
Will this speed up development times long-term?
Epic Games has reportedly delayed a shooter based on Disney’s Marvel and Star Wars franchises, with its developers told to use more AI. According to Bloomberg, the yet-to-be-named game was supposed to be released in March of 2027, but its launch date has been pushed back to an unspecified date. Aside from that, the company also told the people working on the project to switch to an “AI first” production model. One of the game directors was quoted telling staff that there will be “no more handwritten code” and that the game’s art would now be “generated with full AI workflows.”
Around the same time this news came out, Epic boss Tim Sweeney posted an update on X that seemingly confirms the change. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” the Epic founder said on the platform. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Sweeney has previously criticized Steam for putting AI tags on games, calling it “irresponsible of Valve.” He says that AI is just a tool and that it’s useful for handling boring, menial, and repetitive tasks like finding errors in code or rigging 3D models. “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” Epic Games communications director Jake Jones told the publication.
The announcement still reportedly left some of the developers working on the project in a state of astonishment. They were hoping that the directive wasn’t serious or that Epic Games would change its mind about the decision, while others jokingly asked if they should ask Claude to fix its own errors. The delayed title was supposed to be the first in a series of games involving Disney intellectual property, which had invested $1.5 billion in the game developer and publisher in 2024. However, Bloomberg reports that progress on the game has suffered because it lacked the number of people required to keep the schedule on track. It seems that the company is trying to make up for lost time by pushing its people to use AI in the hopes that they’ll be able to work much more quickly.
AI is indeed quite a useful tool, with some developers using it to build surprisingly complicated vibe-coded games, like this GTA clone set in Taipei or this decompiled version of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. One group even used Gemini for their free game demo, leading to a cost of $1,000 a day in AI usage bills. Despite that, many creators and developers have been against the use of AI in the industry, with one major gaming convention in the UK outright banning games that were built mostly using AI.

articles.title: Apple quiere llenar tu casa de cosas: nuevos Apple TV 4K, HomePod Mini 2 y Apple Home Collection
articles.text:
Como bien había anunciado hace unos días, Apple acaba de presentar varios productos enfocados en el hogar inteligente. Ya te hemos contado todo sobre el protagonista del evento, el nuevo HomeView, pero también hay otros acompañantes que completan un catálogo (ahora sí) bastante interesante para quien quiera hacer de su casa un entorno más inteligente gracias a Apple. Y, a diferencia del HomeView, el resto de opciones sí están disponibles en España desde el primer día.
Apple ha lanzado un nuevo Apple TV 4K más rápido, más potente, con mejor resolución y capaz de hacer mucho más por ti y tu hogar. A su vez, ha renovado el altavoz más pequeño del catálogo, el HomePod Mini. Su segunda versión también es más potente, capaz de gestionar la nueva Siri AI y cuenta con una especie de pantalla que Apple ha llamado Sound Glow.
Por último, Apple también ha tenido tiempo para anunciar Apple Home Collection, una serie de dispositivos centrados en el hogar inteligente fabricados en colaboración con otras marcas. Destaca su nueva cerradura inteligente, un nuevo termostato o varias cámaras para diferentes usos dentro y fuera del hogar.
Todo el conjunto de dispositivos destaca por incluir compatibilidad total con Siri AI, aunque Apple sigue sin ofrecer este asistente en Europa, lo que significa que todos los productos llegan, de alguna forma, capados en este sentido. De hecho, se cree que es el principal motivo por el que el HomeView no llega a España.
Nuevo Apple TV 4K
El nuevo Apple TV 4K llega como lo que se esperaba, una renovación con más resolución, mejor rendimiento, novedades para el control del resto de dispositivos del hogar y una compatibilidad total con SiriAI. Esta última no está disponible en España, pero sí el resto.
Su CPU ahora es un 50% más potente y su GPU dobla el rendimiento de la versión anterior. Todo gracias al chip A19, que permite tener un Apple TV 4K con una mejor respuesta y una fluidez total incluso con contenidos en alta resolución. Además, también incluye un nuevo decodificador AV1 que permite reproducir contenido en 4K de una forma mucho más eficiente con el ancho de banda, consumiendo menos cantidad y haciendo que con una conexión más modesta se pueda reproducir cualquier contenido.
Su mando ahora incluye un sistema de búsqueda con el iPhone similar al de los AirTags para encontrarlo allá donde lo hayas dejado. El Apple TV 4K ahora tiene 3 micrófonos integrados que permiten aislar a la perfección el "Oye, Siri" incluso cuando hay ruido de fondo o música sonando.
Además, Apple ha hecho del Apple TV 4K un centro del hogar mucho más completo, permitiendo controlar muchísimos más dispositivos con una mejor interfaz, tener la posibilidad de reproducir sonido envolvente al conectar 4 altavoces HomePod o HomePod Mini y crear un sistema de cine en el salón.
Ya está disponible para reservarlo en la web de Apple por 349 euros con recogida en tienda o envío a domicilio a partir del 13 de noviembre.
Nuevo HomePod Mini 2
Por el lado del sonido, la nueva generación del HomePod Mini llega con internas y externas. Para empezar, si bien mantiene el diseño y la dinámica de la generación anterior, ahora cuenta con una especie de panel interactivo en la zona superior. Apple lo ha llamado Sound Glow, y permite visualizar patrones de colores difuminados en función de la carátula de la canción que suene o adaptarse al entorno y mostrar colores que vayan en función del día.
El nuevo HomePod Mini 2 también está disponible en nuevos colores y tienen una compatibilidad completa con Siri AI en los países donde esta esté disponible. Apple no ha destinado demasiado tiempo a hablar de su potencia o las capacidades de audio, por lo que no está claro cómo mejora a nivel técnico respecto al HomePod Mini original.
Al igual que el Apple TV 4K, el HomePod Mini 2 está disponible para reservas desde hoy mismo para entregas a partir del 13 de noviembre. Su precio es de 169 euros para todos los colores disponibles.
Apple Home Collection
Apple ha colaborado de forma directa con LG Electronics y Schneider Electric para lanzar varios productos que se complementan a la perfección con el resto de novedades propietarias. Dentro de Apple Home Collection hay una buena cantidad de cámaras fabricadas por LG, un nuevo termostato más inteligente y una cerradura para controlar el acceso a tu hogar sin necesidad de cámaras.
La mala noticia, eso sí, es que gran parte de estos productos no llegará a tierras europeas por ahora. Y, de hecho, en Estados Unidos la serie Home Collection estará disponible a partir del mes de diciembre con algunos lanzamientos a principios de 2027.
Estas son las novedades dentro de Apple Home Collection:
- Home Climate. Hay una versión de LG Electronics y otra de Schneider Electric. Ambas son similares, aunque cuentan con diferencias dependiendo del sistema de calefacción que tengas en el hogar. Se pueden configurar dentro del sistema de HomeKit para controlarlos desde el iPhone, el HomeView o con la voz y cuentan con un precio de 199,95 dólares.
- Home Access. Es la nueva cerradura inteligente fabricada por LG que permite olvidar la llave para acceder a tu casa con un PIN o utilizando los diferentes sensores de tu iPhone o el Apple Watch. También se puede controlar desde el interior para cerrar la puerta o abrirla desde cualquier altavoz inteligente o acción de voz. Su precio es de 349,95 dólares.
- Timbre con vídeo. También colaborando con LG, Apple ha lanzado un timbre con vídeo para poder utilizarlo de telefonillo inteligente y abrir la puerta o conocer quién intenta acceder a tu casa desde cualquier parte. Su precio es de 249,95 dólares.
- Cámaras de vídeo. Apple ha presentado un total de 3 cámaras de vigilancia para diferentes escenarios: una para interior, otra para exteriores y una tercera con un sistema de luz que permite establecer una vigilancia perimetral nocturna y detectar el movimiento. En orden, los precios son de 199,95 dólares, 299,95 dólares y 399,95 dólares.

articles.title: MediaMarkt renueva su campaña Oktubre con ofertas top en móviles, televisores y más
articles.text:
MediaMarkt ha renovado su campaña Oktubre con ofertas en muchos dispositivos, por lo que, tras la Fiesta de Ofertas Prime de Amazon, es un buen momento para aprovechar los descuentos en móviles, teles y más dispositivos. Por esta razón, vamos a repasar los mejores chollos que hay ahora mismo disponibles.
- TCL 65C6K Pro por 699 euros, un tele muy completa con una diagonal de 65 pulgadas.
- HP OmniBook 3 por 849 euros, un portátil pequeño y potente que es ideal para estudiar o trabajar.
- LG OLED C6 por 1.015 euros, uno de los televisores más interesantes por su relación calidad-precio.
- Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra por 1.234,05 euros al iniciar sesión en la tienda, un móvil de gama alta que se puede comprar más barato en PcComponentes.
- Philips One Blade Pro por 49,99 euros, una maquinilla para barba y cuerpo con una muy buena relación calidad-precio.
Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (256 GB)
TCL 65C6K Pro
Si buscamos un buen televisor que tenga un precio muy ajustado, el modelo Mini LED TCL 65C6K Pro ahora mismo se encuentra de oferta por 699 euros en lugar de 899 euros. Incorpora una pantalla de 65 pulgadas y es compatible con los formatos Dolby Vision y Dolby Atmos. Su sistema de sonido está firmado por Onkyo, ofrece una tasa de refresco de 144 Hz y su sistema operativo es Google TV.
TCL 65C6K Pro

Incorpora una pantalla de 14 pulgadas que ofrece una resolución 2K, monta el procesador Intel Core Ultra 5 322, incluye Windows 11 Home preinstalado y su configuración es de 16 GB de RAM y 512 GB de almacenamiento interno.
HP OmniBook 3
LG OLED C6
Durante la campaña Oktubre de MediaMarkt tenemos a muy buen precio la LG OLED C6 en su configuración de 55 pulgadas, ya que ha bajado hasta los 1.015 euros (antes 1.899 euros). Se trata de un televisor con pantalla OLED que ofrece una tasa de refresco de hasta 165 Hz, cuenta con HDMI 2.1, viene con las tecnologías gaming AMD FreeSync y Nvidia G-Sync y es compatible tanto con Dolby Vision como con Dolby Atmos.
LG OLED C6 (55 pulgadas)

Se trata de un móvil de gama alta que cuenta con pantalla de privacidad, su batería soporta carga rápida de 60W, las cámaras están a muy buen nivel en esta generación e incluye un S-Pen.
Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (256 GB)

Ofrece un buen resultado e incluye varios accesorios para barba y cuerpo; uno de ellos permite ajustar la longitud de rasurado.

articles.title: Votre téléviseur pourrait bientôt héberger une IA malveillante, et ce n'est pas de la science-fiction
articles.text:
Et si votre téléviseur ou votre aspirateur robot hébergeait demain une intelligence artificielle malveillante, à votre insu ? Des chercheurs d’Anthropic viennent de démontrer que ce scénario, encore largement théorique, pourrait devenir réalité plus rapidement que prévu.
On savait déjà que les objets connectés pouvaient être piratés et transformés en relais pour des cyberattaques. Mais avec les progrès de l’intelligence artificielle, une nouvelle menace commence à prendre forme : des logiciels malveillants capables de réfléchir, de s’adapter et surtout de se reproduire sans intervention humaine. Dans une étude publiée le 12 octobre, Anthropic s’est intéressé à ces nouveaux vers informatiques, avec quelques résultats pour le moins inquiétants. Et pour mener leurs expériences, les chercheurs n’ont pas eu besoin de serveurs surpuissants. De simples boîtiers Android TV à quelques dizaines de dollars ont suffi.
Quinze boîtiers Android TV pour faire tourner une intelligence artificielle
Les chercheurs d’Anthropic ont réussi à exécuter Gemma4-26B-A4B, un modèle d’intelligence artificielle de 26 milliards de paramètres, sur quinze boîtiers Android TV vendus environ 55 dollars pièce.
Pour y parvenir, ils ont réparti les calculs entre les différents appareils, chacun exécutant une petite partie du modèle. Le résultat n’a rien de spectaculaire en matière de performances, avec seulement 0,39 token généré par seconde. Mais l’essentiel est ailleurs : une IA relativement complexe peut fonctionner sur un ensemble d’équipements grand public, sans dépendre d’un centre de données.
Les équipes de recherche ont ensuite évalué la capacité de plusieurs modèles à installer leur propre environnement d’exécution sur des machines inconnues. Un modèle de neuf milliards de paramètres y est parvenu sur huit des neuf catégories de matériel testées.
Plus inquiétant encore : des modèles plus puissants ont réussi à enchaîner les différentes étapes d’une propagation autonome, depuis la recherche d'une nouvelle machine jusqu’à l’installation d'une copie. Ces expériences ont toutefois été réalisées dans des environnements simplifiés, notamment avec des accès volontairement peu sécurisés. Anthropic n'a donc pas créé un ver capable d’infecter spontanément des appareils domestiques.
Des boîtiers TV aux autres objets connectés, une menace encore théorique
Le scénario n’est pourtant pas totalement fantaisiste. Les chercheurs évoquent notamment les réfrigérateurs, les fours connectés et les aspirateurs robots, dont certains disposent désormais de processeurs suffisamment puissants pour contribuer à l’exécution d’une IA.
Attention cependant à ne pas confondre puissance de calcul et vulnérabilité. Un appareil équipé d'une puce dédiée à l’intelligence artificielle n'est pas automatiquement capable d’héberger un modèle de langage, encore moins de se laisser infecter.
Les objets connectés constituent néanmoins des cibles intéressantes pour les pirates. Le botnet Kimwolf a déjà compromis près de deux millions d’appareils, principalement des boîtiers Android TV, pour mener des cyberattaques. La menace existe donc, même sans intelligence artificielle.
Anthropic estime que de petits modèles pourraient acquérir les capacités nécessaires à leur propre réplication d’ici la fin de l’année 2026. C’est une projection, pas une certitude. Les chercheurs reconnaissent d’ailleurs que ces vers pourraient mettre plusieurs jours à se reproduire, ce qui laisserait du temps aux systèmes de sécurité pour les détecter.
Il y a un autre risque, plus sournois. Contrairement aux malwares traditionnels, ces IA pourraient apprendre à s’adapter à de nouveaux appareils et poursuivre leur propagation sans serveur central à neutraliser. De quoi compliquer sérieusement la tâche des spécialistes en cybersécurité. Pour l’instant, nos aspirateurs robots se contentent encore de traquer les miettes sous le canapé. Espérons qu’ils ne se mettront pas demain à chercher de nouvelles machines à infecter.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon passe un cap : déploiement mondial et bonne surprise pour les abonnés Pro — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le 30 septembre, Google présentait Gemini 4 Argon, son nouveau modèle d’IA haut de gamme. Par contre, il ne disait pas quand on pourrait s’en servir. Seules des équipes de cybersécurité triées sur le volet (membres du Fairwind Program) y avaient accès.
Ce mardi 13 octobre, Google déploie Argon à l’échelle mondiale pour les développeurs, les entreprises et les abonnés payants de Google AI. Pour nous, utilisateurs, le modèle arrive dans l’application Gemini et dans le Mode IA du moteur de recherche Google.
    À lire aussi : 
Gemini : notre guide pour tout comprendre l’IA de Google
Qui peut utiliser Argon, et à quel prix ?
Côté particuliers, Argon est réservé aux abonnés Google AI Pro et Ultra. La version gratuite de Gemini et l’offre AI Plus, à 4,99 euros par mois, n’y ont pas accès. En France, Google facture AI Pro 21,99 euros par mois et AI Ultra à partir de 99,99 euros. Fin septembre, Google ne citait que les abonnés Ultra parmi les premiers servis. C’est donc une bonne surprise pour les abonnés Pro.
Pour coder avec Antigravity, en revanche, il faut passer à l’abonnement Ultra. Google Antigravity est la plateforme de développement de Google où des agents IA écrivent et testent le code. Elle ne propose Argon qu’aux abonnés Ultra. Les développeurs Android peuvent aussi utiliser le modèle dans Android Studio, soit via Antigravity dans la version de test Canary, soit via l’offre payante de l’API Gemini.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Les développeurs qui passent par l’API paient en fonction de leur consommation, comptée en jetons. Un jeton (token) correspond à un morceau de mot. Jusqu’au 30 novembre 2026, Google fait un prix de lancement : 2 dollars par million de jetons envoyés au modèle (environ 1,80 euro HT) et 10 dollars par million de jetons générés (environ 8,90 euros HT). Ensuite, le prix double, à 4 et 20 dollars (environ 3,60 et 17,90 euros HT). Les jetons déjà envoyés et gardés en cache coûtent 95 % moins cher.
Au tarif normal, Argon coûtera autant que Claude Opus 5.5, le modèle haut de gamme d’Anthropic. Il restera moins cher que GPT-6 Astra d’OpenAI, facturé 10 et 50 dollars.
Google ouvre aussi le Fairwind Program à des centaines de nouveaux partenaires. Ils reçoivent une version d’Argon sans les garde-fous qui limitent ses capacités en cybersécurité. Côté recherche, 10 000 scientifiques pourront aussi utiliser gratuitement le niveau d’usage le plus élevé d’Antigravity pendant six mois, sur candidature.
Ce que Google promet avec Argon
Google présente Argon comme un modèle pensé pour les tâches longues et complexes, dans le code, la finance, le droit, la cybersécurité ou la recherche scientifique. Via l’API, il peut générer jusqu’à 1 million de jetons en une seule réponse,. Il peut donc travailler sur de gros projets sans s’interrompre.
Dans l’application Gemini, Google promet des réponses plus directes et avec moins de répétitions. Un bouton permet aussi de passer de la discussion aux tâches, que Gemini peut accomplir même quand on n’est pas devant son ordinateur. L’assistant se connecte désormais à plus de 40 applications, dont Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe et Shopify. Sur Mac, l’application Gemini intègre en plus l’interface de code d’Antigravity.
Pour appuyer ces promesses, Google cite surtout l’usage qu’en font ses propres équipes. Selon l’entreprise, Argon leur a permis de soumettre plus de 35 % de code supplémentaire écrit par des agents IA. Les retours en arrière, c’est-à-dire les modifications qu’il faut annuler parce qu’elles cassent quelque chose, ont baissé de près d’un tiers. L’équipe de Chrome s’en est aussi servie pour réorganiser un dossier d’environ 6 millions de lignes de code, sur les 40 millions que compte Chromium, la base de code de Chrome. Le travail a pris quelques semaines au lieu de plusieurs mois.
Google met aussi en avant la robotique dans un billet destiné aux développeurs. Argon y obtient 87 % à ERQA, un test qui mesure la capacité d’un modèle à résoudre des problèmes physiques dans un environnement en 3D. Lors d’un essai interne, Argon a regardé la vidéo d’une personne qui jouait au cornhole (un jeu où l’on lance des sacs sur une planche percée). Il a ensuite écrit le code de simulation qui a permis à Apollo, le robot humanoïde d’Apptronik, de réussir sept lancers d’affilée.
Sur les benchmarks, Google met en avant la première place d’Argon au Vals Index. Ce classement de la société Vals AI évalue les modèles sur des tâches de finance, de code, de droit et de fiscalité. Argon y obtient bien 68,9 %, contre 67 % pour Claude Opus 5.5. Restons prudents sur ce point, car le cabinet indépendant Artificial Analysis le classait huitième au général début octobre, cinq points derrière Claude Opus 5.5.
Les abonnés Pro et Ultra peuvent choisir Argon dans l’application Gemini à partir de ce mardi. Les développeurs, eux, ont jusqu’au 30 novembre pour profiter du prix de lancement de l’API.
