articles.title: Pour refroidir l’iPhone Duo pliant, Apple fait passer un conduit de graphite dans sa charnière
articles.text:
Pour évacuer la chaleur de l’A20 Pro dans un appareil qui double d’épaisseur une fois plié, Apple a fait passer un conduit de graphite flexible à travers la charnière de l’iPhone Duo. Les ingénieurs de la marque détaillent cette pièce, qui relie les deux moitiés du pliant.
L’iPhone Duo, premier pliant d’Apple, doit gérer la chaleur d’une puce gravée en 2 nm dans un châssis en deux parties. Selon un entretien accordé par Apple à PCMag, la charnière joue ici un rôle thermique inattendu : elle sert de pont pour répartir la chaleur sur une plus grande surface.
Un conduit de graphite flexible traverse la charnière
Banafsheh Barabadi, responsable senior de la conception thermique chez Apple, qualifie ce point de « l’un des aspects techniquement les plus difficiles » du design. Le conduit transfère la chaleur d’une moitié de l’appareil à l’autre, ce qui augmente la surface disponible pour la dissiper. Sur un pliant, l’épaisseur double une fois l'appareil refermé, d’où l’intérêt de mettre les deux moitiés à contribution.
La pièce a dû être conçue conjointement par les équipes thermique et mécanique. Il s’agit d’un matériau flexible qui doit encaisser de très nombreux cycles d’ouverture tout en conservant sa conductivité thermique et son intégrité structurelle sur toute la vie du produit. Autrement dit, la même pièce doit être un bon conducteur et un bon ressort, deux qualités qui s’accordent rarement.
Une puce A20 Pro légèrement adaptée au pliant
Cette puce équipe les iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max et iPhone Duo. C’est la première puce d’iPhone d’Apple gravée en 2 nm, après les débuts de cette finesse avec la M6 du Mac mini en août. La version du Duo diffère un peu, Dan Murray, vice-président de l’ingénierie silicium, explique qu’Apple a ajouté un second moteur d’affichage pour faire fonctionner simultanément l’écran intérieur et l'écran extérieur.
Le circuit prend aussi en charge une caméra FaceTime placée sous l’écran intérieur. Le refroidissement général repose par ailleurs sur une chambre à vapeur et sur un matériau baptisé « metal over foam », que l’iFixit a également examiné lors de son démontage de l’iPhone 18 Pro. Barabadi le décrit comme un couplage thermique et mécanique direct entre la puce et la chambre à vapeur, dont la mise au point a demandé des mois.
Deux écrans à alimenter, une seule enveloppe thermique
Le second moteur d’affichage a un coût : deux dalles pouvant s’activer ensemble, c’est davantage de chaleur à évacuer dans un châssis qui ne se dilate pas. Le conduit de graphite apporte la réponse côté dissipation, là où une chambre à vapeur classique ne peut pas franchir une charnière.
L’iPhone Duo arrive en magasin le 23 octobre. Les ingénieurs ne donnent à ce stade aucun chiffre de température ou de performance soutenue : c’est à l’usage, sous charge prolongée, que ce conduit fera ses preuves.

articles.title: XWorm RAT Evolves Into Surveillance Platform
articles.text:
The XWorm RAT developers have expanded the malware’s capabilities with fresh plugins that turn it into a surveillance platform, cybersecurity firm Netskope reports.
A sophisticated, multi-functional Windows RAT first observed in 2022, XWorm provides attackers with full control over the infected systems, offering keylogging, screenshot capture, webcam access, and payload execution capabilities.
The malware’s developers have been constantly updating its codebase and adding new functionality, and the threat has remained highly active, with Netskope observing over 1,200 incidents across 100 organizations during the third quarter of the year.
Alongside new variants, the developers have also increased the number of plugins XWorm supports, from 35 in July 2025 to 46 in October 2026.
Some of these have been clearly designed for surveillance: enabling location tracking, live audio streaming, webcam capture, and interactive control over authenticated browser sessions.
“The Maps plugin provides victims’ GPS location without a user prompt. The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser hijacks authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand,” Netskope says.
According to the cybersecurity company, the activity surrounding XWorm has increased since a cracked version of its builder was released publicly in June 2025, and the source code for RAT’s 6.4 version was leaked in August 2025.
With the addition of the HBrowser plugin, the RAT moves beyond harvesting credentials and user data from browsers: it provides the operator with a real-time view of the browser and can relay attacker inputs to the browser.
Operator’s interactions are encoded as command-and-control (C&C) commands, transmitted over the standard XWorm AES-encrypted communication channel, and executed on the victim’s system.
“The victim machine receives them and executes the corresponding input on the active browser window. The operator receives a continuous stream of screenshots. From the operator’s perspective, it is a full remote browser session. Every authenticated tab is accessible, bypassing the need for logging in and dealing with MFA,” the company explains.
The Maps and Microphone plugins allow operators to monitor the victim’s location and to capture audio without privilege escalation and without a user warning.
“XWorm continues to evolve and has now added surveillance capabilities. Since its builder and source code were leaked, we expect continued upgrades and use of this toolkit,” Netskope notes.

articles.title: Nigeria's data consumption hits 90% of 2025 total in eight months
articles.text:
Nigerians consumed 11.94 million terabytes of internet data in the first eight months of 2026, around 90% of the volume recorded throughout 2025, pointing to growing demand through more intensive use of internet services.
In August alone, consumption reached 1.76 million terabytes, according to the Nigerian Communications Commission’s latest industry statistics.
The surge in internet data consumption intensifies pressure on Nigeria’s telecom operators to expand network capacity as users consume more data through existing and new connections. Operators must therefore accommodate rising traffic while maintaining service quality.
Part of the increase comes from additional internet connections. Osita Odafi, a telecom industry expert, said NCC figures showed approximately 800,000 new internet subscriptions in August alone, expanding the pool of connections generating data traffic.
But new subscriptions are only part of the explanation. Existing users are also using more data-intensive services, he said, particularly video platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels and Netflix. High-definition streaming and autoplay can further increase consumption.
“The critical question is no longer just how many Nigerians are connecting to the internet, but how intensively they are using it,” Odafi told TechCabal.
He also pointed to online banking, digital payments, cloud services, remote work tools, online education, and AI applications as drivers of demand. His assessment identifies potential drivers rather than a measured breakdown of how much traffic each activity generated.
The growing adoption of 4G and 5G is also supporting more data-intensive activities. 4G’s share of mobile subscriptions rose from 54.31% in July to 54.77% in August, while 5G increased from 4.74% to 4.92%. Together, the technologies accounted for approximately 60% of mobile subscriptions.
Monthly consumption was lowest in February, at 1.26 million terabytes, before rising to 1.4 million in March and crossing 1.5 million in June. By August, it had reached 1.76 million terabytes.
Faster connections can make streaming, cloud applications and other demanding services easier to use. Their rising subscription share does not, however, establish how much of the increase in consumption came from either technology.
Nigeria recorded 197.42 million telecommunications subscriptions in August, an increase of approximately 2.31 million, or 1.18%, from July. Data consumption therefore grew faster than total telecommunications subscriptions over the month.
The two indicators measure different things. Telecommunications subscriptions include connections used for voice and other services, while data consumption measures the volume of internet traffic. Subscription figures also count connections, not unique individuals.
The more relevant comparison is with internet subscriptions, including the approximately 800,000 additional connections in August. Even then, determining consumption per connection would require a consistent comparison of internet subscription totals and traffic over time.
MTN recorded 84.56 million internet subscriptions in August, followed by Airtel with 56.94 million and Globacom with 15.76 million. MTN and Airtel accounted for most subscriptions among the three networks.
For operators, sustained growth in consumption means more traffic to accommodate, whether it comes from additional connections or heavier use of existing ones.
“Continued investment in fibre infrastructure, network capacity and spectrum will be vital to accommodating this growth while maintaining service quality,” Odafi said.
He also identified zero-rated access to educational platforms, an initiative the NCC introduced on October 1, as a potential source of further demand. Under the initiative, eligible users are qualified to receive up to 100 megabytes of free daily data allowance to access designated educational platforms.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: The agent did the work. The audit log couldn’t say who asked.
articles.text:
The agent did the work. The audit log couldn’t say who asked.
More than 20 percent of the MCP-related access policies that Shawn Petty’s team reviewed across customer and prospect environments were broken or missing, according to a recent account published in The New Stack. In most cases, the MCP server ran on someone’s personal token rather than a service account.
At 12 p.m. Eastern/9 a.m. Pacific on Tuesday, October 27, Petty, Chief Customer Officer at CloudBolt, and Mike Bombard, Director of Global Pre-Sales Engineering at CloudBolt, will join The New Stack host Viktor Farcic for a live demo of how to trace an agent’s actions back to the person responsible for them.
You have successfully registered for the webinar.
The problem, though, usually shows up after an incident: That personal token puts an engineer’s name into the audit trail for everything the agent did. Meanwhile, a shared service account puts the account’s name there instead. In both cases, the audit trail isn’t able to identify who precisely asked the agent to do the work or who approved the access it used.
Access that goes through a request, approval, and grant in the identity provider is provisioned, and the identity provider records it. Access that an agent picks up along the way is emergent: A role inherited from the service that launched it, or a developer’s own token lent out to finish a task. The identity provider holds no record of those grants, so when an agent touches something it shouldn’t, you can’t trace it back.
In this live conversation, the CloudBolt team will explain how agents end up with access nobody approved, then show how to trace that access back to a person with CloudBolt: linking agent activity to your existing identity provider, setting limits on what an agent can touch, and reading the audit trail that results.
Live attendees can ask these experts questions in real time. Register today to join us!
You’ll learn:
- How to tie agent activity back to your existing identity provider instead of building a parallel system
- Which infrastructure actions an agent should be allowed to take without a human signing off
- What a usable audit trail for agent behavior contains, and how to keep one without slowing teams down
- A live trace of one agent’s credentials and actions, from the task it ran to the person responsible

articles.title: Un robot camina sin batería gracias a un truco: usar el suelo como energía
articles.text:
Un pequeño robot caminante logró moverse durante 150 días sin depender de ninguna batería convencional. La clave está en una membrana instalada en sus patas, capaz de generar electricidad cada vez que toca una superficie metálica. El desarrollo, liderado por Yue Gao, del Departamento de Ciencia Macromolecular de la Universidad Fudan, se publicó en la revista National Science Review.
El problema de fondo es conocido en la robótica miniaturizada: cuanto más chico es un robot, menos espacio queda disponible para una batería, y las que logran entrar ofrecen muy poca autonomía.
Un robot de menos de dos gramos con una batería comercial apenas se sostiene en movimiento un par de minutos. Frente a esa limitación, el equipo de Fudan decidió invertir la lógica y convertir el propio terreno en fuente de energía.
Cómo funciona la membrana que convierte el suelo en energía
El mecanismo se apoya en una membrana de gel de poliacrilato de potasio, un polímero que retiene agua y que mide apenas 135 micrómetros de espesor, un grosor comparable al de una hoja de papel. Ese material se coloca en las patas del robot y entra en acción cada vez que hay contacto con el suelo.
Cuando la pata pisa una superficie de aluminio, zinc o silicio, se desencadena una reacción electroquímica. El metal del piso cede electrones, mientras que el oxígeno y la humedad del aire los reciben del otro lado de la membrana. El suelo pasa a funcionar como uno de los componentes de una pila, de manera similar a las baterías de metal y aire.
Un robot camina sin batería gracias a un truco que consiste en usar el suelo como energía: una membrana ubicada en sus patas genera electricidad apenas toca una superficie metálica, mediante una reacción electroquímica entre el metal del piso y el oxígeno del aire, sin necesidad de ninguna fuente de carga externa.
La velocidad de esta reacción es uno de los datos que más llamó la atención del equipo de investigación. El proceso arranca en apenas una décima de milisegundo cuando la pata toca el suelo y se detiene de inmediato en cuanto se levanta.
Según los investigadores, la membrana entrega 133 milivatios por centímetro cuadrado sobre zinc y 103 sobre aluminio, una potencia unas diez veces superior a la de las microbaterías típicas usadas en este tipo de dispositivos.
Las pruebas que confirmaron la resistencia del sistema
Para comprobar si la idea funcionaba más allá del laboratorio teórico, el equipo construyó un robot caminante impreso en 3D, de unos 6,7 por 5,7 centímetros. Con él realizaron una serie de ensayos pensados para exigir al sistema en condiciones variadas.
Durante las pruebas, el robot funcionó de forma intermitente a lo largo de 150 días. En ese período, dio más de 10.000 pasos sin que se registraran caídas de voltaje y, más adelante, superó el millón de pasos acumulados. La membrana también mostró resistencia térmica: soportó temperaturas de entre 20 grados bajo cero y 80 grados.
El robot llegó incluso a subir planchas de metal inclinadas gracias a la energía generada por sus propios pasos, y la membrana alcanzó a alimentar una luz LED y un transmisor Bluetooth.
A esas funciones se suma una capacidad adicional, no prevista como objetivo inicial: la membrana actúa también como sensor, porque las señales eléctricas varían según el material y la rugosidad de la superficie pisada. Eso permitiría al robot identificar sobre qué tipo de suelo se desplaza.
Los límites de usar el suelo como fuente de energía
El sistema no está exento de contrapartidas. Como es el propio metal del suelo el que aporta los electrones necesarios para la reacción, ese material se consume con el uso. A lo largo de las pruebas, el robot llegó a gastar alrededor de 2 gramos de aluminio del terreno sobre el que caminó.
A ese desgaste se suma otro, interno: la membrana se degrada con el tiempo por la acción del dióxido de carbono del aire. Por esa razón, los investigadores debieron reponer manualmente parte de sus componentes químicos durante los ensayos para mantenerla operativa.
Existe además una restricción de terreno. El sistema no funciona sobre plástico, vidrio, tierra o materiales orgánicos, superficies donde no se produce la reacción electroquímica necesaria. Para atravesar esos tramos, el robot necesita un pequeño supercondensador que almacena energía de manera convencional y la libera cuando no hay metal disponible bajo sus patas.
Posibles usos de los robots que se alimentan del metal
Los metales y el silicio que aprovecha la membrana están presentes en buena parte de la infraestructura moderna: tuberías, edificios, centros de datos y maquinaria industrial son solo algunos ejemplos. Esa disponibilidad abre un campo de aplicación concreto para la tecnología desarrollada en Fudan.
Los autores del trabajo imaginan robots pequeños capaces de recorrer conductos de ventilación, subestaciones eléctricas o espacios reducidos dentro de instalaciones industriales, con el objetivo de inspeccionarlos sin depender de cables ni de recargas periódicas. La energía la obtendrían directamente del entorno metálico que recorren.
Entre las aplicaciones todavía lejanas que se mencionan en el estudio figura también la búsqueda de sobrevivientes entre escombros tras un terremoto, un escenario donde la autonomía energética de un robot diminuto podría resultar determinante para operar sin asistencia externa durante períodos prolongados.

articles.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
articles.text:
Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.
Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

articles.title: Undecimal Bio lands €16 million to develop targeted RNA medicines beyond the liver | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cambridge-based Undecimal Bio, a spin-out from Eleven Therapeutics advancing targeted delivery of siRNA therapeutics, today announced a €16 million ($18 million) Seed financing round to expand DELiveri, its proprietary AI-enabled platform for identifying conjugates that can direct RNA medicines to defined cell types.
The round was co-led by 4BIO Capital and IQ Capital, with participation from Verve Ventures, Harel Tech, Entree Capital, Kerna Ventures and Saras Capital. The funding will also be used to progress Undecimal’s renovascular programmes and enable expansion of the team at their laboratories based at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.
“The hard problem in RNAi was never the silencing, it was getting the molecule to the right cell,” says Dr. Yaniv Erlich, CEO and co-founder of Undecimal Bio. “Our in-vivo validated DELiveri platform can screen large chemical spaces at an unprecedented pace, generating massive data for our legions of AI agents to decipher the structure-activity relationship and score the best candidates. We are excited to bring these advances to develop the next generation of siRNA therapeutics for the benefit of patients.”
Undecimal Bio’s Seed financing comes amid a series of European investments in RNA-based therapeutics, targeted drug delivery and AI-enabled biotechnology platforms in 2026.
Related announcements include Dublin-based Aerska‘s €32 million Series A to advance RNA interference medicines targeting neurological diseases, Paris-based WhiteLab Genomics‘ €23.2 million Series B for AI-driven genomic medicine design and delivery, and Cambridge-based STORM Therapeutics‘ €47.5 million Series C to progress RNA-modifying cancer treatments.
In the UK, Thalia Therapeutics also secured €3.1 million to develop its RNA therapeutics portfolio, while London-based Helical raised €8.4 million for its AI-powered pharmaceutical R&D platform.
Alongside additional investments in Spain’s Gate2Brain, Belgium’s Sightera Biosciences and the UK’s Houdini Bio, these announcements represent approximately €125.9 million in 2026 funding, rising to €141.9 million including Undecimal’s round.
Founded in 2026, Undecimal pairs massive scale combinatorial chemistry with transformer-based AI to guide siRNA therapeutics into the tissues that need them.
According to the company, RNA interference has transformed the treatment of liver-expressed diseases, but reaching tissues beyond the liver remains a key obstacle limiting the broader potential of the modality. DELiveri addresses this challenge as a technology that screens massive-scale combinatorial libraries of candidate ligands, converting cells to act as molecular radars that detect productive delivery at single molecule resolution.
This high throughput data is analysed by agentic AI to decode the resulting structure-activity data and identify conjugates capable of carrying siRNA into target cells.
Undecimal is initially applying the DELiveri platform in renovascular diseases, which pose significant unmet clinical need. Existing treatments of these indications largely address symptoms rather than the underlying etiological factors.
Th company believes that targeted siRNA delivery holds the potential to bring the digital-like precision of genetic medicines, enabling durable, target-specific silencing of the disease-driving pathways.
The Board of Directors comprises representatives of 4BIO Capital, IQ Capital and Harel Technologies, together with co-founders Dr. Yaniv Erlich and Shaul Ilan. Alongside the financing, Verve Ventures joins the Board as an observer.

articles.title: Store-bought hardware crypto wallets had secret chips installed that enabled stealing crypto recovery phrases — $93 million and counting stolen thanks to implanted eSIM and LTE modules in Ledger wallets
articles.text:
Store-bought hardware crypto wallets had secret chips installed that enabled stealing crypto recovery phrases — $93 million and counting stolen thanks to implanted eSIM and LTE modules in Ledger wallets
Hardware sold directly by Ledger appears safe, but some reseller supply chains may be compromised.
Cryptocurrency enthusiasts are often advised to acquire a hardware wallet like one of the Ledger models, theoretically adding the ultimate layer of security. And yet not even that approach is 100% safe, as a currently unfolding investigation revealed that Ledger resellers in Southeast Asia and Europe are carrying hacked wallets laden with eSIM and LTE modules for exfiltration of recovery phrases. At least $93 million (and going) has already reportedly been siphoned off users' balances. Hardware sold directly by Ledger is so far unaffected.
The first booby-trapped wallet originated from reseller Cryptobilis, which has currently ceased all sales of hardware wallets of all brands. The offending unit came from a store in Malaysia, though Cryptobilis also sells in Indonesia and the Philippines. Researcher Mark Karpelès has been looking into hacked wallets for a while now, and one of them came via Amazon Japan, bought from a Chinese seller and shipped from Malaysia. Cryptobilis also sells other brands of wallets such as Trezor, Coolwallet, and Tangem, though so far there is no news of contamination beyond Ledger.
Ledger recommends that users who bought wallets from Cryptobilis in the past 90 days do not perform their initial setup, as that's where the private key exfiltration reportedly occurs. To those who have already done so, Ledger recommends moving their assets to a new wallet with a new seed. The data theft is performed by hiding a flexible PCB under the display assembly to capture the pixels showing the private key entered during the first setup. The information then heads off to the aforementioned eSIM+LTE combination for exfiltration.
Meanwhile, new reports have come in from Europe, as techie Johannes, seemingly located in Germany, found at least two hacked wallets at MediaMarkt, a well-known tech and appliances retailer. He bought one unit and found that it had the same exact hardware modifications as its Asian counterparts, suggesting that the Asian and European events may be related. Johannes then bought a second one at a different MediaMarkt location, and sure enough, it was also modded.
Notably, most hacked wallets found so far are confirmed to be brand-new units instead of returns. Malfeasants will often buy new hardware and return it to the store with modifications, so that the next unsuspecting customer gets bit.
Johannes had a MediaMarkt employee at one of the stores look up the wallets' stock information, and at least the one unit came from Aqipa GmbH, a Europe-wide distributor — meaning the blast radius may be much wider than MediaMarkt or Germany. Since this is a recent development, Ledger hasn't published any guidance, though we imagine it'll be similar to the aforementioned steps.
In his blog post, Mark Karpelès notes that earlier iterations of hacked wallets with eSIM cards had hand-made implants, but that, concerningly, the hardware bolt-ons inside the latest finds appear to be manufactured to order. If true, this might mean that there's a production line somewhere intercepting Ledger wallets and manufacturing hacked wallets in bulk.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Ledger publishes instructions detailing how users can verify the physical integrity of their wallets, including pictures of every component, for every model of wallet the company offers, so they can closely inspect for add-ons. Likewise, prospective users should only download software from the official Ledger website URL — a task made harder by numerous scam sites with booby-trapped software, pretending to be the official ones.

He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
articles.text:
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Why the open-closed AI debate is more complicated than it seems
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.
Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.
These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.
“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.
Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.
But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”
Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.
Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.
“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?
The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.
There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.
Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.
But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).
In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.
Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.
Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.
Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.
The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?
A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.
Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint.
But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.
Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.
Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

articles.title: Netflix compra los derechos exclusivos del Mundial 2030 y emitirá todo el torneo en España
articles.text:
Netflix acaba de anunciar que ha adquirido los derechos exclusivos de la Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030. La plataforma de streaming redobla una vez más su apuesta por el contenido deportivo y emitirá el evento más importante del mundo del fútbol en España y Andorra. Así, el servicio ofrecerá en directo a sus suscriptores los 104 partidos de la mayor competición deportiva del planeta.
La Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030 conmemorará el centenario de la competición. Curiosamente España, vigente campeona del mundo, será uno de sus tres países anfitriones. El país compartirá la organización con Portugal y Marruecos. Además, con motivo de ese centenario, Argentina, Paraguay y Uruguay acogerán algunos de los primeros partidos de la fase de grupos.
Todos esos encuentros del Mundial 2030 se podrán ver en Netflix tanto en España como en Andorra. Además, como parte del acuerdo, en España podrá verse gratis un partido de cada jornada. Y también se ofrecerá a una cadena nacional de televisión en abierto (todavía por determinar cuál) un paquete de partidos que incluirá todos los de España, las dos semifinales y la final.
Como parte de su estrategia de emisión del Mundial 2030, Netflix tiene previsto también ofrecer la cobertura íntegra y en directo del torneo, con emisión de programas —con un planteamiento genuinamente español— antes de cada partido, durante el descanso y después del encuentro, además de un programa resumen diario los días de partido y otros contenidos destinados a generar expectación en la antesala del torneo.
Netflix emitirá el Mundial 2030
El acuerdo se suma a la creciente oferta de deportes en directo de primer nivel de Netflix en todo el mundo, que abarca las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA, partidos y eventos de la NFL, la MLB, WWE y algunos de los principales combates de boxeo y de artes marciales mixtas (MMA).
"Pocos acontecimientos unen tanto a la gente como un Mundial. Este año, yo estaba en el estadio cuando España levantó el trofeo y viví de primera mano la pasión, el orgullo y las historias que acaban formando parte de la cultura de un país y perduran en la memoria durante generaciones. Ahora que España va a ser uno de los países anfitriones en 2030, nos hace muchísima ilusión ofrecer en Netflix todos los partidos a los aficionados de España y Andorra", confiesa Bela Bajaria, directora jefe de Contenidos de Netflix, en un comunicado remitido a la prensa.
"Para los aficionados españoles al fútbol, recibir al mundo como vigentes campeones y poder seguir todos los partidos en Netflix hará que esta ocasión sea única. Además, nuestra creciente colaboración con la FIFA, que incluye las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA en Estados Unidos y Canadá, refleja nuestro compromiso constante por acercar a los aficionados a los grandes momentos del deporte mundial", añade.

articles.title: Cette filiale de Microsoft vient d'être condamnée à une amende de 8,5 millions d'euros
articles.text:
La Norvège sanctionne Xandr pour avoir relayé sans base légale des données d'utilisateurs de Grindr, et notamment leur orientation sexuelle. Le régulateur refuse que la régie publicitaire se défausse sur l'application.
L'amende atteint 92 millions de couronnes norvégiennes, soit environ 8,6 millions d'euros. Aucune sanction de la Datatilsynet, l’autorité norvégienne de protection des données, n'avait atteint ce niveau.
Xandr ne pouvait pas s'appuyer sur le consentement recueilli par Grindr
Xandr servait d'intermédiaire dans les enchères publicitaires en temps réel (real-time bidding). Cette société de publicité en ligne est aujourd’hui une filiale de Microsoft. Le mécanisme est rapide. Quand une application a de la place pour une annonce, elle transmet des informations sur son utilisateur à des plateformes. Les annonceurs surenchérissent alors en une fraction de seconde pour afficher leur publicité. Xandr y participait côté offre comme côté achat. Avec Grindr, les données ont pu atteindre des milliers de sociétés, à l'insu des utilisateurs.
Ces données sont sensibles. Grindr s'adresse aux hommes gays et bisexuels, aux personnes trans et queer. Rien que le fait d'utiliser l'application laisse deviner une orientation sexuelle, une information que le RGPD protège davantage. La justice norvégienne l'a confirmé dans le dossier visant Grindr, sanctionné de 65 millions de couronnes (environ 5,7 millions d'euros). Nous rapportions déjà le partage de ces données avec des régies, localisation précise comprise, lorsqu'une amende de 11,7 millions de dollars avait été annoncée contre l'application.
Pour traiter de telles données, il fallait un consentement explicite. Xandr a supposé que Grindr l'avait obtenu. Elle n'a donc rien vérifié et n'a prévu aucune base légale pour son propre traitement. La Datatilsynet la juge alors coresponsable avec l'application. Sa directrice, Line Coll, rappelle que chaque société doit pouvoir prouver qu'elle avait le droit d'utiliser ces informations. Selon elle, quand tout le monde se renvoie la balle, les droits des utilisateurs deviennent "sans valeur en pratique". Elle insiste aussi sur le fait qu'une fois diffusées, ces données échappent à la personne concernée et peuvent être croisées avec d'autres pour dresser un portrait détaillé de sa vie.
Les faits courent de juillet 2018 à avril 2020. Cette durée a aggravé la sanction, tout comme le profit que Xandr a tiré de ces données. L'amende se base sur son seul chiffre d'affaires. Celui de Microsoft n'entre pas en compte, car Xandr n'en faisait pas encore partie à l'époque. Le rachat à AT&T s'est finalisé en juin 2022. La décision n'est pas définitive, Xandr dispose de trois semaines pour la contester. Si la Norvège est hors de l'Union européenne, le RGPD s'y applique quand même depuis juillet 2018 via l'Espace économique européen.

articles.title: Workday goes headless, opening its HR and finance data to outside AI agents
articles.text:
Workday goes headless, opening its HR and finance data to outside AI agents
Workday is opening up its platform and allowing developers to build their own HR and finance agents in Claude Code, Cursor, and other tools, as long as those agents follow the same rules as the people using them.
On Tuesday, at its Workday Rising conference in Las Vegas, the company made its Trusted Agent Platform “headless.”
With this, its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, SQL access to live Workday data, and a shared runtime for agents are now generally available, and customers can run their own agents on models from Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, Nvidia, and OpenAI.
As Workday CTO Gabe Monroy noted in a press briefing ahead of the event, “No matter who builds the agent, it runs under Workday permissions, approvals and audit trail — no agent gets a side door.”
Workday notes that many companies currently connect their agents to HR and finance data through copies in a data lake or through service accounts, but, the company argues, those approaches bypass those access controls (though companies like SAP, Microsoft, and others would surely argue that they, too, have access control in place).
MCP tools, SQL, and a shared runtime
For AI developers, the main entry point to the Workday ecosystem is Agent-Ready Tools. That’s the company’s MCP server, which ships as part of Workday Extend AI. Users sign in with their own Workday credentials, and Workday says an agent acting for them can’t reach anything their own account can’t. That’s a key feature here, that ties an agent directly to a user’s account.
Monroy said the server currently offers 275 read tools and 54 tools that write or delete data.
Live Data Query, part of Workday Data Cloud, lets BI tools and agents run SQL queries directly against Workday’s data. Monroy described it as JDBC access to Workday’s object graph, and the company says each query returns only what the requesting user is cleared to see.
Three more components are generally available today. Agent Harness is the shared runtime that Workday’s own agents and those built by customers and partners run on. It passes each agent the user’s identity, org position, and access rights, limits what the agent can do, and picks which model handles each task based on cost and performance. Developer Agent generates Workday agents and apps from a natural-language prompt in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or the Workday Developer Site. Custom Agents lets teams deploy agents they built with LangChain or Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK) onto Agent Harness, though ADK support is limited to design partners for now.
Two more pieces are on the roadmap for early access in early 2027. Agent Context Service will preload only the Workday data a task calls for, which Workday says speeds agents up and limits their exposure to sensitive records. Grounded Reasoning will check a planned action against the customer’s policies, process rules, and Workday records before the agent carries it out.
Workday says customers have built more than 500 agents and more than 6,000 apps with Developer Agent and Agent-Ready Tools in the past four months.
“Headless, the lawless way”
In the briefing, Monroy demoed what he called “headless, the lawless way.” An agent connected to a custom MCP server — a setup he said Workday commonly sees among its customers today — returned job requisitions its user had no business seeing and then moved the wrong employee between teams with no approval. When pointed at a copy of Workday data in Snowflake, the same agent produced the CTO’s salary when asked.
“When it fails, it isn’t just a wrong answer,” Monroy said, “it’s a wrong action that nobody approved.”
When the agent went through Workday’s own MCP server and Data Cloud instead, with the user signed in, the same queries unsurprisingly returned only the requisitions that user was allowed to see (it wouldn’t have been much of a demo of those access controls otherwise, of course).
“A small set of use cases”
Asked whether headless matters as much to Workday as it does to Salesforce, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said that Workday is giving customers a choice: “I’d always prefer if they use our user interface, but headless will be equally good.”
Kazmaier noted that building agents directly on Workday’s tools and APIs is “only possible for a small set of use cases where you don’t need to have HR or finance domain logic.” For everything else, he pointed to an AI-to-AI integration in which Claude hands requests to Sana, Workday’s agent orchestrator, which then calls Workday’s own domain agents.
Lakes for analytics, not for agents
It’s worth noting that the Snowflake example is a bit of an awkward one for Workday. When the company announced Data Cloud in September 2025, the pitch included zero-copy sharing of Workday data with Databricks, Salesforce, and Snowflake. Snowflake made its Workday Data Cloud integration generally available on Oct. 7, and Databricks put its Workday connector for Unity Catalog into public beta a day later.
According to Databricks, a Workday admin sets up the connector by registering an Integration System User (ISU), the kind of system account Workday customers use for traditional integrations, with read access to the shared tables. After that, Unity Catalog permissions at the catalog, schema, and table level decide who can query the data.
Monroy said data lakes still make sense for analytics and for joining Workday data with the rest of a company’s data, but that an external lake is “the wrong place to build agents” that need governed access to Workday.
“You can export your data, but you can’t export the rules that govern the data,” he said, adding that rebuilding those rules in the lake means “maintaining a second copy” of Workday’s security model, “and the day it drifts, it’s all wrong.”
Everybody is losing their heads
Headless is the way to go right now, it seems. Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Microsoft, for example, already let outside agents into their systems of record. Salesforce launched Headless 360 at its TDX developer conference in April, so agents in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or a terminal can work with Salesforce data. ServiceNow made its Action Fabric MCP server generally available in May, with Anthropic as a launch partner, and Microsoft offers an MCP server for Dynamics 365 ERP.
All four vendors say outside agents stay within their existing permission models.
Whose identity does the agent use?
When it comes to agent identity, different vendors are currently taking very different approaches.
Salesforce, for example, is preparing to have agents that connect over MCP or its APIs register with their own credentials and permissions instead of acting under a user’s identity, according to Salesforce Ben. MCP clients will eventually need to switch to OAuth credentials tied to those agent identities.
Workday’s documentation says its agents can already get up to two system accounts of their own, called Agent System Users (ASUs), one for acting on a user’s behalf and one for “ambient” work, each with its own OAuth 2.0 client. Workday creates the ambient account automatically when a customer turns on an ambient skill.
Unified.to, which sells a Workday MCP integration, says every Workday MCP path, “official or not,” starts with creating an ISU. Cequence’s setup guide for its Workday MCP integration asks customers to create one “with appropriate security groups.” An agent working through an ISU sees whatever those security groups allow, no matter who is prompting it.
The more telling signal may be Kazmaier’s caveat. If building directly on the MCP server only works for a small set of use cases, the version of headless Workday expects most customers to use is Claude talking to Sana talking to Workday’s own agents, with Workday’s runtime in the middle of every call.

articles.title: 15 startups selected for Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Fifteen startups have been selected for the Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa, a three-month programme designed to support growth-stage, AI-driven startups with equity-free funding, technical mentorship and access to Google’s advanced AI technologies.
The programme forms part of Google’s plan to support 50 South African startups between 2024 and 2028. Each selected startup receives up to ZAR1 million (US$60,000) in equity-free funding, allowing founders to retain full ownership of their business while using the capital to accelerate growth.
They also gain direct access to Google’s AI tools, cloud infrastructure and models, including hands-on access to Gemini, helping them strengthen their products and enhance their technical capabilities.
Applications for the latest cohort opened in July, and received over 1,000 expressions of interest. From that, 15 South African-led, revenue-generating startups have been selected for the 2026 cohort.
They include Ambani Africa, an African language learning app that helps children connect with their mother tongue; Anvaya Legal AI, an AI legal assistant that speeds up research, drafting and document review; Boleka Africa, a community-based fintech helping underbanked adults access fair credit, savings and payments; Bro, a mobility platform connecting passengers with affordable transport; and Buddy Learning, an AI tutor on WhatsApp that delivers low-data, multilingual tutoring.
Also selected are Daedalis, which builds verified data infrastructure and enterprise AI for supply chains; Dataseka, an AI analytics platform that turns scattered business data into usable insights; Fly n Pay Later, a travel fintech that lets people book flights and pay in manageable installments; Kasicoach, an AI mentorship platform on WhatsApp and Telegram for township and rural youth; and Muna Africa. infrastructure that helps retailers run circular fashion resale programmes.
The cohort is completed by Propela Health, a marketplace connecting African healthcare professionals with global employers; Scale, which lets startups launch and issue card products; Thuto, an ed-tech building AI tools to improve learning outcomes; Tradeflow, an AI platform that automates supplier invoicing and ordering for restaurants; and Zumii, a WhatsApp platform that sources, packs and delivers school stationery to parents.

articles.title: Kubo Care uses radar technology to keep elders safe at home
articles.text:
Kubo Care uses radar technology to keep elders safe at home
Bengaluru-based startup Kubo Care uses millimetre-wave radar devices to monitor seniors and detect falls without intrusive cameras or wearables.
As families increasingly live in different cities and countries, keeping ageing parents safe at home can be a challenge. Full-time attendants require trust and may not always be reliable, while video cameras can feel intrusive, particularly in bathrooms, where more than half of serious falls occur. Wearable devices such as smartwatches and panic pendants offer another option, but seniors may forget to wear or charge them.
Bengaluru-based Kubo Care is addressing this problem with a system that monitors movement continuously without recording video or audio, while keeping families informed.
The healthtech startup was founded in 2024 by CEO Ayush Agrawal and COO Anurag Ram Chandran. Agrawal, who previously co-founded senior care ecommerce platform Seniority and worked as an AVP at CARS24, experienced the problem firsthand when his father suffered a stroke and fell while alone at home. He remained undiscovered for hours.
Chandran, a Schwarzman Scholar who previously ran an Indian NGO, became the primary caregiver for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. His experience exposed him to gaps in elderly care.
The two met in early 2024 at Antler’s Bengaluru residency and combined their experience in age-tech to develop a system for monitoring seniors at home.
Monitoring movement through radio waves
Kubo Care’s main device is mounted on a wall or ceiling and uses 60 GHz millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar technology. Similar to how bats use echolocation, the sensor transmits radio signals to map a room in three dimensions, tracking human presence and movement without capturing video or audio.
The system uses proprietary AI to analyse this spatial data and identify patterns of movement. It can detect sudden falls in less than a second while distinguishing them from deliberate movements, such as someone slowly lowering themselves onto the floor.
Beyond emergencies, the software establishes a baseline of daily habits, tracking sleep restlessness, night-time awakenings, and washroom visits. Changes in these routines can help care teams identify possible health issues, including urinary tract infections or gradual vision decline.
Kubo Care holds patents in India and the US for software that converts raw point-cloud data into real-time skeletal models to assess posture and gait. It also has a patented method that reduces false alarms by more than 99%.
The startup develops its technology in-house, including hardware, custom firmware, cloud applications and AI analytics. In larger spaces, its software transfers tracking data between multiple wall-mounted devices, allowing continuous monitoring as a resident moves between rooms, including areas with blind spots.
For institutional operators, the system provides customisable alerts for bed exits, prolonged washroom stays, and wandering. The hardware can also be connected to ambient sensors that measure room temperature, humidity, lighting and air quality.
The information is available through an enterprise management portal for care facility staff and a mobile application for family members.
Global B2B plans
Kubo Care operates on a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model and plans to charge senior care operators between $50 and $70 per device per month.
The startup is currently pre-revenue and conducting pilots in India, Japan, and the US. In India, retirement community developers are integrating its hardware into model homes as part of the standard infrastructure.
Over the next year, Kubo Care plans to expand its B2B presence in senior care facilities across Japan, the US and India, while preparing for a broader direct-to-consumer launch.
“We are able to reduce false alerts by over 99% through our patented method,” Agrawal says. “The roadmap over the course of the next year is to establish ourselves in B2B, especially in the US and Japan, the two largest senior living markets in the world, while preparing for a direct-to-consumer launch by late next year.”
Kubo Care is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Docker Hub flaw let attackers impersonate users, tamper with images
articles.text:
Docker has disclosed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105445) in Docker Hub that let attackers access another user’s container repositories using a personal access token (PAT).
Docker Hub is an online registry for storing, sharing, and downloading container images - templates that package everything needed for an application to run in an isolated environment.
In Docker Hub, a PAT serves as a secret used to authenticate tools and workflows. It allows you to pull, push, or delete container images.
According to a security bulletin from the Docker team, an attacker could create an account and PAT, then convert the account into an organization and name a target user as its owner.
The CVE-2026-105445 flaw stems from Docker Hub reassigning a personal access token (PAT) to a designated organization owner without changing its secret or obtaining the target's consent. This allowed the attacker to use the token to authenticate as the target.
Depending on the token’s scope and the target’s permissions, attackers could pull, push, or delete images in the target’s repositories and accessible organizations.
“Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access,” Docker explained.
“Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.”
Although the flaw is critical, Docker noted that it did not provide Docker Hub web access or allow attackers to change passwords, email addresses, or two-factor settings, potentially locking legitimate account holders out.
The vulnerability was introduced on August 26, 2024, when the conversion started reassigning the personal account PAT to the new owner. This occurred without revoking or rotating the secret, and without asking the named owner to confirm the change.
On September 30, 2026, Docker received a vulnerability report describing the issue, confirmed it, and deployed a fix to production less than four hours later.
Docker says it found no evidence of exploitation after examining 304,000 pushes made with transferred tokens and analyzing high-risk public images.
Affected users and organization owners were notified on October 2, and transferred PATs were deactivated on October 8, except for those whose owners explicitly requested to retain them.
Docker says users who didn’t receive a notification should assume they were not impacted and did not need to take any action.
The platform no longer transfers PATs during conversion and requests user consent before naming them an organization owner.

articles.title: El CNI busca 17 perfiles técnicos para anticiparse a las amenazas de la IA y la cuántica: lo que piden dice mucho de cómo se prepara
articles.text:
El Centro Nacional de Inteligencia ha abierto una campaña para incorporar ingenieros y analistas técnicos. Son 17 perfiles, desde el análisis de malware hasta el despliegue de modelos de IA, para los que el CNI está recibiendo currículums durante este mes de octubre.
Qué está ocurriendo. El CNI se prepara para un escenario de amenazas dirigidas por máquinas. En ese sentido está trabajando sobre dos cuestiones: la IA y lo que la computación cuántica puede hacer con el cifrado de las comunicaciones.
Su brazo de ciberseguridad, el Centro Criptológico Nacional, llevará esos temas a las Jornadas STIC, que se celebran del 24 al 27 de noviembre en Madrid. Y las contrataciones van en la misma línea: formar ahora a quienes tendrán que estar preparados cuando esas amenazas maduren.
La amenaza. Un ordenador cuántico lo bastante potente podrá romper el cifrado de clave pública que protege casi cualquier comunicación, del RSA a las curvas elípticas. Ese ordenador todavía no existe, pero un adversario puede guardar hoy tráfico cifrado y esperar a tenerlo.
- Lo que viaja protegido en 2026 tal vez pueda leerse en 2035.
- Para quien maneja información clasificada con una vigencia de décadas, el plazo para prepararse ya ha empezado.
Migrar a criptografía poscuántica exige gente que sepa dónde vive cada clave dentro de cada sistema. Es un trabajo que encaja con perfiles como los de consultoría de ciberseguridad, acreditación de sistemas clasificados o comunicaciones.
Entre líneas. Las fichas dan pistas de cómo trabaja el CNI:
- Pone a prueba sus propias defensas. Uno de los puestos incluye desarrollar pruebas de concepto de malware para sus propios equipos de pentesting. La idea es atacarse primero para saber por dónde entraría otro.
- Quiere la IA en casa. El perfil de Data Science pide desplegar modelos on-premise, ajustarlos y conocer el hardware necesario para ejecutar modelos grandes. Un servicio de inteligencia no puede ir subiendo documentos clasificados a un chatbot comercial. Necesita su propio LLM funcionando en sus propias máquinas.
- Analiza la tecnología. Otro puesto se dedica a buscar vulnerabilidades en Bluetooth, Zigbee, Matter o Thread, los protocolos domóticos que gobiernan enchufes inteligentes o timbres con cámara.
El contraste. En la misma lista que los modelos de IA aparece un ingeniero TEMPEST. Su trabajo es certificar que un equipo no filtra, a través de su radiación electromagnética, lo que muestra su pantalla.
Es una disciplina nacida en la Guerra Fría que sigue haciendo falta hoy. Para las amenazas nuevas no sobra ninguna de las viejas.
En detalle. Los requisitos comunes son bastante terrenales: un grado o una ingeniería superior (Telecomunicaciones, Informática, Matemáticas, Física o Ciencia de Datos, según el puesto), carné B y un nivel B2 de inglés.
Hay un detalle en ese último requisito: el B2 se puede acreditar durante los dos primeros años. Así, un buen ingeniero no se queda fuera por el idioma. El CNI dice además que impulsa activamente el equilibrio entre hombres y mujeres, algo que considera necesario para cumplir sus objetivos en un sector técnico todavía mayoritariamente masculino.
Entre bambalinas. Quienes superen la primera criba irán a un encuentro presencial y restringido en Madrid a principios de 2027. Allí no solo les entrevistará el departamento de selección, que valorará el perfil personal. También lo harán sus futuros jefes y compañeros de despacho, que evaluarán los conocimientos técnicos. El propio CNI lo presenta como algo nuevo entre los servicios de inteligencia.
En una empresa privada, un candidato puede preguntar a un conocido o mirar en LinkedIn quién hace exactamente qué. Aquí nada de eso es posible, y ese encuentro es la única ventana. Funciona en las dos direcciones: el equipo puede comprobar de primera mano los conocimientos técnicos del candidato, y el candidato verá con quién pasará los próximos años en un trabajo del que sentirse orgulloso.
Los currículums se envían a través de la web del CNI.
