articles.title: Apple presenta ‘Remnants’: su película de terror inmersiva para Vision Pro provoca pánico en su primera proyección
articles.text:
Apple estrenará el 16 de octubre ‘Remnants’, la primera película de terror inmersiva producida para Apple Vision Pro, escrita y dirigida por Ti West y protagonizada por Lucy Boynton y Ralph Ineson. Como parte de la promoción, la compañía proyectó el filme en el Castillo de Woldmere ante un grupo selecto de personas y grabó sus reacciones en tiempo real, material que luego difundió en un video a través de las redes sociales de Apple TV.
Qué es ‘Remnants’ y cómo se vivió su primera proyección
El video promocional muestra a distintas personas sentadas en sillas, con los visores de Apple Vision Pro puestos, bajo una iluminación roja que acompaña la experiencia. Sus reacciones incluyen sustos, gritos y gestos de pánico mientras atraviesan la historia desarrollada por Ti West.
Cabe señalar que el propio material audiovisual aclara que se trata de reacciones reales de personas que experimentaban el filme por primera vez.
‘Remnants’ no llega como una película convencional, sino como una producción pensada específicamente para el formato de video inmersivo de Apple. Esa condición explica el énfasis puesto en documentar las respuestas físicas y emocionales de los espectadores, un recurso que busca transmitir la intensidad de la experiencia antes de su estreno oficial.
Dentro del video también se incluyen fragmentos breves y oscuros de la propia experiencia inmersiva. Entre ellos aparece una mujer que camina por un túnel sosteniendo un candelabro y otra escena en la que un personaje se oculta bajo sábanas, imágenes que anticipan la atmósfera de tensión que propone el filme.
La pieza promocional cierra con el eslogan “Face Evil” (“Enfrenta al mal”) y remarca que ‘Remnants’ estará disponible en exclusiva para Apple Vision Pro a partir del 16 de octubre de 2026.
Cómo funciona Apple Vision Pro, el dispositivo que aloja el estreno
Apple Vision Pro es una computadora espacial que combina contenido digital con el entorno físico del usuario. El dispositivo permite a quien lo utiliza mantenerse presente y en contacto con las personas que lo rodean mientras interactúa con contenidos tridimensionales.
El sistema propone lo que la compañía describe como un lienzo infinito, que supera los límites de una pantalla convencional mediante una interfaz completamente tridimensional. Esa interfaz se controla a través de los ojos, las manos y la voz del usuario, sin necesidad de mandos externos.
Este funcionamiento es posible gracias a visionOS. Mediante este sistema, Vision Pro permite que los usuarios interactúen con el contenido digital como si este estuviera físicamente presente en el mismo espacio que ellos, una característica que resulta determinante para experiencias como la que propone ‘Remnants’.
Cómo funciona Apple Vision Pro
El funcionamiento de Apple Vision Pro se sustenta en la computación espacial, una tecnología que elimina la necesidad de mandos o controles externos. El dispositivo se opera mediante la mirada, los movimientos de las manos y comandos de voz, procesados a través del sistema operativo visionOS.
Para seleccionar e interactuar con los elementos que aparecen en pantalla, Vision Pro combina seguimiento ocular con gestos mínimos de las manos. El usuario solo necesita fijar la vista sobre un botón, una aplicación o un enlace para que este quede resaltado. Después, al unir y separar los dedos índice y pulgar en un movimiento de pellizco, se ejecuta la acción equivalente a un clic.
Ese mismo gesto, sostenido mientras se desplaza la mano, permite mover ventanas de lugar, recorrer páginas hacia arriba o abajo y cambiar el tamaño de los elementos dentro del entorno virtual. Las cámaras de seguimiento reconocen las manos incluso cuando permanecen apoyadas sobre las piernas, sin necesidad de mantenerlas elevadas.
En cuanto a la gestión del entorno y la navegación, el dispositivo combina controles físicos con órdenes por voz. La corona digital, ubicada en la parte superior del visor, regula el nivel de inmersión y permite pasar del modo Passthrough, que muestra el entorno físico real, a una inmersión total en un espacio virtual tridimensional.
Otro recurso de navegación consiste en mirar la palma de la mano, gesto que activa un menú flotante desde el cual se accede a la pantalla de inicio o al Centro de Control. Para escribir, el usuario cuenta con dos alternativas: tocar un teclado virtual que se despliega en el aire o dictar el texto mediante comandos de voz.

articles.title: AI Turns Familiar Cyberattacks Into a Race Against Time
articles.text:
In the AI era, phishing remains the top attack vector in both use (17% of breaches) and breach costs (averaging at $5.29 per breach) according to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026. AI creates more personalized content for phishing with higher success rates. At the same time, AI can identify vulnerabilities, use the phished entry point and elevate privileges for lateral movement at greater speed.
None of this is new – cyberattacks haven’t changed with AI. “It just allows attackers to do the same familiar things much faster and at greater scale than ever before. The pressure comes from minimizing the time for defenders to respond,” says Steve Wallin, director of core integration and R&D labs leader at IBM UK.
For now, AI-generated attacks are still in the minority – little more than 20% of all attacks. But the writing (written by AI) is on the wall, and it is incumbent on enterprises to improve their security defenses now before the tsunami arrives in full.
SecurityWeek talked to Wallin on how enterprises should respond to this growing AI threat. Again, it is nothing new – it must just be done better.
It starts with a basic maxim that is as old as the ancient Delphic Oracle: ‘know thyself’. “Organizations must understand their existing security posture. The key to defending against this increasing volume of attacks and decreasing time to respond is again nothing new. It means focusing on proactive rather than reactive defense. It is security by design from the ground up rather than a bolt-on reaction,” said Wallin.
Proactive cyberdefense is a combination of understanding how attacks work, understanding the enterprise infrastructure and business, and being prepared for all possibilities.
“Zero trust is fundamental to stay in control of credentials, access, and enterprise data. You can no longer build a moat or wall around the infrastructure, so zero trust security by design must be built into the infrastructure, the applications, the API entry points, and the data management,” said Wallin. “This can only be achieved with a full understanding of what is important to the business.”
Interestingly, the father of zero trust, John Kindervag, has published a new book titled Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed: The Zero Trust Model for the AI Era. “Any AI-generated packet still has to move across the same network that attackers have always had to traverse – and correctly implemented zero trust can still halt it,” he told SecurityWeek. He echoes Wallin’s view: the principles of cybersecurity have not been altered by the arrival of AI-driven cyberattacks.
The only thing that has really changed is the statistical likelihood of a breach. This likelihood increases the need for resilience. But if defense starts from the position of ‘know thyself’, the enterprise will understand its key areas. Defensive use of AI can help here. “It is increasingly difficult for everything to be completely free of all unknown vulnerabilities. We can use AI to help us with prioritization, and risk management. We can use it to automate, to discover and to understand, so that we can continuously improve the environments that we’re running as an organization.”
This still doesn’t guarantee that a catastrophic breach won’t happen, so resilience must also include recovery of damaged data to ensure business continuity. This isn’t new, just more pressing – a cyber vault backup facility is necessary. This can be built internally using air-gapping and WORM technology; or acquired externally. The IBM Z mainframe, for example, offers a cyber vault designed for high-end workloads such as banking and core financial services, using automated validation, forensic tools, and immutable backups to test and recover corrupted data rapidly.
AI hasn’t changed the fundamentals of cybersecurity, it has simply made good cybersecurity by design, resilience and recovery more important.

articles.title: Apple refreshes its HomePod mini with a new chip and $149 price tag | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple’s new HomeView device was the center of the show at its smart home event on Tuesday, but the company also refreshed its HomePod mini smart speaker with a new chip and Siri AI integration, the latter of which will be available through a future update.
The $149 update is $50 more expensive than the original version launched over six years ago in 2020. The new HomePod mini has an S10 chip that helps improve optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.
With the new HomePod mini, users can control their smart home devices through voice commands. Plus, the speaker can listen for sounds like a smoke alarm and send a notification to users’ phones — a feature that Alexa devices have offered for years.
Apple said that with Siri AI, users will be able to have multi-turn conversations, but it didn’t provide a date for when the new assistant will be available to HomePod mini 2 buyers.
The company also said the new speaker works better with its other devices. For instance, users could form a four-speaker home entertainment system paired with the new Apple TV 4K. Plus, the HomePod mini 2 speakers can be the default speaker for Mac for video calls or music playback instead of built-in speakers.
The device has another new feature, as well: a visual canvas called “Sound Glow,” which uses the color scheme of the album art to turn the top of the HomePod mini into a visual canvas that will glow and pulse in sync with the music. Users can also pick soundscapes like rain or ocean waves to start animations.
The new speaker comes in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight colorways and will be available starting October 30. Consumers can preorder starting today.

articles.title: Voyager connecté en Europe : ce qu’il faut savoir sur l’eSIM Ubigi
articles.text:
Pas besoin d’un gros forfait mobile pour quelques jours en Europe
Pour un court séjour en Europe, l’eSIM Ubigi permet de rester connecté sans changer de carte SIM ni craindre les frais d’itinérance. Une solution pratique à préparer avant le départ.
Une eSIM pour rester connecté sans complications
Pour un week-end à l’étranger, mieux vaut anticiper la question de la connexion Internet avant de partir. L’eSIM Europe d’Ubigi permet de préparer son accès aux données mobiles en amont et de se connecter dès l’arrivée, sans acheter de carte SIM locale ni dépendre du Wi-Fi de l’hôtel. Une solution pratique pour consulter ses itinéraires, trouver une adresse ou organiser ses déplacements au fil du séjour.
Le principe est assez direct. Il suffit de choisir un forfait de données adapté au séjour, puis de le recevoir par e-mail. Un QR code permet ensuite d’installer l’eSIM sur un appareil compatible. Une fois la configuration effectuée, la connexion peut être utilisée à destination, selon les conditions du forfait choisi.
Ce fonctionnement présente un intérêt particulier pour les courts voyages. Consulter un itinéraire, réserver un transport, retrouver une adresse ou envoyer quelques photos devient plus simple lorsqu’une connexion mobile est disponible. En plus, la carte SIM habituelle reste en place : inutile de manipuler le tiroir du téléphone ou de risquer de perdre sa carte physique.
Voici ce qui distingue l’offre Ubigi :
●	Installation avant le départ : le QR code est envoyé par e-mail.
●	Connexion 4G et 5G :la 5G est disponible dans plus de 90 destinations, selon la couverture locale.
●	Partage de connexion autorisé : pratique pour connecter un ordinateur ou un autre appareil.
●	Recharge depuis l’application : il est possible de recharger son forfait même sans Wi-Fi ni données restantes sur le compte.
●	Couverture internationale : Ubigi propose des forfaits dans plus de 200 destinations.
Attention toutefois : l’offre Europe ne signifie pas nécessairement que tous les pays européens sont inclus dans chaque forfait. Il vaut mieux vérifier la liste des destinations couvertes, la quantité de données et la durée de validité avant de payer.La compatibilité eSIM du smartphone est également indispensable.
Une solution pratique pour éviter les mauvaises surprises
L’aspect qui me plaît le plus chez Ubigi, c’est la possibilité de choisir un forfait adapté à la durée du voyage et à ses besoins en données. Cela permet d’anticiper sa consommation plutôt que de découvrir une mauvaise surprise sur sa facture au retour. L’application facilite également les recharges en cours de séjour, même sans connexion Internet disponible.
Au final, cette eSIM prépayée s’adresse surtout aux voyageurs qui veulent anticiper leur connexion mobile et garder le contrôle sur leur consommation. Le bon réflexe reste de comparer les forfaits disponibles pour les pays visités et de configurer l’eSIM avant de partir. De quoi commencer un court séjour avec un souci en moins.

articles.title: Workday is using TypeSafe's Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
articles.text:
Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
Workday on Tuesday made Sana, its AI assistant, the new home screen for its HR, finance, and IT software. If you’re not an HR pro, that may not be all that exciting for you, but the way the team built this is maybe one of the most interesting use cases of Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model. Workday is building the user interface on the fly — and all of that is managed by Jev.
In a demo during a press briefing ahead of the announcement, a question about a paycheck brought up a card with the amount hidden behind a click, for example, while a request for time off produced a date picker, with Sana filling in the rest of the form.
Sana, which Workday bought for $1.1 billion last year, is available now, and admins can roll it out to their users without making it the default.
Picking components instead of writing them
Joel Hellermark, Workday’s chief AI officer and Sana’s founder, said in a press briefing that the usual approach to generative UI, in which a model generates the full interface, is “quite slow.”
“If you use a classification model instead and you just give it all of the design components to pick from, you can literally do it instantly,” he said.
Workday gave Jev every atomic component in its design system and hard-coded none of the selection logic, Hellermark said, though the team also had to get data preloading right. In the demo, the paycheck card appeared before he finished typing, for example.
TypeSafe claims Jev answers in 70 to 500 milliseconds, which makes it ideal for this kind of real-time use case.
In many cases, Hellermark said, AI that works through real interface elements does significantly better than pure back-and-forth chat.
A model built to choose
According to TypeSafe, developers send Jev application data and a set of typed questions, and it returns a pick from a list of up to 255 options, a score, or a yes-or-no answer, each with a probability attached. It doesn’t generate text.
TypeSafe launched Jev on Sept. 15 with a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. On Friday, it said it raised an $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz, at a $7.5 billion valuation. TypeSafe says a third of the Fortune 500 already use Jev but hasn’t named them. Andreessen Horowitz’s own announcement puts the figure at 25 percent, and TypeSafe’s only published case study features Jack & Jill, an AI recruiting marketplace.
There is no dearth of competition in this field, of course. OpenAI, Amazon, Cloudflare, and Perplexity have already shipped their decision models too, with Microsoft following on last week.
A pattern developers are already testing
Using Jev and similar models for building user interfaces isn’t completely new, though. CopilotKit, an open source framework for adding AI copilots to apps, published a recipe in which Jev picks which prebuilt panel to show, with an OpenAI model as the fallback.
Vercel Labs is testing a Jev mode in json-render, its framework for rendering AI-generated UIs from developer-defined components.
Andrew King, who leads solutions architecture at app developer Very Good Ventures, wrote last month that handing every closed question (one with a fixed set of answers) to Jev cut his generative dashboard’s median render time to 3.8 seconds, from 29 seconds with a frontier model composing it. His tests ran on synthetic data.
“A shape nobody anticipated cannot appear on screen,” King writes. Anything Jev answers with less than 50 percent confidence goes to a language model instead, a setup he calls “a cage with a door.”
In a test on OpenRouter’s blog using the Banking77 intent-classification set, Jev answered in a median 175 milliseconds and scored 81 percent accuracy. Claude Opus 5 scored 84.4 percent but took 2.3 seconds and cost about 22 times as much.
TypeSafe’s own documentation says Jev struggles with counting, arithmetic, and dates, leans toward whichever option is listed first, and doesn’t treat injected content as hostile by default.
Workday hasn’t said how large its design system is or what Sana does when no combination of components fits. King wrote in September that he was keeping client data off Jev because the vendor was “weeks old with no published security certification yet.” TypeSafe now offers a SOC 2 Type II report on request.
What leaves Workday
Workday recently added TypeSafe to its list of subprocessors, the outside companies that can process customer data (the ones you only think about when a SaaS service you subscribe to emails you about a change of subprocessors that you promptly forget). This entry, it’s worth noting, covers all of Workday’s product lines, not just Sana, for natural language processing, intent classification, and confidence scoring.
According to TypeSafe, Jev runs only on its hosted API and processes data in the U.S., and the company offers zero data retention to enterprise customers.
Staying inside Workday
Hellermark also showed Sana working inside Anthropic’s Claude. That’s an AI-to-AI integration, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said in the briefing, and users lose the Jev-driven interface and some context along the way.
Workday’s May partnership with Google Cloud already covers A2UI, Google’s spec for agents to describe interfaces that host apps then render. MCP Apps, a Model Context Protocol extension, brings interactive UI into Claude and ChatGPT. Neither shows up in Workday’s announcements this week, so for now, it seems, employees who reach Sana through Claude get the conversation without the date picker.

articles.title: Whiterock deploys €82 million to support SME growth across Northern Ireland | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Belfast-based fund manager Whiterock has announced their investment of €82 million (£70 million) in Northern Ireland SMEs across their two funds – both backed by the British Business Bank.
The two funds are the Growth Capital Fund and the Investment Fund for Northern Ireland.
Paul Millar, Chief Executive of Whiterock, says: “Whiterock has been supporting local SMEs’ growth for over 14 years, and our strong, dedicated team has spotted investment opportunities across multiple sectors from advanced manufacturing to tech to consumer products.
“We are an NI based funder with local knowledge, and we find that local businesses really value the insights and partnership that we bring to the table. We are proud of the resounding success of our equity and debt funds since they launched in early 2024 and we hope to continue working as the go-to strategic partner for local companies to achieve their growth ambitions.”
Whiterock’s investment milestone comes amid wider British Business Bank activity aimed at increasing access to finance for UK businesses in 2026.
EU-Startups has reported comparable commitments of €58 million to London-based Soho Square Capital, €46 million to FPE Capital, up to €11.5 million to Ascension Ventures, €11 million each to SFC Capital and Fuel Ventures, and up to €53.6 million to Zinc Capital Management.
Together, these commitments represent approximately €191 million in financing for investment managers supporting businesses at different stages of growth. Including Whiterock’s €82 million already deployed across Northern Ireland, the announcements account for approximately €273 million in reported financing activity.
EU-Startups previously covered Whiterock’s €7.7 million investment in Belfast-based Drinksology Kirker Greer and its €1.8 million funding package for Solarfix in 2024.
Sue Barnard, Senior Investment Manager at the British Business Bank, adds: “Reaching £70 million of investment in Northern Ireland businesses is an important milestone and demonstrates the impact that public and private finance can have in supporting ambitious smaller businesses to grow.
“Through the British Business Bank’s programmes, we are proud to work with fund managers such as Whiterock to increase access to finance for businesses that can drive jobs, innovation, and economic growth across the region. The breadth of businesses supported through these funds highlights the importance of a diverse funding landscape, and we look forward to seeing the continued impact of this investment across Northern Ireland.”
Founded in 2012, Whiterock manages over €420 million (£255 million) across five funds. Its Growth Capital Fund provides minority investments in scaling Northern Ireland companies, with capacity for further follow on funding as required.
Since 2024, Whiterock has invested €47 million (£40 million) into 15 companies across Northern Ireland, including Drinksology, MANTIS and Around Noon, through its €88 million (£75 million) equity fund and a further €35 million (£30 million) invested into 60 companies through its €71 million (£60 million) IFNI debt fund, supporting NI SMEs such as Neighbourhood Café, Nomadic Watches, Axial 3D and BLK BOX.
To date, the company has deployed in excess of €224 million (£190 million), which has leveraged over €177 million (£150 million) of further funding from other funders, and supporting the creation of over 3000 jobs.
A prime example of its investment thesis is Neighbourhood Café, which since opening its new site in February 2025 with loan support has delivered strong growth and is reportedly on track to more than double its revenue in FY26, its first full year of trading from the expanded premises. The business now serves an average of 11,000 guests per month across its café operations.
Building on this performance, management is focused on growing its events offering as a key driver of future revenue diversification and revenue growth.

articles.title: Nintendo stands by physical games as Sony embraces a digital-only future — 'There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic,' says a Nintendo exec
articles.text:
Nintendo stands by physical games as Sony embraces a digital-only future — 'There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic,' says a Nintendo exec
While Sony remains committed to phasing out physical media, Nintendo is taking the opposite approach. In a recent interview with the Brazilian YouTube channel Coelho no Japão, Bill van Zyll, Nintendo's VP and General Manager for Latin America, confirmed that the company has no plans to abandon cartridges.
"Historically, we’ve been very agnostic, right?" stated van Zyll in the interview.
The Nintendo executive firmly continued, "We go off what the consumer prefers, and take that into account very heavily. We also have a platform that was just launched. We're barely just over a year into NS2. It's got both digital and physical – that capability. There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic."
In an era where the gaming industry is rapidly shifting toward digital distribution, it is comforting to see at least some companies still supporting physical media. The core issue with digital purchases is that you do not truly own what you buy; instead, you are purchasing a license to access the game, unlike owning a cartridge or game disc. Some storefronts, such as GOG or itch.io, offer DRM-free downloads of the titles you purchase, but only a handful of them exist.
However, even cartridges cannot completely escape the march toward digitalization. With the release of the Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo introduced game-key cards, physical cards that contain a license to download the full game data. Modern AAA game releases have exceeded the storage capacity of traditional cartridges or discs. For instance, Black Myth: Wukong and the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI use this code-in-a-box model.
On the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2, cartridges max out at 32GB and 64GB, respectively. That is not much capacity by modern standards, so publishers turn to game-key cards as a compromise for a physical release. Compared with fully digital releases, game-key cards bind the license to the card, so owners can still trade or sell them like normal cartridges.
Owning physical copies can sometimes cost more than going digital, especially for Nintendo’s first-party titles. Effective as of May 2026, physical versions of first-party Nintendo titles sell for $10 more than their digital counterparts. The price increase was due to manufacturing, packaging, and distribution costs for cartridges. However, Nintendo frames the pricing adjustment differently, claiming it lowered digital game prices by $10 to pass the savings on to consumers.

Nintendo has announced plans for the Switch 2 to mirror its predecessor's lifespan, about six to seven years. No one anticipated Sony's decision to phase out game discs, so Nintendo's future remains uncertain, even though the company pledged to continue physical releases. With the Switch 2 launching just last year, we can at least look forward to another six good years of physical media.

articles.title: Microrganismo com genoma minúsculo desafia definição do que é estar vivo
articles.text:
Um microrganismo com um dos menores genomas já identificados pela ciência está levando pesquisadores a questionar os limites do que caracteriza a vida. Batizado de Sukunaarchaeum mirabile, ele possui apenas 238 mil pares de bases de DNA e apresenta uma estrutura genética tão reduzida que pode depender de outro organismo para sobreviver.
A descoberta aconteceu por acaso, durante uma pesquisa com o plâncton unicelular Citharistes regius, coletado em águas superficiais do mar na costa de Shimoda, no Japão. Os cientistas investigavam o material genético de cianobactérias que vivem em associação com esse plâncton quando encontraram uma pequena sequência circular de DNA que chamou a atenção da equipe.
O estudo foi publicado na revista científica Current Biology e reúne pesquisadores das áreas de biologia e ciência da computação.
Organismo tem menos DNA do que alguns vírus
- O Sukunaarchaeum mirabile pertence ao domínio Archaea, formado por organismos unicelulares que, assim como as bactérias, não possuem o DNA protegido por um núcleo envolvido por membrana. Apesar dessas semelhanças, as arqueias têm uma história evolutiva própria e características distintas das bactérias;
- O tamanho do genoma recém-identificado é particularmente impressionante. Existem vírus com genomas maiores do que o do microrganismo, alguns com 730 mil pares de bases e outros com até 2,5 milhões;
- A comparação chama a atenção porque os vírus não são considerados seres vivos por muitas definições convencionais, entre outros motivos, por não possuírem metabolismo próprio.
O Sukunaarchaeum mirabile também apresenta limitações importantes. Seu genoma não contém quase todos os genes normalmente necessários para manter o metabolismo de forma independente. Isso significa que ele aparentemente não consegue produzir sozinho tudo de que precisa para sobreviver.
Quando os resultados preliminares foram divulgados, em 2025, os pesquisadores chegaram a descrever sua existência como semelhante à de um vírus. Na versão final do estudo, porém, essa comparação foi abandonada para evitar confusão sobre sua classificação biológica.
Leia mais:
- Cientistas descobrem o segredo genético dos gatos laranjas
- O mistério do genoma obscuro. Ele representa 80% do nosso DNA
- Estudo aponta que duas aves brasileiras estão entre as mais barulhentas
Microrganismo pode depender de um hospedeiro
Uma das principais questões levantadas pela descoberta é como o organismo consegue sobreviver com tão pouca informação genética.
Segundo os pesquisadores, o microrganismo perdeu quase todos os genes necessários para produzir nutrientes e energia, mas preservou boa parte dos mecanismos responsáveis por copiar seu próprio genoma e fabricar proteínas a partir das informações contidas no DNA.
Essa combinação sugere que ele pode estar próximo do limite mínimo de informação genética necessário para uma célula continuar sendo capaz de se reproduzir e manter seu material genético.
Thorsten Allers, biólogo molecular da Universidade de Nottingham, no Reino Unido, explica que a capacidade de se replicar e o grau de autonomia desse processo são questões centrais para definir a vida.
A descoberta, segundo o pesquisador, oferece novas pistas sobre o quão simples uma célula viva pode se tornar e ainda preservar a capacidade de reprodução e manutenção de suas informações genéticas.
Os únicos organismos conhecidos com menos material genético do que o Sukunaarchaeum mirabile são bactérias que se tornaram tão dependentes de hospedeiros simbióticos que praticamente perderam sua identidade como organismos separados.
Parasita ou parceiro de outro organismo?
Os pesquisadores também consideram a possibilidade de o microrganismo ser um parasita, em vez de um parceiro que oferece algum benefício ao organismo que o abriga.
Uma das hipóteses é que ele esteja em processo de integração com seu hospedeiro, em fenômeno que pode ajudar a compreender como células mais complexas surgiram ao longo da evolução.
As mitocôndrias, estruturas responsáveis por grande parte da produção de energia nas células humanas, são um exemplo desse tipo de relação evolutiva. Segundo a explicação científica apresentada no artigo, elas descendem de bactérias que passaram a viver dentro de células eucarióticas há cerca de 1,5 bilhão de anos e mantiveram seu próprio DNA.
No caso do Sukunaarchaeum mirabile, entretanto, os cientistas não identificaram evidências suficientes para concluir que exista uma relação de benefício mútuo. Como o organismo aparentemente não oferece vantagem metabólica clara ao hospedeiro, o parasitismo é uma possibilidade considerada pela equipe.
Outro indício é que aproximadamente um quarto de seu genoma está dedicado à produção de grandes proteínas de membrana. Proteínas semelhantes já foram identificadas em outras arqueias parasitas, nas quais participam de mecanismos de invasão de hospedeiros.
Até o momento, o Sukunaarchaeum mirabile é conhecido apenas por meio de seu genoma: os pesquisadores ainda não o observaram diretamente em um microscópio. Por isso, sua forma de vida e sua relação com o plâncton continuam sendo questões em aberto.
A investigação amplia o conhecimento sobre os limites da redução genética e sobre as diferentes estratégias que organismos podem desenvolver para sobreviver, mesmo quando dispõem de um conjunto extremamente limitado de genes.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
articles.text:
Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the EV company’s secretive robotics startup.
Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics spinoff at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”

articles.title: ¿Gemini te va peor? No eres tú: la versión gratis ahora es mucho peor
articles.text:
Si Gemini no te funciona igual desde hace unos días, no es casualidad. De hecho, ni siquiera es un error de tu móvil o la propia Google: la compañía ha hecho un cambio histórico en la forma de gestionar los modelos de lenguaje. En pocas palabras, se puede decir que las cuentas gratuitas ya no tienen acceso a las IAs más avanzadas de la compañía, algo que estaba estandarizado desde que la gran G se metió de lleno en el sector. Por supuesto, los usuarios que no pagaban obtenían límites más estrictos, aunque estos eran suficientes para poder hacer un buen uso de algunos modelos complejos.
Hoy esto acaba. Desde el día 9 de octubre, Google ha eliminado la posibilidad de que las cuentas gratuitas utilicen los modelos Gemini 3.6 Flash y Gemini 3.1 Pro. Ahora, quien no pague, obtiene acceso directo a Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, una IA rápida para solucionar cuestiones sencillas, pero que no está destinada a los grandes volúmenes de datos o la resolución de problemas avanzados.
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite es un modelo que consume pocos recursos, pero sumamente eficiente con cada token que gasta. Es una IA interesante para utilizarla de forma gratuita, aunque supone un gran downgrade respecto a lo que se podía venir haciendo desde hace tiempo con la IA de Google sin necesidad de pagar.
Ahora, para poder tener acceso a los modelos 3.6 Flash y 3.1 Pro que utilizabas antes, es necesario suscribirse a un plan de pago de AI Plus. Además, Google ha actualizado los límites de Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: ahora son 32.000 tokens. ¿Cuánto es eso? A fines prácticos, este modelo es capaz de retener unas 24.000 palabras antes de olvidar el contexto inicial.
¿Es realmente un drama que Gemini no pueda utilizar los modelos más avanzados?
Todo depende de cómo utilizases Gemini antes del 9 de octubre. El nuevo modelo 3.5 Flash-Lite es rápido para traducir, responder cuestiones sencillas y responderte preguntas sin demasiado contexto. Es un modelo más que capaz para el día a día, pero la diferencia con los anteriores modelos es grande cuando utilizas otras características.
Si sueles enviar a Gemini muchos documentos PDF, preguntas que necesitan analizar grandes volúmenes de datos o investigaciones más avanzadas, entonces sí es posible que notes una diferencia notable en las respuestas. No solo en el tiempo que puede tardar en contestarte, sino en la calidad de la respuesta.
Así que, a partir de ahora, si quieres obtener la misma calidad que antes en tus respuestas de Gemini, tendrás que valorar una suscripción a alguno de los planes de pago de AI Plus.

articles.title: Europe’s Advanced Packaging Gap: Fraunhofer, Swissbit Target the Missing Middle - EE Times
articles.text:
Europe has no shortage of semiconductor research. The harder problem often begins after the prototype works.
A company may need an advanced packaging process for a specialized product, but only at volumes of tens, hundreds, or thousands of units. That can be too much for a research organization to support indefinitely and far too little to interest a conventional high-volume outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider.
Rolf Aschenbrenner, deputy director of the Fraunhofer Institute for Reliability and Microintegration (IZM), sees that gap regularly. “Companies come to us because their volume is too low to get access to advanced packaging,” he told EE Times. “We can help with prototypes, and in some cases we can also do small-volume manufacturing.”
That doesn’t mean Fraunhofer wants to become an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider. Its role, according to Aschenbrenner, is to adapt packaging processes to customer requirements, demonstrate their viability, and ultimately hand them off to industry. “The goal is that we also transfer our processes,” he said.
The problem is what happens when no industrial manufacturer is ready to take them.
Too small for the OSATs
Aschenbrenner cited fan-out wafer-level packaging as an example. A company developing RF products might require only around 100 wafers per year. For a large packaging provider, that volume barely registers.
“If you go to a large OSAT and ask for 100 wafers per year, that’s nothing for them,” he said. “They won’t do it.”
Fraunhofer has encountered even smaller production runs. Aschenbrenner described one customer making miniature cameras for medical applications that requires only about 20 wafers annually. A single wafer can contain tens of thousands of cameras, making that small wafer count sufficient for the customer’s entire market.
“Twenty wafers per year is the full volume,” he said. “They don’t need more. But nobody else can do those 20 wafers.”
He also pointed to work for a medical technology company on detector arrays for a novel CT scanner. The application requires sensors to be placed very close together; conventional wire bonding creates gaps that can affect imaging performance, so the design uses through-silicon vias to route connections to the backside.
The customer wanted that work performed in Europe, Aschenbrenner said. But again, the volume was too low to attract a conventional packaging house. “There was no company in Europe with the technology available at that volume,” he said. “So we do it.”
For Europe, that problem is especially relevant because many of its industrial strengths lie in specialized markets rather than mass consumer electronics. “We have many small and medium-sized companies that are champions in very narrow areas,” Aschenbrenner said. “They also need access to advanced packaging, and often no one is there to help them.”
The capital requirements make it harder for those companies to solve the problem themselves. Advanced packaging is no longer a matter of buying a few relatively inexpensive wire bonders. Wafer-level packaging lines require substantial investment.
That leaves a missing industrial layer between pilot production and mass manufacturing.
The industrial answer
Swissbit provides one example of how that middle ground might work. The company develops memory and security products in Europe and increasingly uses advanced packaging to move toward system-level products combining memory, controllers, security functions, compute, and potentially AI.
According to Lars Lust, executive director of Swissbit Germany, the company’s core competency is not semiconductor manufacturing. “We integrate semiconductors,” he told EE Times. “Advanced packaging is a must-have for our products.”
Lust argued that low-volume manufacturing doesn’t necessarily have to be uneconomic. The key is to avoid building a unique process flow for every product. “If you have a standard tool chain and a common platform, you can produce low volume in the same way as higher volume,” he said. “You don’t need a new setup every time.”
Swissbit’s own production illustrates the model. The company has roughly 3,500 products in its catalog and around 150 active products moving through production in a typical month. Some products may run in quantities of only hundreds, while others reach thousands or tens of thousands, but they can share equipment, process steps, and tooling.
“We scale over the platform,” Lust said. “If you have a good platform for low-volume products, you can produce them on the same line as volume products.” That changes the economics of the “missing middle.” The challenge is not necessarily low volume itself, but low volume combined with a bespoke process that cannot be reused.
For Europe, that could be important. Rather than trying to replicate the enormous Asian packaging ecosystem built around highly standardized, high-volume products, European manufacturers could aggregate many specialized products onto common advanced packaging platforms.
The handoff cannot come at the end
Lust also sees room for improvement in the way Europe transfers technology from research institutes to manufacturers. He argued that industry should become involved around technology-readiness levels five or six, once early demonstrators have shown that a process works, rather than waiting until researchers have pushed the technology close to production.
“The RTO should not develop everything to TRL seven or eight and then hand it over,” he said. “Industry needs to come in earlier, when the first demonstrators are there, to define applications, requirements, and scalability.” That makes the transition less like a relay race and more like an overlap between research and manufacturing.
Aschenbrenner described Fraunhofer’s current role in similar terms. Its packaging equipment is deliberately close to what’s used in industry, making it easier either to transfer processes or to manufacture initial volumes while an industrial route is established.
But he was clear that Fraunhofer should not remain the manufacturer indefinitely. “We can fill a gap,” he said. “But manufacturing should be industrialized. We are very interested in transferring our knowledge and processes so industry can do it.”
Build around Europe’s actual strengths
Both Aschenbrenner and Lust argued that Europe should be selective about what kind of packaging capacity it tries to build.
Aschenbrenner pointed to automotive and industrial markets, where Europe already has strong customers and specialized requirements. “We have to look at the real applications in Europe,” he said. “Do we really need to copy what is being done for extreme high-performance computing? I don’t think so. We should focus on the needs we actually have here.”
Lust made a similar argument. “Me-too is not the right approach,” he said. “Traditional packaging is already established elsewhere. Europe should strengthen the things it is already good at and scale those strengths into advanced packaging.”
That means complex integration, specialized industrial products, flexible manufacturing, and packaging platforms able to support many different applications rather than one enormous product family.
For Lust, Europe already has evidence that such a model can work. “In the industrial market, Europe is very strong,” he said. “We can handle complexity and variation. The key is to have your own platforms, your own ecosystem, and scale them across different applications.”
The missing piece is turning that capability into sustainable industrial infrastructure.
Fraunhofer can keep technologies alive through the dangerous interval between prototype and volume production. But if Europe wants a resilient advanced packaging supply chain, the final destination cannot be the pilot line.
It has to be industry.

articles.title: Turning the connectivity gap into a blockchain opportunity - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Unreliable and expensive internet access locks millions out of the digital economy, but as XMesh founder Benjamin Yan explains, blockchain could help equip ordinary people to act as a hyper-local connectivity provider and earn an income from their unused bandwidth.
What problem were you trying to solve when you came up with XOneFi?
I love adventure travelling and I use Starlink in remote areas. I was paying a fair amount of money for that service and I’d find that people around me also wanted to get online, but there was no way to share the connection and there was no way to charge people who want to use my internet, so that’s when I began thinking about a usage-based solution for sharing the internet.
How does XOneFi work?
Anyone with an internet connection can become a provider. They purchase their upstream connection, and then install an XOneFi-enabled router, set their rate and they are good to go.
Nearby customers can use their phones or computers to discover the network, purchase internet access by time or data usage, and the XOneFi firmware meters the session and automatically sends the payment from the customer to the provider.
Where does blockchain come in, and why is it essential?
The blockchain is valuable because we are facing an open network with many independent providers and customers who don’t know the infrastructure owners.
Blockchain is fully transparent, offers tamper-resistant usage accounting – so that providers and customers cannot cheat– and automated micro payments. If a customer is paying $4 a month, maybe every hour you are only paying several cents, which is a very small amount of money, and without blockchain we really cannot transact that.
How are prices set so they work for providers and customers?
We provide a default rate, but providers can adjust it based on their own payment for the internet. When the customer connects they see how much they need to pay and, if they agree, they click, and the transaction starts.
How does the connectivity gap you are bridging affect children and schools?
School administrators tell us connectivity issues are really a big problem: their internet is not reliable, the data rate is very low. Sometimes they cannot sustain a Zoom call or YouTube video, and you can’t even talk about coding or using AI. It is really a missed opportunity for the kids to get a better education, to get the opportunities that they want.
Why did you choose Nigeria to test XOneFi?
Nigeria is a growing economy with big cities and a large population of young people looking for opportunities. They want to utilise the digital economy to improve their living standards.
What is happening on the ground now?
We are running a pilot project at two Nigerian schools and planning to expand to community centres and business centres. Our chief financial officer and our director – both are women – are really moving things forward and identifying and solving challenges on the ground.
Looking ahead, what is your vision for connectivity and local digital economies?
The ultimate vision is that a child or any other user does not need to know where the connection comes from – whether it’s fibre, cellular, satellite or any other technology – but will be able to find an affordable network that they can use. For providers, they can operate their own access points, earn income and reinvest in the hardware to get a better connection. So, everyone has the opportunity to become a mini, hyper-local provider of connectivity, and everyone can get affordable and reliable internet.

articles.title: Control Resonant composer says Dylan is an 'involuntary hero' who 'provided a lot of writing material' for the soundtrack — 'His path from a blank, soulless, and partially mindless being into something willing to sacrifice himself to find his sister is worth a dozen stories alone'
articles.text:
Control Resonant composer used Dylan's 'involuntary hero' backstory and his 'dysfunctional' relationship with Hedron to inform him of the soundtrack, which offered 'a whole dimension' for the score
"Larger than life," and "gut-wrenching" were some terms the composer used when approaching Dylan
- Control Resonant composer Petri Alanko tells TechRadar Gaming how he approached the game's musical aesthetic
- He says "human vocals" and the "significant" relationship between Dylan and Hedron helped inform his writing
- Alanko says Dylan being an "involuntary hero" provided "a lot of writing material"
Control Resonant composer Petri Alanko has shared how the game's new setting and the relationship between protagonist Dylan and antagonist Hedron informed the soundtrack.
"Usually, it’s the scenery that hits best, and how the main character is related to the scenery, be that a connection or a disconnection," Alanko told TechRadar Gaming in an interview when asked about his design process. "It’s interesting, as there also are no rules whatsoever; again it’s a classic case of 'Hey, I think THAT would make you think this…'
"It’s basically psychological to an extent, really. Trying to play with your brain first, and later on with the player’s brain."
Alanko said "human vocals" was a term he and Remedy identified as part of the Resonant's core music aesthetic, "offering a whole dimension, practically." In addition, the "significant" relationship between Dylan and Hedron, a powerful Resonant entity, was another angle that "drove this first phase onwards."
"The path of the main character [Dylan] and the main antagonist’s [Hedron] relationship with him, it’s indeed a very conflicted pairing," he said. "Dysfunctional, one would say, but that provided a very human layer to the original setting.
"Dylan, being one might call 'an involuntary hero', or 'anti-hero' even, provided a lot of writing material; his path from a blank, soulless and partially mindless being into something willing to sacrifice himself just to find his sister is worth a dozen stories alone, not to mention the fact that their relationship hasn’t been exactly peaceful."
The composer went on to say that terms like "rough," "larger than life," "gut-wrenching," "human, yet inhuman," and "organic" were all on his Post-It notes at the beginning of development, concerning how he approached Dylan.

On the other hand, for Hedron, he had "strangely familiar yet frightening," "clangorous," "structured and sequenced," "mathematical and procedural" as his terms.
"And when I mention 'procedural', I mean the appearance," Alanko added. "It’s almost as if Hedron communicated with circular shapes, hence the term."
