articles.title: The X Subscription bundles Cursor with Grok and X Premium. But Claude now costs extra.
articles.text:
The X Subscription bundles Cursor with Grok and X Premium. But Claude now costs extra.
Elon Musk’s mission to unify his sprawling tech empire continues apace, with the news that X, Grok, and Cursor are being bundled together as a single plan dubbed The X Subscription.
Taking to X late on Monday, SpaceXAI announced the new pricing structure. It has five tiers, from free up to $200 per month, with the cheapest paid option costing $8. Paid tiers share a single pool of Grok-model usage across eligible products, and existing Cursor subscribers can keep their current plans — for now, at least.
However, arguably the bigger news for developers is the change to how Cursor charges for AI models. While the new subscriptions offer more included coding usage with Grok, customers who prefer competing models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI will face additional charges.
Musk’s businesses come together
To rewind a little, Musk’s efforts to consolidate his businesses have been several years in the making. He acquired Twitter for $44 billion in October 2022, rebranding the social network as X the following July. That same month, he founded xAI, an OpenAI rival that unveiled its Grok chatbot later that year before making it available directly through X. In March 2025, the corporate structure changed again when xAI formally acquired X.
The consolidation continued back in February, when SpaceX acquired xAI, bringing Grok and X into the rocket company’s portfolio. Meanwhile, SpaceX agreed to buy AI coding company Cursor in a deal reportedly valued at $60 billion, which closed in mid-August. That same month, SpaceX launched Grok Bot, an autonomous AI assistant that can carry out tasks across third-party apps.
Some of these products were already bundled. X Premium has long included Grok, for example, and Cursor plans have included Grok Bot since August. But the X Subscription is the first plan to cover Cursor, Grok, Grok Bot, and X Premium together, with a single shared usage pool.
As an aside, SpaceXAI is in the midst of changing its name to SpaceXSI after Musk confirmed in early October that he would be following President Trump’s directive to use “super intelligence” (SI) in place of artificial intelligence (AI) — a move that is already reflected in its social media branding.
What the X Subscription means for Cursor users
The five tiers differ in the amount of AI usage they include, as well as which features customers can access. The free option offers limited use of Grok and Cursor’s coding agents, while the $8 Plus plan increases those allowances and adds X benefits, including a verification checkmark, creator tools, and fewer advertisements.
The $30 Premium tier is where the offering expands more substantially, adding access to Grok Bot, more advanced X features, and four times the AI usage included with Plus. The $100 Super plan increases that allowance to 15 times the Plus allocation, while the $200 Ultra tier raises it to 50 times. SpaceXAI says Premium combines benefits that previously cost $90 per month when purchased separately through SuperGrok, Cursor Pro, and X Premium+.
It’s also worth noting here that previously, its $20 Pro plan included cloud agents and Origin, the company’s GitHub alternative launched in August. Under The X Subscription, both features require at least the $30 Premium tier, meaning developers switching from the old Pro plan would have to pay an additional $10 per month to retain access to them.
For developers more broadly, there’s a pretty important distinction in how these various allowances work. Subscriptions come with a weekly allocation for using Grok models, which customers can draw on across Cursor, the Grok apps, and X. Grok Bot also consumes that allowance on eligible plans. So someone using Grok heavily for other activities could find themselves with less included usage available for coding. SpaceXAI, though, claims the new plans provide at least twice as much coding usage with its own models as comparable older Cursor subscriptions.
Third-party models now cost extra on Cursor
The economics of all this change considerably for developers who prefer to use third-party models from the frontier labs.
Previously, Cursor’s $20-per-month Pro plan included $20 worth of usage on third-party models such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT and Google’s Gemini, calculated at their respective API prices. Cursor also provided additional usage beyond that allowance. Its $60 Pro+ and $200 Ultra plans included $70 and $400 worth of API-priced model usage respectively, before accounting for any additional allowances.
“The economics of all this change considerably for developers who prefer to use third-party models from the frontier labs.”
Under The X Subscription, access to third-party models starts with the $30 Premium tier, but the subscription fee no longer covers any of their usage. Instead, developers are charged at the models’ standard API rates from their very first request, with payments handled through prepaid credits. This applies even to customers paying $100 or $200 per month for the higher tiers.
To put that into perspective, a developer who previously paid $20 for Cursor Pro and consumed $20 worth of Claude usage could have had their entire bill covered by their subscription. Under the new Premium plan, that same usage would bring their monthly spending to $50 — comprising the $30 subscription and $20 in additional model charges.
“If most of your usage is on third-party models, the new plans might cost you more, so check your usage before switching.”
In a post on X explaining the changes, Matt Palmer, who works in developer experience at SpaceXAI, acknowledges that existing Cursor subscriptions effectively subsidize the use of competing AI models, allowing customers to access them at rates below what the providers charge directly.
“If most of your usage is on third-party models, the new plans might cost you more, so check your usage before switching,” Palmer writes. “That’s one of the main reasons these plans are opt-in.”
There are changes for businesses, too. Team subscriptions now start at $30 per user per month, down from the previous $40 entry-level Cursor Teams plan, with higher tiers available at $100 and $200. The company claims that its revised team offering provides three times more coding usage than its predecessor, alongside administrative features such as single sign-on, centralized billing and usage analytics.
Existing Cursor subscribers can continue with their current plans and included third-party model allowances for now. However, the announcement sparked a flurry of questions on Cursor’s community forum, particularly from existing Pro, Pro+ and Ultra subscribers trying to understand how the new plans compare with their current subscriptions. Some questioned whether switching would leave them paying more for the same usage, while others wanted to know whether they could simply stick with their existing plans indefinitely.
Responding to these concerns on Tuesday, Colin Mueller, a technical support engineer who joined SpaceXAI from Cursor in August, indicates that existing customers could stay put for the time being, though a mandatory transition may eventually be on the cards.
“Users who don’t choose to migrate will, sometime in the future, be migrated with advance notice.”
“Nothing happens to your Pro plan automatically,” Mueller writes. “You can keep it at the same price with the same features for now. Users who don’t choose to migrate will, sometime in the future, be migrated with advance notice.”
That would suggest a move to the new subscriptions is inevitable. But in a separate response to another user discussing the existing Ultra plan, Mueller is more cautious about what the company may or may not do.
“On how long the current plan lasts: it isn’t going away today, and there’s no timeline for moving remaining customers,” Mueller adds. “If that changes, you’ll get advance notice first.”
However, some developers are questioning what the changes mean for Cursor’s longstanding appeal as a platform that lets users choose between different AI models. One self-described longtime Ultra subscriber, posting under the username coco_max, argues that the new pricing risks alienating the developers who helped establish Cursor’s reputation, particularly those who rely heavily on Claude and GPT.
“Cursor earned its place next to Codex and Claude Code not because of its own model, but because it was ‘one editor where you can use the best models,’” the user writes. “A lot of us have all three installed, and Cursor is the one that stays open all day, precisely because it isn’t locked to any single vendor. The new plans change that.”
“Cursor earned its place next to Codex and Claude Code not because of its own model, but because it was ‘one editor where you can use the best models.’”
A battle over AI models and subscriptions
SpaceXAI’s pricing shake-up comes as Cursor is already losing access to one of its most popular model providers. In August, OpenAI announced plans to withdraw direct access to its models through Cursor, with a proposed cutoff date of November 12, citing concerns about Elon Musk’s track record on compliance with its terms of service.
Anthropic, for its part, pledged to continue supporting Claude in Cursor, despite competing directly with Grok. The relationship is complicated further by Anthropic’s multibillion-dollar agreement to purchase computing capacity from SpaceX.
There’s also a certain irony in the new pricing structure. Just last week, Musk confirmed that Grok Bot would use whichever AI model was best suited to a particular task, explicitly naming Anthropic’s Claude among the options. Yet developers who want to use Claude directly through Cursor now face additional charges under the new subscriptions.
Meanwhile, OpenAI is pursuing its own subscription strategy. At its DevDay conference in September, the company expanded its Sign in with ChatGPT offering, allowing paying subscribers to use their existing AI allowances inside third-party developer tools such as Devin, Amp and Warp. The move essentially gives OpenAI another way to keep developers using its models across competing products, without requiring separate API payments for eligible usage.
Ultimately, the new X Subscription raises questions about Cursor’s future as a model-agnostic coding platform. SpaceX clearly wants to encourage greater adoption of Grok, and its new pricing provides a financial incentive to do so. But with developers accustomed to choosing between Claude, GPT and other models, it remains to be seen whether the new offering will persuade them to embrace Grok — or prompt some to look elsewhere.

articles.title: So skalierst du dein E-Commerce-Business durch smarte Daten-Logistik
articles.text:
So skalierst du dein E-Commerce-Business durch smarte Daten-Logistik
Viele traditionelle Third-Party-Logistics-Anbieter (3PL) arbeiten jedoch nach wie vor mit starren Standardsystemen, die durch intransparente Dashboards und teure Zusatzlizenzen für jede neue Funktion limitiert werden. Das Ergebnis für Händler sind fehlende Echtzeit-Einblicke in den Warenfluss und steigende Kosten bei jedem Wachstumsschritt.
Vertikalisierung: Logistik trifft auf Software-Entwicklung
Einige Akteure am Markt brechen mit diesem traditionellen Ansatz, indem sie Software und Logistik-Infrastruktur vollständig vertikalisieren. Der Fulfillment-Dienstleister Monta agiert hier primär als Tech-Unternehmen, das seine Systeme seit 1999 komplett in-house entwickelt. Durch standardisierte Schnittstellen zu allen gängigen ERP- und Shopsystemen sowie eine offene API für individuelle Architekturen ermöglicht Monta eine Live-Schaltung in der Regel innerhalb von ein bis drei Wochen.
Real-Time-Daten statt Kontrollverlust
Herkömmliche Warehouse-Management-Systeme (WMS) bilden Daten häufig erst zeitversetzt ab. Ein proaktiver Steuerungsansatz setzt früher an: Das System von Monta bildet Daten nicht nur passiv ab, sondern ermöglicht das direkte Eingreifen in laufende Prozesse. Erkennt die Software beispielsweise eine fehlerhafte Lieferadresse, wird der betroffene Auftrag automatisch gestoppt. Die Korrektur kann direkt im Dashboard vorgenommen werden, sodass das Paket fehlerfrei das Lager verlässt – was unvorhergesehene Retourenkosten minimiert und die Marge schützt.
Die technologische Differenzierung vom klassischen Markt erfolgt dabei über drei zentrale Säulen:
Monta ist der Fulfillment-Partner für E-Commerce-Unternehmen, die ihr Backend technologisch skalieren wollen. Komplett in-house entwickelte IT, kombiniert mit DHL-Infrastruktur – von der offenen API bis zur paneuropäischen Cross-Border-Logistik.
- Das Labor-Prinzip: IT-Entwickler arbeiten räumlich direkt verzahnt mit den Logistikteams im Lager. Jede neue Funktion und jede API-Kopplung wird sofort im operativen Betrieb getestet. Bottlenecks oder Systembrüche werden dadurch ohne Verzögerung identifiziert und direkt im Code angepasst.
- All-in-One-Software statt Lizenz-Flickenteppich: Viele Wettbewerber arbeiten mit modularen Systemen, die ständige Upgrades erfordern. Monta bietet stattdessen eine extrem umfangreiche Standardsoftware, für die Händler keine teuren Zusatzlizenzen benötigen. Smarte Features wie ein Einkaufsberater-Tool, ein integriertes Retourenmodul und detaillierte Bestandsreportings sind bereits vollumfänglich enthalten.
- Großes Carrier-Netzwerk bei voller Wahlfreiheit: Ohne feste Bindung an einen einzelnen Versanddienstleister bietet Monta Zugriff auf ein breites Netzwerk an Carriern. Dabei bevormundet das System den Händler nicht durch automatische Zuweisungen: Der Shop-Betreiber entscheidet selbst, mit wem er versendet – oder er bietet gleich mehrere Carrier an und überlässt seinen Endkunden im Checkout die freie Wahl des bevorzugten Paketdienstes.
Fulfillment entwickelt sich damit vom reinen operativen Kostenfaktor zum strategischen Wachstumsmotor, der E-Commerce-Unternehmen im Backend den Rücken freihält.
Bereit für ein Fulfillment-Setup, das mit deinen Tech-Ambitionen mitwächst? Lerne jetzt die datengetriebene Logistik-Infrastruktur von Monta kennen.
Unverbindliches Angebot anfordern

articles.title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements
Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization.
In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants.
Why automate grant activation
With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them.
Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms.
Solution overview
The sample repository provides two paths:
- Path 1 – The lightweight path is a standalone script that lists received licenses and prints a dry-run plan. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id. It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account.
- Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account.
Choose one of the following implementation paths. Use Path 1 for one-time activation without CDK. Use Path 2 for ongoing event-driven automation.
Path 1: Lightweight script (one-time activation)
Use this path when you need one-time activation without deploying CDK. The script lists every received license in the management account, so use the dry run as your review gate before applying changes.
- Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory.
- Run the lightweight script in dry-run mode.
- Review every listed license and confirm that the ISV Partner issuer and account scope match the private offer you expect.
- Apply the reviewed plan from the same AWS Organizations management account.
- After the grant is active, validate the billing path before you rely on the private offer in production. Billing data in AWS Cost Explorer can lag, so use it to compare the effective charge for covered Amazon Bedrock usage after charges appear. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and confirm the expected discount path.
Path 2: CDK automation (ongoing activation)
Use this path when you want new private pricing agreements handled automatically. The CDK stack listens for eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events, checks your seller allowlist, creates distributed grants, and retries activation when License Manager needs more time. The solution contains three components:
- Amazon EventBridge rule: The stack listens for AWS Marketplace agreement events on the default event bus in us-east-1. The rule matches source aws.agreement-marketplace and detail type Purchase Agreement Created - Acceptor, then invokes the AWS Lambda function.
- AWS Lambda function: The function receives the AWS Marketplace agreement event, verifies the seller allow-list, discovers the license, creates the distributed grant, and requests activation with CreateGrantVersion(Status=ACTIVE). The function logs the outcome to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for auditability.
- AWS License Manager entitlements: The grant targets your organization, selected organizational units (OUs), or specific accounts. Negotiated pricing applies only after the grant is activated and reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED.
The following diagram shows the event-driven flow.
Key benefits of this approach:
- Faster time to negotiated pricing. The negotiated rate applies after the distributed grant reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED, without waiting for a manual console check.
- Consistent handling across accounts. The same AWS Lambda function and Amazon EventBridge rule pattern can be deployed for each organization that receives third-party model grants, so activation logic doesn’t vary by operator.
- Built-in audit trail. Every activation attempt or skip decision is logged to CloudWatch Logs, giving you a record of when each grant was activated, deferred, or ignored.
Prerequisites
Before you deploy this path, confirm these prerequisites:
- Use the AWS Organizations management account in us-east-1 with Python 3.12+, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and AWS CDK v2 configured.
- Confirm that AWS Organizations uses all features and that the private offer is for a License Manager-backed Bedrock model. Software as a service (SaaS) products are out of scope for this automation.
Implementation steps
- Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory.
- Verify or enable organization prerequisites. 
         
         Review any APPLY or MANUAL items before making changes. The bootstrap script can enable License Manager organization integration, License Manager trusted access, AWS Marketplace license-management trusted access, and required service-linked roles.
- Configure deployment inputs. 
         
         Review config/sellers.json. Configure your Organization ID, seller allow-list, notifications, and optional grant targets. By default, grants target the full organization. Use grantTargets to scope grants to selected OUs or AWS accounts.
- Deploy the CDK stack.
- Seed the Amazon DynamoDB seller allow-list from config/sellers.json. Treat the seller allow-list as a security boundary. Verify each seller account ID against your accepted AWS Marketplace private offer or received License Manager license before seeding the table. Don’t add broad or unverified seller entries, because matching sellers can trigger grant creation and activation across your configured grant targets. After deployment and seller seeding, the stack is ready to process eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events. Grant creation and activation happen only for verified sellers in the allowlist, and activation may be deferred until License Manager finishes processing the grant workflow.
- Validate the deployed automation.
- Verify grant activation after an eligible AWS Marketplace agreement event. 
         
         Activation and billing visibility can take hours or days. After the event-driven workflow accepts and activates the grants, confirm the grant state in AWS License Manager, then validate covered Amazon Bedrock usage in AWS Cost Explorer after billing data appears. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and target linked account.
Clean up
If you deployed this stack for testing, remove it to avoid the small ongoing Lambda and Amazon EventBridge charges:
Voice of customer
        “As an AI Care Partner supporting millions of clinician consults every week, Heidi Health relies on third-party foundation models at real scale. Private pricing on AWS Marketplace gives us a cost-effective and efficient way to manage that growth: we can granularly attribute usage and pricing across AWS accounts and organizational units, and automate grant management as we adopt new models. That lets our platform team scale cost governance without scaling manual work.”
— Marcus Lau, Head of Platform Engineering, Heidi Health
Conclusion
This post showed two ways to activate managed entitlements for Amazon Bedrock private pricing offers. Use the lightweight script for one-time activation of trusted received licenses, or deploy the CDK automation when you need ongoing event-driven processing for new AWS Marketplace agreements. Both approaches reduce manual effort and help negotiated pricing apply after distributed grants are activated.
To get started, try the code sample in your AWS management account to automate model subscriptions.

articles.title: Circle Gas has $67 million in carbon credits awaiting delivery
articles.text:
Circle Gas, the UK parent of Kenyan pay-as-you-cook liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplier M-Gas, reported $67 million in contracted carbon credits awaiting delivery and $57 million in cash prepayments in 2025, according to its financial statements.
The company’s dependence on carbon-credit revenue exposes the financial risks facing Kenya’s clean-cooking businesses, where government authorisation can determine whether contracted credits deliver their expected value.
The company’s accounts, filed in September, show the financial stakes. Circle Gas lost $39.3 million in 2025, held $1.1 million in cash at year-end and reported net liabilities of $156.7 million. It needs about $28 million in new funding to finance its growth plans.
Carbon credits are central to the economics of clean cooking businesses such as M-Gas. The company supplies LPG in small, affordable amounts with smart meters so households can pay as they cook. Revenue from the resulting emissions reductions can help support that model. Koko Networks, another Kenyan clean-cooking company, entered administration after the government declined to authorise the carbon-credit sales on which its business depended.
Circle Gas’s annual report says it received a “Letter of Acceptance” confirming that its carbon-credit projects met eligibility criteria and could proceed to apply for a “Letter of Authorisation.”
M-Gas announced in January 2026 that its clean-cooking carbon project had received a Letter of Approval. The report does not clarify whether this is the same document it calls a Letter of Acceptance.
Kenya’s carbon-market rules distinguish project approval from authorisation to transfer credits internationally. Under the relevant framework, the final authorisation requires government approval and determines whether specified emissions reductions can be transferred abroad.
Circle Gas did not respond to a request for comment.
The value of carbon credits
Circle Gas reported $67 million in contracted carbon credits yet to be delivered as of the end of 2025, and $57 million in cash already received as prepayments against carbon-credit contracts. The first figure represents credits awaiting delivery, while the second is money buyers have already paid.
The accounts do not disclose how much of the contracted portfolio depends on the outstanding authorisation or how much of the prepayments remains available.
Circle Gas says authorised credits can command significantly higher prices than credits sold in advance. It has not disclosed the expected premium. The company also excludes the higher value from its financial projections, leaving the potential upside outside its current funding assumptions.
Circle Gas grew revenue to $40.8 million in 2025 from $36.1 million, but remained loss-making, with a $39.3 million loss after tax. Its cash reserves fell to $1.1 million, while net liabilities climbed to $156.7 million from $116.5 million.
The company says it needs about $28 million to fund its 2026 growth plans. Without additional funding, it expects to limit investment and remain stagnant.
“At the date of approval of these financial statements, the additional third-party funding of approximately US$28.0m necessary to finance continued growth funding for the base case in 2026 is yet to be fully secured, and there is no certainty that funding will be available to the Group (Circle Gas),” the statement said.
The losses and funding needs cannot be attributed solely to the outstanding authorisation. But the delay leaves a potentially more lucrative source of carbon revenue uncertain as Circle Gas seeks new capital.
Koko’s carbon debt
Koko Networks built a business selling subsidised bioethanol stoves and fuel to low-income households, relying on carbon-credit sales to cover part of its operating costs. When the Kenyan government declined to authorise those sales, the company lost access to a revenue stream it needed to sustain the business.
Koko shut down in January 2026, laying off more than 700 employees. Its Kenyan and UK entities entered administration in February. The administrators now face the task of recovering money owed to creditors, with the carbon credits held by its UK arm a central asset. Without a sale, FirstRand Bank is owed $60 million, while other unsecured creditors are owed about $171 million.
Koko’s collapse shows how a clean-cooking business can accumulate substantial debts when it cannot sell the carbon credits expected to fund its operations.
The government rejected Koko’s application in early February 2026, with Trade Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui saying the volume of credits sought could have exhausted Kenya’s allocation for international transfers, leaving other projects in agriculture and manufacturing with little room to sell their credits abroad.
Unlike Koko Networks, Circle Gas has not had its authorisation request rejected. M-Gas announced that its project had received a Letter of Approval. However, Circle Gas’s accounts indicate it is still seeking a Letter of Authorisation and do not disclose how much of its contracted carbon credits depends on it.
Koko is the clearest warning of what is at stake: carbon credits may be recorded as assets, contracted to buyers and used to secure financing, but they cannot generate the expected cash if the company cannot sell them.
Kenya’s carbon-credit rules give the government control over which emissions reductions can be sold abroad, leaving companies exposed to decisions that can affect their revenues and debts.
Circle Gas secured earlier approval for its project but is still seeking authorisation, leaving the value and delivery of some contracted credits uncertain.

articles.title: Recharge en 5 minutes et 653 km d’autonomie : le BYD Atto 8 arrive officiellement en France
articles.text:
La recharge en 5 minutes devient réalité en France avec BYD qui commercialise chez nous son premier modèle équipé de la technologie Flash Charging. Remplaçant pressenti du vieillissant Tang, l’Atto 8 est encore plus imposant en pointant à 5,04 mètres de long. Il devient ainsi le nouveau porte-drapeau de la marque en Europe. En plus d’être ultra rapide à recharger, le chinois propose dans son portefeuille des technologies de premier plan.
En version de base Design propulsion avec 462 ch et 365 Nm de couple, sa grande batterie de 115 kWh lui permet ainsi de proposer une autonomie de 653 km sur le cycle WLTP. Même si cela ne constitue aucun record, c’est de bon goût pour tenir correctement la distance. Pour faire fondre le chrono, on se rabattra plutôt sur la version Excellence intégrale avec deux électromoteurs produisant en cumulé 775 ch et 775 Nm de couple.
1 500 kW de puissance : la recharge la plus rapide chez BYD arrive en France
Suffisant pour effacer le 0 à 100 km/h en 4,6 secondes. L’autonomie est quant à elle réduite à 602 km, rançon d’un appétit supérieur. Dans les deux cas, le Flash Charging casse la barque avec une puissance de recharge pouvant atteindre les 1 500 kW en courant continu DC. De quoi passer de 10 à 70 % de batterie en 5 minutes et de 10 à 97 % en seulement 9 minutes. Et pour information, 12 minutes seront nécessaires pour faire le 20 à 97 % par -30°C.
Impressionnant, car en France, cette technologie était jusqu’alors réservée à l’exclusive Denza Z9GT. Le seul hic est de trouver une borne compatible : BYD prévoit l’installation de 3 000 points de charge en Europe d’ici fin 2027. Patience car il n’y en a encore aucun en France. Il faudra donc se rabattre en attendant sur des bornes 600 kW qui suffiront déjà à écourter l’attente par rapport aux rivaux.
Un habitacle 7 places digne d’un salon avec réfrigérateur intégré
À bord, c’est l’espace qui prime pour les 7 passagers. Et la qualité, aussi : la marque évoque « des matériaux doux au toucher, notamment du cuir suédé, sur les principales surfaces ». Côté numérique, c’est plutôt classique avec une instrumentation de 10,25 pouces secondée par un affichage tête haute de 26 pouces. Un écran central de 15,6 pouces intégrant les services Google est aussi de la partie.
Les sièges avant et latéraux du second rang sont chauffants, massants et ventilés. La climatisation trizone arrive en série sur toutes les versions. Ajoutons que sur les modèles Design RWD et Excellence AWD se drapent de cuir véritable. L’engin inclut aussi une sonorisation à 21 haut-parleurs et un réfrigérateur avant. Les prix du BYD Atto 8 n’ont pas encore été communiqués.

articles.title: Apple's new smart home lineup includes a smart lock, thermostat, and video doorbells | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple is getting serious about the smart home space. The company on Tuesday showed off its new Apple Home Collection, which includes a new smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor, and a range of security cameras.
The new devices are designed to work with HomeView, the company’s new smart home hub which can be used to control connected accessories and interact with Apple’s software.
This new range of smart home accessories could help Apple compete better with Amazon Ring and Google Nest, two established players in connected home security. The products will become available in December.
Apple says the devices were built in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — an interesting move for the company, which has long sought to build and support every smart home accessory itself.
The smart lock, priced at $349.95, stands out for its support for ultra-wideband (UWB), a wireless technology that enables more precise proximity detection than traditional Bluetooth. This could allow the lock to recognize when an authorized user approaches and automatically unlock the door, reducing the need to pull out a phone or reach for a physical key.
The $249.95 wired video doorbell, meanwhile, will let homeowners see who’s outside, monitor visitors, and receive notifications when someone approaches their property. When someone rings it, a chime will sound through Apple devices like HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Users will also be notified on their iPhone or iPad.
As for the temperature sensor, it can provide insight into conditions in individual rooms, helping users identify temperature differences between areas and make adjustments.
For security, Apple is also introducing indoor and outdoor cameras, as well as a floodlight camera ($399.95) that combines exterior lighting with video monitoring. The camera lineup includes features such as live viewing, motion detection, intelligent alerts, and video storage.

articles.title: La emotiva despedida de Bryan Cranston a RJ Mitte, su hijo en 'Breaking Bad': "Le conocí con solo 14 años"
articles.text:
El actor Bryan Cranston, protagonista de Breaking Bad, no ha tardado en dedicarle una emotiva despedida a RJ Mitte, quien en la ficción interpretó a su hijo Walter Jr. Mitte ha fallecido este lunes 12 de octubre a causa de suicidio a los 34 años de edad. Una terrible noticia que ha impactado con especial fuerza entre los fans de la serie, una de las más importantes y reconocidas de todos los tiempos.
"Estoy profundamente abatido mientras escribo esto. RJ Mitte, mi querido hijo en Breaking Bad, ha fallecido", comienza Bryan Cranston su despeddia publicada en Instagram junto a una fotografía de ambos sonrientes. "Lo conocí cuando solo tenía 14 años, al ser elegido para interpretar a Walter White Jr., un papel que desempeñó con mucha alegría y entusiasmo", prosigue.
"Nació con parálisis cerebral, pero nunca —jamás— permitió que ese reto fuera una excusa para nada. Afrontó el exigente calendario de rodaje con gran determinación. Siempre escuchaba los consejos que le daban sus padres en la serie (Anna Gunn y yo). Aunque, como buen adolescente, a veces los ignoraba con picardía para aprender por las malas… Era una de las estrellas de una serie de éxito, pero seguía siendo un niño", continúa el escrito.
"Ese chico era bastante inexperto cuando empezamos a rodar el episodio piloto en febrero de 2007. Pero poco a poco le vimos convertirse en un actor realmente excelente. Aprovechó su experiencia en la serie para convertirse en un firme defensor de los intérpretes con discapacidad y ser el director de una organización filantrópica dedicada a ayudar a la comunidad de personas con discapacidad", celebra Bryan Cranston a su vez el legado que deja RJ Mitte.
"Toda esa promesa y ese potencial suponen ahora una gran pérdida. Es especialmente devastador saber que se quitó la vida. ¿Por qué? Hace solo unas semanas nos estábamos enviando mensajes de texto, intentando concretar cuándo podríamos quedar para comer. No sé si esa comida habría cambiado su futuro… Pero sí sé que le quería y que disfruté muchísimo de su compañía a lo largo de todos esos años en la serie, y también después de que se apagaran los focos de Breaking Bad… Te echaré de menos, hijo", sentencia. La despedida de Bryan Cranston a RJ Mitte concluye incitando a pedir ayuda a todos aquellos que se estén planteando el suicidio: "Hay esperanza".
Muere RJ Mitte, actor de Breaking Bad
"Con profunda tristeza comunicamos el trágico fallecimiento del querido actor, filántropo y apasionado defensor de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad RJ Mitte", anunciaban sus representantes en un comunicado remitido a la prensa. Con esas palabras se daba a conocer la triste noticia de su muerte.
El actor se convirtió en parte fundamental del reparto de Breaking Bad. Y, a partir de aquella irrupción, consiguió labrarse una carrera en la industria. Entre sus papeles destacan películas como Triumph (2021) junto a Terrance Howard o Love Me Dead (2024) junto a Dove Cameron. También las series Cambiadas al nacer (2014) y Los guardianes de la justicia (2022).

articles.title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
articles.text:
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
The Good
- I don’t feel like a creep wearing these
- Long battery life
- Lightweight
- Stylish
- Good for open-ear audio
The Bad
- Expensive for what they are
- Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives.
Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge
Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters.
If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu.
The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including:
Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.

articles.title: Enterprise IT infrastructure isn’t built for AI inference
articles.text:
Enterprise IT infrastructure isn’t built for AI inference
AI inference requires fundamentally new, distributed enterprise infrastructure
As global AI investment continues to climb — it surpassed $300 billion in 2025, according to IDC — enterprise IT remains primarily focused on supporting the development of training models, with architecture such as large GPU clusters and high-density compute taking center stage.
But now AI inference is becoming the dominant workload, and the architecture that supports models in production, at scale, and to real users and systems has quickly become the future of AI.
The demand for AI inference is there — according to Deloitte, inference already accounts for roughly two-thirds of compute, while McKinsey projects that it will represent between 30% and 40% of total data center demand by 2030 — however, the dedicated infrastructure is not.
CEO of Megaport.
Inference is more than a scaled-down training environment
What training and inference require from an IT point of view are very nearly polar opposites. Enterprises have facilitated AI training via data centers with massive, centralized data GPU clusters for extreme power density and specialized, high-speed interconnects meant to maximize communication within a single room.
Inference, on the other hand, is defined by a continuous flow of information and unpredictable user demand as opposed to a pre-defined workload. Once the prompts start coming in, you need geographically distributed compute that responds to and scales with real-time demands.
Because inference runs 24/7 and requires millisecond-fast responses for end users, it relies on commodity ethernet, geographically distributed edge sites, and low-latency network connections rather than isolated throughput within a single data center. The very design choices that make an enterprise data center optimal for training actively work against running inference at scale.
The cost structure is entirely different, too. Training is a one-time capital event — once a model is built, that cost is already sunk. Organizations that continue to optimize their spending for training are now being hit with the reality that they have the wrong foundation.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Inference, meanwhile, is a recurring operational cost that scales with every user, query, agent interaction, and more. It’s more like a living, breathing organism which needs to grow alongside the kind of workload that is going to determine the future of AI economics.
Agents are creating new strain on architecture
Autonomous AI agents are also compounding the infrastructure deficit. Agents don’t generate a single response and then stop; they plan, execute across multiple steps, call external tools, coordinate other agents, and pass outputs between systems. The ripple effect of an agentic workload multiplies the data traffic flowing through a network. As demand for agentic solutions grows, so will the demand for supporting infrastructure.
That growth is already consequential. Gartner predicts that by the end of 2026, 40% of enterprise applications will be integrated with task-specific agents, while IDC projects that agent usage will surge tenfold by 2027, with token and API call volumes multiplying by a factor of thousands.
Inference is also acting as a north-south traffic multiplier in ways that traditional WAN and data center network architectures aren’t designed to handle. McKinsey found that most enterprise WANs are currently unable to support AI data traffic patterns, and must evolve as AI now ranks as the second-highest infrastructure investment priority.
Burst traffic is another issue impacting architecture strain. Agentic workloads aren’t a steady flow, they’re a torrential downpour that comes and goes. A single orchestration event can trigger dozens of downstream API calls simultaneously.
This causes networks that are sized for average loads to hit capacity ceilings when agents coordinate at scale, creating the same latency and reliability problems that lead enterprise AI pilots to crash before reaching production. To thrive in the AI era, enterprises must build the proper infrastructure from the ground-up.
Inference is now the critical CPU use case
Building inference-forward architecture starts at the most basic layer: hardware. CPUs are critical for planning, scheduling, tool-call coordination, and the multi-step reasoning loops that define agentic workloads.
However, the industry’s heavy focus on the GPU market during the AI training boom has directed attention away from the necessity for CPUs in AI inference workloads. As inference workloads increase in scale, CPUs move from a supporting role to a critical one, acting as the main filter to the orchestration layer.
When viewed through a purely agentic lens, high-core-count server CPUs can handle the workload more economically than GPU accelerators. But it’s important to understand that one cannot function without the other. Inference still demands GPU function; it’s simply that CPU capacity is the bottleneck that most organizations aren’t accounting for.
Aligning compute, network, and storage is key
The reality is that AI use cases are generating abysmal ROI in most cases. Gartner’s most recent survey of infrastructure and operations leaders found that only 28% of AI use cases fully succeed and meet ROI projections, while 20% fail outright. The leading cause of failure was expecting too much, too fast from infrastructure that was incapable of supporting the workload.
How can enterprises avoid that trap? Take the time to set up their underlying infrastructure before diving headfirst into building systems they can’t support. Putting real effort into building dedicated compute, network, and storage that function as individually managed resources is the key.
Inference at production scale requires all three to work in tandem, with compute handling model execution, storage determining how quickly context, embeddings, and retrieval data are available, and network defining whether compute and storage can communicate externally with the appropriate latency
The organizations that can make this distinction early will be better prepared for the next phase of AI, and will spend less time managing infrastructure failures during production, and more time actually focusing on generating value through AI inference.

articles.title: Lightspeed lays off staff as part of “organizational changes” | BetaKit
articles.text:
Lightspeed Commerce has laid off staff and closed vacant roles at the company, impacting a total of 250 roles.
The news: Last week, multiple former Lightspeed employees across content and sales roles announced on LinkedIn that they had been laid off. When reached for comment by BetaKit, the Montréal-based e-commerce and point-of-sale company confirmed the “organizational changes” and said that 250 roles across the company were impacted, including “vacant roles that are being closed.” The company did not break down how many of those jobs were cut compared to how many roles were no longer open.
From the source: “These decisions support Lightspeed’s long-term objective of growing responsibly and profitably so we can continue to invest in our business, our products, and the customers we serve,” a Lightspeed spokesperson wrote to BetaKit in an email on Friday.
The context: Founded in 2005, Lightspeed sells point-of-sale and commerce software and hardware to restaurants, retailers, and hospitality providers. Since last year, the company has been executing a transformation plan to focus on two key markets: North American retail and European hospitality.
The company has tried to balance growth and profitability in part to raise its share price, which never regained its 2021 zero-interest-rate period high. It dropped from a peak of $159 CAD on the Toronto Stock Exchange in September 2021 to a third of its value in three months, and now hovers around $15 CAD.
Final thought: Lightspeed also made roughly 100 job cuts earlier this year, across a team of about 2,000 people, to find further efficiencies in the business, CEO Dax Dasilva told BetaKit in July. In March, the company divested a US hospitality business unit and has told The Globe and Mail that it’s open to more divestitures. A Lightspeed spokesperson said the company would share more details about its organizational changes on Nov. 5 when it reports its fiscal second-quarter earnings.

articles.title: 10 points de permis perdus en 20 minutes : j’ai testé la voiture autonome à Paris
articles.text:
La conduite 100% autonome est la promesse faite notamment par Tesla à ses clients depuis de nombreuses années. À l’occasion du Mondial de l’automobile qui se déroule à Paris du 12 au 18 octobre, la marque américaine — tout comme la chinoise Xpeng — permettent d’ailleurs aux plus curieux de tester le dispositif qu’elles aimeraient bien voir chacune homologué en France. Mais ces deux constructeurs ne sont pas les seuls sur les rangs. Il y a quelques jours, c’est Denza, l’enseigne haut de gamme du groupe BYD, qui nous a convié à parcourir les rues de Paris « sans les mains ». Du gâteau ? Pas vraiment…
La capitale française n’est pas spécialement connue pour être un cadeau fait aux automobilistes de chair et d’os. Ronds points aux règles très parisiennes, zones de travaux, rues étroites, signalisation verticale pas toujours visible ou entretenue, marquage au sol aléatoire : nombreux sont les conducteurs qui voient monter le stress au passage du panneau Paris. Qu’en sera-t-il pour le robot de conduite de Denza ?
Le CNOA — pour City Navigation On Autopilot — de Denza existe depuis déjà environ deux ans en Chine. Baptisé God’s Eye (l’œil de Dieu, rien que ça !), le système fonctionne en mode « map free », c’est-à-dire qu’il ne repose pas sur des cartes de haute définition mais utilise plutôt une batterie de capteurs (27 en tout), dont un lidar haute précision à très longue portée, des caméras ultra-haute définition, des radars à ondes millimétriques et d’autres capteurs à ultrasons connectés au cerveau unique de la machine via l’architecture Xuanji maison pour décider de ses manœuvres telles que le passage aux carrefours (conduite en ligne droite, virage à gauche, virage à droite, demi-tour, etc.), dans les giratoires, le franchissement des feux tricolores, les dépassements, l’évitement intelligent des obstacles, les changements de voie, le maintien de voie, la conduite en régulateur de vitesse, le passage d’une voie à l’autre et la priorité aux piétons et aux véhicules non motorisés.
L’ensemble est en outre connecté en 5G, par satellite et aux éventuels véhicules également connectés qui circuleraient dans la zone. Mais en premier lieu et pour faire simple, la voiture voit et perçoit son environnement puis adopte ce que son cerveau pense être la bonne stratégie à chaque étape de son évolution urbaine. Pour l’aider dans ces décisions, des milliers de kilomètres de tests sont nécessaires, durant lesquels les opérateurs apprennent à la machine les bonnes décisions au regard des règles de conduite locales.
On ne conduit pas à Paris comme à Shanghai, où tous les feux de circulation sont connectés, par exemple. Dans la capitale française, il n’est pas rare d’en trouver cachés derrière un utilitaire, une branche d’arbre, ou qui sont tout simplement défectueux. Alors qu’il s’agit déjà souvent d’un défi pour un humain, à la machine de se débrouiller avec. Enfin, la cartographie Google Maps intégrée à la voiture sert quant à elle à définir le parcours à suivre pour arriver à destination.
Une voiture immense dans les rues bondées de Paris
C’est par paire que les cobayes — nous autres journalistes, donc — sont invités à monter à bord d’une Denza Z9 GT, grande berline électrique de plus de 1150 chevaux. Ce n’est évidemment pas cette caractéristique qui fera la différence à 30 km/h maximum, vitesse autorisée à Paris et que l’auto est évidemment tenue de respecter. En revanche, son encombrement — 5,18 mètres de long, 2 de large — constitue un handicap sérieux pour se faufiler dans la circulation de ce milieu d’après-midi de fin de semaine.
Le reste de l’équipage est constitué d’un superviseur formé spécialement pour la tâche et dont le rôle est de reprendre les commandes si cela s’avère nécessaire, ainsi que — nous concernant — d’une ingénieure venue de Chine pour assurer le suivi de l’opération, prendre en note tout ce qui ne va pas et, éventuellement, remettre en route le logiciel s’il venait à défaillir.
D’ailleurs, Denza nous prévient dès le départ : pas question de proposer cette technologie au client avant au moins l’année prochaine, nous sommes réellement en phase de test et de développement. Et des bugs, certaines des autos en ont rencontré, parfois avant même de prendre leur premier départ.
Un circuit de 20 mn et quelques grosses frayeurs
Pour nous, la sortie de la place de stationnement située au pied de la concession BYD des Champs-Élysées se déroule sans difficulté, mais toujours sous l’œil inquiet du staff pléthorique chargé de sécuriser les abords, au cas où. Quelques minutes plus tôt, certaines autos ont eu plus de mal. Il faut dire que le tempérament du conducteur parisien est rarement caractérisé par la patience, et nombreux sont ceux qui veulent prendre les devants en se glissant sous le nez de la Denza, stoppant net sa procédure de départ.
Nous voici partis pour un tour d’un peu plus de 5 kilomètres dans Paris : Étoile, Trocadéro, Passy, Tour Eiffel, Iéna et retour vers la rue Pierre Charron. Premier feu, à l’angle des Champs-Élysées, nous mettons cap à droite vers la place de l’Étoile, ce fameux giratoire à 12 sorties que plus de 100 000 voitures empruntent chaque jour et qui met souvent au défi même le plus chevronné des Parisiens.
L’engagement se passe bien, la voiture prend sa place dans le flot remontant. D’abord sur la file de gauche, puis elle se décale vers la droite, plus roulante. Loin d’être fluide, la circulation ne semble pas poser de problème particulier à la Z9 GT. À l’Étoile, le parcours prévoit trois-quarts de tour, avec une sortie Avenue Kléber. L’engagement est plutôt bon, la berline chinoise se positionne sur une des files du milieu, file toute virtuelle puisque ce giratoire ne dispose d’aucun marquage au sol. Particularité : c’est l’un des seuls, sinon le seul giratoire en France à imposer la priorité à l’entrée. À allure modérée, l’auto franchit la moitié du rond-point mais, au lieu d’anticiper sa manœuvre pour s’engager tranquillement vers les voies extérieures et prendre sa sortie, attend d’être rendue à la perpendiculaire de celle-ci pour virer à 90 degrés droite.
Coup de chance, aucun automobiliste énervé n’a cherché à forcer sa priorité. À ce stade, le code de la route suggère plutôt de refaire le tour. Engagé avenue Kléber, une nouvelle épreuve attend l’œil de Dieu environ 200 mètres plus loin. Un poids lourd en livraison, hayon ouvert et feux de détresse allumés, occupe la chaussée. Nous sommes loin de l’intersection suivante et la voie opposée est dégagée.
L’auto peut doubler… mais préfère laisser mourir son freinage littéralement au cul du camion, s’interdisant toute manœuvre pour s’échapper, tous les capteurs frontaux étant aveuglés par l’obstacle. Seule solution pour l’opérateur : reprendre la main et relancer le système une fois le camion contourné. Un peu plus loin, imperturbable, elle ignore un passage protégé sur lequel un piéton est pourtant déjà engagé sur une bonne moitié de la voie opposée. Une infraction sanctionnée d’un retrait de 6 points sur le permis de conduire, sans parler de l’amende pécuniaire qui l’accompagne.
L’œil de Dieu ne voit pas le rouge
Au Trocadéro, le parcours prévoit de remonter quelques dizaines de mètres puis de bifurquer à gauche sur la rue Benjamin Franklin. Mais alors qu’elle se prépositionne plutôt correctement, la Denza préfère finalement continuer tout droit. Une situation que l’ingénieure de bord semble ne pas vouloir lui laisser gérer. Tandis que Google Maps recalcule l’itinéraire, elle demande au chauffeur de reprendre la main et de prendre la rue prévue au départ. Demi-tour, donc.
Le giratoire de la place du Costa-Rica est négocié sans problème, direction les bords de Seine, avenues du Président-Kennedy, puis de New York. Face à la Tour Eiffel, au Pont d’Iéna, la Z9 s’engage avenue des Nations-Unies et prolonge avenue d’Iéna sans difficulté. Elle attend même le bon moment et la place nécessaire pour dépasser quelques cyclistes à la peine dans la côte sans les frôler. Place d’Iéna, tout semble aller pour le mieux. La voiture salue la statue équestre de Washington et vise la sortie pour continuer sur l’avenue d’Iéna.
Nous sommes à environ 50 mètres du feu de circulation lorsque celui-ci passe à l’orange. Calé à un peu moins de 30 km/h, la Denza n’hésite pas une seconde : elle garde l’allure et, en bonne Parisienne, franchit le feu alors qu’il est au rouge vif depuis une bonne seconde. Voilà quatre points supplémentaires supprimés sur son permis, tout virtuel qu’il soit !
Le virage à droite de la rue Georges Bizet passé, la Denza continue son chemin. On ignore comment elle s’assure que personne ne va prendre la priorité de la rue de Chaillot, mais tout se passe sans encombre. À 30 km/h, elle aurait probablement eu le temps de s’arrêter en cas de trafic transversal, difficile à détecter dans les rues parisiennes sans s’avancer un peu au-delà du début de l’intersection.
Une centaine de mètres plus bas : feu rouge. Comme si elle avait voulu se faire pardonner son loupé de la place d’Iéna, la Z9 s’arrête cette fois… une bonne trentaine de mètres avant le feu ! Pas vraiment d’infraction, mais une bizarrerie de plus sur ce parcours semé d’embûches.
Nous voici avenue Pierre Iᵉʳ de Serbie avec notre point d’arrivée presque en vue. La voiture en double file n’est cette fois pas ignorée : clignotant, la Z9 l’efface, non sans avoir pris en compte l’auto qui sortait de son stationnement sur la voie opposée pile à ce moment-là.
Mais être presque arrivé ne signifie pas la fin des curiosités. Un peu plus loin, aux abords de la rue Pierre Charron, une petite file de quatre véhicules se forme au niveau d’un feu de circulation. Deux voitures, suivies par deux side-cars promène-touristes. La Denza s’en approche et… engage une manœuvre de dépassement ! In extremis, l’opérateur reprend la main, se remet dans la file et adresse un petit signe d’excuses à l’automobiliste qui se présentait en face au même moment.
Allez, encore quelques mètres avant le point de stationnement. Le chauffeur engage le mode de parking automatique puis, au niveau de la concession BYD, indique la place qu’il souhaite occuper d’un clic sur l’écran. Manque de chance, il commande un stationnement à contre-sens. La voiture, qui ne semble pas savoir qu’il est interdit de stationner à contre-sens, entame tranquillement son demi-tour, que le chauffeur avortera avant d’appuyer sur le bon bouton. Nous voici garés, ouf !
Bilan : encore du travail
Quiconque prend le volant à Paris mesure le monde qui peut séparer la conduite parisienne de celle de n’importe quelle autre ville de province. Si BYD propose déjà cette conduite autonome de niveau 2+ dans les rues des villes chinoises, elle sait qu’il lui reste encore beaucoup de travail avant de délivrer cette fonction à ces clients européens, voire français.
À vrai dire, la marche vers une conduite déléguée fiable à Paris nous paraît encore si loin pour Denza qu’il faut saluer la sorte de courage, voire de témérité, dont elle a fait preuve en proposant à quelques dizaines de journalistes plutôt exigeants d’effectuer in vivo les premiers tests français de sa technologie.
Il ne serait pas très juste de vouloir comparer le CNAO au FSD de Tesla, que la marque américaine pousse aussi fort qu’elle le peut pour obtenir son homologation. Si les démos européennes de Tesla semblent se passer plutôt bien malgré quelques couacs notables (dépassement de vitesse maximum autorisée en ville, par exemple), il faut se rappeler que la marque a engrangé des milliards de données depuis plusieurs années, issues de la conduite de ses clients, pour alimenter l’IA de son autopilot. Denza, qui de plus ne roule pas aux USA, part donc avec quelques longueurs de retard, retard que des milliers d’ingénieurs tentent aujourd’hui de combler.
Tests de conduite autonome en ville : que permet la loi française ?
En France, les constructeurs automobiles peuvent expérimenter des systèmes de conduite autonome sur la voie publique, y compris en pleine ville. Mais cette liberté est encadrée. L’ordonnance du 3 août 2016 et le décret du 28 mars 2018 imposent une autorisation préalable du ministère chargé des Transports pour les essais impliquant une délégation effective de conduite. Cette autorisation précise notamment les fonctionnalités testées, les conditions de sécurité, la durée des essais et les voies sur lesquelles ils peuvent être réalisés.
Un constructeur autorisé à expérimenter son système dans certaines rues parisiennes ; ici BYD-Denza ne peut donc pas décider librement de poursuivre ses essais en mode autonome dans une autre ville. Les véhicules concernés doivent par ailleurs disposer d’un certificat spécifique et être sous la supervision d’un opérateur formé à cette tâche et seul habilité à se trouver derrière le volant lorsque la voiture évolue en mode autonome.

articles.title: La NASA cree que las cuevas de la Luna sirven como "búnkeres" para astronautas y tiene una misión en marcha
articles.text:
La NASA ha seleccionado tres proyectos que se encargarán de analizar el terreno lunar para maximizar la seguridad de los astronautas que viajen en el futuro a nuestro satélite. Los astronautas del programa Apolo pasaron muy poco tiempo en la Luna y aun así se enfrentaron a peligros desconocidos, como el efecto del polvo lunar en sus mucosas. Los astronautas de Artemis irán mucho más preparados para esas misiones cortas, gracias a todas las naves y robots que han estudiado nuestro satélite desde dentro y desde fuera. Sin embargo, aún queda analizar los riesgos que podrían darse en estancias mucho más largas. Ahí es donde entra en juego el programa PRISM, compuesto por tres investigaciones: LEMS-SP, GIMLI y DISCO.
Un concurso de propuestas. Con el fin de analizar mucho mejor la Luna, la NASA abrió un concurso de propuestas, dirigido tanto a universidades y centros de investigación públicos como a empresas privadas. Todo esto está dentro del marco de CLPS, una iniciativa de la NASA dirigida a contratar empresas para transportar y entregar instrumentos científicos a la Luna. Para el programa PRISM, se han elegido propuestas de la Universidad de Maryland, el Planetary Science Institute y la NASA Ames. Tienen objetivos muy distintos, pero todos pueden servir para elegir los mejores lugares para construir asentamientos lunares.
LEMS-SP. Esta misión, dirigida por Mehdi Benna, de la Universidad de Maryland, se encargará de analizar el medio ambiente lunar mediante el estudio de tres pilares. Por un lado, los impactos de micrometeoritos. La Luna no tiene una atmósfera como la nuestra, que desintegra o frena la mayor parte de rocas que intentan atravesarla, por lo que sufre un constante bombardeo de meteoritos de distintos tamaños. En una misión corta, como las del programa Apolo, sería mala suerte sufrir un impacto, pero en estancias largas la cosa se complica. Por eso es tan importante este análisis. En segundo lugar, LEMS-SP analizará la abundancia de los gases en la fina capa que rodea la Luna.
Y para terminar, se enviará a la Luna un sismómetro. Estudiar los terremotos que suceden en la Luna es vital para seleccionar los mejores lugares para construir asentamientos.
GIMLI. Si Gimli y el resto de enanos de la Tierra Media vivían bajo tierra, los astronautas podrían necesitar hacerlo para huir de posibles amenazas. Por eso, esta misión, dirigida por Nathaniel Putzig, del Planetary Science Institute, se encargará de estudiar el pozo de Marius Hills, una abertura en la superficie lunar que podría conectarse a un extenso tubo de lava subterráneo. Este tubo de lava, una vez vacío, podría convertirse en una serie de cuevas y pasadizos subterráneos que funcionarían como búnker, en caso de que las construcciones superficiales estuviesen en peligro.
DISCO. Es bien sabido que en la Luna hay hielo, que podría obtenerse para obtener agua en los asentamientos lunares. Con esta misión se analizarán las microtrampas frías, unas zonas que nunca reciben luz solar y, por lo tanto, son buenas candidatas para albergar grandes cantidades de hielo. No obstante, ese no será su único objetivo. También se estudiará la consistencia del terreno, en busca de lugares en los que se pueda caminar fácilmente. Además, esta investigación permitirá comprender cómo se comportará el polvo lunar durante el alunizaje de las naves, algo que también es muy importante si ya se ha construido un asentamiento. No queremos una tormenta de arena con cada llegada de suministros. Esta misión la dirige Ariel Deutsch, de la NASA Ames.
El lugar ideal. En conjunto, estas tres misiones buscan seleccionar los mejores lugares para construir asentamiento y, a su vez, recopilar información útil para construir los instrumentos que utilizarán los astronautas en su día a día. Aún no se ha anunciado la fecha de lanzamiento de ninguna de estas misiones, pero lo lógico sería que lleguen a la Luna antes de que se empiecen a realizar estancias largas en nuestro satélite.
Imagen | NASA

articles.title: Beats x Pokémon : une collaboration insolite se prépare autour de l’enceinte Pill
articles.text:
Attrapez-les tous… à commencer par cette enceinte Beats aux couleurs de Pikachu ! Beats vient de dévoiler un premier teaser pour une collaboration avec Pokémon, qui devrait donner naissance à une version de la Pill aux couleurs du célèbre Pokémon électrique.
Les collaborations entre marques et licences de jeux vidéo réservent parfois quelques surprises. Cette fois, c’est Beats, la marque audio d’Apple, qui s’associe à Pokémon. Une courte vidéo publiée par le fabricant laisse entrevoir une nouvelle version de son enceinte Pill. Des photos d’un mystérieux emballage aux couleurs de Pikachu avaient d’ailleurs déjà circulé sur les réseaux sociaux.
Une enceinte Beats Pill aux couleurs de Pikachu
Dans la vidéo partagée par Beats, une enceinte Pill apparaît aux côtés de symboles associés aux deux marques, dont une Poké Ball. Ce premier teaser est accompagné d’un message qui ne laisse guère de place au doute : « Il est temps d’attraper quelque chose de nouveau ». Une référence directe au célèbre slogan de la franchise, qui laisse entrevoir une collaboration aux couleurs de Pikachu.
On ne va pas se mentir, ce premier aperçu reste relativement bref et ne révèle pas encore de détails en lien avec le produit. Il vient néanmoins consolider les indices apparus plus tôt dans le mois. Le créateur de contenu Pokémon BritBratTV avait en effet publié il y a quelques jours deux photos présentées comme celles de la boîte d’une Beats Pill aux couleurs de Pikachu, repérée dans un magasin Target aux États-Unis.
La vidéo ne donne malheureusement aucune date de commercialisation. Le tarif de cette édition spéciale n’a pas non plus été annoncé. Aux États-Unis, l’enceinte Beats Pill est habituellement affichée au prix de 149,99 dollars, contre 169,95 euros en France.

articles.title: Logitech prépare une MX Master 4 Special Edition, et seul le look change — Frandroid
articles.text:
Roland Quandt, journaliste du site allemand WinFuture spécialisé dans les fuites, a publié ce mardi 13 octobre des visuels marketing officiels d’une souris pas encore annoncée, la Logitech MX Master 4 Special Edition.
    Pour aller plus loin
Test de la Logitech MX Master 4 : tout simplement la meilleure souris bureautique ?
            
Si vous avez acheté une MX Master 4 depuis sa sortie il y a un an, vous n’avez rien raté côté technique. D’après ces images, Logitech ne change que l’habillage, avec des graphismes sur tout le dessus et un bouton coloré en rouge-orange.
Pour rappel, la MX Master 4 avait été lancée le 30 septembre 2025, à 129,99 euros. C’est sans doute la souris la plus populaire de Logitech en ce moment, adoptée par beaucoup de gens qui travaillent toute la journée sur ordinateur.
Sous les graphismes, la même souris
Sur les visuels, des motifs graphiques couvrent toute la coque supérieure. La différence la plus visible se trouve au-dessus des boutons principaux, où une touche passe au rouge-orange. Pour le reste, WinFuture indique que le poids et les dimensions ne changent pas.
La MX Master 4 classique pèse 150 grammes d’après la fiche technique de Logitech. C’est 9 grammes de plus que la MX Master 3S, qui l’a précédée.
À l’intérieur, rien ne change non plus d’après WinFuture. Le capteur monte toujours à 8 000 DPI, ou points par pouce, l’unité qui mesure la sensibilité d’une souris (plus le chiffre est élevé, moins on bouge la main pour traverser l’écran). Selon le site, il suffit aussi pour jouer de temps en temps (pour jouer plus sérieusement, des souris gaming existent à moins de 50 euros). Il fonctionne même sur une table en verre, donc sans avoir besoin d’un tapis de souris.
La molette MagSpeed est elle aussi conservée. Elle utilise un système électromagnétique pour passer d’un défilement cranté, ligne par ligne, à une rotation libre qui fait défiler jusqu’à 1 000 lignes par seconde. C’est pratique pour remonter un long tableur en un coup de doigt.
Logitech garde aussi le retour haptique, la grande nouveauté de la MX Master 4 l’an dernier. Un petit moteur placé dans le repose-pouce vibre pour confirmer une action (un Rumble Pak de Nintendo 64, version bureautique).
Pas encore de prix ni de date
Ob ne connaît ni la date de sortie ni le prix de cette Special Edition, et Logitech n’a rien annoncé. Pour avoir un repère, Logitech vend la MX Master 4 classique environ 130 euros.
Rien n’indique non plus que la batterie soit plus facile à changer sur cette version. Sur le modèle classique, la fiche de Logitech décrit sa batterie de 650 mAh comme « non remplaçable ». Pourtant, le règlement européen sur les batteries (source) imposera à partir du 18 février 2027 que les appareils portables vendus dans l’Union européenne aient une batterie que l’utilisateur peut retirer et remplacer lui-même.
    Pour aller plus loin
Fin des smartphones jetables : ce qui change radicalement pour votre batterie dès 2027
            
Si les graphismes vous laissent froid, la MX Master 4 classique offre a priori la même technique, et elle est déjà en vente. Vous pouvez aussi comparer d’autres modèles dans notre sélection des meilleures souris sans fil.
