articles.title: Apple dévoile le HomeView et nous donne vraiment envie… mais ne le sort pas en France et en Europe
articles.text:
L’Apple HomeView est officiel après des années de rumeurs. Le 13 octobre 2026, à l’occasion d’un événement dédié à la maison où un nouveau HomePod mini et une nouvelle Apple TV ont aussi été présentés, Apple a dévoilé sa vision pour le futur de la maison. Son rêve est d’imposer le HomeView dans tous les foyers des propriétaires d’iPhone, en allant au-delà du simple pilotage d’accessoires domotiques. « Apple HomeView est conçu pour être partagé par tout le foyer, tout en restant complètement personnel pour chaque utilisateur », indique Apple.
L’écran HomeView utilise Siri AI pour exécuter vos ordres, peut se transformer en interrupteur tactile, dispose de fonctions de reconnaissance faciale et réunit tout l’écosystème Apple des différents membres d’un foyer au même endroit. Apple le décline en deux versions vendues au même prix : une avec un socle-enceinte qui se pose sur une table, l’autre qui s’accroche au mur. Le HomeView est en précommande dès aujourd’hui aux États-Unis, au Royaume-Uni, au Canada, en Australie, en Inde et en Nouvelle-Zélande, à 299 dollars, pour une sortie le 13 novembre. L’Europe, sans surprise, en est privée. Apple écrit dans son communiqué de presse que l’UE est privée du produit.
Apple dévoile le HomeView et veut en mettre dans toutes les maisons (sur une table ou sur un mur)
Le HomeView se décline en deux versions. La première se pose sur une table, un plan de travail ou une table de chevet : l’écran est relié à une base-enceinte en forme de dôme par une charnière en acier inoxydable, qui permet de l’incliner. Elle existe en quatre couleurs (argent, lumière stellaire, rose et gris sidéral), avec un câble assorti.
La seconde s’accroche au mur, dans l’entrée ou un couloir, et n’existe qu’en gris sidéral et argent. Il faut lui ajouter une fixation signée Schneider Home, vendue à part : un modèle USB-C à installer soi-même (59,95 dollars), un modèle raccordé au secteur (79,95 dollars) et un modèle Power over Ethernet (129,95 dollars, disponible début 2027), les deux derniers étant pensés pour une installation par un professionnel. Le HomeView n’a ni batterie ni bouton. L’idée d’Apple n’est pas de proposer un iPad qui reste à la maison mais d’aller sur un produit surtout conçu pour être commandé à la voix.
Contrairement à ce que suggéraient les rumeurs, le HomeView embarque un écran carré Liquid Retina de 7 pouces (et non 6), compatible True Tone. Sa luminosité peut descendre de 500 à 0,3 nit, la plus faible jamais proposée par Apple, de quoi l’installer sur une table de chevet. L’interface s’adapte aussi à la distance : elle affiche des informations simples quand on est loin, puis plus détaillées quand on s’approche. À l’intérieur, on retrouve une puce A18 (comme l’iPhone 16). En façade, une caméra 12 Mpx Center Stage et quatre micros servent aux appels FaceTime et à la reconnaissance des utilisateurs.
Côté son, deux haut-parleurs sont proposés et gèrent l’audio spatial. La version avec un socle dispose d’un meilleur son que la version murale.
Le HomeView fonctionne avec un nouveau système d’exploitation, sobrement baptisé HomeView. Son interface emprunte beaucoup à l’Apple Watch : l’écran affiche des cadrans personnalisables et un glissement vers le haut ouvre un écran d’accueil façon iPhone, avec des applications et des widgets propres à chaque utilisateur. N’espérez pas y installer vos applications préférées : il n’y a pas d’App Store, seulement une sélection d’applications Apple (Musique, Podcasts, News, Apple TV, FaceTime, Messages…) et des applications audio et vidéo tierces compatibles, récupérées depuis l’iPhone. L’installation nécessite un iPhone ou un iPad compatible.
À quoi sert le HomeView ? Il faudra le tester pour en avoir le cœur net, mais Apple a mis en avant plusieurs idées lors de sa présentation de l’appareil :
- L’écran reconnaît jusqu’à six personnes par leur visage et change d’interface automatiquement. Il affiche les messages, le calendrier ou les rappels de chacun… à condition que son iPhone ou son iPad soit à proximité et ait été déverrouillé récemment.
- Le HomeView est un super-interrupteur tactile : le cadran « Maison » donne accès aux accessoires favoris (lumières, thermostat, serrures, volets…), tandis que le cadran « Caméras » affiche jusqu’à neuf flux vidéo en direct.
- Le HomeView peut passer des appels FaceTime, lire et répondre aux messages à la voix ou au clavier, et sert d’interphone avec les autres HomeView, HomePod, iPhone ou Apple Watch de la maison.
- Grâce à Handoff, il suffit d’approcher son iPhone pour y transférer une chanson, un podcast, un appel ou une recette.
- En cuisine, le HomeView transforme une recette trouvée sur le web en instructions étape par étape, avec des minuteurs pilotables à la voix.
- Le HomeView détecte le son des détecteurs de fumée et de monoxyde de carbone et prévient les membres du foyer sur leur iPhone ou leur Apple Watch.
- Quand il n’est pas utilisé, le HomeView devient un cadre photo, y compris avec des albums partagés que les proches peuvent alimenter à distance.
Le cœur du produit reste Siri AI. Avec un iPhone ou un iPad compatible, l’assistant exploite le contexte personnel de chaque utilisateur (Messages, Calendrier, playlists Apple Music…) et peut agir dans les applications. Les autres membres du foyer profitent quand même de ses connaissances générales et de conversations plus naturelles. Apple fait le choix de limiter la sortie du produit à l’anglais… et de le bloquer dans l’Union européenne.
Sur de nombreux aspects, l’Apple HomeView reprend les idées de Google (Nest Hub) et d’Amazon (Echo Show). Mais Apple, fidèle à ses habitudes, mise sur son écosystème, avec les iPhone au cœur de la machine, pour vous donner une raison d’adopter son système. La vie privée est aussi mise en avant : la puce A18 traite les flux de la caméra et des micros dans un compartiment isolé.
Une sortie le 13 novembre aux États-Unis… et un blocage en Europe
Contrairement au HomePod mini et à l’Apple TV, disponibles dès le 30 octobre, le HomeView se fera un peu attendre. Apple annonce une sortie le 13 novembre, au prix de 299 dollars pour la version de table comme pour la version murale. Les précommandes sont ouvertes dès aujourd’hui aux États-Unis, au Royaume-Uni, au Canada, en Australie, en Inde et en Nouvelle-Zélande, et le 15 octobre à Singapour. Il sera aussi vendu en Afrique du Sud via des revendeurs agréés.
Malheureusement et comme nous le pressentions, la France n’est pas sur la liste. Apple l’écrit noir sur blanc dans son communiqué : le HomeView n’est pas commercialisé dans l’Union européenne, car Siri AI n’est pas disponible sur iOS dans l’UE. La marque assure « travailler de manière constructive avec l’UE » pour trouver une solution. Le HomeView lui-même n’est pas concerné par le DMA, qui bloque Siri AI sur iPhone, iPad et Apple Watch, mais il dépend de l’iPhone à tous les niveaux : pour l’installation, pour afficher les données personnelles de chacun et pour donner à Siri AI son contexte personnel. Sans Siri AI sur nos iPhone, le HomeView perd une bonne partie de son intérêt.
Autre question pour l’instant sans réponse : pourra-t-on l’importer des États-Unis ou du Royaume-Uni ? Apple indique que Siri AI fonctionne sur le HomeView même sans iPhone compatible pour les questions générales, ce qui laisse imaginer un usage partiel. Mais l’assistant n’est disponible qu’en anglais et dans les huit pays de lancement, et l’installation passe par un iPhone ou un iPad. Tout ce que l’on sait est qu’à partir d’iOS 27.2, Siri AI parlera français.… mais pas sur le HomeView.

articles.title: EON Space Labs is building India’s indigenous optical payloads after Falcon 9 Success
articles.text:
EON Space Labs is building India’s indigenous optical payloads after Falcon 9 Success
After Mira’s Successful Launch on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, Hyderabad spacetech startup EON Space Labs is positioning itself as India's pioneer in end‑to‑end optical systems by indigenising payloads and securing flight heritage.
EON Space Labs has spent the last few years building optical systems for satellites, drones, and ground-based platforms, with a focus on reducing India’s dependence on imported imaging technologies.
The Hyderabad-based startup has now crossed an important milestone with Mira, its flagship earth-observation payload, reaching orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 Transporter-18 mission on October 2, 2026. The company expects to receive its first images in the next 10 days.
For Punit Badeka, Co-founder and COO of EON Space Labs, the mission is also about establishing indigenous capability.
“This proves and enables us to make sure that now the product is indigenised. We do not claim it. We prove that the product is designed and manufactured here in India itself,” he says.
The company has also secured an Indian patent for Mira. Its current portfolio spans three segments — space, aerial, and ground — covering earth-observation payloads, electro-optical/infrared (EONIR) systems for drones, and surveillance systems for ground applications.
Moving beyond space
Badeka says the spacetech startup is currently working with more than seven companies in the space segment, while its aerial business has received inbound interest from around 120 Indian companies seeking its EONIR payloads. In the ground segment, it is working with about 12 companies looking at perimeter surveillance, counter-drone systems, and airport monitoring.
One of its key developments is a handheld imaging system being developed through iDEX. It combines short-wave infrared (SWIR), long-wave infrared (LWIR) and a conventional day camera. Its LWIR system uses germanium-free lenses, replacing a material that has faced supply constraints.
“We have these germanium-free lenses, which are designed, developed, and manufactured from materials synthetically grown in India. They are affordable and easily available, which brings down the lead time from six months to six weeks,” the COO says.
The system has undergone trials aboard Indian Navy ships, where EON says it was able to identify vessels at around 30 km, including in low-visibility conditions.
“We have also developed a DIY telescope for school students, designed to let children assemble the instrument and observe the craters on the moon. A future version will add motorised tracking and AI features,” he says.
Badeka adds that the company's three-way positioning is a deliberate differentiator. “There is no company in the country that is designing, developing, and manufacturing these optical payloads that we are doing,” he says.
Building its own optical manufacturing capability
EON's longer-term ambition is to control more of the optical manufacturing process. The COO says the company wants to launch its own payloads so it can control the resulting imagery and use that data to improve its optics.
The company wants to use this flight heritage to improve the quality of its optics through better surface finishes and ultra-precision manufacturing. “Only a few machines in the country can do such precision optics manufacturing,” Badeka says. EON has applied for government support to build this capability.
At present, EON's optics are manufactured by strategic investor Hind High Vacuum (HHV). The startup plans to eventually install its own ultra-precision machines in Hyderabad and transfer its designs to the facility.
EON has secured payload orders from Indian spacetech companies including Orbited Labs and Kepler Aerospace. Orbited Labs will use an EON payload on its SSLV mission, while Kepler Aerospace has placed an order worth around Rs 6–7 crore for an iDEX programme.
“For Kepler Aerospace, it is going to be a bulk constellation of satellites that we are going to have with them,” Badeka says. “While we are designing and manufacturing these optics for them, we will also ensure that we are sending this with our own optics and readout electronics.”
EON is now preparing to raise around Rs 40 crore in a planned Series A1 round. The funding would support international commercialisation of its Lumira aerial products, its own payload launches, R&D, and a cleanroom facility for precision-optics work.
EON Space Labs is part of YourStory’s Tech30 cohort — a showcase of India’s most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: DJI Romo P2 : cartographie, détection, déplacements… Découvrez en vidéo comment fonctionne son système de navigation
articles.text:
DJI Romo P2 : cartographie, détection, déplacements… Découvrez en vidéo comment fonctionne son système de navigation
Cartographier son environnement, reconnaître les obstacles et se faufiler sous les meubles : le DJI Romo P2 s'appuie sur plusieurs technologies pour optimiser ses déplacements. Mais comment fonctionne son système de navigation ? Réponse dans notre vidéo YouTube.
La navigation d’un aspirateur-robot ne se limite pas à suivre un itinéraire. Elle repose aussi sur divers systèmes qui lui permettent de se repérer, planifier ses déplacements et s’adapter aux contraintes du logement.
 
Le DJI Romo P2 s’est montré particulièrement convaincant sur ce point lors de nos essais. Dans notre nouvelle vidéo YouTube, nous vous expliquons notamment comment fonctionnent ses différentes technologies de navigation.
Cartographie du DJI Romo P2 : une modélisation 3D rapide et précise
L’aspirateur-robot de DJI associe un LiDAR 3D ToF à deux caméras fisheye et une caméra centrale. Le premier calcule les distances pour dessiner une carte 3D de la pièce, les caméras fisheye analysent l'espace global autour du robot, et la caméra centrale utilise l'IA pour reconnaître les obstacles à éviter sur son passage.
Dans les faits, cette alliance technologique porte ses fruits : le Romo P2 établit une carte fidèle du logement dès son premier passage. Il identifie correctement les pièces et suit un parcours méthodique sans multiplier les déplacements inutiles.
DJI Romo P2
Évitement des obstacles : comment le Romo P2 ajuste sa trajectoire en temps réel
Une fois son parcours défini, le Romo P2 doit composer avec les obstacles qui se présentent à lui et adapter ses déplacements en temps réel. Lors de nos essais, il s’est aisément faufilé sous les meubles, entre les pieds de chaise, derrière un rideau et le long des plinthes. Il a également franchi sans difficulté la transition entre le sol dur et le tapis.
Par ailleurs, l’aspirateur-robot dispose d’un bras articulé qui pivote sur 123° afin de réorienter son capteur LiDAR et ainsi atteindre les zones les plus difficiles d'accès. Lorsque la luminosité est faible, une led intégrée éclaire les zones observées par les caméras.
Sa détection n’est toutefois pas infaillible : nous avons observé quelques contacts avec un câble ou un pied de chaise lorsque le robot circulait à proximité immédiate d’un obstacle.
Franchissement de seuils : un châssis relevable pour grimper jusqu'à 4 cm
Se déplacer efficacement implique aussi de franchir les séparations entre les pièces. Dans ce contexte, l'aspirateur-robot de DJI se dote d'un système d'élévation du châssis. Cette fonctionnalité lui permet de franchir des seuils jusqu'à 4 cm de hauteur, même s'il s'y prend parfois à deux fois avant d'ajuster sa hauteur.
Ces légères hésitations n'entachent pas un bilan globalement très positif : la précision de sa navigation lui permet de gérer sans encombre la plupart des obstacles du quotidien.
Rendez-vous dans notre vidéo complète pour le voir évoluer en conditions réelles et juger de son comportement par vous-même.

articles.title: SAP warns of maximum severity OAuth2 SSRF security flaw
articles.text:
SAP has addressed 20 security flaws across multiple products in its October 2026 security updates, including a maximum-severity vulnerability in the Cloud SDK for Python.
The SAP Python SDK is the official programmatic toolkit for developing AI agents and Python applications on the company's SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) services.
Tracked as CVE-2026-89111, the maximum-severity vulnerability patched this month can be exploited by remote attackers without privileges to steal credentials.
Customers who can't immediately deploy the October 2026 SAP patches can temporarily mitigate the issue by using an allowlist to validate tenant_subdomain values.
"The SAP Cloud SDK for Python contains an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications. An attacker who controls the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated," according to a Tuesday advisory.
"Consumer applications can mitigate the vulnerability by validating tenant_subdomain against a known allowlist of registered tenant subdomains before passing it to any SDK call."
Today, SAP also addressed CVE-2026-89110, a critical broken access control vulnerability in the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer that could let remote attackers with limited privileges fully compromise vulnerable systems.
Another critical flaw patched today in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (tracked as CVE-2026-89108) lets threat actors with administrator privileges gain admin control over the underlying system by provisioning an elevated-privilege account on the underlying Java app.
In recent months, SAP has fixed several other maximum-severity flaws in multiple components. For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after it was addressed.
More recently, in September, it also fixed the CVE-2026-44756 memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code, dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it. According to Onapsis estimates at the time, over 10,000 Internet-facing SAP systems use the vulnerable component and may be exposed to attacks that exploit CVE-2026-44756.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added 14 SAP security flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities since November 2021, three of which were abused in ransomware attacks.
SAP is a German multinational software company that serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide and reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025.

articles.title: Cómo China está transformando una zona rural donde se cultivan papas en el centro de su competencia tecnológica con EE.UU.
articles.text:
En los campos de patatas de Ulanqab, los agricultores cosechan junto a unos vecinos que no dejan de crecer: enormes bloques rectangulares donde se alojará buena parte del cómputo de la inteligencia artificial china.
Cientos de obreros con casco amarillo mueven maquinaria entre andamios y chispas de soldadura, y las grúas levantan tejados a toda prisa.
Cientos de grúas y 500.000 millones de yuanes
La prisa tiene una razón de Estado. El plan 'IA Plus' del Consejo de Estado fija para 2030 una penetración de terminales y agentes de IA superior al 90 %, y eso necesita cómputo.
Ulanqab, según las cifras de un análisis reciente, ha atraído 84 proyectos de centros de datos (81 de IA; otros recuentos suben a 89) y más de 500.000 millones de yuanes (unos 66.000 millones de euros), y el consumo eléctrico de sus servicios de datos subió un 85,2 % interanual en el primer semestre de 2026, hasta los 4.000 millones de kWh.
Los nombres propios ya están sobre la mesa. Envision puso en marcha el 6 de agosto su campus Galaxy: 120.000 metros cuadrados, hasta un millón de aceleradores de IA y, según la compañía, margen para superar los 2 GW con electricidad renovable conectada de forma directa. DeepSeek prepara cerca de 1 GW, con operación parcial a finales de 2027 o principios de 2028 y sin confirmación oficial. ByteDance quiere añadir entre cinco y seis gigavatios en dos años, apunta una fuente cercana a las conversaciones con proveedores locales.
¿Por qué una estepa y no en pleno Shanghái?
Por el frío (4,3 grados de media a 1.500 metros), el viento y una electricidad verde de 0,30-0,35 yuanes por kWh. Un centro de datos de 1 GW funcionando a carga constante consume unos 8.760 millones de kWh al año: a 0,35 yuanes, serían unos 3.066 millones de yuanes de factura (cuenta propia). Y Pekín queda a unos 4 milisegundos de latencia.
Nada de esto es improvisado. Ulanqab es uno de los nodos del plan ‘Datos del Este, Computación del Oeste’, lanzado en 2022 por la NDRC con ocho ‘hubs’ y diez clústeres, para llevar el cómputo pesado adonde sobra energía.
Wang Chaoyang, de Alibaba Cloud, lo explica con un reparto: el entrenamiento de modelos se va al oeste, por la energía barata, y la inferencia (lo que usamos los usuarios) se queda cerca del este.
Hay peros. China quiere que la mayoría de sus centros de datos funcionen con energía verde en 2030, pero parte de su red todavía tira de carbón, y el agua sigue siendo un problema en la Mongolia Interior árida.
Pekín juega la carrera desde tres puntos de vista
La carrera tiene meta política. A finales de septiembre, Trump y Xi se vieron en Washington, con la IA entre los temas. Poco antes, el consejero delegado de Anthropic, Dario Amodei, había defendido en un ensayo frenar el ritmo de los modelos más potentes y mantener las restricciones a la venta de chips avanzados a China; Trump respondió que no piensa frenar, porque quien gane en IA, gana. El portavoz de Exteriores chino, Guo Jiakun, lo tachó de alarmismo.
La carta del talento. Jack Zhang, de la Universidad de Ciencia y Tecnología de China (pasó por Yale y Cambridge), asegura que cada vez van menos estudiantes a EE.UU. y que más regresan. El país forma, se suele estimar, unos cinco millones de graduados en ciencia y tecnología al año frente a medio millón de EE.UU., aunque las estimaciones varían bastante.
La tercera vía son los chips propios. DeepSeek prepararía un pedido de chips Ascend de Huawei, con su modelo V4 optimizado para el Ascend 950, aunque ni el volumen ni el modelo están confirmados.
A la hora de comparar tamaños, el seguimiento de Epoch AI sitúa hoy a Colossus 2 (el de xAI) con 946 MW y a New Carlisle (Anthropic y Amazon) con 910 MW, y a Fairwater Wisconsin con 2.263 MW previstos para 2028, y en su lista no aparece ningún centro chino. Los 2 GW de Envision son capacidad de diseño, no consumo actual.
Mucho gigavatio y poco enchufado
Ahora, las cuentas. Los 4.000 millones de kWh del primer semestre equivalen a unos 0,92 GW de consumo medio (181 días, 4.344 horas, cuenta propia). Lo que ha trascendido de solo tres proyectos (Envision, DeepSeek y ByteDance) suma entre 8 y 9 GW: casi diez veces lo que Ulanqab gasta hoy, aunque solo lo de Envision es oficial.
Además, el oeste llega con sobrecapacidad. En 2025, apenas el 36,8 % de la capacidad de cómputo inteligente se utilizó, según la Academia China de Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación. Un análisis de mayo habla de centros de datos occidentales con tasas del 20-30 % frente al objetivo de más del 60%.
Y a pie de campo, la vara de medir es otra. Se han reubicado pueblos enteros, aunque nadie precisa cuántos ni con qué compensación, y pocos se atreven a hablar. Un vecino que pide anonimato asegura que pocos lugareños han encontrado trabajo en los centros y pregunta: “¿Qué beneficios nos han aportado?”. Otro hombre, que recoge patatas junto a las obras y solo da su apellido, ve el futuro con optimismo: sus hijos ya trabajan en las instalaciones.
Los centros de datos están al lado; el cambio, de momento, no.

articles.title: Linkbuilding auslagern: Warum es in der Praxis oft nicht klappt
articles.text:
Offpage SEO: Woran ausgelagertes Linkbuilding in der Praxis wirklich scheitert
Die Ernüchterung folgt jedoch oft schnell: Wer Prozesse auslagert, spart erst dann wirklich Zeit, wenn die internen Abläufe nahtlos andocken und klare Verantwortlichkeiten vorhanden sind.
Schlägt ein Linkbuilding-Partner beispielsweise drei potenzielle Publisher vor, im eigenen Team fehlt jedoch die Zeit zur Prüfung von Zielseite und Umfeld, kippt das Modell: Die ausgelagerte Aufgabe wird prompt wieder zum internen Zeitfresser.
Um das zu verhindern, müssen Verantwortlichkeiten rund um Textfreigaben, Zielseiten-Anpassungen und Ankertexte vorab glasklar definiert sein – inklusive fester Vertretungsregelungen. Denn oft sind es schlicht unvorhergesehene Engpässe wie Urlaube oder Krankheitsfälle, die eingespielte Abläufe ins Chaos stürzen und Platzierungen verzögern. Nur mit strukturierten Freigabeprozessen, klar benannten Vertretungen und kurzen Kommunikationswegen landen die Inhalte pünktlich beim Publisher – ohne dass das eigene Marketing-Team im Mikromanagement oder Vertretungs-Chaos versinkt.
Verantwortung abgeben – aber wie viel?
Erfolgreiches Linkbuilding erfordert weit mehr als den bloßen Einkauf von Platzierungen. Es braucht ein präzises Briefing und eine verlässliche interne Qualitätssicherung. Gute Partner-Modelle, wie sie eine spezialisierte Linkbuilding-Agentur oder Managed Services bieten, setzen deshalb bereits bei der Strategie an: Sie verknüpfen eine fundierte Linkprofilanalyse und strategische Priorisierung direkt mit der operativen Umsetzung und dem anschließenden Monitoring, damit die Platzierungen auch ihre nachhaltige Wirkung erzielen können.
Damit die Zusammenarbeit reibungslos funktioniert, müssen vor Kampagnenstart glasklare Leitplanken definiert werden:
- Aufgabenverteilung: Welche operativen Schritte übernimmt der Partner, was bleibt inhouse?
- Freigaben & Veto: Wer sichert die Zielseiten (Landingpages) ab und wer darf unpassende Publisher-Quellen ablehnen?
- Eskalationspfade: Bei welchen Sonderfällen oder Abweichungen ist eine direkte Rücksprache erforderlich?
Den tatsächlichen Engpass im Prozess finden
Bevor du dich für ein externes Modell entscheidest, lohnt sich ein Blick auf die Historie. Analysiere die letzten Kampagnen rückwirkend, um herauszufinden, an welcher Stelle im Prozess konkret Zeit verloren ging – und um typische Prozess- und Strategiefehler beim Linkbuilding künftig systematisch zu vermeiden. Stell dir dabei wichtige Fragen:
- Quellenauswahl: Wie viele Publisher-Vorschläge wurden verworfen – und aus welchen fachlichen Gründen?
- Freigabelaufzeiten: Wie lange lagen Themenkonzepte, Zielseiten (Landingpages) oder Ankertexte zur Prüfung im eigenen Team?
- Nacharbeit: Wer bemerkte im Nachgang fehlerhafte Verlinkungen, schwachen Content oder fehlende Werbekennzeichnungen (z. B. fehlende rel=“sponsored“-Attribute)?
Vier Modelle im Vergleich
Ob Freelancer, Agentur oder Managed Service: Die reine Bezeichnung des Betriebsmodells sagt im Linkbuilding noch wenig darüber aus, wie viel Arbeit tatsächlich abgegeben wird. Entscheidend ist, wie hoch der verbleibende interne Ressourcenaufwand im Unternehmen ist.
| Modell | Strategiebedarf | Interne Ressourcen | Qualitätskontrolle | Skalierbarkeit | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inhouse | intern | hoch | vollständig intern | nur mit Personal | 
| Freelancer | vorgegeben | mittel | interne Endabnahme | begrenzt | 
| Agentur | gemeinsam | niedrig bis mittel | interne Endabnahme | nach Kapazität | 
| Managed Service | extern begleitet | niedrig bis mittel | interne Endabnahme | flexibel | 
Ein Freelancer eignet sich ideal für klar abgegrenzte Einzelpakete, sofern Strategie und Qualitätskontrolle fest inhouse verankert sind. Eine Agentur fängt schwankendes Auftragsvolumen gut ab. Bei einem Managed Service wandern zusätzlich die laufende strategische Beratung und Priorisierung nach außen – was maximale Flexibilität bei geringer interner Belastung ermöglicht.
“Auch das beste Dienstleister-Modell löst keine trägen internen Freigabeprozesse.”
Qualität lässt sich nicht delegieren
Das Vetorecht – also das gezielte „Nein“-Sagen – ist eine Kernaufgabe, die zwingend im eigenen Unternehmen verbleiben muss. Benenne intern eine feste Person, die Publisher-Quellen, Themenumfeld, Zielseiten und Ankertexte rigoros prüft.
Der Grund ist simpel: Google führt den Kauf von Links zu Rankingzwecken explizit als Verstoß in den Google Search Essentials (Spamrichtlinien) auf. Eine verantwortungsvolle Auswahl der Quellseiten ist daher essenziell. Die Entscheidung über eine Platzierung sollte idealerweise vor der Content-Erstellung fallen – doch auch unmittelbar vor dem Go-Live muss ein finales Veto möglich sein.
Im Bericht zählen auch die Umwege
Grüne Statusfelder in Excel-Listen erzählen nur die halbe Wahrheit. Ein sauberes Indexierungs-Monitoring gehört heute zwar zum Standard, ein aussagekräftiger Report muss aber weit darüber hinausgehen: Auch abgelehnte Quellen, Kostenstrukturen, Zielseiten, Nachbearbeitungsschleifen und interne Wartezeiten gehören transparent in die Auswertung.
Nur so lässt sich objektiv analysieren, ob ein Engpass beim Dienstleister lag oder das interne Briefing mehrfach angepasst werden musste. Tipp: Vereinbare vorab eine klare Stoppregel für den Fall, dass qualitativ passende Quellen knapp werden oder die Standards sichtbar sinken.

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – A not-so-Flash deal - TechCabal
articles.text:
Wazzup. ☀️ ️️️
Half of yesterday’s TC Daily edition was about IPOs: Airtel Money and OPay. But apparently, we missed an important one: Banque du Caire, Egypt’s sixth-largest commercial bank by assets. On October 11, the bank announced plans to sell a 30% stake on Egypt’s stock exchange, the country’s second major IPO this month after MNT-Halan. Quite the season for public listings!
Meanwhile, Abuja, Nigeria’s capital city, is hosting the Defence Futures Summit on October 14–15, 2026, bringing together Nigeria’s technology, creative, and defence communities to explore homegrown innovation. Register here.
Finally, before you scroll, one quick favour: help us make TC Daily better. Tell us what you love, what you skip, and what you want more of. Share your thoughts here.
Let’s dive in.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Fintech
Pepkor’s $1.3 billion fintech deal draws shareholder pushback
When Pepkor, the South African retailer behind PEP and Ackermans, announced its Flash-Shop2Shop merger in July, the pitch was growth: combine two large merchant networks, build a bigger fintech business, then list it separately. Three months later, the deal is attracting attention for a different reason.
What happened? Some Pepkor directors and investors believe shareholders should have been allowed to vote on the R21.3 billion ($1.3 billion) transaction. Pepkor will own 57.1% of the combined entity, FintechCo. Pieter Erasmus, Pepkor’s chief executive officer (CEO), will indirectly own 13.2%, worth roughly R2.8 billion ($170 million) at the deal valuation, according to the company’s filing.
Erasmus recused himself from discussions and decisions. Pepkor also obtained independent valuations and a voluntary fair opinion. JSE rules did not require a shareholder vote because the deal is classified as a Category 2 transaction—which must be publicly disclosed but does not require shareholder approval—while Erasmus’s interest falls below the threshold that would make it a related-party transaction.
Explain like I’m new here: Erasmus’s link to Shop2Shop is not new. An associated company owned 31.2% of Shop2Shop before the merger, and Flash and Shop2Shop had already been doing business together since 2020. Pepkor disclosed those relationships in previous financial statements.
Between the lines: Pepkor did not need shareholder approval under JSE rules. But some investors still think a deal this important—especially one in which the CEO has a financial interest—should have gone before shareholders. FintechCo is central to Pepkor’s next phase, and its CEO stands to own a valuable stake in the private company being brought into the group. A shareholder vote, even a non-binding one, would have given investors a direct say on that conflict.
Zoom out: Pepkor is moving quickly beyond retail. Financial-services revenue jumped 41.6% in the first half of 2026, and the group plans to launch a bank in April 2027. As more of Pepkor’s growth comes from finance and payments—as it eyes banking—as well as other private deals, investors will care just as much about how those businesses are put together and how fast they grow.
Happy customer service week.
Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com.
Ecommerce
Quickmart cuts founder-linked contracts before IPO
Quickmart’s owners are selling half the supermarket chain to the public. But before those new shareholders come on board, the retailer has been cleaning up some old arrangements with the people who built and owned the business.
What happened? Quickmart terminated several consultancy and management contracts with founder- and director-linked businesses in July, months before its initial public offering (IPO). In 2025 alone, Quickmart paid KES 208.4 million ($1.6 million) in management fees to its parent companies, KES 268.7 million ($2.1 million) to Basic Land Investment, and KES 161 million ($1.2 million) to Resource Business Investments.
Those three payments alone came to about KES 638 million ($4.9 million), roughly 43% of Quickmart’s KES 1.5 billion ($11.6 million) net profit that year.
Explain like I’m new here: Founder-linked transactions are not automatically a problem. Private companies often lean on their owners for property, advice, or other services. The calculation changes once strangers are invited to buy shares. Investors want to know that money leaving the company is being spent on the best available terms, not simply routed to insiders.
Between the lines: Ending the contracts makes Quickmart easier to scrutinise as a public company, but it does not mean the entire KES 638 million ($4.9 million) suddenly becomes profit. The retailer may still need some of those services and could pay outside advisers or build the work in-house. The more important change is who gets to decide what those services cost.
Some links to the founders remain. Eighteen Quickmart stores are still leased from businesses connected to founders or directors, though the retailer said those leases are on normal commercial terms.
Zoom out: Governance matters more here because Quickmart itself is not raising money. Its owner, Sokoni Retail Kenya, is selling two billion existing shares for KES 15 billion ($116 million), and will collect the proceeds from the public offer in a much-needed listing for Kenya’s capital market. Quickmart has already opened the offer, with full trading expected by November 12.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
E-mobility
Eskom opens its first public EV chargers in Durban, South Africa
Eskom has spent decades keeping South Africa’s lights on, mostly by burning coal. Now, it wants to help keep the country’s electric cars moving, too.
What happened? The state-owned electricity company has opened its first public electric vehicle (EV) charging stations at the Gateway Theatre of Shopping in Umhlanga and The Pavilion Shopping Centre in Durban, South Africa. Eskom’s two new charging stations each have two fast direct-current (DC) charging ports capable of delivering up to 120 kilowatts (kW), plus one alternating-current (AC) port offering up to 22kW.
Explain like I’m new here: Eskom may be best known for generating electricity, but charging electric cars can be a natural extension of that business, using its operating experience with electricity infrastructure to support the growth of electric transport. E.ON, one of Europe’s largest investor-owned electric utility service providers, operates a network of public and home electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure across Europe and the UK.
Eskom has been trying its hand at clean business for a while. In August 2024, the company, in partnership with GridCars, a South African charging-network operator, launched a pilot with 10 charging stations across five of its properties, but kept it closed to the general public. In September 2025, it introduced 20 electric vehicles (EVs) and said it wanted to transition its entire fleet to electric by 2035. It also announced plans to roll out 55 public charging stations over two years. Eskom also signed an agreement with BYD, the Chinese car-maker, to support electric mobility and expand public charging infrastructure in South Africa.
From generating power to selling a charge: Eskom is entering the EV charging business, giving it an advantage because it already runs South Africa’s electricity system. Charging operators make money by selling power to drivers, but they also pay for equipment, maintenance, grid connections and demand fees.
Some industry players have raised concerns that Eskom may have offered certain sites lower demand charges, which could let them price charging more cheaply than rivals. Eskom says its pilot pricing follows existing tariffs and regulations.
What does this mean for drivers? Eskom’s new DC chargers cost R5.88 ($0.045) per kilowatt-hour (kWh), compared with R7.35 ($0.057) at GridCars’ public stations, making Eskom’s rates 20% cheaper. For a driver buying 50 kWh of electricity, that means paying R294 ($2.27) at an Eskom station instead of R367.5 ($2.83) at GridCars, the country’s largest EV charging station operator, helping them save about R73.50 ($0.57) on a single charge. Eskom’s lower prices offer drivers a cheaper alternative to existing charging networks, although its ability to compete with established operators will depend on how widely it expands its public charging stations.
South Africa recorded sales of over 16,000 new-energy vehicles in 2025, but expanding its public charging network remains important to making electric driving more practical, especially for drivers who cannot charge at home or travel frequently between cities.
Capital Markets
Investors get a two-week extension to buy into Dangote Refinery shares
The Dangote Refinery initial public offering (IPO), originally scheduled to close on October 13, has been extended by two weeks, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The extension gives retail investors more time to buy shares in the company, amid growing interest from investors in other African countries.
What happened? Dangote Refinery says it has received strong interest from eligible investors across Africa and other markets. The IPO, which opened on September 14, will now remain open until October 27.
Explain like I’m new here: Dangote is giving everyday investors a chance to own a piece of its refinery. Each share costs ₦525 ($0.40), and the company plans to sell 4.1 billion shares to raise ₦2.15 trillion ($1.6 billion). The extra two weeks will allow it to bring in investors from more African countries and complete the arrangements needed for them to buy shares across borders.
Many people want in: In Kenya, Renaissance Capital, a Kenyan investment bank, worked on a new vehicle that would allow Kenyan investors to participate in the IPO through Kenya’s stock exchange, for KES 49 ($0.38) per share. In Zimbabwe, asset manager Bard Santner Investors is facilitating local participation by securing the required approvals and moving clients’ money from Ecobank Zimbabwe to Ecobank Nigeria.
More time, more shares? Not necessarily. The extension gives more investors time to participate; it does not automatically increase the number of shares on offer. Dangote has regulatory approval to sell additional equity if demand warrants it, potentially raising to $2.1 billion, but the company has not said that the extension itself will trigger a larger offer.
What does this mean? The extension gives Dangote more time to increase participation and benefit from the possible cross-border demand in its refinery. Dangote’s IPO has become a major test of how easily investors can buy shares across African borders. Kenya’s route and Zimbabwe’s bank-transfer arrangement show that investors are finding ways in, and Dangote wants a pan-African shareholder base.

articles.title: AMD's RDNA 5 graphics cards tipped to arrive in late 2027
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Given the state of the graphics card market, it feels like we'll be waiting forever to see next-generation GPUs. But according to a popular leaker, AMD will launch its RDNA 5 lineup in the second half of 2027 – so the first cards could be here in less than 12 months.
The information comes from Kepler_L2, who has a long history of correctly predicting graphics card releases. The leaker previously said RDNA 5 would land in 2027. Now, the timeframe has been narrowed to the second half of the year.
Writing on the AnandTech forums, Kepler_L2 said Team Red's next-generation cards could be unveiled at Computex 2027 at the earliest, though they're more likely to be announced later that year.
Computex 2027 starts on June 1. That'll be 2 years and 3 months since the RDNA 4-based Radeon 9000 series launched in March 2025. The gap between the Radeon RX 7000 series and RX 9000 cards was 2 years and 2 months, and it was 2 years and 25 days between the Radeon RX 6000 cards and RX 7000. So, the timing fits.
AMD might also depart from its usual habit of launching the higher-end cards first. Previous reports point to the mid-range AT2 GPU arriving in 2027, with the rest of the RDNA 5 family – including the rumored flagship AT0 and lower-end AT3 and AT4 chips – following in 2028.
Kepler_L2 also responded to a question about RDNA 5's potential use of the rumored 4GB GDDR7 memory chips, which are expected to be mass produced in the next two years along with 6GB GDDR7 chips. The leaker believes that 4 GB GDDR7 won't be used for next-generation consumer parts, suggesting they'll be reserved for AI-focused and other enterprise products.
Another unanswered question is the all-important price of the cards. Thanks to the memory crisis, most mid-range GPUs no longer carry mid-range prices, while flagships have reached second-hand car levels. There are opposing opinions about whether things will get better or worse over the next few years, but it's hard to be optimistic.
As for when Nvidia will launch what is presumed to be the RTX 6000 series, another leaker, Kopite7kimi, says it won't be here until 2028. And don't expect to ever see any RTX 5000 Super cards.

articles.title: $86 Million Crypto Heist Linked to Ledger Signer Hardware Implant
articles.text:
A hardware implant in Ledger signers is blamed for the theft of at least $86 million in cryptocurrency from multiple users.
Ledger provides users with a secure cryptocurrency wallet that is backed by a signer, an offline hardware device used to securely authorize blockchain transactions.
Ledger signers sold via Southeast Asia reseller CryptoBilis were found to include an unauthorized hardware implant designed to intercept user data and send it to the attackers.
The cryptocurrency theft was disclosed on October 9 and was immediately pinned on devices sold through CryptoBilis. Ledger asked the company to stop selling its devices and instructed customers to stop using them.
“We recommend Ledger users who purchased from this reseller in the last 90 days to not initiate set up if you have not done so yet. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with new seed),” the company said.
On October 13, Ledger confirmed that all confirmed fund losses linked to the incident involved a signer sold through CryptoBilis.
It appears that someone along the distribution chain modified the signers to manually solder the hardware implant to the device’s circuit boards.
“The implant sits inside the enclosure and reads the data shown on the screen. During setup, the signer displays the 24-word recovery phrase. When the implant detects these screens, its microcontroller decodes the words and transmits them over LTE using a provisioned eSIM,” Ledger said.
The implant was designed only for information interception and does not modify the device’s OS, transactions, or signatures.
According to on-chain investigator Specter, the total losses associated with the supply chain attack may top $86 million.
Ledger, on the other hand, says it has not confirmed the number of impacted users or the total stolen.

articles.title: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results).
To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock. Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph.
In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline.
Bridging natural language and structured queries
Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema.
To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text.
Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale.
Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement.
The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock.
Solution overview
Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model.
Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline.
The following diagram illustrates the nine-stage pipeline architecture.
The Discovery AI pipeline converts a natural language request into a validated Discovery filter through nine steps.
- Request Entry and Context Setup: The pipeline starts by combining the user’s natural language request with relevant context, including the user’s organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata. This context helps the pipeline interpret the request accurately and generate a Discovery filter that matches the customer’s environment.
- Quick Deterministic Matcher: The Quick Matcher identifies structured inputs such as IP addresses, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), ARNs, file hashes, Amazon Machine Image IDs, Oracle Cloud Identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs. It uses regex and rule-based matching to detect high-confidence patterns.When a match is found, the pipeline can return a predefined Discovery filter through a fast path, without using large language model (LLM) inference. When no match is found, the request continues to the next step.
- LLM Guardrail Screening: The Guardrail component checks whether the request is safe, relevant, technical, and supported. It blocks prompt injection attempts, off-topic requests, and unsupported inputs before they reach the rest of the pipeline. Requests that fail the guardrail checks are rejected with an appropriate error. Approved requests continue to example retrieval.
- Embedding-Based Semantic Candidate Recall: The pipeline searches for relevant previously validated query examples using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. It retrieves the 20 nearest examples from the vector store based on semantic similarity. These candidates provide the pipeline with examples of how similar natural language requests were previously translated into Discovery filters.
- Neural Relevance Reranking: The retrieved candidates are reranked using Cohere Rerank 3.5 on Amazon Bedrock. It identifies the examples that are most relevant to the current request and selects the five highest-signal examples. When an exact or high-confidence match is found, the pipeline can reuse the known-good filter directly. Otherwise, the reranked examples are passed to the generative stages.
- LLM-Driven Relevant Model Selection: Model Selection narrows more than 900 Sonar models to the small set relevant to the request. It considers the user’s request, connected providers, and retrieved examples when selecting the appropriate models. The selected models are provided to the Generator using the appropriate schema level, ranging from compact micro schemas to more detailed mini schemas. This reduces unnecessary context and makes generation more efficient.
- Tool-Augmented Agentic Filter Generation: The Generator uses a tool-augmented agent to construct the final Discovery filter. It reasons over the selected model schemas, retrieved examples, user context, and available tools. The agent can iteratively refine the filter as it works toward a valid representation of the user’s request.
- Static and API-Backed Validation: The generated filter is checked for syntactic and semantic correctness. The pipeline first applies static validation and then verifies the filter against Orca’s Sonar API. When validation fails, the validation error is returned to the Generator so the agent can correct the filter and try again. If the maximum number of retries is reached without producing a valid filter, the pipeline returns an invalid-filter response. The Generator is constrained to the reranked examples and selected schemas. Static validation resolves every model, field, and operator back to those schema definitions. Each validation error goes back to the agent with the offending element identified, so retries re-ground rather than re-guess.
- Post-Processing and Response: After a valid filter is produced, whether through the Quick Matcher, reuse of a known-good example, or agentic generation, the pipeline prepares the final response.The team allocated different foundation models on Amazon Bedrock across components based on each stage’s requirements. Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 powers the Model Selector and Generator. These components require strong reasoning for accurate query construction. Amazon Nova 2 Lite handles the Guardrail and Validator, where fast inference at lower cost is prioritized. Amazon Titan provides embeddings for semantic search in the Example Retrieval component. Cohere Rerank 3.5 reranks retrieved candidates to maximize relevance. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
Maximizing relevance and diversity in example retrieval
Example retrieval emerged as the single biggest accuracy lever in the pipeline. Strong examples teach the Generator how to translate questions into Sonar queries more efficiently than schema alone, so the Orca team benchmarked several retrieval strategies on Amazon Bedrock. Each strategy traded off relevance, diversity, or speed in a different way, and comparing them directly showed which combination worked best.
Pure top-K semantic search on Amazon Titan embeddings performed quickly, but it tended to return near-duplicate examples that starved the Generator of diversity. Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) improved diversity, but it traded off relevance when the top candidate was actually the right answer. Retrieving a larger candidate set and then reranking it pulled in a broader pool and used a reranker to select the most relevant subset, which pointed toward the winning approach.
The winner was top-20 nearest-neighbor retrieval using Amazon Titan embeddings. Orca then reranked these results with Cohere Rerank 3.5 down to the top five. This approach gives the Generator a small, diverse, highly relevant set of examples without forcing a trade-off between coverage and precision at retrieval time.
Loading over 900 models into context
A core constraint shaped the architecture. It wasn’t feasible to include 900+ Sonar model schemas into every prompt. Even with long-context models, doing so degrades both cost and accuracy.
The Model Selector resolves this. Running on Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5, it works against compact, semantically rich representations of each model (name, purpose, key fields, and key relationships). Given the user’s question, it returns only the models the Generator actually needs. The Generator then receives full schema detail only for those selected models plus the relationships that connect them.
Evaluation methodology
To iterate confidently, the Orca team built a continuous evaluation harness early in the project. The harness combines a curated dataset, an automated scoring layer, and a slice-based measurement approach so the team can trust every change before it ships. Together these elements turn evaluation into a routine step rather than an afterthought.
The curated evaluation dataset spans the question types, model families, and complexity tiers seen in production, so it reflects real usage. An LLM-as-judge scoring layer grades generated queries on correctness, completeness, and semantic equivalence to a reference query, which gives the team a consistent quality signal. The measurement methodology then breaks deltas down by slice, allowing the team to identify exactly where regressions occur and what to correct.
Every change to a prompt, a model, a retrieval parameter, or an example flows through the harness before it ships to production.
Domain-expert-in-the-loop labeling system for continuous improvement
Sustaining accuracy as customer environments evolve and new question patterns emerge required more than a strong initial deployment. The Orca team built an internal labeling tool for product managers, support engineers, and security researchers. With the tool, they can flag queries, correct outputs, and push corrections into the example bank in one action. Furthermore, the system automatically collects production queries with low-confidence matching examples and routes them to the appropriate domain expert for daily labeling. The next pipeline run retrieves the new example through Cohere Rerank 3.5, and accuracy on that class of question improves the same moment, with no deployment.
        “The labeling UI is the single most important investment we made for long-term quality. It turns Discovery AI from a static deployment into a living system, with our domain experts continuously improving it inside their normal workflow.”
— Or Gabay, Director of AI, Orca Security
Combined with end-to-end pipeline observability and shared dashboards spanning product, engineering, and customer-facing teams, this feedback loop is what keeps Discovery AI improving after initial launch.
Results
After deploying Discovery AI to production, the new solution outperformed the initial baseline across cost, latency, and accuracy. Input token usage fell by 93 percent, from approximately 2 million tokens down to 140,000 per comparable workload. Overall cost fell by 90 percent, driven by that lower token consumption together with per-stage model allocation across Amazon Bedrock.
Latency also improved, with end-to-end response times dropping by 75 percent, from approximately 60 seconds to 15 seconds. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries also improved, measured continuously through the team’s evaluation harness.
Discovery AI now handles thousands of queries per day in production since March 2026, with internal subject matter experts and customer feedback validating quality.
Conclusion
In this post, we shared how Orca Security built Discovery AI on Amazon Bedrock. The solution reduced query costs by 90 percent, input token usage by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. The solution combines several key technologies. These include RAG-based example retrieval with Cohere Rerank 3.5, per-stage model allocation across Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 and Amazon Nova 2 Lite, and semantic search powered by Amazon Titan. Additionally, a continuous human-in-the-loop labeling system provides ongoing improvement. This combination allowed Orca to turn a working prototype into a production-grade solution that is both cheaper to run and more accurate.
To get started building similar solutions, explore Amazon Bedrock for foundation model (FM) access, Cohere Rerank on Amazon Bedrock for retrieval optimization, and Amazon Titan for embeddings. To learn more about Orca Security’s cloud security tool, visit orca.security.
To learn more about how Orca Security applies AI across its framework, see how Orca drives security outcomes with AI and how Orca secures AI adoption, including Amazon Bedrock.
For more on the techniques used in this post, read related posts on the AWS Machine Learning Blog.

articles.title: Nárnia: O Sobrinho do Mago ganha primeiro trailer e já tem data de estreia; assista
articles.text:
O primeiro trailer de Nárnia: O Sobrinho do Mago, novo filme dirigido por Greta Gerwig, foi divulgado nesta terça-feira (13). Baseada na obra de C.S. Lewis, a produção apresenta a origem do mundo fantástico de Nárnia e tem estreia prevista nos cinemas para 12 de fevereiro de 2027, antes de chegar à Netflix em 2 de abril do mesmo ano.
A história acompanha Digory e Polly, duas crianças que descobrem o Bosque entre os Mundos, uma passagem para diferentes lugares fantásticos. A prévia mostra os protagonistas explorando esses ambientes após receberem um anel mágico de Andrew Ketterley, personagem interpretado por Daniel Craig, conhecido como o mágico que dá nome ao livro.
O trailer também apresenta criaturas e personagens importantes da trama, como Jadis, interpretada por Emma Mackey. Ela é a futura Feiticeira Branca, última rainha de Charn. Outro destaque é Aslan, o leão mítico que dá vida a Nárnia e tem voz de Meryl Streep. A prévia utiliza a música “Stairway to Heaven”, da banda Led Zeppelin, para acompanhar as imagens.
Em entrevista durante um evento de apresentação do trailer em Nova York, Gerwig contou que cresceu conhecendo os livros de Lewis e que sugeriu à Netflix começar a adaptação pela história de O Sobrinho do Mago. A diretora também explicou que procurou milhares de audições gravadas durante meses até escolher David McKenna e Beatrice Campbell para os papéis centrais.
O longa será o primeiro filme de Gerwig desde Barbie, lançado em 2023, e marca uma mudança na estratégia da Netflix: será o primeiro título da plataforma a receber lançamento mundial nos cinemas antes da estreia no serviço de streaming. A diretora afirmou que a música é um elemento central da produção, que deseja aproximar de uma ópera rock.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Europe cannot be sovereign without control of its own AI | EU-Startups
articles.text:
AI is steadily being integrated further into the systems and workflows that run many European businesses. What was once a tool for analysing information and assisting employees with basic administrative tasks, is now an integral part of how many of these businesses operate.
The problem with Europe’s growing dependence on AI, is that much of the technology they are dependent upon comes from elsewhere.
The companies producing the most sophisticated AI models and supporting infrastructure are concentrated heavily in the US and China, giving them huge influence over the technology that is becoming so important to the global economy. That influence is becoming more significant as these nations continue to develop competing AI ecosystems, with their rivalry increasingly tied to their wider geopolitical interests.
Recent reports suggest that the US is preparing to tell dozens of countries to choose between rival US and China-led AI ecosystems, and China last week called for countries to respect their “digital sovereignty”. AI sovereignty is no longer an abstract debate. We are watching AI divide along geopolitical lines in real time, and Europe is now at risk of becoming a customer of whichever superpower controls the intelligence it relies upon.
Europe needs choice, not complete self-sufficiency
The vulnerability this presents was arguably already demonstrated in June, when the US ordered Anthropic to restrict foreign nationals’ access to its most advanced AI models, prompting European concern about how reliant businesses and governments could become on American frontier AI.
For Europe, the question is how much autonomy will it have to make its own decisions as this divide widens?
Europe should be able to use the best models available, wherever they might be developed, but it cannot build its economy on imported AI that might get cut off.
This is not to say that Europe needs to be completely self-sufficient in AI, but it needs enough choice to switch suppliers and maintain viable alternatives.
That choice becomes more important as AI continues to become embedded into the everyday running of businesses.
In July, The European Commission launched a call for up to seven AI Gigafactories, backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding and intended to unlock at least €20 billion in private investment.
However, the question of sovereignty goes beyond the models themselves, it also extends to the knowledge businesses create through AI.
Businesses risk renting back their own knowledge
Every time an employee uses AI, they are writing down how their work gets done, often for the first time. The companies that hold onto that knowledge can use it to fuel their AI transformation. But many risk handing it to their vendors, teaching them how to commoditise their businesses, and will end up renting back their own know-how.
The consequences of this extend beyond technology. AI will shape which companies become most productive and which industries adapt quickest. If European companies are importing these capabilities from foreign entities, the value created will likely flow outside of Europe, also.
This creates a different type of dependency. A business might be able to switch model or supplier, but separating from a system that has spent years learning its processes and organisational knowledge is much more difficult. The longer a business spends building its operations around external AI providers, the harder it will be to separate themselves from it.
For startups and scale-ups, this is particularly important. Their advantage often lies in their specialist knowledge, their understanding of a problem and the distinctive way they carry out their work. If that knowledge becomes trapped within an external platform, they risk giving away part of what makes the business valuable.
This does not mean that European businesses need to stop using foreign AI. This is unrealistic, and also poses the threat of Europe falling further behind.
Europe’s opportunity is applied AI
Europe’s opportunity instead lies in building on top of these models and turning them into systems that are designed around the needs of its own businesses. This is where European businesses can build intellectual property and competitive advantage around AI, even if the technology is developed elsewhere.
The opportunity is also in building the infrastructure that lets businesses use different models, without rebuilding their systems each time the market changes. This flexibility can help businesses avoid vendor dependency and maintain greater control over how they use AI.
This applied layer is where AI is connected to a company’s systems and put to work. It is also where businesses can govern what agents are allowed to do, monitor their actions, test their performance and investigate when something goes wrong. Europe may not lead every part of the race to build the largest model, but it can lead in making AI safe, accountable and useful for the companies deploying it.
Europe has a large industrial base, strong expertise across sectors, and businesses that understand their own processes better than any general-purpose model ever could.
Sovereignty means control and continuity: control over what AI agents can do, ownership of the workflows and knowledge they create, and the freedom to choose or change the underlying technology.
Europe has the talent, industry and trust to become a genuine power in AI, but that does not mean it has to be a distant third participant.
It must be the counterbalance to this race: deploy its talent and expertise into the applied layer, and build systems that are safe, sovereign and equitable by design, for the benefit of everyone, not just those in Europe.
We need AI that works for us, not the other way around. Building a sovereign applied AI layer that can be deployed in good faith, creating productivity and lasting values for businesses across the globe, is Europe’s decisive opportunity in this race.

articles.title: UK workers are handling personal tasks during work hours — and they say it makes them more productive
articles.text:
UK workers are handling personal tasks during work hours — and they say it makes them more productive
UK workers are spending more time taking personal breaks
- Half of UK workers admit to taking personal breaks daily, four in five take 30 to 120 minutes
- Household chores and personal errands are the most common activities
- European workers take fewer breaks and spend less time on them
New research has claimed three in four (76%) UK employees handle personal tasks during working hours at least a few times a week, with half (48%) doing so every single working day, but it might not be such a bad thing.
The vast majority (86%) of respondents in a new LiveCareer study reported that taking short personal breaks during working hours actually helps to improve overall productivity, with a further 11% seeing no meaningful impact. That leaves just 3% who believe there could be harmful effects.
In fact, only 5% of workers choose never to handle personal tasks during working hours, challenging traditional definitions of productivity at work.
Taking personal breaks at work helps to improve productivity
Spread across the working day, nearly three in five (57%) spend between 30 and 60 minutes on personal tasks, with another one in five (19%) spending between one and two hours.
And by far the leading distraction are household chores (54%) and personal errands (51%), which are likely most synonymous with hybrid and remote working.
But despite illustrating just how widespread personal breaks, LiveCareer's data reveals some interesting geographical differences, positioning the UK in a totally different ballpark to other European countries.
While around half (48%) of British workers take personal breaks daily, only around a quarter (27%) of European employees do the same. The figures also point to European workers spending less time on breaks when they do take them.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
What the report fails to note is just how productive workers are from each country, to detail whether taking personal breaks has a positive or negative impact on work, however British workers are clearly redefining what productivity looks like in a hybrid working landscape thanks to the added flexibility.
"For employers, the findings suggest that occasional personal breaks are no longer viewed by employees as time lost but as part of a more sustainable approach to managing work and life throughout the day," the report concludes.
