articles.title: Muere RJ Mitte, el hijo de Walter White en 'Breaking Bad', a los 34 años
articles.text:
El actor RJ Mitte, conocido principalmente por su papel de Walter Jr. en la serie de Breaking Bad, ha fallecido este lunes 12 de octubre a los 34 años. El intérprete, que vivió con parálisis cerebral, se había convertido en todo un icono en la lucha por los derechos de las perdonas con discapacidad.
Tal y como han confirmado sus representantes a la prensa, el RJ Mitte se ha suicidado en su domicilio en Brownsville, Texas. Según el reporte de la agencia Associated Press, la jueza de paz del condado de Cameron, Cyndi Hinojosa, declaró la muerte de Mitte alrededor de las 13:30 hora local del lunes. Próximamente se le practicará la autopsia.
"Con profunda tristeza comunicamos el trágico fallecimiento del querido actor, filántropo y apasionado defensor de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad RJ Mitte", anunciaban sus representantes en un comunicado. A su vez, destacaban el papel de Walter Jr. en Breaking Bad. "Aportó autenticidad al papel y creó una plataforma para la sensibilización sobre la discapacidad y la inclusión", añaden.
Muere RJ Mitte, el eterno Walter Jr. de Breaking Bad
RJ Mitte interpretó a Walter Jr. en Breaking Bad durante los 5 años que la serie estuvo en emisión, entre 2008 y 2013. El título es considerado a día de hoy una de las mejores series de todos los tiempos. Ganó 16 Premios Emmy y obtuvo un total de 58 nominaciones. Mitte fue parte fundamental de su elenco, que en 2014 ganó el premio a mejor reparto de una serie dramática en los SAG Awards, los galardones entregados por el Sindicato de Actores.
Antes de aquella serie, ya había tenido algunas apariciones esporádicas y papeles menores y puntuales en proyectos como Hannah Montana y Vegas. Pero su irrupción en la industria con Breaking Bad fue lo que llevó a RJ Mitte a construir una carrera como actor. En 2014 apareció en la serie Cambiadas al nacer, aunque algunos de sus otros papeles más destacados han llegaod en esta década. Por ejemplo, las películas Triumph (2021) junto a Terrance Howard, Love Me Dead (2024) junto a Dove Cameron o la reciente Westhampton (2025) junto a Finn Wittrock. También la serie Los guardianes de la justicia (2022).

articles.title: The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
articles.text:
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school.
The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.
NHTSA:
The Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) received a DP on September 23, 2026, requesting an investigation into model year (MY) 2026 Tesla Robotaxis (Model Y and Cybercab) with the Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged. The Petitioner alleges that the ADS exceeds posted speed limits in active school zones.
The Cybercab launched earlier this year, and is already under investigation for its lack of side mirrors, pedals, and a steering wheel. NHTSA has also opened an investigation into Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system for traffic violations, like blowing past red lights and driving on the wrong side of the street.

articles.title: Dominion Dynamics strikes deal to build Ukrainian uncrewed ground vehicles in Canada | BetaKit
articles.text:
Dominion Dynamics has struck a partnership that will send uncrewed ground vehicles from Canada to Ukraine’s front lines.
The news: The Ottawa-based defence contractor signed a memorandum of understanding with Ukrainian defence tech firm Tencore at the Association of the United States Army defence conference in Washington, DC, on Tuesday afternoon. The agreement will see Dominion Dynamics manufacture Tencore’s TerMIT uncrewed ground vehicle in Canada and integrate its AuraNet command-and-control platform to Ukraine’s front lines.
The TerMIT is a modular light armour vehicle that can be modified for logistics, evacuation, or weaponry, and operate without a human on board. Tencore claims it has delivered more than 5,000 uncrewed ground vehicles to Ukrainian military units since 2024.
From the source: “Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback, and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale,” Tencore co-founder Roman Tkachenko said in a statement. “Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles.”
The context: Since launching in June 2025, Dominion Dynamics has raised $169 million CAD to become an explicitly Canadian competitor to big-name defence contractors like Lockheed Martin. Earlier this year, it raised a $139-million CAD Series A round and moved into a 25,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Ottawa’s west end.
The Tencore agreement comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy struck a 100-year partnership and drone collaboration agreement last month. As part of the partnership, Carney committed Canada to producing millions of drones within the next two years, with one third of those earmarked for Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
Hamilton-based drone company Sentinel R&D has inked similar deals with the Ukrainians and faced threats from Russian officials as a result. Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence told BetaKit in an email that his company isn’t concerned about potential threats, and that it “will never be afraid of defending democracy and western values.”
Final thought: While the companies are still ironing out a definitive agreement, Dominion Dynamics said initial TerMIT production is planned for 2027, following Tencore transferring its technology and training technicians in Canada. Dominion also said it is aiming to develop an “Arctic-hardened” version of the TerMIT for Canadian operations and to export to NATO allies.
Feature image courtesy Dominion Dynamics via X.

articles.title: 'Companies do realize that they need to do a better job of earning consumers' trust, not letting them feel like there's an invasion of privacy’: I asked Bose's President of Premium Audio why the company released $99 wired earbuds with no app, Bluetooth or AI in 2026 — 'There's definitely something larger happening'
articles.text:
‘There's definitely been a return to less technologically driven products’: Bose president Raza Haider talks releasing $99 wired earbuds with no app or AI, and why they're only here because his daughter thinks they’re cool
‘There's definitely something larger happening …and there's something oddly satisfying about this lovely silicone wire’
- Bose recently launched $99 / £99 'Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds'
- Also, Bose is 'happy to take credit for making open-ear mass market'
- Bose's President of Premium Audio spoke to me about both developments
Last month was huge for Bose's earbuds output, thanks to the release of not one but two successors to the excellent Bose Ultra Open, a delightfully emo collab on the company's flagship cans and a set of wired, inexpensive earbuds that boast ANC, controlled by the inline remote.
So hang on, on the one hand we've got an evolution on a groundbreaking, clip-style, wire-free product Bose pioneered just over two years ago, (something President Raza Haider says he's "happy to take credit for — making open-ear mass market"). And on the other hand we have… wired earbuds like it's 2003?
Yes. And Bose President of Premium Audio, Raza Haider, is happy to talk about the nostalgia-driven technology trend many of us are seeing. After all, who could forget the various 'digital detox' resolves at the start of the year, compounded by the advent of the great privacy revolt concerning glasses, TVs and even wireless earbuds that want to know a little too much about us?
I start off asking Haider simply, "Who knew wired earbuds would be so popular in 2026?"
"Right? I know", Haider laughs. "It was a funny story actually. Over the last three, four years, the team's done a really good job of being able to capture insights and turn them into products much faster than we historically were able to.
"So the idea [for the wired earbuds] actually came a year and a half ago, when I was dropping my daughter off at university. We saw them everywhere. And my daughter was like, 'You know, these are the coolest things ever.'
"And she's like, 'A year ago, we would have made fun of kids who had wired products, and now we all wear them.' So we came back and as a group back in the office, we're like, 'You know, we should do something about it.'
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"We saw the trend, but we saw that all the products in the market didn't have great quality audio — none of them had noise cancellation. So, typical Bose, we wanted to redesign something that was a big part of our history and DNA, and bring back something a little bit more retro, a little bit more fun.
"It's a little bit of an homage. I don't know if you remember the old Bose [wired earbuds], it had the little block in the middle, so we kept the block, except it's more like retro color blocks versus the large, big thing.
"These launch in Europe on the 15th October, but we launched them for presale in America on Monday. It is now Wednesday, and they're gone. They're sold out."
'Something is definitely happening'
I'm always keen for presidents of audio companies to talk to me about any trends they're seeing. Haider doesn't shy away from telling me how much he thinks this particular trend might stem from buyers avoiding apps that require data collection, as well as trying to bypass the more intrusive aspects AI.
Is that why people are heading back to wires? "There's two dimensions to it. One, there is something larger happening, whether it sticks or doesn't," he said. "You used the term 'digital detox' — now whether it's trust or whatever it is, there's something happening.
"Most tech companies will figure out a way around it. There's no way we're going to back away from technology — the technology is here to stay. But companies, I think, do realize that they need to do a better job of earning consumers' trust, not letting them feel like there's an invasion of privacy. So I think one part is definitely that, there's a return to less technologically driven products. That being said, there's a lot of tech in these that makes these great, right?"
He shows me the earbuds and I have to agree, they're pretty cool. But Haider isn't done. "The second part is this: there is a certain convenience and almost comfort in this," he continued, "and I think this is where technology actually should help.
"So, you can leave these in your bag for weeks on end and never lose a charge, never worry about a connection, never have to worry about a sensitive area. You just pull them out and you plug them into your phone physically. There's no app, no settings, and you just go — that's it!
"There's something oddly satisfying about taking this lovely silicone wire, playing around with your hands, hearing the physical click into the interface; you've got actual buttons for volume, and so it's just oddly fun."
'I think the average consumer doesn't know what a Bluetooth codec is, and they couldn't care less'
I ask Haider how much he thinks the knowledge that Bluetooth codecs (however improved) still can't quite compete with wired audio for resolution plays a factor in the wired trend? Or is it simply that physical media is having a moment and if you've got a CD Walkman, you want wired buds?
"It's both", he answers. "I think the average consumer doesn't even know what a Bluetooth codec is, and they couldn't care less. All they know is that when they have a wireless headphone, it sometimes drops out, and this doesn't.
"That goes back to my earlier point; it's reinforcing to technology companies that technology needs to work in a way that's invisible to consumers. The days of people using technology just for technology's sake? We've moved past that for certain categories.
"It also goes back to my point on re-plumbing our company's operating model and product development to be able to move faster to capitalize on trends, because there always will be trends.
"The trend of wired now? There'll be a trend for something else. There are trends for colors too. We've done a great job over the last couple of years of launching I think 60 colors to take advantage of that. Companies have to be a lot more nimbler in listening and adapting to consumer trends."
Let's be completely open
As well as literally writing the book on active noise cancellation, Bose pioneered what I like to call the 'ear cuff style' open earbuds, with the Bose Ultra Open. To be clear, this was in February 2024, a time when nobody else was doing that.
Did Haider anticipate how popular that particular design would become, and why does he think production of such designs has skyrocketed since? "Yeah! I think as a category overall, it's like the fastest growing category in consumer wearables, right?" he said. "We saw there was a huge need for people to have an alternative to in-ear products.
"For many reasons, starting from the obvious simple logic, in-ear products don't fit in everyone's ear. Some people don't like jamming stuff in their ear. Then, there are many instances where you want to actually be more aware of your surroundings, where it's actually safer to be aware of your surroundings. You're walking home late night, you're going for a run, you're out walking the dog, you want to hear the cars, the roads, the fire trucks.
"There are also many places where there's a social cue — where having one earbud in is disrespectful, people don't engage with you, you lose the human connection. But having a cue or clip which looks and feels like jewelry? It feels more inviting, you don't feel disconnected.
"And so as a result of that, we took a bunch of technology we had, and we spent a lot of time actually designing that cuff, much more than the 10 months it took for the wired earbuds.
"We were very deliberate about form, fit, feel, design, design intent and look. And when we launched it, people actually asked us whether this would take off, whether people would understand what it is, whether it'd be alienating, would men want to wear something that looks like jewelry? Our answer was, 'We don't know. We've heard our consumers, they said they wanted it, we're giving them an option for something new.'
"And the best thing that can happen is, everyone copies us. And that's what happened. In the last two years, this thing has blown up."
La vie en Bose?
Our time together is coming to an end, but I'm keen to ask where Haider, as head of a market leader and pioneer in the portable audio space, thinks consumer audio will be in 10 years?
"Given how fast things are changing now, it seems almost impossible to make a prediction," he said. "But let me give you a few just general trends, right? There's always a nostalgia-driven customer, and companies have to be positioned to be able to successfully capitalize on trends.
"Companies well-positioned to capitalize on trends will be at an advantage. But from a tech standpoint — especially with what's happening right now with AI and the pace at which things are getting smarter — I think you'll see edge or wearable devices becoming a lot more intelligent and contextually aware of what a user wants to do.
"As a result, I think you're going to see a lot more fragmentation in the combination of things a user puts on their body, to optimize something that they're passionate about.
"People will soon realize that most of us have a passion point around something. For some people it might be music, for some it might be health and fitness, for some might be wellness, some might be an active lifestyle, some might be content creation, some might be creating and producing.
"And for all of those people, there's a different set of both awareness and sensory capture and sensory orchestration, let's say, that will allow you to do what you're passionate about better. And companies that realize that, and deliver something that's more consumer and passion point-centric, win.
"So, what my daughter will want to do with the combination of her earbuds, her phone, and her watch would be very different than what you and I might want to do, which will be different from someone who wants to go on a run, which will be different from someone who might be interviewing someone at a concert."
It's an insightful and hopeful look at a more tailored wearable future. Will we still be embracing wires, or will wireless audio finally be hi-res enough (and carefree enough) to be the better standard? Time will tell. But as a daughter myself, I for one really hope the people in charge will always listen to theirs.

articles.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Bahn, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global.
Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand, an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets.
In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1).
Business challenge
The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part.
The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch:
- Employees posted more than 1,500 threads, and volume kept growing.
- With employees in the US, UK, Spain, Poland, Australia, and the Philippines, more than a fifth of questions arrived outside US business hours.
- Answers were split across different places: Confluence articles, intranet pages and PDFs, IT-maintained guides, and the channel’s own history.
- Repetitive questions consumed time that structured self-service steps could have handled.
        “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’”
— Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global
Solution overview
Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers.
The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2:
- Slack service: A FastAPI and Slack Bolt application, hosted on AWS App Runner. It receives Slack events, decides whether the bot should respond, and builds a user-context payload from the requester’s Slack profile, including name, email, time zone, and manager.
- Agent service: A Strands agent, deployed as a container on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, manages the multi-turn tool agent loop using Anthropic’s Claude in Amazon Bedrock.
- Tools and knowledge: A single AWS Lambda function, exposed as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, classifies requests, creates and updates Jira tickets, and analyzes images. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base indexes content from Confluence, the company intranet, Slack, and marketing pages, storing it in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
- Operations and feedback. Amazon DynamoDB stores feedback, AWS X-Ray traces request paths using OpenTelemetry, and the services log to Amazon CloudWatch.
When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4).
Deckhand workflow
This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment.
Prerequisites
To implement this pattern, you need the following:
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore runtime, and AgentCore Gateway.
- A Slack app with event subscriptions, a signing secret, and a bot token scoped to your use case.
- A container image registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
- An Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.
- AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles scoped to each runtime and tool, and AWS Secrets Manager entries for third-party credentials.
Building the agent with Strands Agents and AgentCore
The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK, an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python.
The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code.
Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild.
AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically.
Knowledge base design and answer routing
Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources:
- Articles synced from Confluence.
- Internal pages, PDFs, and events synced from the company intranet.
- Resolved support threads mined from Slack (covered in the next section).
Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office.
Mining Slack history with Recursive Language Models (RLMs)
The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. Indexing an unverified fix or a garbled summary means the knowledge base surfaces an incorrect answer with the same confidence as a correct one, so extraction needs to be precise.
The mining process follows a three-stage pipeline (Figure 5):
- A script exports the channel’s full history via the Slack API, retrieving complete replies for every thread and writing a structured dump that includes thread markers, timestamps, and reply counts.
- DSPy’s Recursive Language Model (RLM), running Claude on Amazon Bedrock, treats that export as a navigable memory space inside a sandboxed Python read-eval-print loop (REPL) rather than a single prompt. Working iteratively over the data, it classifies each thread as resolved, unresolved, or escalated and filters out announcements and non-questions. Strict criteria keep quality high: a thread counts as resolved only when the full, workable fix is visible in the thread itself.
- For each resolved thread, the RLM orchestrates recursive sub-LLM (large language model) calls to extract structured fields, each validated against a Pydantic model. The fields include an issue summary, the original question, and the resolution. They also capture whether the fix is self-service or needs a ticket, the self-service steps, the application and system involved, error messages, and tags. When a sub-LLM call returns something that fails the schema, the RLM’s code-based loop catches the validation error in the interpreter and retries. The results are written as a markdown document organized by issue. The pipeline uploads it to Amazon S3 for the knowledge base to index.
We chose RLM because it maintains the entire Slack history in a persistent sandbox variable space, allowing iterative reasoning over the export and consistent output structure. As a result, when an employee encounters a problem previously solved by a colleague, Deckhand provides the proven solution, often as actionable, numbered steps.
Knowing when not to answer
An AI bot in a shared channel fails socially before it fails technically. Deckhand’s most refined logic decides when to stay quiet:
- The agent’s first decision on every message is whether it’s an announcement, a social message, or a conversation between people. If so, it outputs “SKIP,” and the Slack service suppresses the reply.
- In threads, it replies only to the original poster.
- If the last reply came from another human helper, it stays silent, because a person has taken over.
- If a reply starts by @naming a person, the message isn’t for the bot.
Collecting feedback
Each answer includes feedback buttons. A thumbs-up is recorded directly, while a thumbs-down prompts a brief “what went wrong” field. Ratings are stored in DynamoDB with the original question and the bot’s response.
Negative feedback is a valuable dataset used to improve the system prompt and agent behavior, and to update incorrect knowledge base information.
Security and validation
Prompt rules enhance behavior but do not replace access controls. Enforcement is managed through code and infrastructure:
- Ticket creation requires explicit confirmation. When Deckhand offers to create a ticket, the Slack service adds a Create Ticket button, and selecting it sends confirmation through the agent. Ticket updates only accept valid keys matching the helpdesk project pattern and reject empty comments.
- Classification is validated before it acts. Request classification runs as a separate Amazon Bedrock Converse API call that returns structured ticket fields, validated with Pydantic before anything reaches Jira.
- The image tool is restricted to downloading only from Slack’s file host. It authenticates with the bot token, limits each request to five images of up to 5 MB each, and sends the files to a vision model using the Converse API.
- Credentials stay out of code. Slack tokens, the signing secret, and Jira credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager, and each service and tool runs under its own scoped IAM role.
- The prompt enforces behavioral safeguards: never request passwords or multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, never write credentials in ticket comments, and never expose profile metadata used for ticket fields.
Outcome
Deckhand launched in April 2026. It started at about 30 messages a day and reached as many as 100 by early summer. In its first three months it handled 1,935 messages, started 1,221 agent conversations, and opened 409 Jira tickets. It replied to 97.5 percent of messages. A third of the questions came in after hours, when no one on the IT team was working, and Deckhand answered 94 percent of those. People who would have waited until the next morning got an answer that night.
Feedback improved as the team worked on it. Positive ratings went from 82 percent in April to 96 percent in June, after they revised the system prompt and knowledge base to fix what people complained about.
The clearest win was ticket deflection. An agent conversation is a question that would otherwise have become a Jira ticket. Of the 1,221 conversations, only 409 turned into tickets. The other 812 were handled in chat. Filing a ticket and then working and closing it runs about 30 minutes. Those 812 conversations add up to roughly 406 hours over three months, or around 1,600 hours a year. Employees kept that time for their own work, and IT never spent it on intake.
Conclusion
Deckhand took repetitive IT questions off people’s plates and gave the time back to employees and the IT team. It works because each part of the stack has one job and runs as a managed service: AgentCore runtime hosts the agent, AgentCore Gateway turns a Lambda function into MCP tools the agent can call, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles retrieval. The team shipped it without standing up servers or maintaining orchestration code.
To build a similar solution, begin with a well-maintained knowledge source and a clearly defined action. Refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and Strands Agents SDK for agent development, and the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation for connecting content sources.
To discuss an agentic AI use case for your organization, contact your AWS account team.

articles.title: Apollyon Dynamics quits building drones to make defencetech for the military
articles.text:
Apollyon Dynamics quits building drones to make defencetech for the military
Hyderabad-based student startup Apollyon Dynamics sold drones worth over Rs 1.5 crore last year. It has now moved to a jet-powered target drone, a multirotor interceptor, and a marine unmanned system.
When Jayant Khatri and Sourya Choudhury started in May 2025, the focus of the Hyderabad-based defencetech startup was building drones. Its early portfolio included trainer, endurance, multirole, and FPV systems, with the company selling drones worth more than Rs 1.5 crore last year.
But foresight prevails over immediate success. Anticipating saturation in the market, Apollyon has now pivoted.
“We have stopped building regular drones. Instead, we have completely shifted towards making higher value products,” says Khatri, Co-founder and CEO of Apollyon Dynamics.
The founder says the conventional drone market had become too crowded, with limited room for differentiation. “It’s basically a race to the bottom now. People are just assembling stuff. That included us as well. There’s not a lot of value addition,” he says.
The startup’s current portfolio has been rebuilt around three core products: Nightshade, Ahuti Mk II, and Project Piranha.
Apollyon now has around 20 full-time employees, two manufacturing labs, and an office in Hyderabad.
The new defencetech portfolio
Khatri says Nightshade is a jet-powered platform that can be configured as a target drone, decoy, or loitering munition. The company has already conducted multiple tests. “We were the first company in India to launch it from top of a car, a jet-powered system,” he says.
The startup plans to begin supplying pilot batches of the target-drone variant to the Indian Army by December, while trials of the loitering-munition version are expected to begin next year.
Nightshade's three configurations are designed for different battlefield roles. The target-drone variant is intended to simulate threats during air-defence training, while its decoys can help identify enemy radar positions. The loitering-munition variant combines a jet-powered platform with components typically associated with more expensive missile systems.
Khatri says that Apollyon has also repurposed Ahuti, its earlier flagship drone, into an interceptor.
“After several iterations, it has reached a top speed of 498 kmph, making it the fastest multirotor drone in India. The India Book of Records has certified this,” shares the CEO, adding that the platform is part of a Make II programme (a special system used by the Indian army to build military hardware) and is being developed with defence partners.
Project Piranha expands Apollyon's ambitions beyond aerial systems. The company hasn’t revealed much about it, only that it is a marine-based unmanned system.
“We wanted to make a family of products, a family of unmanned systems, and we don’t want to be just known as a UAV-making company,” Khatri says. “We want to be a proper defencetech company with multiple products in our portfolio.”
The evolving industry of military tech
Apollyon has also stopped selling its mobile drone lab and is instead integrating its systems into command-centre products with companies like the Noida-based Raphe mPhibr and Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space in a collaborative effort. Raphe and Dhruva Space are also customers of Apollyon; they buy Ahuti interceptors.
In June 2026, the startup had conducted a pre-seed round raising $480,000 led by Naandi Ventures. The startup is now looking to raise $5 million through a seed round within the next six months.
Started as a drone-making student startup, Apollyon’s ambition is now considerably larger: developing cruise-missile-class systems capable of carrying thousands of kilograms and travelling at least Mach 1 by 2030. M R M Babu, who led DRDO’s Agni-V missile programme, has joined as an advisor to help with hiring, programme planning and fund allocation.
For 21-year-old Khatri, collaboration will be important as Indian defence companies become larger. “If we want to survive, we can’t do it alone,” he says. “Others have realised that too and have become a lot more collaborative. It’s a good thing for the long term.”
Apollyon Dynamics is part of YourStory’s Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India’s most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: El motivo para temer a la IA no es que nos extinga a todos, es lo que acaba de pasarle a 300 supermercados franceses
articles.text:
La noche del domingo al lunes, los frigoríficos de cientos de supermercados franceses se descongelaron a la vez. Alguien activó a distancia los ciclos de desescarche de sus controladores. El ataque alcanzó al menos 300 establecimientos de Intermarché y Netto, más de 100 de Coopérative U y varios de E.Leclerc; Carrefour ha comunicado 80 supermercados afectados.
No sabemos quién lo hizo ni si hubo IA implicada. Pero lo importante de este caso no depende de eso. Porque es un ejemplo de manual de lo que ya permite la IA.
Por qué es importante. Cuando hablamos de los riesgos de la IA pensamos en cosas de película de ciencia-ficción. Pero el problema real, el que ya podemos ver este año, se parece más a este caso: algo medio aburrido, físico y barato de hacer, pero con consecuencias destructivas.
El contexto. El fallo no es nuevo. Danfoss, el fabricante de los controladores, ha reconocido que algunos de los controladores afectados ya no reciben actualizaciones, y que ya hubo ataques parecidos en supermercados de Rusia e Israel en 2022.
La diferencia con aquellos ataques es la escala. Antes eran casos sueltos, pero ahora hablamos de más de 500 tiendas en una noche.
Entre líneas. Estos aparatos llevan años “protegidos” porque atacarlos daba mucha pereza: había que encontrarlos uno a uno, entender un software extraño y adaptar el ataque a cada versión. Ese trabajo tedioso, casi disuasorio, es justo lo que la IA abarata.
UN VISTAZO A...
Anthropic lo contó en su informe de septiembre: los atacantes ya le pasan fases enteras del ataque a la IA, y eso acerca mucho lo que puede hacer un grupo pequeño a lo que antes solo podía hacer alguien con muchos recursos, alguien como un Estado.
Y ni siquiera hace falta mala intención. A un modelo de OpenAI en pruebas le pidieron hace unos meses buscar datos de gasto en medicamentos en Australia. Acabó colándose en un portal sanitario, ejecutando comandos y llevándose archivos y credenciales. La propia OpenAI tardó meses en enterarse.
No es la primera vez. En agosto, en una base militar de Arizona, todos los congeladores se pusieron en modo desescarche a la vez durante la noche. Pasó en tiendas de bases de al menos nueve estados casi al mismo tiempo.
No hay ninguna conexión demostrada con Francia y es muy posible que no la haya, pero el truco es el mismo, en dos continentes, con dos meses de diferencia.
Sí, pero. El problema de fondo no es solo la IA, es el ritmo:
- El que ataca va a velocidad de software. El que defiende, a velocidad de hardware.
- Un controlador viejo a menudo no se arregla con una actualización OTA sin más: hay que cambiarlo, tienda por tienda, con un técnico.
- Hemos conectado a Internet dispositivos pensados para durar veinte años justo cuando atacarlos se ha vuelto muy fácil.
En resumen. Lo que ha protegido a esta infraestructura durante todos estos años era que atacarla era viable, pero costaba mucho esfuerzo y el "premio" no compensaba. La IA va de quitar esfuerzo. Por eso el riesgo no va a llegar con una máquina que decide hacernos daño, sino con algo mucho más tonto: que hacernos daño entre nosotros sea cada vez más fácil.
Imagen | Jack Lee
