articles.title: The Xteink X4 Pro is a great, tiny e-reader, and it’s cheaper than ever
articles.text:
If you’re looking for an e-reader that can easily fit in your pocket (or snap onto your magnet-equipped phone), the tiny Xteink X4 Pro might be worth a look. It features a 4.26-inch, 800 x 480 E Ink display, making it significantly smaller and thinner than Amazon’s smallest six-inch Kindle. It’s also quite a bit cheaper. Right now, you can pick it up for $84.15 ($25 off) at Amazon, which is its best price to date.
The Xteink X4 Pro is a great, tiny e-reader, and it’s cheaper than ever
The X4 Pro adds a touchscreen, lighting, and improved software, making it even easier to recommend.
The X4 Pro brings several welcome upgrades over its predecessors, including a touchscreen that gives readers another way to interact with it. It still has physical page-turning buttons, though. There’s also a new touch-sensitive button below the display for quickly returning to the home screen, along with a built-in light with adjustable brightness and color temperature, so you can read in the dark. It ships with the excellent CrossPoint Reader software, which makes navigating your library and reading books a much better experience than on previous Xteink models we’ve tested, though it’s still not quite as polished as Amazon’s software.
Understandably, not everyone is a fan of Xteink’s decision to swap the X4 Pro’s USB-C port for a proprietary charging connector. If you can look past that, the X4 Pro is a great, little e-reader that features magnets that let you attach it to compatible smartphones, just like previous models. The magnetic connection is stronger this time around, though we still wish it were a little more secure. All the same, my colleague Andrew Liszewski still considers the X4 Pro the best tiny e-reader you can buy, calling it a device he “won’t leave the house without.”

articles.title: Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio join 400 scientists calling for international AI regulator | BetaKit
articles.text:
More than 400 members of the scientific community are pushing for an international AI regulator to curb cybersecurity incidents.
The news: The open letter, released on Tuesday, calls for the creation of an international body to standardize AI containment practices and record and track containment failures. The letter recommends that every security incident involving containment failure be reported to the body and eventually made public, arguing that such transparency is required for learning and accountability.
The open letter counted signatories from all over the world, including nearly 70 Canadians, such as Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton and Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio. Both AI pioneers have signed many previous open letters warning about AI’s potentially devastating effects.
From the source: “As scientists, we thought that the current situation with AI models breaking containment during testing was a concern,” University of Toronto professor and signatory David Lie told BetaKit over the phone. “We drafted this letter after talking with people across both the AI and security communities in hopes it would improve the situation.”
The context: The new open letter’s recommendations follow an OpenAI model escaping its test environment and breaching the systems of Hugging Face and other platforms this past summer. That incident was just the first in a growing number of similar disclosures.
The scientists’ proposed solution may already be in the works. Canada’s AI minister Evan Solomon recently floated the idea of an international “technology stability board,” which would regulate testing, model evaluation, and model release, as well as include incident reporting mechanisms.
Final thought: While Canada is talking about potential solutions, the threat of rogue AI cybersecurity incidents persists. The scientists behind the open letter say that more emphasis is needed on AI safety research and containment technologies, and warn that cybersecurity incidents will become “far more damaging” to critical infrastructure without immediate changes to AI development.
Feature image courtesy LawZero via LinkedIn.

articles.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
articles.text:
GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
GitHub’s context-aware secret classifier improves detection quality, raises weighted acceptance by 11.5%, and reduces median scan execution time by 86%.
Smarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost
11.5%
higher acceptance
Owner-weighted alert precision
86%
lower median scan execution time
Post-push scanning
98%
lower serving cost
Compact model vs. remote LLM calls
Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.
Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.
To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.
In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.
What we enabled
GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:
Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.
Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.
We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.
Why secrets are hard to detect
Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.
Likely real credential
Likely harmless lookalike
A password assigned beside a production database URL
The same password-shaped value in a test fixture
A connection string in deployment configuration
A localhost connection string in a setup guide
A high-entropy value bound to an API credential
A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash
These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.
That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:
Candidate generation: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.
Context-aware classification: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.
Impact:
11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.
More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.
How our pipeline works
As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.
HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS
Broad first, careful second
STEP 1
Scan
Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces.
STEP 2
Generate candidates
Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.
STEP 3
Classify
Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.
STEP 4
Alert or suppress
High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.
The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”
A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real
Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.
ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.
We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.
That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.
How we trained
The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:
Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.
High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.
Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.
Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.
Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.
Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.
We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.
The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.
The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.
Evaluation results
Online result
Change vs. previous LLM pipeline
What it measures
Repository owner-weighted acceptance
11.5% higher
Customer acceptance of detected findings
Median post-push scan execution time
86% lower
Production scan execution time
Serving cost
More than 98% lower
Cost of the compact classifier compared with remote LLM calls
Customer A/B evaluation results for our fine-tuned model compared to the previous LLM pipeline.
We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment.
Offline evaluation: On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved 13% higher precision and 19% higher recall than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic.
Online evaluation: We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%. We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average.
Take this with you
The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.
For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.
Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.
We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.
This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:
Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.
Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.
Acknowledgments
Huge thanks to the engineering, science and product teams across GitHub and Microsoft who helped build the training data, evaluation suite, serving stack, and rollout plan for this new secret scanner.
As a Senior Research Scientist in Microsoft CoreAI, I develop agentic model orchestration and routing techniques for GitHub Copilot. My research focuses on adaptive model selection, multi-model coordination, long-horizon agentic workflows, and developer security.
As a Partner Applied Science Manager in Microsoft CoreAI, I lead an applied research team that measurably boosts developer productivity with ML and AI. We evolve GitHub Copilot in Completion, Chat, Code Review, and agentic workflows by continuously refining models and applying in-context learning for deeper, context-aware assistance.
As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team spotlights @vaib25vicky, exploring their methodology, techniques, and experiences hacking on GitHub.
Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.
We do newsletters, too
Discover tips, technical guides, and best practices in our biweekly newsletter just for devs.

articles.title: KI wird lascher kontrolliert als Milch: Microsoft-Funktionäre fordern mehr Kontrolle
articles.text:
Microsoft-Präsident Brad Smith : KI wird lascher kontrolliert als Milch
Am 10. Oktober 2026 hatte Microsoft-CEO Satya Nadella in einem Social-Media-Beitrag die Notwendigkeit einer strengeren Kontrolle für KI-Systeme angemahnt und einen entsprechenden Kill-Switch gefordert. Zuvor hatte Microsoft-Mitgründer Bill Gates in deutlich drastischeren Worten vor den potenziellen Gefahren gewarnt, die von KI ausgehen könnten.
Microsoft-Granden wollen mehr KI-Regulierung
Gegenüber der New York Times hatte Gates erklärt, dass KI das Gefährlichste sei, mit dem die Menschheit sich je befasst habe. Dagegen seien Atomwaffen eine Kleinigkeit. Zudem sei es an der Zeit zu handeln, die Gefahrenschwelle habe man schon Anfang 2026 überschritten. Wie Gates und Nadella spricht sich auch Microsoft-President Brad Smith für mehr Kontrolle und eine KI-Regulierung aus.
Jede Milch im Supermarkt werde strenger überwacht als KI, kritisierte Smith im BBC-Podcast Big Boss Interview. Die Technologie sei sowohl Werkzeug als auch Waffe und gehöre dringend reguliert. Am besten sofort, so Smith, der zudem ebenfalls eine Einführung der von Nadella ins Spiel gebrachten KI-Notbremsen forderte.
Gesetzliche Verpflichtungen für Anbieter
Außerdem sollte es eine gesetzliche Verpflichtung für Unternehmen geben, Berichte zu möglichen Vorfällen zu erstellen und Betroffene zu informieren. Unabhängige staatliche Prüfer:innen sollten neue KI-Technologien vor deren Release unabhängig begutachten. Bei anderen Produkten funktioniere das ja auch, so Smith gegenüber der BBC. Und weiter: „Wir sollten auf diesem Wissen aufbauen und überlegen, wie wir es auf KI anwenden können“.
Cnet zufolge hat Microsoft derweil schon ein auf diesen Überlegungen basierendes Produkt an den Start gebracht. Bei den sogenannten Execution Containers handelt es sich um eine Sicherheitsfunktion für Unternehmen, die den Zugriff von KI-Modellen auf bestimmte Dateien und Programme einschränkt. Außerdem verfügt das Feature über einen Notausschalter, der die Modelle bei Bedarf umgehend stoppen kann.
US-Präsident lehnt staatliche Regulierung ab
Derweil sehen offenbar nicht alle Branchenvertreter:innen eine Notwendigkeit zu strengerer Regulierung. US-Präsident Donald Trump hatte bei einem Treffen mit den führenden US-Anbietern erklärt, dass sich die Tech-Konzerne mehr oder weniger selbst regulieren sollten. Trump ist der Überzeugung, anderenfalls das KI-Rennen gegen China zu verlieren.
Nicht gefallen dürfte der KI-Konkurrenz eine weitere Forderung des Microsoft-Presidents Smith: Gegenüber dem britischen Sender ITV sagte er, dass im Falle einer durch KI ausgelösten Katastrophe die dafür verantwortliche Firma rechtlich haftbar gemacht werden soll. Vorausgesetzt, das Unternehmen habe fahrlässig gehandelt. Die zentrale Herausforderung, so Smith, bestehe darin, sicherzustellen, dass der Mensch die Kontrolle behalte.

articles.title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way.
An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run.
In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs.
The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production.
We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid.
What SpaceXAI reports about Grok 4.7
According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context.
SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers.
| Benchmark | Category | Grok 4.6 | Grok 4.7 | 
| Terminal-Bench 4.0 | Multi-hour terminal work | 20.3% | 37.6% | 
| EEBench | Electrical engineering | 53.0% | 64.0% | 
| Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark | Legal work | 15.8% | 19.6% | 
| CursorBench 4.0 | Longer-running coding | 40.4% | 46.3% | 
| HealthBench Professional | Clinical reasoning | 48.5% | 56.7% | 
| AA Briefcase v1.1 | Multi-hour office work | 1,546 | 1,657 | 
Source: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7 (https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7). Scores are as published by SpaceXAI at the time of the model launch.
Benchmarks show how a model performs across standard tasks. For your own workload, the useful next step is to measure on tasks shaped like yours, which is what the rest of this post walks through.
SpaceXAI lists a 500K token context window for Grok 4.7, with text and image input and text output. On Amazon Bedrock, the model supports configurable reasoning effort, tool calling, and structured output.
How you access Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
Grok 4.7 runs on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and is accessed through a cross-Region inference profile. Two profiles are available:
| Inference profile | Routing | Use when | 
| us.xai.grok-4.7 | Within the US geography | You have US data residency requirements | 
| global.xai.grok-4.7 | Commercial AWS Regions | You have no residency constraints and want the widest capacity | 
Cross-Region inference routes requests across multiple AWS Regions, which gives you higher throughput without managing capacity Region by Region. Requests name one of the inference profiles rather than a bare model ID.
The model supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. On Converse, reasoning is returned as a reasoningContent block alongside the text block. In inferenceConfig, set maxTokens only, and put model-specific parameters, such as reasoning effort, in additionalModelRequestFields.
For the current list of supported Regions, service tiers, and token prices, see the Grok 4.7 model card in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page (https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/).
Prerequisites
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, and model access enabled for Grok 4.7.
- Python 3.9 or later, with openai, boto3, and aws-bedrock-token-generator installed.
- AWS credentials configured in your environment.
Your AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity needs bedrock:InvokeModel on both the inference profile and your account’s default project:
- arn:aws:bedrock:{region}::inference-profile/us.xai.grok-4.7 or the global. equivalent.
- arn:aws:bedrock:{region}:{account-id}:project/default.
Include both resources in the policy statement. The default project permission is required in addition to the inference profile.
Connect to the model
For production use, we recommend generating a short-term bearer token from your existing AWS credentials, so authentication stays tied to your IAM identity and no long-lived secret is stored:
Reasoning tokens count as output tokens and draw down max_completion_tokens before the answer text is produced, so size the limit to leave room for both. If the limit is reached during reasoning, the response returns without answer text, so check for empty content in agent code and raise the limit if you see it. Our runs used a limit of 32,768 tokens, which left headroom at every effort level.
Grok 4.7 supports four effort levels: low, medium, high, and xhigh. Effort levels can change between model versions, so it is worth confirming them against the service rather than hardcoding a list:
Design tasks that need reasoning
Many agent evaluations test diligence: read a record, filter it, add it up. Those tasks are worth having, but to see what reasoning effort contributes, a task has to require search: the answer can’t be read off the data, it has to be proposed and then checked.
We built a synthetic environment of 20 services, exposed through seven tools, and three tasks on top of it. Every task has exactly one correct answer, and each is built so that a quick heuristic is not enough to find it.
| Task | What the agent has to do | What makes it a reasoning task | 
| two_fault_diagnosis | Two services failed silently at 03:00 and 12 others raised alerts. Identify the two that failed | Failed services raise no alerts, so the answer is not among the alerting services. 190 possible pairs, and only one explains exactly the alerts observed | 
| maintenance_schedule | Patch eight services over four nights, two per night, under ten constraints and a rule that two services from the same team never share a night | 2,520 possible schedules, one valid. The team rule depends on data the agent has to look up | 
| migration_budget | Choose candidates to migrate that maximize risk reduction within a budget, including transitive prerequisites | 53 feasible sets, one optimal. Picking the best ratio first gives a set nine points short of the optimum | 
Four practices keep a measurement like this trustworthy, and they apply to most agent evaluations.
State every rule the grader relies on. If the prompt leaves an edge case open, a reasonable answer can be scored as wrong, and the evaluation ends up measuring the specification rather than the model. The diagnosis prompt, for example, says explicitly that a failed service raises no alert of its own.
Prove each task has one answer. Each environment is small enough to enumerate, so we checked every candidate answer before running anything. For the schedule, that is a few lines:
Grade a required final line, not the whole response. Each prompt asks the agent to end with a line such as FINAL: auth, checkout. The grader reads only that line, so a response that discusses other candidates while explaining its reasoning is graded on its conclusion:
Track format separately from correctness. A missing final line is a different signal from an incorrect one. In our runs, all 72 responses included a gradeable final line.
Constrain tool parameters with an enum where the valid values are known, so every tool call targets a real resource:
The system prompt is deliberately short, and asks the agent to check its answer before giving it:
The agent loop is a standard tool-calling loop: call the model with reasoning_effort set, execute each returned tool call, append the result keyed by tool_call_id, and repeat until the model stops requesting tools. Tracking prompt_tokens and completion_tokens across the loop gives the token counts reported in the following section.
Results
Six runs of each task at each effort level, 72 runs in total. The agent answered 67 correctly.
| Task | low | medium | high | xhigh | 
| two_fault_diagnosis | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| maintenance_schedule | 5 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| migration_budget | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| All three tasks | 15 of 18 | 17 of 18 | 17 of 18 | 18 of 18 | 
| Per run | low | medium | high | xhigh | 
| Mean output tokens | 1,184 | 6,430 | 6,778 | 9,147 | 
| Output tokens relative to low | 1.0x | 5.4x | 5.7x | 7.7x | 
| Mean tool calls | 17.2 | 18.7 | 17.8 | 18.1 | 
| Median elapsed time | 18s | 98s | 89s | 106s | 
Three observations.
xhigh answered every run correctly. All 18 runs across the three tasks were correct at xhigh, and medium and high answered 17 of 18 each. With six runs per task and level, the differences between levels are indicative rather than statistically conclusive, and the direction was consistent across all three tasks.
Effort changes how much the agent reasons, not how much it explores. Tool calls were essentially flat, between 17.2 and 18.7 per run at every level. The agent gathered the same facts regardless of effort, and what changed was how much reasoning it applied to them, with output tokens rising from 1,184 at low to 9,147 at xhigh.
low offers a strong cost-to-quality ratio. At low, the agent answered 15 of 18 runs correctly using about an eighth of the output tokens of xhigh, with a median run of 18 seconds. Where a slightly lower completion rate is acceptable, or where answers are reviewed downstream, low is an efficient choice. Where every answer needs to be right first time, higher levels are the safer default.
How effort level shapes the answer
The tasks were designed around a specific kind of difficulty, and looking at how each effort level handled them clarifies when the extra reasoning is worth it.
Optimization. The migration task rewards considering combinations rather than ranking options one at a time. Selecting the candidates with the best individual ratios produces a reasonable answer that is nine points short of the optimum. At medium and above, the agent found the optimal set in all 18 runs.
Hypothesis testing. The diagnosis task requires checking a candidate pair in both directions: every alert has to be explained, and every service that stayed silent has to be consistent with the answer. At medium and above, the agent identified the correct pair in all 18 runs.
Constraint satisfaction. The scheduling task combines ten listed constraints with a team rule that depends on looked-up ownership data. xhigh produced the valid schedule in every run, and this was the task where the highest level made the clearest difference.
The pattern across the three is that additional reasoning effort is most valuable where the agent has to weigh several candidate answers against each other, rather than follow a single path to the result.
Monitoring reasoning in production
In production you don’t have a known answer to grade against, but you do know how many output tokens and tool calls each run used. Those give you a useful operational signal.
Correct runs at each level stay above a clear floor of reasoning volume. Every correct run at medium and above used at least 1,739 output tokens, and the typical run used several thousand. A run that makes no tool calls, or that produces far less output than is normal for its level, is worth flagging for review:
Calibrate the baseline from runs you have graded, per task and per effort level, then apply it to runs you have not. Treat a flag as a prompt to inspect or re-run. At low, where every run is brief, output volume is a weaker signal, so pair it with spot checks.
Asking the agent to verify its answer in the system prompt is worth keeping, because it makes the agent’s reasoning straightforward to follow when you review a run. Pair it with automated grading wherever a known answer exists, so that quality is measured independently of the transcript.
Choosing a reasoning effort
These results suggest a few practical rules.
Match effort to the kind of task. Tasks that involve search, optimization, or testing a hypothesis benefit most from medium or higher. Tasks that follow a single path, or whose answers are reviewed downstream, can run efficiently at low.
Set effort per request, not per agent. Effort is a request parameter, so an agent can run its planning and verification steps at a higher level and its mechanical steps, such as formatting a tool result, at low. That combines much of the reliability of a higher level with a lower token cost.
Measure on your own tasks, with repeats. A single run per configuration gives a single observation. Repeating each configuration several times shows how consistent it is.
Monitor reasoning volume. Output tokens and tool calls per run, tracked by effort level, give you an early signal to review a run before its result is used.
Limitations of this measurement
Six runs per task and effort level. Enough to show a consistent direction across three tasks, not enough for a confidence interval. Treat the differences between levels as indicative.
A synthetic environment. The tools read from data generated in code, which is what makes it possible to prove each task has exactly one answer and to grade automatically. Real tools add latency, partial results and errors, none of which are tested here.
Minutes, not hours. Median run time ranged from 18 seconds at low to 106 seconds at xhigh. This is a scaled-down proxy for long-horizon work. The method transfers. The absolute figures do not.
One model version, one Region, one prompt per task. Different phrasings of the same task may change the results, which is part of why stating every rule explicitly matters.
Token counts, not costs. To convert to currency, apply the current rates for your inference profile and service tier from the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. The Global and US Geo profiles are priced differently, and the Flex and Priority service tiers apply multipliers.
Operational controls for agent workloads
Build in retries. Agents that issue a high volume of calls should treat retries as part of the design. Set a request timeout, retry only errors that are retryable, back off exponentially with jitter, and honor a Retry-After header when one is returned:
On-demand throughput scales up over time, so ramp a new high-volume workload gradually rather than starting at full rate.
Auditing a run. Model invocation logging writes request and response data to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. This gives you the full transcript of runs you want to review after the fact.
Monitoring reasoning volume at scale. Amazon CloudWatch metrics give you the aggregate view of token usage, which is where the per-level baselines described earlier become something you can alarm on.
Attributing spend across agents. Cost itemization in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report breaks usage out per model, which combined with per-task token counts gives you both unit economics and the aggregate bill.
Matching cost to urgency. Service tiers are set per request, so one deployment can send an overnight analysis through the Flex tier and an interactive request through Priority. For a workload that runs at a higher effort level, tier selection is a further lever on cost.
Choosing a routing profile. Cross-Region inference widens the capacity pool a long run draws from. The Global profile serves from your choice of commercial AWS Region and is typically priced lower per token than geographic routing. The US profile keeps processing within the United States. Choose based on your data residency requirements as well as cost.
Clean up
The examples in this post do not create billable AWS resources beyond per-request token usage. If you generated a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key, delete it in the Amazon Bedrock console when you are finished, because it remains valid until revoked. Short-term tokens generated from IAM credentials expire on their own.
If you enabled model invocation logging to Amazon S3 while testing, review the bucket and remove objects you no longer need.
Conclusion
SpaceXAI trained Grok 4.7 to work longer on more difficult tasks and to know when to check its own work. On three tasks that required search rather than lookup, the agent answered 67 of 72 runs correctly, and every run at xhigh. Because reasoning effort is set per request, you can choose where each step of an agent sits on the trade-off between thoroughness and token cost.
Three things are worth carrying into your own evaluation. Design tasks with one provable answer and state every rule the grader depends on. Repeat runs, so you see how consistent each configuration is. And monitor output tokens and tool calls by effort level, so you have an operational signal alongside your quality measurements.

articles.title: Sony lance une PS5 noire deux fois moins chère pour GTA 6 (mais pas en France)
articles.text:
Sony prépare l’arrivée de GTA 6, dont la sortie est prévue pour le 19 novembre 2026. Dans un communiqué publié sur le blog japonais de PlayStation ce mardi 13 octobre, la firme nippone officialise un nouveau modèle de PS5, qui sera disponible le même jour que le blockbuster de Rockstar Games. Il s’agit d’une édition numérique, dépourvue de lecteur de disque, en finition Midnight Black (couleur noire).
Tout l’intérêt de cette console tient dans son prix : 55 000 yens TTC, soit environ 310 €. Seulement, cette PS5 est réservée au marché japonais. Sony précise qu’elle ne peut être utilisée « qu’avec un compte PlayStation configuré avec la langue de la console sur ‘Japonais’ et le ‘Pays / Région’ sur ‘Japon’ ». Avec un compte d’un autre pays, elle ne fonctionne pas du tout.
Les Japonais vont pouvoir acheter une console plus abordable
Cette nouvelle déclinaison de la PS5 est donc strictement la même que celle lancée au Japon en novembre 2025, à l’occasion de l’anniversaire des cinq ans. Seule la couleur change, le noir remplaçant le blanc. Sony vendra le même jour un lecteur de disque assorti, lui aussi noir, à 11 980 yens (environ 70 €). Un comble, puisque Sony rappelle dans la même annonce que les nouveaux jeux PlayStation sortis à partir de janvier 2028 ne seront plus vendus qu’en téléchargement (les disques plus anciens resteront lisibles).
En somme, n’espérez pas profiter d’un futur voyage au Japon pour ramener cette PS5 dans votre valise en pensant faire des économies. Vous ne pourrez pas mettre votre compte PSN français dessus. Même avec un compte japonais créé pour l’occasion, impossible d’y transférer ou d’y restaurer les données d’un compte rattaché à un autre pays. La page d’assistance de Sony indique noir sur blanc que cette PS5 n’a accès qu’au PlayStation Store japonais et ne peut lire que des jeux PS4 et PS5 numériques achetés sur le PlayStation Store japonais.
Sony déconseille d’ailleurs tout usage hors de l’archipel. Cette PS5 ne répond qu’aux normes de sécurité japonaises et elle est prévue pour le courant à 100 volts du Japon, quand les prises françaises délivrent 230 volts.
En France, il n’existe pas de PS5 régionalisée, qui ne fonctionnerait que chez nous. On ne peut y acheter que la version internationale. La PS5 Digital Edition, sans lecteur de disque, coûte 599,99 € depuis que Sony a augmenté ses prix de 100 € en avril 2026, soit presque deux fois plus que cette PS5 japonaise. Même au Japon, l’écart est net : la PS5 Digital Edition internationale y coûte 72 980 yens, soit 17 980 yens de plus que le modèle japonais. Il existe aussi une Switch 2 régionalisée plus abordable.
