articles.title: WhatsApp va enfin vous laisser programmer vos messages
articles.text:
La fonctionnalité semble anodine et pourtant il aura fallu attendre des années avant de la voir implémentée. Pour certains testeurs utilisant la version bêta de WhatsApp sur Android, il est enfin possible de planifier l'envoi d'un message. Les textes, les liens, les photos ou les vidéos partiront à l'heure choisie, même si le téléphone est hors ligne.
Pouvoir planifier un message, c'est quand même bien pratique, notamment pour gérer les fuseaux horaires ou écrire en dehors des heures de bureau. Si une telle option est disponible depuis longtemps pour les emails, sur les messageries mobiles, cela reste anecdotique. Les utilisateurs réclament cette option depuis longtemps. Telegram la propose déjà, et WhatsApp vient de l'intégrer à sa bêta Android 2.26.40.7.
Entre 10 minutes et deux semaines, vous choisissez l'heure d'envoi
Pour planifier un envoi, il suffit de rédiger son message, puis d'appuyer longuement sur le bouton d'envoi, comme sur Telegram. Une fenêtre apparaît en bas de l'écran pour choisir la date et l'heure. Le message part ensuite tout seul à l'horaire prévu, même si l'application est fermée ou si le téléphone est hors ligne. L'envoi doit être programmé 10 minutes à l'avance au minimum, ce qui laisse le temps de se corriger. Le maximum est de deux semaines. Cela permet par exemple de prévoir un message dans la journée ou de souhaiter un anniversaire en avance.
Les photos et les vidéos sont acceptées, mais une seule à la fois. Les liens sont aussi pris en charge. L'éditeur de dessin permet aussi de retoucher une image ou d'ajouter une légende avant de fixer l'horaire. Le chiffrement de bout en bout reste actif. Autrement dit, seuls l'expéditeur et le destinataire peuvent lire le contenu.
Les messages en attente sont listés dans l'écran d'informations de la conversation. Il est possible de les consulter, les gérer ou les supprimer avant leur envoi. Cette section permet de garder la main jusqu'au dernier moment. Si l'un des messages planifiés est supprimé, le destinataire n'est pas prévenu et ne voit pas que ce dernier était programmé. Dans un groupe, seuls les membres présents au moment de la programmation le reçoivent. Quelqu'un qui arrive ensuite ne le verra pas. Cela évite qu'une information soit transmise à une personne qui était absente à l'origine.
- Chiffrement de bout en bout.
- Appels audio et vidéo gratuits.
- Compatibilité multiplateforme.

articles.title: One of Spain’s largest recent FinTech deals sees ID Finance secure €545 million to scale Plazo | EU-Startups
articles.text:
ID Finance, a Barcelona-based FinTech group, has announced €545 million of debt and equity funding to support further growth for their flagship consumer finance app; Plazo.
This funding saw participation from Spice Expeditions, WashU, Kingsway Capital and global investment firm i80 Group, who provided asset-based financing. EU-Startups previously covered ID Finance in October 2019, when the Barcelona-based group secured over €1.7 million through crowdfunding.
Alexander Dunaev, co-founder of ID Finance says: “This investment is a strong vote of confidence in Plazo and in the model we’ve built to modernise consumer credit in Spain. Plazo tripled its portfolio in 2025 and reached profitability, proving that responsible, AI-driven underwriting and a genuinely better product experience can scale together.
“This new capital from some of the most reputable global investors in FinTech lets us build on that foundation, expand Plazo’s product suite and keep pushing on innovation, including through Turrón“.
ID Finance’s debt and equity financing comes amid wider investment activity in European consumer credit, flexible payments and specialist lending during 2026.
According to EU-Startups’ coverage, London-based Plend secured a credit facility of up to €58.3 million, fellow UK FinTech Vuelo raised €64 million for its travel financing platform, and Manchester-based Firenze secured €6.8 million for investment-backed lending.
In Spain, Madrid-based BCAS raised €30 million in debt financing to expand its flexible education payment solutions. Meanwhile, Paris-based Aria announced €247 million in equity and debt financing capacity for its embedded B2B finance platform.
Together, these five announcements represent approximately €406 million, rising to around €951 million when including ID Finance’s latest transaction.
Tamir Saeed, Managing Partner at Kingsway Capital, adds: “It has been a pleasure to partner with ID Finance over the last few years, supporting their mission to provide access to financial services to all consumers in Spain and Mexico. We are pleased to continue investing in this exciting next phase of ID Finance’s journey, exemplified by the high growth and disruptive potential of new products like Plazo and Turron.”
Founded in 2015, ID Finance provides alternative lending in both Spain and Mexico, specialising in providing innovative financial solutions. Plazo plays a key role in this strategy. Launched in 2021, the app brings together debit and credit solutions on a single platform.
As part of its continued expansion, ID Finance recently launched Turrón by Plazo, a flexible payment solution that enables customers to make online and in-store purchases. Turrón combines an e-money account, debit card and Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) solution.
The addition of BNPL services marks another step towards in creating Spain’s “go-to” consumer credit platform.
Peter Frank, Managing Director at i80, says: “ID Finance has done a tremendous job of managing risk while growing the portfolio. We’re delighted to deepen our relationship and increase the scale of the asset-based financing that will support Plazo’s next phase of growth as it continues to modernise consumer credit in Europe.”
Today’s transaction is reportedly one of the largest closed by a Spanish FinTech in recent years and comes two years after the €134 million ($150 million) debt financing round provided by i80 Group in early 2024, that was utilised to grow Plazo’s credit portfolio.
In 2025, the Group reported €243 million in revenue, while profit nearly doubled in the same period. Plazo achieved bottom line profitability in 2025 as its revenue grew 300% YoY, growing client base to over 400,000 users.
Together with additional financing, Plazo is expected to grow another 300% in 2026, supported by AI-powered technology infrastructure.

articles.title: Under the hood, off the hot path: how D1 scales to millions of databases
articles.text:
Under the hood, off the hot path: How D1 scales to millions of databases
Traditional database architecture assumes you have one or two big database clusters per application, usually accompanied by a connection pooling solution. AI-assisted development and vibe coding platforms turn this model inside out and are driving applications toward many small databases: one per user, application, preview environment, or tenant.
That model fits D1 particularly well. D1 is Cloudflare's managed, serverless database based on SQLite. It allows you to create millions of databases and only pay for what you use.
The question becomes: how do you scale the control plane for millions of databases without making every query slower by sending it through centralized bottlenecks?
We made a lot of architectural changes to scale out D1 to support platforms with millions of created databases, hundreds of thousands of which are active at any point.
This post is a behind-the-scenes deep dive into how the D1 control plane works. Many of the architectural patterns we will describe can be used by anyone building on top of Cloudflare’s Developer Platform. The post also gives a glimpse into how we build our own control planes.
Growth in numbers
There was already a steady growth in D1 usage when we started planning these changes, but we knew we would need to support a much bigger scale once large platforms started building with D1.
Here is how things have played out so far.
D1 has seen a 15x growth in the number of live non-deleted databases over the past one year, and a 65x growth over the past 2 years (as of October 8, 2026).
We have also seen 18x growth in the number of daily active databases over the past year (as of October 8, 2026). A database is considered active if it executed at least one query during that day.
Established and successful platforms are already building with D1, using the same tools available to all Cloudflare users.
"ChatGPT Sites lets anyone turn ideas into shareable experiences. D1 gives our users a simple, scalable way to add features like custom metrics, leaderboards, and comments to their dashboards, games, and tools."
- Jon Abrams, ChatGPT Sites @ OpenAI
While we were making the changes described in this blog post, we periodically load-tested against a target well above our expected growth. This guided where to focus our optimization efforts.
Guiding engineering principles
Applications built on the Cloudflare Developer Platform range from full-stack applications to service APIs, from internal single-user portals to massive multi-tenant vibe coding platforms, and everything in between.
While building out the D1 control plane to support millions of databases, the following tenets and principles were guiding our architecture decisions and are useful for anyone building their control and data planes on our platform.
- Design all processes with failure and idempotency in mind. Failures will happen, so the system needs to self-correct where possible and continue making progress.
- Avoid centralized single-region components in any hot path for data plane operations (in our case all query requests).
- Use Workers KV, a globally distributed KV store, for critical routing metadata so that cache misses only rarely need to query central databases.
- Use Hyperdrive to access central Postgres databases for efficient connection pooling and optimized routing and caching, using read replicas wherever possible.
- Periodically precompute aggregations in the database to avoid scan queries during user request processing.
- Use eventual consistency and queuing between components that don’t need strong consistency to increase reliability and availability.
- Load-test the application with realistic workloads to discover bottlenecks and inefficiencies, and focus on optimizing those first.
There are more engineering principles we follow internally to build our systems, but the above are generic enough and apply to anyone building on Cloudflare.
The following sections will dive into the main system components and processes of the D1 control plane regarding the lifecycle of a D1 database, and showcase how to put these principles into practice with a real-world system.
High-level architecture
Let’s start off by introducing the main components of D1.
There are a few more arrows and boxes missing from the diagram for secondary processes supporting D1, but these are the ones providing D1’s public feature set. We will explore the rest in dedicated sections in the rest of the blog post.
First of all, each D1 database is backed by one SQLite Durable Object, which makes it very easy to create millions of them.
The “HTTP API” shape represents all our API surfaces including the Cloudflare dashboard, Wrangler, and Cloudflare CLI. All API requests go through Cloudflare’s edge gateway and are served by the D1 Edge API Worker.
The diagram shows the HTTP endpoints that allow users to execute SQL queries against their databases as the “Query endpoints”. The remaining endpoints include the usual database operations like creating, deleting, and listing databases, along with import/export and time travel features. These are shown as the “CRUD endpoints”.
The CRUD endpoints use Hyperdrive to query a Postgres cluster in our central data centers (referred to as “Core”). There are two configurations. One configuration has caching enabled and targets the Postgres read replicas. The other configuration has caching disabled and targets the Postgres primary.
The Edge API Worker might invoke the D1 Eyeball Worker (depending on the type of request). The Eyeball Worker is our proxy for all requests that need to be handled by the underlying D1 Durable Objects (DO). This allows us to put all query handling inside the Eyeball Worker, including observability, automatic retries, error handling, and other query-specific behaviors.
Workers KV acts as our caching layer at the edge for read-heavy metadata and can be read by all the D1 Workers.
The “Worker Binding” shape represents all users’ Workers with a D1 Worker binding. Requests from the D1 Binding go directly to the D1 Eyeball Worker, which in turn forwards the request to the Durable Object backing the database and proxies the response back to the User Worker.
We have two methods for users to execute queries in their databases. One is over the HTTP API query endpoints, and the other is through a Worker they deploy in their accounts with a D1 Binding.
In terms of operations, we fold each operation into one of the following categories:
- Data plane: any database query related request; should be as fast as possible and always at the edge.
- Control plane: any HTTP API operation or internal flows that run in response to a non-query user request; they can depend on central single-region components.
- Background asynchronous plane: any analytical and billing-related workflow; can be eventually consistent and runs anywhere.
There is a lot more under the hood, so let’s dive into the key flows.
Fast on-demand database creation close to the user
Multi-tenant platforms and AI agent-driven development require creating a lot of database instances in a fast, cost-efficient, and reliable way.
The following is an example Wrangler command to create a D1 database:
% time wrangler d1 create "demo-01"
✅ Successfully created DB 'demo-01' in region WEUR
...
0.56s user 0.13s system 42% cpu 1.614 total
When a user creates a D1 database, several things need to happen before the database is ready to receive queries.
- Check that the account can create more databases against the free tier limit or its account limits.
- Generate a unique D1 database UUID, a unique Durable Object ID (newUniqueId()), and initialize the underlying Durable Object (DO) with the account and database information.
- Persist the newly created database’s information in Postgres (one row per database, including metadata and the mapping to the initialized Durable Object ID).
- Write the mapping from a database ID to the Durable Object ID in Workers KV (later used by the data plane and the query endpoints).
Let’s examine the actual flow and how we recover from failures at each step.
Once a database creation request comes in, our Edge API Worker handler is invoked in the nearest Cloudflare location at the edge. Edge API queries our Postgres read replicas over Hyperdrive with caching enabled (with cache TTL of a few seconds) to get the number of non-deleted databases for the given account.
The Edge API Worker forwards control plane requests to data centers near our Postgres cluster for endpoints that do multiple round-trips to Postgres (step 2), and the “create database” endpoint is one of them. The reason is that a round-trip from afar can be hundreds of milliseconds, whereas being near Postgres can be a few milliseconds. For endpoints that do at most one Postgres query we don’t need to do this optimization since Hyperdrive already handles efficient routing through the Cloudflare network.
Creating a D1 database without any options places the database near the request’s location by default. You can influence the location of the database by providing an explicit location hint or a jurisdiction. The location hints and jurisdiction options are identical to what Durable Objects support, so when these are provided they are just passed straight through to the underlying Durable Object initialization.
With the default creation we want the D1 databases to be created near the original location of the request, close to the user. To achieve this, during step 4 of the diagram, we internally forward the request execution to a data center close to the original request’s location and invoke the underlying Durable Object from there. This ensures that the underlying Durable Object is placed near the user.
You can implement similar routing techniques by using explicit Worker placement hints and at runtime invoking the right Worker via Service Bindings.
The creation endpoint is a bit of a weird case in terms of placement because even though we query Postgres at least two times, we also do a long-distance call to the underlying Durable Objects, which differ per request, so running the request to either side of the world could be inefficient. That's why we leaned towards forwarding the initial request near Postgres.
The next step is to generate the database UUID along with a new unique Durable Object ID using the newUniqueId() API and invoke the init(options) RPC function on the new Durable Object’s stub. The Durable Object stores the information in its durable storage so that every incoming request from that point on has all the metadata for the linked database.
Once the Edge API Worker gets the initialization response, it persists the database metadata into our central Postgres primary database over Hyperdrive, one metadata row per database.
The steps above are wrapped in a retry loop (steps 5-7 in the diagram). When the DO initialization or the write to Postgres fails we retry with different IDs (this is important, as we will see in the next section).
The write to Postgres is the “creation checkpoint” where a database is considered created even if the final response fails to reach the user. The database from that point on is included in all the control plane operations and can be bound to a Worker to serve queries.
At this point the D1 database is ready to receive queries.
The final creation confirmation RPC to the Durable Object happens in a waitUntil() and is OK to fail. This call signals the DO that the database is now active, and the DO updates Workers KV with the database metadata so that any subsequent query can immediately read the information from Workers KV cache without needing to query Postgres.
A common question is why can’t the creation flow run entirely inside a Postgres transaction to simplify the process? The answer is simply that it cannot scale, since it leads to connections being held while the Durable Object is being initialized, which could be on the other side of the world.
Heartbeats for self-correcting databases
Each D1 Durable Object periodically heartbeats the control plane to get the latest database state (active or deleted) and account limits (more on this in the enforcement sections later). The interval is 30 seconds with a per-database jitter on top. We also have knobs to change the interval by database or account, or disable heartbeats entirely.
Heartbeats can tolerate slightly out-of-date data, meaning they can be served by Hyperdrive’s multiple caching layers or by a Postgres read replica. This heartbeat flow enables the Durable Object to self-correct to reflect the source of truth (Postgres) regarding the creation and deletion of databases.
One clarifying detail before we move on. The reason we use different database UUID and Durable Object IDs for each retry in the creation flow of the previous section (step 5) is that if we reused the database UUIDs with fresh Durable Object IDs, multiple Durable Objects would think they own the same database leading to difficult-to-debug situations. The periodic heartbeats also act as a cleanup for orphaned objects.
Also, it’s important that we first initialize the Durable Object before we persist the database mapping in Postgres, otherwise query requests could start to flow to the Durable Object and would be rejected due to uninitialized state.
For example, let’s assume the following failure scenario and why it is self-correcting:
- We executed everything from the previous section until we initialized Durable Object A, and then, the write to Postgres fails.
- The Worker retries the loop and initializes a new DO with a different ID B, and this time it persists to Postgres.
- We now have two Durable Objects initialized and running as part of this request, but only one of them is valid.
- The user can only query Durable Object B because that’s the only ID available in Postgres, which is our source of truth.
- Within 30 seconds, DO A sends its next heartbeat to the control plane and receives back a response that its database does not exist. This will trigger DO A to mark itself as deleted.
A similar flow happens for the deletion endpoint.
Another self-correcting behavior of the heartbeats is making sure the Workers KV data eventually reflects reality: whether a database is active or deleted.
The final step of the creation flow to update Workers KV is “best-effort” and can fail without causing problems. It’s eventually consistent, and the next time the Durable Object heartbeats it will ensure that the Workers KV item has been written with the correct value. Since Workers KV is eventually consistent without a way to do a consistent read, the Durable Object acts as the serialization point for the writes to the Workers KV items.
Deletion works the same way in reverse: the Durable Object owns writing its “deleted” state to Workers KV, again best-effort during the actual deletion operation, and if that fails the heartbeat will correct it eventually. The Durable Object stores the active or deleted state in its storage too, so it can reject or accept query requests immediately, even if Workers KV is stale and allows requests through.
Overall, the database heartbeats are the fallback mechanism for getting into a consistent state when operations need to write into an external datastore and also update the Durable Object itself.
Decoupling the hot path: keeping queries off the central database
The key principle for query endpoints is to avoid talking to Postgres or any other centralized single-region component. Each query request over HTTP executes our Edge API Worker close to the original user request location, and then goes straight to the D1 Durable Object via the Eyeball Worker.
The Edge API Worker is responsible for doing standard HTTP API authentication, resource-based authorization, rate limiting at the account and database level, request validation, checking the entitlements of the account, and other API-related functions before executing the actual business logic.
The Eyeball Worker, on the other hand, skips these extra checks (apart from its own dedicated rate limiting), since under the hood, a D1 Binding is a Service Binding to the D1 Eyeball Worker. Each user Worker’s D1 Binding carries encoded information that authorizes access to one specific D1 database that the D1 Eyeball Worker validates and allows the request through.
The following diagram shows the execution of a query through the HTTP API.
- A user sends a query request over the HTTP API.
- The Edge API Worker first tries to load the mapping from a D1 UUID to the database metadata from Workers KV.
- In rare cases, the item cannot be found in Workers KV, either because the write failed as described earlier or potentially due to an availability issue. We then fall back to reading the mapping from Hyperdrive targeting the Postgres replicas. Before querying the actual replicas, Hyperdrive first checks its cache in the caller location, then its cache near the Postgres cluster location, and only if both are cache misses queries the Postgres replicas for the mapping.
- Once we have the mapping, the Edge API Worker calls the Eyeball Worker over Worker Service Bindings passing the relevant IDs.
- The Eyeball Worker does its validation and forwards the query request to the D1 Durable Object.
- The D1 Durable Object executes the SQL query and returns the result through Eyeball Worker to the Edge API Worker, which returns it back to the user.
// Edge API Worker
const parsed = parseQueries(request);
const cachedDB = await withRetries(getCachedDatabase(parsed.dbUuid));
const response = await env.EYEBALL_WORKER.query({
  db: cachedDB,
  queries: parsed.queries,
});
return response;
If you are wondering why we use newUniqueId() during the database creation rather than addressing Durable Objects by “name” to eliminate steps 2 and 3 above, the answer is to avoid a lookup round-trip to a central mapping of “name” to “Durable Object ID” during query requests. The Durable Object ID alone would not be enough, since we also need other metadata to help us pick the right Durable Object Namespace to use in our Eyeball Worker. Hence, we would replace one lookup with two.
In most cases, even with many of our own applications, addressing Durable Objects by name works great, and it removes the need for a lookup from your own IDs to a Durable Object ID, so use that as a starting point and only move to unique DO IDs if you have to.
You might also wonder why we use Workers KV when we already have Hyperdrive Caching.
Workers KV is a durable datastore, not just a cache: if an item falls out of KV's edge cache, the read is served from KV's own storage rather than Postgres, keeping Postgres out of the data plane. In a catastrophic cache purge scenario, a million databases trying to fetch their routing information would lead to metastable failures.
As a reminder, query requests from a user Worker with a D1 Binding do not need to resolve the D1 UUID mapping metadata because the binding itself holds that information internally, so requests go straight to the Eyeball Worker and the Durable Object.
For the query execution itself and how Durable Objects are implemented under the hood, read our blog post about D1 read replication that dives into all the nitty-gritty details.
Next, let's look at the asynchronous processes that support D1.
Enforcing storage usage limits
All platforms that reach a certain scale eventually need to enforce billing and usage limits. At the time of writing, D1 has a 5 GB per-account storage limit on the Free plan and 1 TB on Workers Paid (can be raised on request).
In general, usage limit enforcement and billing systems are good candidates for eventual consistency and asynchronous processing, and in the following sections we will explore how D1 implements the enforcement of these limits.
Asynchronous update processing with queues
The first step of the journey is that each Durable Object publishes storage usage updates to a Kafka-like queue for batching and asynchronous processing. The control plane does not need to process every update synchronously: it is fine if a load spike is not reflected immediately and our usage information is stale. The important thing is that it cannot overload Postgres and impact users of D1. We ensure this by limiting the number of queue consumers, and therefore the write load on Postgres.
The queue consumer system runs inside Cloudflare’s central data centers (“Core”), whereas the Durable Objects themselves are spread everywhere in the world at the edge. The usage is aggregated locally per edge server and then published into the internal queue system.
The guiding principle here is that we use a queue to smooth out and batch writes to our central regional Postgres data store.
Batching usage deltas and pre-aggregations
The queue consumer writes the latest reported size for each database into a Postgres table. This isn’t what we need for enforcement decisions though. For enforcement decisions, we need the sum of all storage usage across the whole account. When we come to read the usage at enforcement time, we can’t afford to run SELECT sum(storage) FROM database_stats WHERE account_id = ?. The cost of this query scales linearly with the number of databases on each account. This doesn’t scale for accounts with millions of D1 databases, like some of the agentic coding platforms built with D1.
Ideally, we want a lookup table that will allow us to go directly from account ID to total database storage. The solution is to use incremental view maintenance to precompute the total, and keep it up to date when we have database storage changes.
Let’s call this table account_database_stats.
In theory, we could make the queue consumer update database_stats and account_database_stats itself for every update that comes in. In practice, this would end up with a lot of write lock contention on a single row for large accounts. Instead, we add a third table called account_database_stats_changes that acts like a queue of changes. This is a log of all changes, and can have multiple entries per account. We then periodically aggregate updates from that table into account_database_stats. The flow looks like this:
- The queue consumer writes usage info to the database_stats table for a specific database.
- A trigger calculates the difference in storage for that database and puts the delta in an account_database_stats_changes table (one row per delta).
- A scheduled job runs every second to consume everything in account_database_stats_changes and update account_database_stats with the sum of those deltas.
Concretely, the scheduled job runs this query:
WITH updates AS MATERIALIZED (
  DELETE FROM account_database_stats_changes
  RETURNING *
),
changes AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT
    account_id,
    SUM(storage_change) AS storage
  FROM updates
  GROUP BY account_id
)
INSERT INTO account_database_stats (account_id, storage)
SELECT
  account_id,
  storage
FROM changes
ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO UPDATE
SET storage = account_database_stats.storage + EXCLUDED.storage;
It gets a list of updates from account_database_stats_changes, aggregates them by account, and then writes the deltas to the per-account table. This avoids write contention on any particular row, because we aggregate the changes before writing them.
The Common Table Expression (CTE) DELETE ... RETURNING atomically consumes the pending changes and passes the deleted rows to the next CTE. Postgres executes the data-modifying CTE exactly once and to completion. The query then groups those changes by account and applies one aggregated update per account, reducing write contention.
This schema design is a pattern used by many other Cloudflare teams, and it lets us scale to millions of resources per account without each additional resource making common operations more expensive.
It’s worth noting that the total is eventually consistent. It’s not like first-class incremental view maintenance that you find in some other databases. We are already using a queue to get the updates from the Durable Objects into Postgres, so we are already fine with eventual consistency.
Cached reads via Hyperdrive
We now have a lookup table for each account’s total storage. What next?
Each D1 Durable Object periodically retrieves the account’s usage through the periodic heartbeat we mentioned earlier. We query Postgres with  SELECT storage FROM account_database_stats WHERE account_id = ? and compare that to the account’s entitlement and tier limits. If the total is over the limit then we forbid all writes that would increase the database size.
The query goes to Postgres replicas through Hyperdrive, and uses Hyperdrive’s built-in cache. Hyperdrive’s cache key is made up of the query and all parameter values, with the expiration time-to-live being a few seconds. By using the account ID as the only parameter, every database on that account will share the same cached value, which is what we want.
Time for a neat cache trick. Cached reads via Hyperdrive by default have a 60s expiration, and the Hyperdrive cache configuration applies to all queries. For specific queries we want cached values with lower expiration time. By adding a dynamic_ttl parameter to the query we generate a different cache key every X seconds, therefore reading fresh values sooner.
-- $2 = Math.floor(Date.now() / (X * 1000))
SELECT storage, $2 as dynamic_ttl
FROM account_database_stats WHERE account_id = $1
It might be tempting to make a query that takes account ID and database ID as parameters. That would let you find the account total and subtract the total for the current database. That would get an exact answer to the question “how much storage is this database allowed to use before we start enforcing?”, which would allow the database to start enforcing limits earlier.
Doing this would mean that the database ID would be included in Hyperdrive’s cache key, which would make cache hit rates very poor. For accounts with millions of active databases, an account-based cache key means that most of the heartbeats use the same cached account information from Hyperdrive and never reach Postgres.
Limit enforcement is slightly slower than it could be in terms of reaction to usage changes, but this is acceptable.
Separately from the above flow, we have a process that periodically snapshots the storage usage information from Postgres into a ClickHouse cluster, so that we can get a historical view of storage over time. These ClickHouse events are also the source of truth for storage usage billing purposes.
Enforcing row usage limits at the edge
D1 also enforces daily execution usage limits for free tier customers. The pattern we use here is different, and is worth mentioning as well.
Whenever an SQL query is executed in a Durable Object, we track how many rows it reads and writes (including index updates if needed) to perform the query. When the query execution completes, we publish a usage event that ends up in another ClickHouse cluster. These events are what drive our row-based usage billing.
A central component, call it “Limiter”, runs in our Core data centers and periodically queries the usage events from ClickHouse since the start of the day:
SELECT account_id, sum(rows_read) as reads, sum(rows_written) as writes
FROM requests
WHERE timestamp > toStartOfDay(now())
GROUP BY account_id HAVING reads > ? or writes > ?
ClickHouse deals with this kind of query better than Postgres, and we also benefit from not overloading our Postgres cluster for analytical queries.
For every account that is over the limit, we check their entitlements and tier (this limit applies only to free tier users). If they are over a limit, we email them (deduplicated throughout the day), and set a key in Quicksilver, our internal globally distributed key-value store with fast sub-second replication, with an expiry date at the end of the day. If the account upgrades to the Workers Paid tier, we receive a message on a queue and clear the Quicksilver key.
Each D1 Durable Object periodically checks Quicksilver at the edge to find out whether its account has been limited, and in case it is, they reject any future query execution until the limit is lifted.
Someone building on the Developer Platform can use Workers KV Instant, which is built on top of Quicksilver.
This pattern avoids any load into the regional Postgres for the entire flow and uses the right tool for the right job. Doing analytics queries with ClickHouse is more efficient than doing them in Postgres.
This pattern is common across the company, but different from the approach we use for storage usage limit enforcement. In the future, we may migrate other limit enforcements to use this pattern instead.
Conclusion
The D1 architecture is designed around separating control plane concerns from hot-path query execution.
Each decision follows our guiding principles: reducing central regional bottlenecks, using caching and read replicas along with eventual consistency when possible to scale out read throughput, and choosing the right data store for each job: Postgres for transactional metadata, ClickHouse for analytics, and Workers KV for globally replicated routing data.
If you are building a vibe coding platform and want to offer your users managed SQLite databases in a fast, cost-efficient, and reliable way, consider using D1.
If you are building applications on Workers and the Developer Platform, the patterns and trade-offs covered here reflect real decisions made for D1. Use them as a foundation in your own applications.
Check out the D1 documentation, and let us know what you build in the D1 Discord channel!
Acknowledgements
Massive thanks to Cloudflare’s internal Databases and Hyperdrive teams, who helped us find problematic usage patterns and suggested improvements.

articles.title: Hypersonic Technologies is turning methane into hydrogen and carbon black
articles.text:
Hypersonic Technologies is turning methane into hydrogen and carbon black
Chennai-based deeptech startup Hypersonic Technologies is betting on two revenue streams to help industrial customers offset production costs while reducing emissions.
Hydrogen is expected to play a larger role in helping industries cut emissions, but conventional production methods can leave a significant carbon footprint. Chennai-based Hypersonic Technologies is working on an alternative that produces hydrogen alongside carbon black, a commercially useful material used in tyres, rubber and pigments.
Founded in 2023 by Jayaraman Kandasamy and Jayakumar Venkatesan, the climate-tech startup uses staged-plasma pyrolysis to convert methane and biomethane into hydrogen and solid carbon. By producing two materials through one process, it aims to help industrial customers offset production costs while reducing emissions.
Kandasamy has more than a decade of experience in Europe, where he worked on plasma technology for aerospace propulsion and explored converting biomass into fuel and hydrogen-rich gases. After returning to India, he founded Hypersonic Technologies to apply this experience to industrial decarbonisation.
“Our main mission is converting methane and biomethane into hydrogen and carbon black using staged-plasma pyrolysis technology,” he says. “The aim is to decarbonise industries, particularly oil refineries, steel, cement, and fertiliser, while also producing carbon black through the same process.”
One process, two outputs
Plasma pyrolysis uses high temperatures to break down hydrocarbons into hydrogen and solid carbon. Hypersonic Technologies combines dielectric plasma with microwave plasma in two stages, which Kandasamy says can improve efficiency and make the process more stable than a single-stage system.
The technology aims to address emissions associated with conventional hydrogen production. Kandasamy says steam methane reforming, a widely used method, can emit around 10 kg of carbon dioxide for every kilogram of hydrogen produced. Carbon black production also generates emissions.
“Both methods have to move towards cleaner, climate-oriented options. That is why this technology is important,” he says. “Methane is available in several places, where it may simply be flared. Instead, we can use it as feedstock to produce hydrogen and solid carbon.”
The company's prototype is at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 5, meaning it has been validated in a relevant environment. Its lab-scale system at IIT Madras produces around 500 grams of hydrogen per hour, according to Kandasamy. The technology has received a patent grant, and the startup says it has also been validated through the government-backed NRDC-NETRA programme.
The carbon black produced is intended for industrial applications, including pigments, and the company is exploring higher-value grades. Kandasamy says Hypersonic has held discussions with established carbon black manufacturers about possible collaborations, although the technology is still at an early stage.
“We are looking at producing carbon black that can be used for pigments and other applications,” he says. “The advantage is that hydrogen and carbon black can both be monetised, rather than relying on hydrogen revenue alone.”
Moving from the lab to industry
Hypersonic Technologies is targeting refineries, steelmakers, cement companies, and fertiliser manufacturers. It is also exploring commercial models that could include equipment sales, operating partnerships, and payments linked to output.
Its immediate challenge is scaling the prototype. Kandasamy says the company needs around Rs 5 crore to advance from TRL 5 to TRL 7, with plans for a larger pilot plant once funding is secured. The startup is also seeking government support and has received a Carbon Zero Challenge grant.
“We are a deeptech hardware startup, so we need funding to take the technology to the next level,” he says. “Once we establish a plant producing five kilograms of hydrogen per hour and reach the required validation stage, we can pursue orders from refineries and steel companies.”
Kandasamy says industrial adoption will depend largely on cost, particularly because major manufacturers cannot easily replace existing infrastructure. He sees new facilities as a more immediate opportunity than retrofitting existing plants.
“Industries are very sensitive to cost. They cannot replace existing technology overnight because they have already invested in it,” he says. “But when they set up new facilities, they can evaluate alternatives such as plasma pyrolysis.”
For Hypersonic Technologies, the next step is to demonstrate that its process can produce hydrogen and carbon black reliably and economically at a larger scale.
Hypersonic Technologies is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: New USFP Pluggable Optics Form Factor for Higher Speeds from Cisco and NVIDIA
articles.text:
Ahead of the OCP Global Summit, Cisco briefed analysts on AI-infrastructure announcements spanning optics, silicon, systems, and software. For us, the headline is clearly the ultra-dense small form factor, or USFP, a pluggable module Cisco developed with NVIDIA for 400G SerDes lanes, which it says enabling higher-density 1.6Tbps fabrics. Cisco also detailed the Silicon One G300 in first systems, a G302 front-end top-of-rack switch coming in Q4 2026, and the Silicon One A100L aimed at lower-cost 10G/1G out-of-band management switches. USFP will be a big one with both Cisco and NVIDIA behind it and because next-generation pluggable optics are a key part of the 1.6Tbps Ethernet generation. To me, the A100L stood out on the briefing call since Cisco’s custom silicon applied to cost-sensitive switching rather than only the high-performance fabric.
Cisco OCP AI Networking Announcements
Cisco and NVIDIA are designing a new pluggable form factor for 400G SerDes lanes rather than today’s common 200G lanes. We will say “common” because there is still a lot of 56G PAM4 SerDes and 112G gear being sold today. Moving to 400G means 1.6Tbps networking can happen on four lanes, scaling to 6.4T aggregate across 16 lanes and 12.8T across 32. Cisco and NVIDIA are jointly drafting the multi-source specification so other vendors can build to it.
It is interesting that QSFP/ OSFP were not sufficient for the next-gen speeds. Pairing that optics work with switch silicon produces the ethernet-to-optical architecture on the next figure, which places the Silicon One G300 in first-shipped Cisco 8000 and N9000 systems at 102.4T of capacity across 1.6T ports. Now, the new G302 drives a 51.2T front-end top-of-rack switch using 200G SerDes.
The Silcon One A100L made me ask a question at the analyst pre-brief. Custom AI silicon usually appears in high-performance fabric switches since that is where the value from doing something custom often can be captured. Lower-end silicon found in management boxes running the 1G/10G networks in racks tends to be mostly just a volume play. Cisco said it was proof the architecture scales and hyperscale clients wanted to run SONiC on everything. I asked what the licensing model would be, more perpetual like a C1300 or more like the Nexus 9K series but did not get a clear answer on that one so I am going to call it a TBD. The reason I asked is that if you are doing custom silicon versus like a Marvell Prestera and not capturing software revenue, that feels like a tough road to take.
Live Protect for Cisco SONiC on Nexus One adds runtime vulnerability shielding to N9000 switches, applying policy to a running system so operators can protect it before scheduling a conventional patch and reboot. Cisco SONiC is set to be available in 2027, but that feels like a big move for Cisco as well.
Cisco positions Live Protect to shrink the exploit window, with availability slated for Q2 2027 in Cisco-validated SONiC environments. Customers will also be able to choose between community or custom SONiC and a Cisco-validated distribution, as the final operating-model figure shows.
Rounding out the software story is how Cisco intends customers to run SONiC. An operating-model figure lays out two tracks. A community or custom path offers full customization and source access for maximum control, while a turnkey Cisco-validated path provides a defined upgrade path and professional services. Notably, Cisco’s use of NVIDIA Spectrum-X is an option we have covered before, but aside from supporting the open-source SONiC, Cisco is also supporting switching platforms from NVIDIA.
Final Words
With Cisco and NVIDIA behind USFP, it will become an industry standard. Hopefully we will get to see some module shells on the OCP show floor this week. Silicon One G302 is a meaningful milestone on its own, but A100L sliding into out-of-band management feels almost crazy to me, since the sub-1Tbps switch space was widely assumed to be largely commoditized.

articles.title: Cyberattaque « opportuniste » contre les supermarchés français : des chercheurs évoquent « une réalité largement sous-estimée »
articles.text:
Des équipements industriels connectés, comme des frigos, peuvent être pris pour cible « avec une facilité déconcertante ». Synacktiv, une entreprise française spécialisée dans la cybersécurité offensive, réagit aux cyberattaques qui ont déréglé les frigos de centaines de supermarchés. Pour Synacktiv, la vague de cyberattaques met en lumière « une réalité largement sous-estimée ».
Des failles connues dans les systèmes de Danfoss
Dans une réaction adressée à 01net, l’entreprise assure que ses chercheurs « connaissent particulièrement bien ces systèmes ». Par le passé, les chercheurs de Synacktiv ont déjà identifié plusieurs vulnérabilités dans des équipements signés Danfoss, le fabricant danois au cœur de la cyberattaque contre les supermarchés. L’entreprise originaire du Danemark a en effet conçu les systèmes de régulation frigorifique qui ont été piratés dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre 2026, et qui ont été déréglés à distance par des cybercriminels.
Parmi les vulnérabilités épinglées par Synacktiv, on trouve une faille permettant de contourner l’authentification. Autrement dit, des pirates pouvaient se connecter à des systèmes sans avoir besoin du moindre identifiant. L’alerte est loin d’être récente. Trois ans avant la cyberattaque, Synacktiv a déjà découvert des vulnérabilités sur d’anciens systèmes de régulation Danfoss, les SM800 et SC255/SC355. « Le problème est loin d’être théorique », insiste Synacktiv.
Le CERT-FR, le centre gouvernemental de veille et de réponse aux attaques informatiques rattaché à l’Anssi, confirme d’ailleurs le problème. Dans une alerte publiée ce 12 octobre, il dit avoir connaissance de « nombreuses compromissions » des équipements Danfoss des séries AK-SM et AK-SC. En cause : des interfaces de gestion exposées sur Internet, ce qui est « contraire aux bonnes pratiques », rappelle l’organisme. Il recommande de déconnecter ces équipements d’Internet ou d’en filtrer strictement l’accès. En cas de piratage, les exploitants doivent réinitialiser les boîtiers, appliquer tous les correctifs disponibles et changer leurs mots de passe.
 ⚠️ CERT-FR Alert ⚠️
The CERT-FR is aware of numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series.
— CERT-FR (@CERT_FR) October 12, 2026
À lire aussi : 200 000 appareils piratés : ce botnet utilise la blockchain pour brouiller les pistes
Des frigos connectés sans mot de passe
Lors d’un audit réalisé récemment, les experts ont cette fois découvert des systèmes de réfrigération accessibles « directement depuis Internet, sans aucun mot de passe ». Pour mener une cyberattaque, il suffit donc théoriquement de trouver l’appareil en parcourant le réseau. Une fois à l’intérieur, un attaquant peut « arrêter les équipements ou modifier à distance les températures de conservation », ce qui peut avoir des impacts « potentiellement importants sur les marchandises et l’activité des magasins », prévient l’entreprise. C’est peut-être ce qu’il s’est passé lors de l’opération qui vient de semer la pagaille dans des centaines de magasins français.
Le chercheur en cybersécurité français Baptiste Robert affirme d’ailleurs avoir recensé 2 752 « systèmes » Danfoss accessibles en ligne. Plus de la moitié d’entre eux, soit 1 590, se trouvent en France.
 We count 2752 Danfoss “systems” online.
We’re gonna do a quick and dirty thread the old-school way.
First observation: 1590 “systems” out of 2752 are in France
— Baptiste Robert (@fs0c131y) October 12, 2026
D’après les recherches de Synacktiv, les équipements vulnérables sont aussi « parfois accessibles depuis les réseaux internes des magasins ». La société affirme avoir pu prouver ses dires lors de plusieurs tests réalisés dans différentes enseignes. Lors des expérimentations, un chercheur s’est s’introduit dans un lieu pour vérifier que les mesures de sécurité étaient à la hauteur.
« Cet incident n’a rien de surprenant. Un réfrigérateur de supermarché n’est plus un simple appareil électrique ; c’est un système informatisé connecté à un réseau, permettant une surveillance et un contrôle à distance. Si cette connectivité permet une gestion efficace des systèmes de réfrigération, elle les expose également à des risques de cybersécurité, en particulier lorsque les équipements opérationnels fonctionnent pendant des années avec des logiciels obsolètes, sans mises à jour de sécurité régulières et avec des interfaces de gestion accessibles depuis Internet », nous explique Oded Vanunu, responsable de la recherche sur les vulnérabilités chez Check Point Software Technologies, soulignant que « les équipements opérationnels sont souvent conçus pour rester en service pendant 15 ans ou plus, alors que les cybermenaces et les technologies évoluent à un rythme bien plus soutenu ».
L’experte recommande d’abord « d’identifier les contrôleurs et les interfaces de gestion directement exposés à Internet et d’éliminer toute exposition inutile ». De son côté, Benoît Grunemwald, expert cybersécurité chez ESET, estime que c’est « un bon rappel que la cybersécurité ne relève plus seulement des équipes informatiques ». Les « systèmes de froid, de chauffage, de production ou de supervision sont devenus des systèmes numériques à part entière », ajoute l’expert.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque chez E.Leclerc : une fuite a exposé les données des clients
Une attaque « opportuniste »
À ce stade, les chercheurs de Synacktiv privilégient l’hypothèse d’une « attaque opportuniste », menée en deux temps. Les cybercriminels auraient d’abord repéré les frigos de Danfoss grâce à des moteurs de recherche spécialisés, tel que Shodan. Ce type de moteur permet de retrouver des appareils connectés à Internet, comme des caméras, serveurs, ou des systèmes industriels. Ensuite, les attaquants auraient exploité des failles connues de Danfoss ou des identifiants faciles à deviner pour prendre le contrôle sur les interfaces de gestion. In fine, ils pouvaient envoyer les commandes qu’ils souhaitaient aux frigos de centaines de supermarchés. Les pirates ont alors activé à distance le mode de dégivrage, qui fait grimper la température au-delà des 50 degrés.
« La dispersion géographique des attaques semble conforter cette hypothèse », estime Synacktiv, qui reconnaît toutefois ne pas pouvoir confirmer le mode opératoire exact « à ce stade ».
Pour l’heure, la faille exploitée le 12 octobre n’a pas encore été identifiée. L’attaque n’a pas non plus été revendiquée. Danfoss s’est contenté d’indiquer que « la majorité des logiciels touchés sont obsolètes, et ne reçoivent plus de mises à jour de sécurité ». Quoi qu’il en soit, la cyberattaque risque de laisser des traces. Interrogé par 01net, le Groupement Mousquetaires, à l’origine d’Intermarché et de Netto, estime qu’il y a environ 180 magasins concernés par cette cyberattaque, et que le « retour à la normale » sera progressif.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Anthropic cree que algunos de sus modelos pequeños ya tienen la capacidad de propagarse sin intervención humana
articles.text:
William Zhou y Daniel Freeman, dos investigadores de Anthropic, han publicado en la página web de este laboratorio un artículo que con toda seguridad va a desencadenar un debate intenso. El título de su texto es muy revelador: "Los modelos de IA pueden ser capaces de autorreplicarse sin acceder a un centro de datos". Es un titular muy directo que nos invita a hacernos una pregunta evidente: si los modelos de inteligencia artificial (IA) no necesitan acceder a un centro de datos, ¿dónde podrían autorreplicarse?
Según Zhou y Freeman, algunos modelos pequeños podrían adquirir en pocos meses la capacidad de propagarse sin intervención humana utilizando el hardware de algunos dispositivos de consumo que muchos de nosotros tenemos en casa, como los televisores, los electrodomésticos u otros aparatos dotados de conexión a internet y un SoC mínimamente capaz. Suena a ciencia ficción, pero no lo es. Los dos investigadores de Anthropic aseguran que han llegado a esta conclusión después de llevar a cabo experimentos que exploran cómo estos sistemas podrían propagarse sin intervención humana.
En su artículo plantean un escenario en el que un modelo de IA lo suficientemente avanzado podría usar dispositivos económicos y poco protegidos para ejecutar su código y continuar propagándose. No le haría falta un centro de datos; solo necesitaría una red de dispositivos conectados a internet y relativamente poco protegidos. Lo más preocupante de esta posibilidad, que para Zhou y Freeman es plausible, es que un ataque a gran escala de este tipo sería muy difícil de contener.
UN VISTAZO A...
Podrían bastar 30.000 millones de parámetros
Durante sus pruebas, estos investigadores de Anthropic no han utilizado únicamente sus propios modelos. En su artículo aseguran que han puesto a prueba GLM-5.2 en este escenario, un modelo de pesos abiertos desarrollado por el laboratorio chino Z.ai, y logró su cometido. Lo probaron en una red aislada de ocho nodos que ejecutaban un emulador de Android, y el modelo logró propagarse a los ocho nodos en cuatro de cinco pruebas y a siete de los ocho en la restante. Da escalofríos.
Anthropic calcula que una réplica basada en un modelo de 9.000 millones de parámetros podría tardar entre uno y dos días en propagarse
GLM-5.2 tiene aproximadamente 753.000 millones de parámetros en total, de los cuales activa unos 40.000 millones por cada token procesado. Sin embargo, Zhou y Freeman creen que un modelo mucho más pequeño, de unos 30.000 millones de parámetros, también podría salir airoso en un escenario como este. Por el momento los modelos pequeños que han probado cometen errores al encadenar las tareas que requiere este proceso, pero estiman que si el desarrollo de la IA continúa al mismo ritmo de los últimos seis meses podrían adquirir esta capacidad antes de que termine 2026.
Más allá de su tamaño, hay una diferencia muy importante entre un modelo de IA grande que está siendo procesado en un centro de datos y una red de modelos pequeños que se han replicado y distribuido en una red de dispositivos: la actividad de estos últimos no puede detenerse 'apagando' un único punto. Eso sí, su propagación sería relativamente lenta. Anthropic calcula que una réplica basada en un modelo de 9.000 millones de parámetros podría tardar entre uno y dos días en propagarse.
Existe cierta similitud entre estos modelos de IA pequeños que presumiblemente podrán propagarse a dispositivos IoT y electrodomésticos, y el malware convencional. Sin embargo, la IA tiene una cualidad que no está presente en el malware: puede ser capaz de identificar qué debe hacer para llevar a cabo su cometido en dispositivos con los que no ha tenido ninguna interacción previamente. Anthropic ya ha observado esta capacidad de adaptación al probar un modelo de 9.000 millones de parámetros que consiguió poner en funcionamiento la inferencia en ocho de los nueve tipos de hardware evaluados.
Imagen | Brecht Corbeel

articles.title: Votre Wi-Fi ralentit loin de la box ? Ces nouveaux kits devolo permettent d’étendre votre réseau — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est un phénomène classique : la connexion est impeccable dans le salon, mais le signal faiblit dans la chambre des enfants, voire disparaît dans le bureau au fond du couloir. Au-delà de la distance avec la box, les cloisons, les miroirs ou les autres appareils sans fil perturbent le signal et provoquent ces ralentissements et coupures.
Dans les grands logements ou les appartements aux cloisons épaisses, il est possible d’obtenir une bonne connexion sans fil dans toutes les pièces grâce à de petits boîtiers, à répartir dans le logement. La marque devolo en propose plusieurs :
- le kit devolo WiFi 7 Mesh BE9300 Tri-Band, à 479,90 € les deux boîtiers ;
- le kit devolo WiFi 7 Mesh BE6500, à 279,90 € les deux boîtiers.
Plusieurs boîtiers pour mieux couvrir votre logement
Lorsque le Wi-Fi peine à atteindre certaines pièces, ajouter un boîtier pour relayer le signal de la box est une solution simple à mettre en place. Un répéteur classique peut remplir ce rôle, mais selon le modèle et sa configuration, le passage d’un point d’accès à l’autre manque parfois de fluidité. Le smartphone peut notamment rester connecté à un signal devenu faible, alors qu’un autre point d’accès offre une meilleure connexion à proximité.
Un réseau Mesh, ou réseau maillé, repose au contraire sur plusieurs boîtiers qui travaillent ensemble, avec un seul nom de réseau et un seul mot de passe. Le système aide les appareils à se connecter au boîtier et à la bande de fréquences les plus adaptés à leur situation. Il facilite ainsi le passage d’un point d’accès à l’autre lorsque vous changez de pièce, par exemple pendant un appel vidéo.
Trois bandes de fréquences pour tirer parti du Wi-Fi 7
Le BE9300 utilise trois bandes de fréquences : 2,4, 5 et 6 GHz. Ces trois bandes permettent de répartir les connexions entre les appareils du foyer, ce qui désengorge le réseau, réduit les interférences et maintient des débits élevés lorsque de nombreux appareils sont connectés en même temps.
Le nom du modèle renvoie à son débit théorique maximal, soit jusqu’à 9,3 Gb/s cumulés sur les trois bandes : 1 200 Mb/s en 2,4 GHz, 2 400 Mb/s en 5 GHz et 5 765 Mb/s en 6 GHz. Ce débit se répartit entre tous les appareils connectés au réseau.
Le BE9300 profite également de plusieurs avancées du Wi-Fi 7, comme le MLO, ou Multi-Link Operation, qui permet aux appareils compatibles d’exploiter simultanément deux bandes de fréquences. Cette fonction peut améliorer le débit et la stabilité de la connexion, notamment pendant les transferts de fichiers ou les appels vidéo.
Sur la bande 6 GHz, le BE9300 peut utiliser des canaux de 320 MHz, contre un maximum de 160 MHz en Wi-Fi 6 et 6E. Cette largeur supplémentaire permet de transmettre davantage de données à la fois, notamment pour télécharger de gros fichiers ou les transférer entre appareils compatibles. Ce modèle utilise par ailleurs le 4K-QAM, une modulation qui permet de transporter davantage d’informations dans un même signal, soit un débit par flux supérieur de 20 % à celui du Wi-Fi 6 selon devolo.
Les anciens équipements restent compatibles avec le réseau, mais seuls les appareils prenant en charge ces nouvelles fonctions peuvent pleinement en profiter.
Une installation prête à l’emploi, une application pour aller plus loin
Pas besoin d’application ni de réglages particuliers pour installer les kits Mesh devolo : les boîtiers sont livrés préconfigurés pour fonctionner ensemble. Il suffit donc de relier le premier à la box avec un câble Ethernet, puis de brancher les autres sur des prises de courant dans le logement, à des endroits où ils reçoivent encore correctement le signal.
Pour celles et ceux qui souhaitent personnaliser leur réseau, l’application gratuite devolo Home Network et l’interface web dédiée permettent d’aller plus loin. Il est possible d’y configurer les appareils en profondeur, mais aussi de créer un réseau invité pour éviter de partager le mot de passe du réseau principal. L’application propose également un test de débit pour comparer plusieurs emplacements et choisir le meilleur.
En plus du Wi-Fi, chaque boîtier peut aussi connecter vos appareils – box, PC, NAS, consoles, domotique – en Ethernet grâce à ses quatre ports RJ45 : un port à 2,5 Gb/s et trois ports Gigabit (1 Gb/s). Sur le boîtier principal, le port 2,5 Gb/s sert à relier la box.
Les kits devolo WiFi 7 Mesh BE9300 Tri-Band, qui bénéficient d’une garantie fabricant de trois ans, sont disponibles sur le site de devolo :
- le BE9300 en kit de 2 est à 479,90 € ;
- le BE9300 en kit de 3 est à 699,90 € ;
- le BE9300 en boîtier seul (de complément) est à 249,90 €.
Le BE6500, une alternative pour un budget plus limité
Si votre budget est plus serré mais que vous souhaitez tout de même profiter des avantages du réseau maillé, le BE6500 est l’option à privilégier.
Également compatible Wi-Fi 7, le BE6500 conserve notamment le MLO et le 4K-QAM, et fonctionne sur deux bandes simultanément : 2,4 et 5 GHz par défaut, ou 2,4 et 6 GHz après configuration. Il peut aussi utiliser des canaux de 320 MHz lorsqu’il est configuré sur la bande 6 GHz.
À 279,90 € les deux boîtiers, le BE6500 propose une alternative plus accessible, lui aussi livré préconfiguré pour une installation sans application. Le BE6500 existe aussi en kit de trois boîtiers à 399,90 €, et un boîtier d’extension vendu 149,90 € permet d’agrandir le réseau par la suite.
Chaque boîtier dispose de quatre ports Ethernet, dont un à 2,5 Gb/s, tandis que le débit théorique atteint jusqu’à 6,5 Gb/s, d’où le nom du modèle. C’est la principale différence avec le kit BE9300 de devolo.

articles.title: If AI prompts can build your product, will African VCs still invest?
articles.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped how the world works, and African AI startups, venture capital and tech ecosystems are no exception. The technology is evolving so fast that many investors are still working out how to evaluate AI startups, let alone how to fund them. Over the past six months, this column has spoken to African investors across regions, sectors, and funding stages about where AI creates genuine value, where it falls short, and what merits institutional capital. They are Babacar Seck , founder of Askya Investment Partners; Eloho Omame , partner at TLcom Capital; Emmanuel Adegboye , head of Madica; Magnifique Ishimwe , fund manager at the Development Bank of Rwanda; Husein Merchant , investment officer at Village Capital; and Benjamin Toulouze, head of corporate venture capital at AXIAN Investment. When we asked them what makes an AI startup fundable, they mostly described something an AI model itself cannot supply. Anyone can build on the same foundational models now, so investors are paying for what sits around them: voice products that work in Wolof and isiZulu, software tied so deeply into a customer’s systems that leaving is painful, licences that take years to win, and revenue. Voice is where they see the clearest opening. Adegboye says the opportunity lies in building on top of foundational models with local data, and above all in voice. He points to a man who speaks only Wolof: what is the easiest way for him to take part in an economy increasingly run by software? Seck makes the same point about South Africa, where census data shows only 8.7% of citizens speak English at home. Building software has also never been cheaper, and the number of AI startups has climbed as costs have fallen. TechCabal Insights counted 207 African AI startups across 17 countries in 2025, roughly double the 104 it tracked in 2022. Most of the newest ones work in software development, business intelligence, finance and education, the areas where off-the-shelf models lowered the barrier most. When code is cheap, investors look for what rivals cannot copy. Eloho Omame of TLcom Capital compares this moment to the arrival of mobile technology in Africa. Once it becomes easy to build the thing, she says, companies defend themselves in other ways: brand, network effects, and the cost to a customer of pulling out software that runs their business. The following responses are drawn from a series of interviews TechCabal conducted with investors between April and September 2026. They have been curated by theme and edited for length and clarity. Babacar Seck. Image Source: Askya Why context is an advantage Local context decides whether an AI tool works in Africa. Founders who have it can build for specific problems, as Pewbeam AI has done with software that projects Bible verses during live church services, and as YarnGPT has done with a speech model for Nigerian-accented English, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa. They can also make something as viral as Lagos Life. Of the 207 African AI startups TechCabal Insights counted across 17 countries in 2025, two-thirds are still early stage and only eight have reached maturity. When that many companies can plug into the same foundation models, saying a product is AI-powered proves very little. That changes what investors ask founders. If AI keeps making software cheaper to write, software on its own protects nothing. What matters is everything around it: data nobody else holds, local knowledge, a way to reach customers, regulatory permission, and how deeply the product sits inside the work a customer already does. Merchant of Village Capital, whose fund has not yet looked at AI as a sector, expects most of the African opportunity to sit at the application layer. Husein Merchant (Village Capital): My personal opinion is that there is going to be a lot of opportunity on the consumer side. Given that Africa may be more of a consumer of AI technology than a creator of it, I think the investments and solutions will lean that way. Eloho Omame (TLcom Capital): AI does not make everything cheaper to build. It is not a panacea. Some things are cheaper. Testing is cheaper, so you can experiment far more quickly with LLMs than before. Whenever a technology has driven down the cost of delivering something, the shape of defensibility has changed. A company could no longer rely on a high cost of entry. AI has lowered the cost of entry the way mobile technology lowered it before. When we look at a company, we ask how it builds defensibility if testing or delivery is now commoditised. It might be the brand. It might be network effects or switching costs. Eloho Omame. Image Source: TLCOM Data and language Seck splits AI startups in two. One group builds the layers of AI itself. The other applies AI to ordinary businesses, and that is where he sees an opening for Africa. Speech data for African languages is scarce. A company that collects it, trains on it, and builds a customer base around what it can do with it owns something rivals cannot easily copy. Caantin, a Zambian startup that replaces call-centre staff with AI voice agents for banks and fintechs, told TechCabal in June 2025 it was approaching $1 million in monthly revenue, charging by the volume of calls it handles. No one has fully cracked it yet. Babacar Seck (Askya Investment Partners): Wherever you have structured data at scale, you can build small AI models that improve performance. That is exciting in the African context because we are digitising in the age of AI. We are creating structured pools of data at the same time as we apply AI to them, so companies build a competitive advantage much faster as they scale. Language is the clearest case of data that is hard to copy. In South Africa, Census 2022 found that 8.7% of people speak English most often at home. IsiZulu (24.4%), isiXhosa (16.3%), Afrikaans (10.6%) and Sepedi (10%) all rank above it. A product that only works in English is built for a small slice of that market. Babacar Seck (Askya Investment Partners): One very exciting area is voice AI in African languages. Many startups operate in that space, and none have fully cracked it. Today in Africa, most people do not speak English, French, or Portuguese at home. They speak their mother tongue, the language they are most comfortable in. The minute you have an application that lets companies talk to their customers in the customer’s own language, you bridge a divide. That applies to companies and their customers, and to governments and their citizens. Emmanuel Adegboye (Madica): I think daily about people in rural areas. What is the easiest way to take part in the global economy if you only speak Wolof? The fastest way is to build platforms that speak Wolof or deliver information in Wolof, so you can do all of that without needing to learn English. That is why I think voice is an important long-term opportunity in AI, and it is why some of our investments have been in voice AI. Emmanuel Adegboye, head of Madica. Image Source: Madica Being one with the customer Omame’s portfolio has shown her a second kind of defence: a company that sits inside a customer’s daily operations. Once its software is wired into thousands of end customers, a rival cannot easily replace it, and the margin that integration earns is protected with it. Eloho Omame (TLcom Capital): We invested in an API infrastructure business. Its API plugs into its customers’ software and delivers a fintech product. Before, each time the customer needed the product, it made an API call. Now, because of agentic technology, the system prompts the customer when they are about to run out of the resource they lease. Revenue goes up, and the company also knows its revenue is going up. The product also costs less to deliver, because there is an agentic layer on the production side too. In principle more people can now build what it builds, as cheaply as it can. But once our software is talking to each other and I am delivering value across thousands of your own customers, it is much harder for you to unplug from my system. I want a clear line of sight to how AI makes the product cheaper to create, and what happens to the margin that creates. The founder can pass it all to the customer or capture it in the business as a higher margin. As an investor, I want to see it captured in the business. Revenue comes first Defensibility answers only half the question. The other half is whether the company earns money while investors are still willing to wait, and on this continent the wait has shortened. An AI company that spends three years on compute before charging anyone fails that test, however good the idea. Magnifique Ishimwe (Development Bank of Rwanda): Basic technology can always be built. I could put together an app like the one I showed you by the next morning. The fundamental question is whether you can execute. I have done a couple of AI deals, and sometimes we cannot see when the company reaches its horizon. You can absorb two or three equity rounds, and we still do not see a path to profitability. In the United States you can be an Uber that loses money for six, eight, or ten years. In Africa, every investor asks where your revenue is, and if you do not have it, what value you have in its place. Think of an AI company that builds a chatbot for students, but nobody is willing to pay for it. You spent a lot on compute, we helped you get credits, you paid expensive engineers, and for three years nothing came out of it. Those deals are misaligned with our instrument, because we are not an equity investor. Some investors back AI infrastructure Some investors do fund the deeper layers, usually for strategic reasons. AXIAN, the Madagascar-based group with telecoms and digital banking operations, frames its infrastructure bets around who controls the data. Benjamin Toulouze (AXIAN Investment): We want to invest in AI infrastructure, and we have already done so. One example is WideBot AI, a proprietary LLM system for Arabic speakers. We invested in Nucleon Security, a Moroccan company that protects devices using zero trust, EDR, and malware tools. We are convinced about the sovereignty issue. African countries need autonomy and control over their own data. That is one of the biggest challenges in the African market, because it is fragmented across 54 countries. Emmanuel Adegboye (Madica): There is also an opportunity in hardware and AI. That is the bet we are making with ChipMango and chip design, and we will see how it evolves. Madica joined ChipMango’s $1.9 million seed round, led by Atlantica Ventures, in September 2026. Even these bets follow the same logic as the rest of the column. WideBot’s edge is Arabic dialect data and a book of more than 350 government and enterprise clients. ChipMango recruits engineers through partnerships with Nigerian universities, trains them and sells chip-design work to global customers. In each case the hard thing to copy is the data, the talent pipeline or the customer list. The cost of inaction in AI investing If African investors back only the application layer, the deeper layers of AI will be financed, built and owned elsewhere. Global capital is already moving that way. Capital is not the only gap. African data centres are chasing customers while the continent says it needs more of them, and universities are training AI engineers who leave for jobs abroad. Emmanuel Adegboye (Madica): Capital is concentrating in a handful of funds and a handful of startups. Most funding globally is going to AI infrastructure companies, and only a few of those. On top of that, most of the funding coming into Africa comes from outside Africa, which exposes the continent to that risk. If I am a Silicon Valley investor who is not close to the continent, Africa is not top of mind when I invest. Babacar Seck (Askya Investment Partners): Most data centres are chasing customers, yet we keep saying Africa does not have enough data centres. One gap is that these operators are not plugged into demand. When you speak to the global cloud players, they will tell you their biggest customers in Africa are startups, with some scale-ups spending upwards of $30 million a year on cloud. We are training a growing number of AI engineers at Carnegie Mellon in Kigali, at the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences, and at some very good Nigerian universities, and many of them find jobs abroad because the companies on the continent are not yet large enough to keep them. For now, the investors in this column have answered the question they can control. They will pay for the parts of an AI company that grow more valuable as the AI underneath gets cheaper. Whether the continent also builds that underlying layer is a question their capital cannot settle on its own. True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Deux USB-C et deux USB-A : la batterie externe JUOVI de 20 000 mAh passe à 29,99 €
articles.text:
La batterie externe JUOVI 20 000 mAh 45 W est à 29,99 €
La batterie externe JUOVI associe une capacité de 20 000 mAh, une charge rapide jusqu’à 45 W et quatre ports pour alimenter les appareils du quotidien.
La batterie externe JUOVI 20 000 mAh 45 W est proposée à 29,99 € sur Amazon, contre un ancien prix de 32,99 €. Cette baisse de 3 € représente environ 9 % de réduction. L’offre concerne le coloris noir, vendu par ZLGYL et expédié par Amazon.
Une réserve d’énergie de 20 000 mAh
Avec sa capacité annoncée de 20 000 mAh, cette batterie externe permet de prolonger l’utilisation d’un smartphone ou d’une tablette loin d’une prise. Elle peut accompagner une journée de déplacement ou servir de réserve d’énergie lorsque plusieurs appareils doivent être rechargés.
Le nombre de recharges dépend toutefois de la capacité de l’appareil branché, de son utilisation pendant la charge et des pertes de conversion. L’affichage numérique indique le niveau de batterie restant en pourcentage : un repère utile pour savoir quand recharger la JUOVI avant de repartir.
Quatre ports et une charge jusqu’à 45 W
La connectique comprend deux ports USB-C servant à la fois d’entrée et de sortie, ainsi que deux sorties USB-A. Cette combinaison permet de conserver des câbles USB-A tout en utilisant les connexions USB-C des appareils plus récents. Jusqu’à quatre appareils peuvent être branchés simultanément.
La puissance maximale annoncée atteint 45 W, avec une compatibilité PD 3.0 et QC 4.0. La vitesse effective dépend du téléphone ou de la tablette, du câble utilisé et des protocoles pris en charge. Les 45 W ne doivent donc pas être interprétés comme une puissance disponible sur chacun des quatre ports en même temps. Pour profiter de la charge rapide, il faut associer la batterie à un appareil et à un câble compatibles.
