articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, C. J. Ballance, R. Srinivas, D. M. Lucas, A. Bermúdez. Aharonov–Bohm interference in a $${\\pmb{\\mathbb{Z}}}_{\\bf{2}}$$ lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6
- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

articles.title: Cyberattack Prompts Grocery Giant Ahold Delhaize to Disconnect Systems
articles.text:
Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize has disconnected some of its systems in response to a cyberattack.
In a bare-bones notice on its website, the company revealed that it identified a security issue within its network, triggering incident response.
“Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them,” the company said.
Ahold Delhaize said its stores remain open and that its ability to serve customers has not been affected.
According to local media, the preventive measures impacted deliveries and online orders at Albert Heijn and Delhaize brands in Belgium and the Netherlands. Stores in the US appear to have been affected as well.
In a Tuesday update, the company confirmed that its brands’ stores are experiencing issues.
“The impact of our preventative measures differs per brand. Each local brand is working hard to serve its customers and minimize disruption,” Ahold Delhaize said.
It also noted that its security team is getting ready to restore the affected systems, but did not provide an estimated timeline.
“Our teams are working with urgency to investigate the incident and restore affected systems safely. As they make progress in assessing and mitigating the issues, we are in the process of starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems,” the company said.
Ahold Delhaize says it has notified the relevant authorities and stakeholders and that it has no evidence that customer and associate data has been stolen in the attack.
Responding to a SecurityWeek inquiry, an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson refrained from sharing additional details on the incident.
It is unclear if the incident is related to the cyberattack that hit refrigerators and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across Europe over the weekend.
In November 2024, Ahold Delhaize was hit by a cyberattack that impacted Giant Food pharmacies and Hannaford supermarkets, as well as Food Lion, The Giant Company, and Stop & Shop.
In April 2025, just as the INC Ransom ransomware group took credit for the incident, the company confirmed that data was stolen from its systems.
In June 2025, Ahold Delhaize notified regulators in the US that the personal information of more than 2.2 million individuals had been compromised in the ransomware attack.
*Updated with new information from Ahold Delhaize.

articles.title: Multa de R$ 138 milhões faz Meta acionar Suprema Corte em Londres
articles.text:
A Meta, dona do Facebook e do Instagram, contestou na Justiça britânica os critérios usados pelo regulador de mídia Ofcom para calcular taxas e multas previstas na Lei de Segurança Online. A empresa considera desproporcional o uso da receita mundial como base para essas cobranças.
O processo começou nesta terça-feira (13), na Alta Corte de Londres, uma semana depois de o órgão abrir uma investigação para apurar se a Meta avaliou adequadamente os riscos do recurso Instagram Instants antes de lançá-lo, em maio.
O que está em jogo no cálculo das multas
Aprovada em 2023, a Lei de Segurança Online permite que o Ofcom aplique multas de até 10% da receita mundial qualificável de uma empresa ou 18 milhões de libras (cerca de R$ 120 milhões), prevalecendo o valor maior. A legislação também autoriza o órgão a cobrar taxas para cobrir os custos de fiscalização, calculadas com base na receita.
A Meta argumenta que o regulador extrapolou os poderes previstos na lei ao adotar uma definição ampla de receita mundial qualificável. Na contestação, a empresa afirma que o método abre caminho para as maiores penalidades possíveis. Também questiona como são calculadas as multas quando duas ou mais empresas do mesmo grupo são consideradas conjuntamente responsáveis por uma infração.
O Ofcom defende sua metodologia. Segundo o órgão, a receita mundial serve apenas para determinar o limite máximo de uma eventual penalidade; a multa efetiva deve ser proporcional à infração.
Meta e Ofcom travam outras disputas
A discussão financeira se soma a outro confronto judicial. Na semana passada, a Meta participou, ao lado do TikTok e do X, de uma audiência sobre a quantidade de informações que o regulador exige das plataformas.
Um porta-voz da Meta afirmou que a empresa está comprometida em cooperar com o Ofcom, mas criticou os critérios adotados para calcular taxas e possíveis multas.
“Estamos comprometidos em cooperar de forma construtiva com o Ofcom. No entanto, nós e outros integrantes do setor de tecnologia acreditamos que suas decisões sobre a metodologia para calcular taxas e possíveis multas são desproporcionais”, declarou o representante.
A Meta também defende que as cobranças considerem os serviços regulados em cada país. Segundo o porta-voz, essa abordagem ainda permitiria ao Ofcom aplicar “as maiores multas da história corporativa do Reino Unido”.
O Ofcom, por sua vez, afirma que sua atuação é necessária para supervisionar um setor que, segundo o órgão, passou mais de 20 anos sem regulamentação e sem prestação de contas. Sobre as contestações judiciais, um porta-voz do regulador declarou: “Em todas essas frentes, defenderemos firmemente nossos fundamentos e decisões”.
A disputa coloca em debate o alcance dos poderes do Ofcom e a forma de calcular as penalidades previstas na legislação britânica. A Justiça deverá examinar os argumentos apresentados pelas partes.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: India delays digital payments fee rollout amid retailer pushback | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Following broad pushback from merchants across the country, India has delayed plans to introduce merchant fees on its digital payments network that aimed to make the business more lucrative for the companies that facilitate the payments service, long dominated by Google and PhonePe.
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which operates the country’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), said on Tuesday it was postponing the planned October 15 rollout of a 0.4% fee on eligible merchant transactions exceeding ₹2,000 (about $21), citing the festive shopping season. The fee, announced last month, would mark a significant departure from India’s years-long policy of keeping UPI payments free for merchants.
The rollout will now take place after Diwali, one of India’s biggest festivals and shopping periods, though the NPCI did not specify a new date. In September alone, UPI processed 24.07 billion transactions worth ₹29.37 trillion (about $305 billion), per NPCI.
The proposed fee drew opposition from retailers and petrol pump operators, some of whom warned they could stop accepting UPI payments if the charge took effect.
Over the past several years, UPI has become the backbone of India’s digital payments system, powering payments through apps such as Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm. Its growth has been supported by the Indian government keeping UPI payments free for merchants and providing subsidies to banks and payment providers to help them cover some of the costs.
UPI was not always free for merchants, however. Banks and payment providers previously charged merchants for transactions, but the Indian government scrapped those fees in January 2020 as it sought to encourage more people to shift away from using cash, long the dominant way people have paid for goods and services in the country. UPI has continued to grow in both transaction volume and value.
In recent years, the government has sought to take UPI overseas. In April 2020, NPCI set up its international arm, and the network is currently available in several countries, including Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and France.
NPCI had sought to limit the impact of the new merchant fee by exempting payments of ₹2,000 or less, as well as small merchants that receive less than ₹100,000 (about $1,033) a month through UPI. It also capped the fee at ₹300 (around $3) for larger transactions. The organization said it would share the money collected among participants in the UPI ecosystem to help pay for infrastructure, cybersecurity, and fraud prevention.
Citing industry estimates, NPCI said last month that the annual cost of running UPI was about ₹200 billion (around $2.1 billion), including spending on server capacity, fraud prevention, and technical support. Banks and payment companies have for years argued that they need a way to recoup those costs as transaction volumes grow.

articles.title: Juan Luis Arsuaga, antropólogo, sobre la IA: “Ojalá esta vez no ocurra, pero no hay precedentes de un cambio de modelo económico que no produzca conflictos”
articles.text:
Juan Luis Arsuaga, especialista en evolución humana, no es economista, y cuando le preguntan por la inteligencia artificial, contesta con lo que sabe: la historia. “Ojalá esta vez no ocurra, pero no hay precedentes de un cambio de modelo económico que no produzca conflictos”, ha dicho en una entrevista.
Para Arsuaga, el problema empieza cuando cambia la estructura económica y parte del trabajo humano deja de hacer falta, más que cuando una máquina aprende a hacer una tarea. Queda por saber qué pasa con quien deja de ser necesario y quién gana con ello.
Un 46 % más de producción, un 12 % más de salario: la última vez que cambió el modelo
Entre 1780 y 1840, la producción por trabajador en Gran Bretaña creció un 46 % (estimación de Nicholas Crafts y Knick Harley) y el salario real un 12 % (la de Charles Feinstein).
El historiador económico Robert Allen bautizó ese periodo como la "pausa de Engels", por Friedrich Engels, que describió la situación de la clase obrera inglesa en 1845. Según su estudio de 2009, la tasa de beneficio de los empresarios se duplicó mientras los sueldos casi no se movían, y solo hacia mediados del siglo XIX los salarios alcanzaron a la productividad: entre 1840 y 1900, la producción por trabajador aumentó un 90 % y el salario real un 123 %. Allen lo atribuye a la acumulación de capital, que tardó en ponerse a la altura del progreso técnico.
No todos los economistas aceptan que existiera esa pausa. Crafts sostiene que la participación del trabajo en la renta nacional pasó del 57,1 % en 1790 al 59,2 % en 1840, es decir, subió ligeramente, mientras que la serie de Allen la baja del 56,2 % al 49,0 %, y dice que esta choca con todas las demás estimaciones. Se discute con datos de hace dos siglos.
Del conflicto sí hay registro. En 1811, los tejedores de medias de Nottinghamshire intentaron negociar salarios más altos y que los fabricantes dejaran de producir los llamados cut-ups, prendas más baratas que exigían menos destreza y pagaban menos.
Al fracasar la negociación, rompieron 63 bastidores en Arnold y unos 200 más en el condado en tres semanas. Según Kevin Binfield, que ha estudiado el movimiento, los luditas no se oponían a la tecnología en sí, sino al uso de máquinas existentes de maneras que recortaban salarios y producían ropa de mala calidad. El Parlamento convirtió romper bastidores en delito capital, el Gobierno envió a unos 14.000 soldados al centro de Inglaterra y unas dos docenas de luditas acabaron en la horca.
¿Cuántos empleos están en juego? Depende de quién haga la cuenta
La Organización Internacional del Trabajo y el instituto polaco NASK calcularon en 2025 que uno de cada cuatro empleos del mundo (el 24 %) está en ocupaciones expuestas a la IA generativa, una cifra que sube al 34 % en los países de renta alta. Los más expuestos son los puestos administrativos, y lo más probable, dicen, es la transformación de los empleos, no su sustitución.
El FMI había medido en enero de 2024 casi el 40 % del empleo mundial y en torno al 60 % en las economías avanzadas. En estas últimas, según el análisis de su directora gerente, más o menos la mitad de los empleos expuestos podría salir ganando con la IA y la otra mitad sufrir menos demanda, salarios más bajos o menos contratación. Añadía que, en la mayoría de los escenarios, la IA probablemente agravará la desigualdad general.
Exposición no equivale a pérdida de puestos. Funcas estimó en 2026 que la IA podría destruir entre 1,7 y 2,3 millones de empleos en España entre 2025 y 2035, con un abanico de 700.000 en el escenario más optimista a más de 3,5 millones en el más pesimista. Suma además unos 1,61 millones de empleos nuevos ligados a la IA (cifra de otros estudios, con un horizonte algo distinto, 2023-2033), de modo que en el escenario central quedaría una pérdida neta de unos 400.000.
Por ahora, los datos de empleo no detectan destrucción
Eso son proyecciones; lo ocurrido lo recoge el Observatorio Trimestral del Mercado de Trabajo que elaboran Fedea y BBVA Research, publicado en septiembre: algo más del 30 % del empleo en España está en ocupaciones muy o bastante expuestas a la IA generativa, y desde 2022 el empleo ha crecido más en ellas que la media. Florentino Felgueroso, de Fedea, dice que no observan desplazamiento de empleo por la IA.
Los autores de BBVA Research, Rafael Doménech y Juan Ramón García, piden no sacar todavía conclusiones causales: los efectos, advierten, no son automáticos ni homogéneos. Los más expuestos son los trabajadores de 25 a 34 años y los titulados (más del 40 % de quienes tienen estudios superiores, frente al 15 % de quienes tienen la ESO, Educación Secundaria Obligatoria, o menos).
El análisis añade que el PIB por ocupado apenas ha variado desde finales de 2019 y que la productividad por hora ha subido un 2,4 %. La nota no ofrece cifras de salarios.
Más miedo donde hay menos formación
En mayo, el análisis de la Dirección General de Economía y Finanzas de la Comisión Europea partió de una encuesta a 21.207 personas de 18 Estados miembros y cuatro países candidatos, hecha en febrero y marzo.
Alrededor del 54 % usa herramientas de IA y algo menos de la mitad de ellas lo hace en el trabajo; el uso es mayor entre directivos y profesionales. Entre los ocupados que la usan en su empleo, el 41 % teme ser desplazado (un 14 % mucho y un 27 % algo), y ese temor es mayor entre operarios, personas de menos renta y menos formación, y jóvenes. Según el texto, la adopción desigual corre el riesgo de ampliar las disparidades económicas dentro de los mercados laborales y entre regiones. No estima el efecto neto sobre el empleo.
En España, según ADP Research (39.000 trabajadores de 36 países), el 15 % usa IA a diario y el 11 % cree que acabará sustituyéndolo.
Bruselas anunció el 22 de julio un grupo de expertos de alto nivel para estudiar cómo transforma la IA el empleo. Entre las tres prioridades de su estrategia social figuran gestionar esos efectos y reducir las desigualdades. La información publicada no dice cuándo empezará a trabajar.

articles.title: What’s old is new: Lightwell discovers novel zero-day vulnerability in core Java framework
articles.text:
Enterprise IT runs on decades-old foundational code. The prevailing assumption around these mature components is that if code has been sitting untouched in production for ten years without breaking, it must be safe. Libraries like the Eclipse Implementation of Jakarta XML Binding (JAXB) quietly power enterprise applications in the background. Embedded deep into middleware stacks and application servers, they carry heavy workloads without drawing attention.
Advanced AI security tooling doesn’t ignore these deep-stack layers, however. It finds zero-day flaws hidden in structural parsing logic that standard static analysis tools miss entirely. And discovery is only part of the story. Any new vulnerabilities impacting these load-bearing pillars need to be discovered, analyzed, and swiftly addressed by the community. This is exactly what Lightwell did with a novel vulnerability within JAXB, identified as CVE-2026-92877.
Addressing novel flaws across the software lifecycle
When a vulnerability is discovered in a new framework, communities and maintainers respond quickly. The code is fresh, developers are actively tweaking it, and patches roll out quickly. Legacy components face a different reality. Unaddressed flaws in fundamental XML binding logic can compromise every application server, middleware pipeline, and cloud service that relies on it.
Left unaddressed, a flaw like this could create severe operational consequences:
- Chained exploits: Isolated parsing bugs can be chained with other system vulnerabilities to escalate privileges, bypass access controls, or even execute arbitrary code.
- Unplanned downtime: Malformed payloads can trigger unhandled exceptions or resource exhaustion deep within key services, bringing critical business workflows to a sudden halt.
- Supply-chain amplification: Because JAXB is buried deep within thousands of enterprise software packages, downstream vendors and IT teams often don't realize they are exposed until an exploit hits production.
Discovering and addressing a novel vulnerability in a legacy codebase in real-time is key, not simply finding the problem and passing the hard work to the community. Lightwell’s work with JAXB shows the value that a collaborative, responsible, and technically innovative security practice brings to global IT infrastructure, as well as the health of upstream open source communities.
True security is upstream security
Scanning a container image and flagging a potential common vulnerability and exploit (CVE) is relatively easy with modern off-the-shelf tooling. Finding a zero-day flaw in a decade-old upstream project, engineering a fix, and contributing that patch back to the open source community is hard.
That is the core value proposition of Lightwell.
Lightwell centers on active engineering at the source and deep-level stewardship. When the Lightwell team uncovers a novel vulnerability or one is brought to our attention by a customer, our mission is to fix it upstream at the source.
By contributing this fix directly to the eclipse-ee4j community, Lightwell helps protect the broader open source ecosystem before downstream enterprise runtimes face exposure. These upstream contributions, however, are only part of the equation.
In many enterprise environments, critical infrastructure runs on older software versions that upstream communities no longer actively patch or maintain. Upstream maintainers eventually move on to new major releases. When a flaw impacts legacy versions, downstream systems are left exposed.
Lightwell steps in during those exact scenarios. Whether fixing current code upstream or backporting security patches to older releases that organizations still rely on, Lightwell helps protect critical workloads without forcing disruptive, unplanned upgrades. 
Durability is an active commitment
Durable enterprise software, the kind that allows critical infrastructure to run reliably for decades, isn’t easy to deliver. It requires continuous, active maintenance and rigorous upstream security engineering. Red Hat delivered this work for the better part of 30 years across Linux, Java, Kubernetes, and supporting projects.
The discovery and upstream acceptance of this patch to JAXB is a major milestone for Lightwell and further validates our core commitment to open source security. Protecting critical enterprise applications starts deep in the software stack, and Lightwell provides the engineering required to keep those foundations resilient.

articles.title: Facebook will let you customize your feed algorithm using AI
articles.text:
Facebook’s new “Your Algorithm” feature will let you directly add and manage topics you want to see in your feed and Facebook Reels. Meta says your recommendations “respond right away” after you make updates using the new feature by hitting “interested” or “not interested” for different topics. Your Algorithm previously launched on Instagram earlier this year, and Meta also launched a similar “Dear Algo” feature on Threads.
Facebook will let you customize your feed algorithm using AI
Meta’s bringing Instagram’s “Your Algorithm” feature to Facebook, and using LLMs more to rank content.
Facebook users will be able to access Your Algorithm or select “interested” or “not interested” from the three dots menu on individual posts. The “interested” and “not interested” buttons may also appear under posts, and Meta says it “may ask follow up questions for more detail on what you liked or disliked. You can easily tell us, in your own words, what you want to see more or less of, and your recommendations will update in real time.”
The new feature is part of a set of “AI-powered” tools Meta says it’s using to customize what users see on Facebook. It also says it’s using LLMs more in its ranking systems: “LLMs can incorporate the interests, context, and intent behind natural language, unlocking an algorithm you can actually talk to. Tell it what you want more or less of, and your recommendations respond in real time, adapting within the same session to reflect what matters to you right now.”

articles.title: Promise Robotics strikes deal to supply largest US homebuilder DR Horton
articles.text:
Toronto-based construction tech startup Promise Robotics is ready to grow south of the border after landing its first United States (US) customer: DR Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder in terms of volume.
Through the multi-year commercial agreement, DR Horton will leverage Promise’s tech and “factory-as-a-service” capabilities to support the production of more than 1,250 largely single-story, single-family homes for buyers in the Phoenix, Arizona area.
Promise CEO Ramtin Attar said a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.”
Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar told BetaKit in an interview that a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.” He said the deal emphasizes the power of the startup’s platform, which aims to help developers build homes faster and more cheaply than traditional construction methods.
“That a company at that scale is able to look at what we have done and say, ‘We’re ready to work with you,’ that, to me, is very significant,” Attar added.
Promise announced the deal today, also revealing it intends to open a 16,000-square-foot factory in Phoenix. There, its AI-powered robots will assemble the components necessary to construct these houses in what marks the start of its broader US expansion. “This is our go-to-market facility in [the] US,” Attar said.
The hub, which will be Promise’s first outside of Canada and the company’s third of its kind after Calgary and Edmonton, is expected to begin manufacturing in early 2027.
“I was actually talking to an investor the other day who said, ‘I really love your odds. If you can build in the frost in Calgary, Phoenix is going to be pretty darn simple,’ and that’s exactly the case,” Attar said.
While the US housing market is very different from Canada’s, Attar said it faces similar challenges, from labour shortages to rising costs, and pressure to build more homes faster.
RELATED: Canada’s housing supply is in crisis. Can robots help?
Promise uses AI to interpret existing home designs, generate production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrate manufacturing, and connect that production with site installation as part of one integrated platform. The company equips off-the-shelf robots with its own tooling and software to produce everything from repeatable modular housing to custom builds.
“We are continuously focused on improving cycle times, increasing production capacity, and bringing greater consistency and predictability to our operations,” DR Horton senior vice president of strategic innovation Brad Conlon said in a statement. “Promise Robotics’ integrated platform gives us a new capability to support those goals.”
Attar claimed Promise, which is now contracted to build just over 2,500 homes for several different homebuilders, has completed over 200 builds to date for a group that includes Brookfield, Hopewell, and Mattamy.
“These are real market homes that people are living in,” the Autodesk alumnus said.
Promise’s factories are currently capable of producing many of the core components that make a house, from the interior and exterior walls to the flooring, stairs, and roof.
The 80-person startup is working to add heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and plumbing, followed by drywall, insulation, and more over time as it looks to grow to 100 employees by the end of 2026.
Feature image courtesy Promise Robotics.

articles.title: Así es HomeView, la última pantalla inteligente de Apple para controlar los hogares con su nueva IA
articles.text:
Así es HomeView, la última pantalla inteligente de Apple para controlar los hogares con su nueva IA
El dispositivo, diseñado para que la renovada Siri pueda rivalizar con la Alexa de Amazon, no se venderá en la Unión Europea porque no cumple con la normativa comunitaria de competencia digital
Apple ha llegado varios años tarde a la carrera de la IA generativa y pretende recuperar terreno donde flaquean sus rivales, que todavía no han sido capaces de lanzar dispositivos que lleven ChatGPT, Gemini o Claude más allá del móvil, la tableta o el ordenador. El gigante tecnológico ha presentado este martes HomeView, una nueva pantalla táctil diseñada específicamente para Siri AI —su asistente de inteligencia artificial de nueva generación—, con el objetivo de llevarla a los hogares y convertirla en el panel de control de todo tipo de dispositivos inteligentes. Además de esa función de central domótica, reconoce la cara de cada usuario de la casa para darle acceso, en pantalla y por voz, a la información personal de sus mensajes, calendarios o recordatorios. También sirve como un marco digital compartido por la familia y para poner música, podcasts, vídeos y programas de televisión.
Este caballo de Troya, con el que Apple quiere abrir una nueva batalla en la guerra tecnológica de la inteligencia artificial, saldrá a la venta en EE UU el próximo 13 de noviembre, a un precio de 300 dólares. Sin embargo, no hay ninguna fecha para la llegada de HomeView a España, “pues Siri AI aún no está disponible para iPhone en la Unión Europea”, según un comunicado de la compañía, que añade que “está trabajando de manera constructiva con la UE en un intento de encontrar un camino hacia adelante”. Con una pantalla cuadrada de 7 pulgadas, similar en superficie a la de un iPad mini o un iPhone Duo abierto, llegará en cuatro colores y en dos modalidades diferentes: una para montar en la pared y otra para poner sobre una mesa, encimera o estante. Esta última añade a la pantalla una base que permite inclinarla y que realza los bajos de su sonido.
John Ternus, el nuevo consejero delegado de Apple (que sustituyó a Tim Cook el pasado 1 de septiembre), se ha estrenado presentando dos dispositivos totalmente nuevos en sus dos primeros meses de mandato. Tras el anuncio del teléfono plegable iPhone Duo, a los pocos días de ponerse al frente de la compañía, ahora Ternus ha desvelado HomeView en un evento privado celebrado en Nueva York. De nuevo, la idea es llevar la manzana a una categoría en la que muchas grandes tecnológicas lo han intentado, y sin mayor éxito. En este caso, en el terreno de las pantallas inteligentes para el hogar, solo Amazon resiste con sus Echo Show; y lo hace de aquella manera: a base de rebajarlas frecuentemente a la mitad de precio en su propia tienda online.
HomeView abre la puerta a los usuarios de Apple a controlar las luces, cámaras de seguridad, persianas, puertas y demás dispositivos inteligentes con un aparato específico para eso —que además sirve para hacer videollamadas, poner música, visualizar recetas o resolver dudas—, en lugar de hacerlo con sus móviles o tabletas. Esto ha sido hasta ahora un lujo reservado para el nicho de usuarios más entusiastas de la digitalización doméstica, que tenían que recurrir al asistente de Amazon y decirle “Alexa, apaga las luces del salón y pon la lavadora” si querían tener un sistema domótico compatible con múltiples marcas de electrodomésticos, bombillas, enchufes y cámaras. O si querían respuestas medianamente fiables y poder conversar con esa IA del hogar para preguntarle cuestiones de actualidad informativa, cultura general o resultados deportivos.
Adiós a la vieja Siri (fuera de Europa)
Hasta ahora, Siri podía hacer eso desde los altavoces HomePod mini de Apple, pero con unas limitaciones que exasperaban a sus usuarios, sobre todo desde que pueden conversar con naturalidad con ChatGPT y demás asistentes de IA generativa. Pero esos HomePod mini, lanzados en 2020, no eran compatibles con Siri AI, la nueva generación del asistente de voz que Apple estrenó finalmente hace un mes, después de no poder cumplir su promesa inicial de lanzarla hace un año y medio; y de tener que recurrir a la tecnología de IA de Google para poder empezar de cero. Junto al HomeView, Apple ha presentado también nuevas versiones de los HomePod mini y de Apple TV —su reproductor multimedia para conectar el televisor—, que ya sí son compatibles con Siri AI y otras funciones de inteligencia artificial generativa.
Al iniciarse la presentación de este martes, quedaba la duda de si este asistente con IA de última generación estará disponible en la Unión Europea, donde Siri AI no ha llegado ni a los iPhone ni a los iPads porque no cumple con la Ley de Mercados Digitales. Los usuarios europeos solo la pueden utilizar —y de momento, solo en inglés— en los ordenadores Mac, que están exentos de esa normativa para garantizar la competencia en los teléfonos y tabletas. Al revelarse las especificaciones finales del HomeView, se ha constatado que necesita estar emparejado a un iPhone o un iPad en el que esté activado Siri AI, lo que descarta la llegada de este producto a España y demás países del espacio comunitario. Al menos, mientras Apple y la Comisión Europea no arreglen sus diferencias.

articles.title: Aldi lanza el miércoles 21 de octubre (por 9,99 euros) este reloj despertador radiocontrolado con termómetro ideal para el dormitorio
articles.text:
Como cada semana, Aldi acaba de renovar su folleto de ofertas con algunas novedades de lo más interesantes. Una de las cuales es este reloj despertador con proyector que, además, se ajusta automáticamente al horario de invierno y verano gracias a que es radiocontrolado. Tiene un precio de 9,99 euros y estará disponible en tiendas Aldi a partir del miércoles 21 de octubre.
Hama | Reloj con proyección
Si no tenemos a mano ninguna tienda de Aldi o preferimos simplemente comprar online, encontramos una completísima alternativa a este reloj Krontaler de Aldi en Amazon: este Hama, disponible por 32,68 euros, con similares características pero que además viene con un puerto USB para cargar el teléfono móvil o la tablet.
Incluye un proyector giratorio de 180 grados
El nuevo reloj despertador de Aldi ya merece la pena a su PVP de 11,99 euros, pero más aún a los 9,99 euros que costará rebajado desde el miércoles 21. Porque además de bastante económico, es súper completo al incluir hora, fecha, día de la semana y hasta la temperatura de la habitación. Siendo ideal para colocar en el dormitorio, sobre todo, por su función de proyector.
Porque no sólo cuenta con una pantalla donde muestra toda esa información, sino que incluye un brazo articulado giratorio de 180 grados a modo de mini proyector, que permite proyectar la hora en la pared o el techo. Un aspecto muy diferencial frente a la mayoría de relojes despertadores.
Sin olvidarnos de otra de sus funciones clave: ajusta automáticamente el horario de verano e invierno, así como la hora, mediante radiofrecuencia. Esto, en esencia, hace que siempre esté sincronizado y en hora, evitando que indique una hora errónea sin tener que ajustarlo nosotros cada cierto tiempo como suele ocurrir con los relojes manuales.

articles.title: « Équipé comme un véhicule à 200 000 € » : le spectaculaire Xpeng G9L débarque en France à moitié prix
articles.text:
Avouons que les gros SUV chinois que nous vous faisons régulièrement découvrir dans nos colonnes n’existent pas réellement en France. Ils ne sont pourtant pas très chers, ultra équipés, hyper autonomes et super rapides à recharger. Beaucoup expriment alors à juste titre leur frustration dans les commentaires… Bonne nouvelle, Xpeng semble aujourd’hui les avoir entendus en parachutant l’immense G9L sur notre marché.
Avec ses 5,12 mètres de long, l’engin parvient à surpasser le déjà très obèse G9. Et contrairement à ce que son nom peut suggérer, le G9L n’est pas une vulgaire version rallongée du G9. Il s’agit d’un modèle inédit de la tête aux pieds se plaçant au sommet de la gamme Xpeng. Pour justifier un tel statut, ce porte-drapeau promet un équipement de pointe drapé dans un confort bluffant.
Écran pliant au toit et frigo intégré : la vie de château aux places arrière
Car ce n’est pas au niveau du style qu’il se distinguera des autres. Le G9L est massif avec des éléments esthétiques vus et revus. C’est plutôt à bord que les choses deviennent véritablement intéressantes avec des configurations en 6 et 7 places. Bien vu pour le confort avec des assises zéro gravité massantes sur 16 points installées sous une climatisation centrale innovante. Un vrai réfrigérateur électrique est également à disposition des gourmands.
Plus impressionnant, l’écran multimédia intégré au toit se déploie devant les passagers arrière pour une expérience numérique haut de gamme. La qualité de finition est d’ailleurs du même acabit, avec des matériaux très soignés y compris en partie basse. Cette atmosphère premium se prolonge naturellement sur la liste des équipements. Le G9L embarque ainsi une suspension pneumatique double chambre optimisant le toucher de route.
Suspension pneumatique et feux projecteurs : la débauche technologique
Ses quatre roues directrices améliorent la maniabilité, tandis que les feux matriciels à LED sont une première chez Xpeng. Ils permettent en outre de projeter des guides lumineux au sol. Les cinq ouvrants sont également électriques, même s’ils manquent parfois de finesse dans leur fonctionnement. En configuration 6 places comme ici, l’accès au troisième rang est plutôt aisé. La modularité sera à confirmer en version 7 places avec une banquette au deuxième rang.
Au dernier rang, les attentions ne manquent en tout cas pas avec des sièges chauffants au dossier électrique. L’espace aux jambes est par ailleurs excellent, quelle que soit la place retenue. Côté conduite, le G9L est bien entendu semi-autonome avec ses 3 puces Turing permettant une puissance de calcul ultra élevée. Sa batterie nickel manganèse cobalt en architecture 800 V garde une capacité encore inconnue.
Dès 74 990 € : des prestations de luxe à prix « cassé » ?
Xpeng promet en tout cas jusqu’à 591 km d’autonomie et un 10 à 80 % de charge en seulement 12 minutes. Cela nous amène alors aux trois versions proposées à la vente. L’entrée de gamme Autonomie Étendue Propulsion s’échange contre 74 990 € avec 367 ch et un rayon d’action de 591 km sur le cycle WLTP. Le niveau supérieur Performance Intégrale attaque à 79 990 €, voit sa puissance grimper à 585 ch et son autonomie freinée à 553 km.
Ces deux modèles peuvent accueillir 7 personnes. Ce n’est pas le cas du haut de gamme Performance Intégrale avec ses 6 places facturé 85 990 €. Oui, c’est bien loin des prix pratiqués en Chine qui sont à minima deux fois inférieurs. Mais il faut rappeler que l’industrie automobile chinoise est massivement subventionnée et que l’Europe taxe lourdement les véhicules provenant de l’Empire du Milieu.
Audi, BMW et Volvo dans le collimateur : le pari audacieux de Xpeng
Cela ne suffit de toute manière pas à effacer l’argument prix brandi sans cesse par les constructeurs chinois. Xpeng explique ainsi que « le G9L offre le niveau d’équipements, la technologie et la norme de confort des marques de luxe traditionnelles dont le prix est supérieur à 200 000 € ». La marque vise en priorité les familles roulant en Audi Q7, Volvo XC90 et BMW X5 avec pour principal argument la garantie et le rapport qualité/prix.

articles.title: SpaceFields is turning solid propulsion R&D into scaled manufacturing
articles.text:
SpaceFields is turning solid propulsion R&D into scaled manufacturing
From winning iDEX challenges to signing MoUs with defence PSUs, IISc-incubated SpaceFields is moving from bespoke propulsion design to large‑scale supply.
In 2025, Bengaluru-based spacetech startup SpaceFields was best known for its work on solid rocket propulsion and an Aerospike engine it hoped could make rocket launches more efficient. The company was then a relatively small, IISc-incubated startup working to develop its propulsion technology and build out its manufacturing capabilities.
Just a year down the line, SpaceFields has expanded both its team and its ambitions, with defence now becoming an increasingly important part of its business.
The startup has raised Rs 53.5 crore to date, including a Rs 42.5 crore pre-Series A round. It has used the capital to establish a 45,000-square-foot R&D facility in Bengaluru's Rajajinagar Industrial area, which has received DSIR certification. Its team has grown to nearly 60 people, with hiring across aerospace engineering, materials, chemicals, avionics, and propulsion.
“We are now developing multiple different types of solid propulsion systems for different applications,” Apurwa Masook, Co-founder and CEO, tells YourStory.
From propulsion R&D to defence applications
The spacetech startup, no longer focused on a single propulsion technology, now develops customised solid propulsion systems for different platforms and applications. Its customers include Bharat Electronics, HAL, Bharat Forge, and multiple drone startups.
The B2B and B2G company has also won five Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) challenges, and now has more than 16 customers across government and private companies.
“The work is sort of similar where we are developing these custom solid propulsion systems for different applications,” Masook says. “It is bespoke to the platform because propulsion is a subsystem of the platform that it is going on.”
One area where the company is working with defence customers is the refurbishment of ageing rocket and missile stockpiles. Many systems have exceeded their shelf life, while access to their original overseas manufacturers can be limited.
“This is a large problem with the armed forces,” Apurwa says. “India needs sovereign capability in this field.” Through its iDEX projects, SpaceFields has secured multiple refurbishment programmes for different missiles.
Building the capacity to manufacture at scale
SpaceFields has also signed MoUs with defence PSUs like Munitions India Limited and Bharat Dynamics Limited. The startup is now building the infrastructure to support larger programmes. It has received 121 acres of land in Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh, where it plans to establish a large-scale solid-propellant manufacturing facility over the next two years. The Bengaluru site will remain its design and R&D centre.
“We plan to set up our production unit in Anantapur,” the CEO says. “In the next two years we'll be planning to set up the factory or the propellant production unit there.”
The company has filed 32 patents, of which 11 have been granted, and continues to leverage IISc's facilities and expertise.
The founder says its near-term focus is converting development work into procurement. SpaceFields says it has embedded its systems through pilot programmes and iDEX projects into strategic programmes involving rockets, missiles and armaments.
“By the time we're production ready, we will have large-scale procurements coming our way parallelly,” he says.
The company has generated around Rs 6.5 crore in cumulative revenue and was last valued at less than Rs 200 crore. Its investors include Globaz Technologies, Rainmatter, Venture Catalysts, Rockstud Capital, and Jamwant Ventures.
Masook believes the broader ecosystem is moving in SpaceFields' favour, with increased investor interest and government reforms opening up the space and deeptech sectors.
“The amount of changes, reforms, and implementation in a few quarters is commendable. For us, the next phase is about turning our propulsion expertise into industrial capacity and moving from developing solid propulsion systems to supplying them at scale, ” Masook says.
SpaceFields is part of YourStory’s Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India’s most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Anthropic warnt: Kleine KI-Modelle könnten sich bald selbst replizieren und ausbreiten
articles.text:
Anthropic warnt: KI-Modelle könnten sich bald selbst auf Smart-Home-Geräten ausbreiten
Die Berichte über potenzielle Risiken durch neue, leistungsstarke KI-Modelle reißen nicht ab. Jetzt hat sich das „Frontier Red“-Team von Anthropic in einem umfangreichen Beitrag zu Wort gemeldet. Die Expert:innen berichten, dass ihre Experimente darauf hindeuten, dass kleine KI-Modelle möglicherweise nur noch Monate davon entfernt sind, sich auf IoT-Geräten selbst zu replizieren. Dazu zählen beispielsweise smarte Heizkörperthermostate und Leuchtmittel, aber auch Video-Türklingeln, vernetzte Haushaltsgeräte oder Smart Speaker. In diesem Fall wären die Modelle nur noch schwer zu stoppen.
KI-Replikation stehe kurz bevor
„In der Cybersicherheit ist ein Wurm ein Programm, das sich ohne menschliches Zutun von einem Computer auf den nächsten kopiert. Frühere Arbeiten haben gezeigt, dass KI-Agenten sich ähnlich verhalten können. Sie scannen ihr Netzwerk, führen einen Exploit aus und kopieren Modellgewichte über einen GPU-Cluster hinweg auf einen Zielrechner“, heißt es in dem Beitrag von Anthropic. So ein „KI-Wurm“ könne „seine Modellgewichte bei der Vermehrung mit sich führen (oder sie von einem öffentlichen Hub erneut herunterladen) und dann Inferenz direkt auf kompromittierter Hardware ausführen. Effektiv würden die Gewichte Teil der Malware-Nutzlast werden.“ Ein solcher Replikator hätte keinen zentralen Punkt zum Abschalten. Die Verdopplungszeit könnte Tage betragen.
In seinen Experimenten untersuchte Anthropic, ob KI-Modelle anfällige Geräte ausfindig machen, sich darauf kopieren und ohne menschliche Hilfe weiterverbreiten können. Das Unternehmen stellte dabei fest, dass kleine Modelle mit weniger als 30 Milliarden Parametern die zahlreichen für die Replikation erforderlichen Schritte ausführen konnten. Die Exploit-Phase war allerdings bewusst vereinfacht, sodass die Ergebnisse nur eine Obergrenze darstellen. Im Gegensatz zu Malware könnten die Modelle laut Anthropic zudem unbekannte Geräte selbstständig identifizieren und Prozessoren in Rechenzentren ins Visier nehmen.
Wie ein „digitaler Schleimpilz“
„Die Fähigkeiten, die KI-Modelle im Allgemeinen zu leistungsstarken Programmieragenten machen, lassen sich auch auf Cyber-Aufgaben übertragen, einschließlich der autonomen Replikation“, heißt es in dem Beitrag weiter. Das Unternehmen verfüge noch nicht über einen voll funktionsfähigen, eigenmächtigen Replikator, aber „die Agenten sind zunehmend in der Lage, die einzelnen Schritte in der Replikationskette auszuführen.“ Welche Form die autonome KI-Replikation genau annehmen wird, sei bisher unklar. Laut den Forscher:innen könnte es sich um einen „digitalen Schleimpilz“ handeln, der auf relativ unsicherer Recheninfrastruktur lebt und sich langsam ausbreitet. Genauso denkbar sei aber auch ein leistungsstarkes Cybermodell, das Rechenzentren in hohem Tempo durchbricht.
Der Bericht von Anthropic erscheint zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem das Risiko der aktuellen KI-Entwicklung im Zentrum der Debatte steht. Seit Wochen melden KI-Labore neue Sicherheitsvorfälle, bei denen sich ihre Modelle der Kontrolle entzogen, aus ihren Testumgebungen ausbrachen und unerlaubt in fremde Systeme eindrangen. Besondere Aufmerksamkeit erregte ein Angriff auf die Open-Source-Plattform Hugging Face. Mehrere OpenAI-Agenten tauschten sich in einem internen Forum aus, teilten Schwachstellen miteinander und wiesen sich sogar Aufgaben zu. Auch Anthropic musste mehrere Fälle melden. In einem davon füllte Claude ein Online-Formular der Polizei aus und gab in einem ungelösten Mordfall falsche Hinweise ab. Daraufhin zog das Unternehmen die Reißleine und sperrte für seine KI-Modelle den Internetzugang.

articles.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.
Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations.
In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example.
Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization
To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle.
This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid.
This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation:
A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N]
Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension.
During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout:
Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096).
Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192).
Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization.
In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096).
In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match.
To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition:
BT[N,K] x AT[K,M] —> CT[N,M]
By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (BT), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (BT) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later.
Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization
Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default FLASHINFER_CUTLASS path.
The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps.
Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing, resolving a severe structural flaw in traditional compilation templates. CUTLASS is natively optimized for dense, large, and predictable matrix dimensions. When it encounters the fluid, ultra-thin batch profiles (M < 64 or M = 1) typical of the live decode generation phase, its default block-tiling and thread-mapping structures become profoundly inefficient. The result is heavy warp under-utilization or expensive memory padding overhead. Conversely, the Triton MoE backend excels at dynamically mapping these small, fragmented token arrays across the physical boundaries of the active expert weights. This keeps the hardware’s internal prefetch streams and Tensor Core pipelines fully saturated even when processing highly unstable workloads at very low batch sizes.
Updating the routing policy is a pure configuration change with no kernel code modified. Still, it yielded a 10 percent end-to-end throughput improvement for FP8 quantized fused MoE models on H200. This improvement is available in the AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) v28 container.
Triton JIT recompilation elimination
One of the most impactful performance pathologies in GPU inference is also one of the least obvious: unnecessary kernel recompilation. Triton, the compiler framework underlying many of vLLM’s custom kernels, specializes integer arguments by default. Every time a kernel is invoked with a previously unseen value for a specialized parameter, Triton triggers a fresh just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In serving workloads where sequence lengths and batch sizes vary continuously, this creates a steady stream of compilation overhead that inflates latency, particularly Time to First Token (TTFT).
In MoE model serving, the _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel (responsible for fused rotary position embedding and FP8 quantization) was recompiling on every new num_tokens value. Adding do_not_specialize annotations to the variable-length parameters removed these recompilations entirely, improving TTFT by 9 percent on H200 at 8-way tensor parallelism (PR #42849).
In a multi-GPU cluster, all 8 GPUs must execute their kernels in perfect, microsecond-level synchronization. If even one GPU must stop to recompile its local _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel because its local token batch count changed, the other seven GPUs sit idle and wait for it. By eliminating recompilations across the entire cluster, we smoothed out the multi-GPU coordination overhead, delivering a 9 percent speedup for the user’s initial response latency. The principle here is to treat the compiler as a first-class optimization surface. Understanding how Triton specializes semantics and recognizing when parameters are dead or variable unlocks latency improvements with minimal code change.
We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.22.0 or later.
Conclusion
Through our collaboration with the vLLM community, we implemented and open sourced multiple kernel optimizations for fused MoE models. We apply these optimizations in the LMI Deep Learning Container on Amazon SageMaker AI. Together, these optimizations have delivered up to 10 percent higher throughput and up to 9 percent faster TTFT. To get started with custom model hosting, see the Amazon SageMaker AI hosting documentation.

articles.title: Jusqu'à 35 % de performances en plus : Nvidia dégaine une option surprise pour ses RTX 40 et 50
articles.text:
Nos jeux vidéo profitent depuis quelques années d’un « boost » fourni par l’intelligence artificielle. Vous le connaissez sous le nom de FSR chez AMD (l’IA n’y est arrivée qu’avec le FSR 4) et de DLSS chez Nvidia, aujourd’hui dans sa version 5.
Pour faire simple, le DLSS fait un rendu des images successives du jeu en basse définition (1080p par exemple) et se sert de l’IA pour reconstruire l’image dans la définition de l’écran (1440p, 4K ou autres). En interne, le jeu calcule donc ses images dans une définition inférieure, ce qui soulage la carte graphique et fait grimper les performances.
Le mode Performance dont il est question ici concerne une autre brique du DLSS, la génération d’images (Frame Generation). Le jeu calcule de vraies images, et l’IA en intercale d’autres entre deux d’entre elles, en s’appuyant sur des données fournies par le jeu, comme les vecteurs de mouvement et la profondeur, pour comprendre comment les objets se déplacent d’une image à l’autre.
L’un des résultats les plus concrets est la hausse du nombre d’images par seconde. Nvidia veut justement la pousser encore plus loin avec une mise à jour du DLSS 5, annoncée ce mardi 13 octobre. Parmi les nouveautés, Nvidia introduit un nouveau mode Performance pour la génération d’images (Frame Generation).
Comment fonctionne le nouveau mode Performance du DLSS de Nvidia ?
Compatible avec les cartes graphiques RTX 40 et 50, ainsi que les PC portables RTX Spark, le mode remplace en réalité, par un algorithme plus rapide et plus léger, l’un des deux modèles d’IA utilisés par le DLSS pour la génération d’images. En l’occurrence celui qui « calcule le flux optique pour des éléments tels que l’interface utilisateur ou les effets de Ray Tracing ».
Baptisé « Preset C » dans l’application Nvidia, ce mode augmente le nombre d’images par seconde avec la génération d’images DLSS, la génération multi-images et la génération dynamique multi-images. « Avec des compromis mineurs en termes de qualité d’image », précise Nvidia.
Attention tout de même pour les possesseurs de RTX 40 : Nvidia réserve toujours officiellement la génération multi-images aux RTX 50. Sur ces cartes, le Preset C ne profitera donc qu’à la génération d’images classique.
La marque donne par ailleurs un chiffre : « Sur une GeForce RTX 5060, ce mode Performance pour la génération d’images est jusqu’à 35 % plus rapide. » Un « jusqu’à » à prendre avec des pincettes, puisque Nvidia ne précise ni le jeu, ni la définition, ni s’il parle du temps de calcul des images générées ou du nombre d’images par seconde affiché au final. Dans le détail, voici ce que ça donne selon les cas de figure, toujours selon le fabricant :
Disponible en bêta depuis ce mardi 13 octobre, le Preset C du mode Performance doit être activé manuellement une fois la version bêta de l’application Nvidia installée. La marche à suivre est indiquée sur le site de Nvidia, dans la partie « New, Faster Performance Mode For Frame Generation Enters Beta ».
Voici les étapes à respecter pour en profiter. Dans l’application Nvidia, il faut d’abord cocher l’accès aux fonctions bêta (dans Paramètres, puis À propos) et installer la mise à jour proposée. Ensuite, dans la section Graphiques, il faut choisir un jeu compatible avec la génération d’images (ou les paramètres globaux, pour l’appliquer à tous les jeux compatibles). Dans les paramètres du pilote, ouvrir « DLSS Override – Model Presets », choisir « Custom », puis « Preset C » dans le menu Frame Generation. Le mode arrivera aussi le 23 octobre dans RTX Remix, l’outil de Nvidia pour remasteriser d’anciens jeux.
