articles.title: iPhone : Apple atteint un record alors que le marché mondial des smartphones s’effondre
articles.text:
Le marché mondial des smartphones enregistre son pire troisième trimestre depuis 14 ans, victime d’une pénurie de mémoire qui fait grimper les prix et réduit les volumes d’expédition. Face à la débâcle générale, l’iPhone affiche une part de marché record pour un troisième trimestre.
Le marché du smartphone traverse définitivement une période difficile. Selon les estimations de Counterpoint Research, les livraisons mondiales ont reculé de 20 % au troisième trimestre 2026, tombant à leur plus bas niveau depuis 2012. En cause, la pénurie persistante de mémoire DRAM et NAND, qui a fait grimper les coûts de fabrication et les prix de vente. Apple n’échappe pas à ces difficultés, mais atteint malgré tout 22 % de parts de marché sur cette période, une première pour le géant à la pomme.
L’iPhone atteint 22 % de part de marché au troisième trimestre
Apple a livré 22 % des smartphones mondiaux au troisième trimestre 2026, contre 18 % un an plus tôt. La firme californienne n’avait jamais atteint ce niveau pour un troisième trimestre. Elle se rapproche ainsi de Samsung, qui reste numéro un avec 23 %.
Ce résultat est d’autant plus surprenant que la marque à la pomme n’a pas lancé de version de base de l’iPhone 18 durant cette période. L’absence de ce modèle d’entrée de gamme a mécaniquement réduit le volume total des expéditions par rapport à la gamme iPhone 17 un an plus tôt, composée, dès son lancement, de quatre modèles (iPhone Air inclus).
Le démarrage des modèles Pro a pourtant été plus solide que celui de leurs prédécesseurs, particulièrement en Chine et en Inde. La dynamique maintenue par la série iPhone 17, incluant les variantes Pro et Pro Max, a également contribué à limiter la baisse des volumes. Apple a rejoint le mouvement généralisé de hausse des prix, mais son effet s’est limité aux dernières semaines du trimestre.
Une crise des composants qui frappe durement tous les autres acteurs
De son côté, Samsung conserve la première place avec 23 % de parts de marché, malgré un recul de 3 % de ses livraisons sur un an. Le lancement du Galaxy Z Fold8 et le maintien d’une offre stable dans la gamme A sur les marchés émergents ont contribué à soutenir sa position. La situation est plus difficile pour ses concurrents. Xiaomi enregistre la chute la plus marquée du top 5, avec un recul de plus de 30 % sur un an et une part de marché tombée à 10 %. OPPO et Vivo accusent chacun des baisses supérieures à 20 %, leurs parts de marché reculant respectivement à 9 % et 8 %.
Shilpi Jain, analyste senior chez Counterpoint Research, résume la situation de la manière suivante : « Le troisième trimestre consécutif à subir de plein fouet la crise des mémoires confirme la pression qui pèse sur le marché. Cette pénurie pousse les fabricants à revoir leurs stratégies et modifie les habitudes des consommateurs, qui conservent leurs appareils plus longtemps, s’intéressent davantage au reconditionné et privilégient les produits offrant une meilleure valeur ». L’analyste souligne également le fossé grandissant entre le segment premium, où la demande résiste relativement bien, et les modèles d’entrée de gamme, davantage touchés par la hausse des prix.
Counterpoint Research n’anticipe pas de reprise des volumes tant que les coûts et l’approvisionnement en mémoire ne seront pas revenus à la normale. D’ici la fin de l’année, les fabricants devraient donc continuer de privilégier leurs marges au détriment des volumes.

articles.title: Los datos de casi nueve millones de daneses, ¿expuestos por usar la contraseña 123456?
articles.text:
Los datos de casi nueve millones de daneses, ¿expuestos por usar la contraseña 123456?
En declaraciones al diario danés ‘Politiken’, el supuesto atacante afirma haber accedido a una base de datos estatal a través de esa clave. Es la mayor filtración de la historia del país
La contraseña 123456 es poco recomendable para una cuenta de Netflix o de banco, pero aún menos cuando es la clave para acceder a una base de datos de todos los ciudadanos de un país. Ha sido el caso de Dinamarca. Unos ciberdelincuentes descargaron en septiembre los nombres, direcciones y números de seguridad social de casi nueve millones de daneses, un número superior incluso a la población, que es de seis millones, porque incluye también a personas ya fallecidas o habitantes en el extranjero, en la mayor filtración de datos de la historia del país. El supuesto pirata informático afirma ahora en una entrevista con el diario danés Politiken que accedió al Registro Central de Población (CPR, por sus siglas en inglés) tras probar la combinación 123456 como credencial de una empresa privada que tenía acceso legal a la base de datos.
El incidente tuvo lugar sin que saltara ninguna alarma, algo que ha sorprendido a los expertos. Jens Myrup Pedersen, catedrático de Ingeniería Informática de la Universidad de Aarhus del país nórdico, explica por llamada telefónica que las autoridades solo se dieron cuenta de la filtración a principios de este mes, cuando preparaban las facturas mensuales para las empresas con permiso para realizar búsquedas en el registro estatal. “Se paga una pequeña tarifa por cada consulta realizada en el sistema”, relata Pedersen. “Y finalmente se dieron cuenta de que había una cantidad enorme y excepcionalmente elevada de consultas”, todas precedentes de una misma compañía.
El Gobierno danés no ha confirmado la versión del supuesto ciberdelincuente, ni ha aclarado si actuó como lobo solitario. La ministra de Investigación, Educación y Digitalización, Christina Egelund, alertó el 5 de octubre en un comunicado de que se trata de “un incidente de extrema gravedad” que se está investigando. Su ministerio aconseja a la ciudadanía danesa que actúe con prudencia ante llamadas telefónicas o correos electrónicos de personas desconocidas que aseguran conocer sus datos personales. Los daneses usan el número del CPR como un identificador personal para todo tipo de trámites, explica Pedersen.
La persona anónima entrevistada por Politiken cuenta que descargó los datos de los 8,8 millones de personas registradas en la plataforma a través de la empresa privada, a la que se saltó con la contraseña 123456. Pedersen, que también es el fundador de una compañía de ciberseguridad, fue consultado por el periódico danés sobre los métodos de la filtración. “No me cabe duda de que la persona que contactó con Politiken dispone de los datos robados”, subraya el profesor. Aunque no ha podido verificar si el ciberdelincuente lo hizo con la clave 123456, lo califica de “posible”.
Pero Pedersen sí cree que “es probable” que sea la mayor filtración de información personal jamás registrada en Dinamarca. El riesgo principal para los daneses es el fraude electrónico, afirma. “Con esta información puedes contactar a las personas afectadas y decirles que llamas de la policía o del hospital, y convencerles porque conoces su número del CPR, su dirección y su cumpleaños”, advierte.
Pedro García Teodoro, catedrático de Ingeniería Telemática de la Universidad de Granada, señala por correo electrónico que el incidente en Dinamarca “se conoce como un ataque a la cadena de suministro (supply chain) porque conlleva realizar un ataque a través de proveedores terceros con un nivel de seguridad menor”. Es una táctica “de una alta prevalencia a fecha de hoy”, agrega. Pedersen apunta a la falta de autenticación de múltiples factores en la compañía infiltrada como una causa principal del robo. “Pero claro, el uso de la contraseña 123456 demostraría que la empresa carecía de políticas de seguridad”, enfatiza.
El experto danés considera “increíble” que la descarga masiva de registros no hiciera saltar las alarmas del sistema estatal. El CPR, el “núcleo de la sociedad digital danesa”, se creó en 1968, lo que convirtió a Dinamarca en “uno de los países más digitalizados del mundo”, según Pedersen. “Pero no hemos invertido lo suficiente en seguridad”, critica. “Y esto es un síntoma de ello”.
Pino Caballero-Gil, catedrática de Ingeniería Informática de la Universidad de La Laguna en Tenerife, alerta por correo electrónico de que “el peligro más habitual en la práctica está en los intermediarios con permisos y en la falta de alertas para detectar descargas masivas”. La profesora cita el caso de Bulgaria, que sufrió el robo de datos fiscales de cinco millones de personas en 2019, y Francia, donde se filtraron los datos de salud de 15 millones de pacientes en 2025, como otros ejemplos del problema.
“En España compartimos demasiado el DNI y el número de la seguridad social en todo tipo de situaciones”, añade Caballero-Gil. “El problema es que esos y otros datos asociados van a parar a bases de datos inseguras, y luego los ciberdelincuentes los usan para hacerse pasar por ti y cometer estafas”.

articles.title: NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Today, NVIDIA is making the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs.
Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference.
By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.
This post details the open source release, which includes the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform and four components that can also be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, Workload Map. Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements.
How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open-source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings.
Deploy the open source platform directly
The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the NVIDIA Run:ai repository within the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently.
The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on NVIDIA NGC as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack.
Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included.
Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners
Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements.
- Crusoe integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure.
- Mirantis extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization.
- Nebius offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes.
- OpenNebula Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds.
- Rafay is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs.
- Saturn Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing.
- Spectro Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure.
- vCluster provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet.
For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering.
For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently.
Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform
This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements.
KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai
KAI Scheduler is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and contributed it to CNCF as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale.
KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating:
- Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly
- Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams
- Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level
- GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HaMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning)
- Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support
To learn more about key features, visit the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform.
Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes
The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in CUDA 13.4. The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what GPU Fractioning Operator provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic.
Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation.
KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer
While the scheduler decides how work is placed, KAI Resource Management governs who gets what:
- Projects and departments: The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them.
- Resource management with an organizational hierarchy: The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics.
- Node pools: Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources.
Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee.
Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters.
Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the KAI Resource Management documentation.
Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes
Workload Map is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management.
In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status.
Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle:
- Describing pods, components, and roles
- Submitting and configuring
- Scheduling with gang and topology awareness
- Observing status and health consistently
- Applying policy at admission or runtime
This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD.
Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters.
Learn more in the dsx-ai-factory/workload-map GitHub repo and check out the adopter projects.
Related open source platform software
The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components.
Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency
Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models.
Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors.
Inference engines
Model Streamer is integrated upstream in vLLM and SGLang, where it can be enabled with the --load-format runai_streamer flag, as well as in ModelExpress. Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below.
Clouds
Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance.
- AWS: Model Streamer ships in the vLLM Deep Learning Container and is the recommended fast path in the official EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference, with tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3.
- Google Cloud: Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA, including GKE documentation for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory.
- Microsoft Azure: Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers. Published benchmarks on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path.
Storage platforms
Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results:
- WEKA loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment.
- VAST Data measured measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe
- DDN streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage.
Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck.
Grove: One API, any inference architecture
Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs.
Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML.
Grove is a modular part of NVIDIA Dynamo that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress.
Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements.
Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources:
- NVIDIA Run:ai full platform
- KAI Scheduler scheduling engine
- KAI Resource Management for projects, departments, quotas, and node pools
- GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA GPU fractions on Kubernetes, with per-pod metrics
- Workload Map workload-management contract
Related open source projects include:
- Model Streamer for fast model weight loading
- Grove for multicomponent inference orchestration
We’re excited to bring this work to the community and to build the next generation of AI workload and GPU orchestration in the open. We welcome your contributions, issues, and feedback.

articles.title: Rewinding the exponential: How we keep hardware usage down
articles.text:
Rewinding the exponential: How we keep hardware usage down
More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, and our team, the Data team, owns the data pipeline responsible for plumbing that data (and more) from our global network to applicable central data centers. The Cloudflare network is a globally distributed system supporting tens of thousands of servers. Data that power Cloudflare Logs, SQL API, observability, internal analytics, and more flow through this network and use our data pipeline to serve customers.
In May of this year, we were providing data delivery at roughly two billion events per second. This includes customer traffic as well as data sent from internal teams. Year after year, we tackle the same problem — exponential traffic growth against linear hardware growth. We have to react to this increase in order to keep resource costs under control. Over the past five years, we’ve made various improvements to compensate for the data volume increase in comparison to hardware allocation, equivalent to deferring two and a half years of hardware expansion. This post details those changes: breaking up our monolithic data schema in 2022, adjusting compression in 2024, rearchitecting pipeline replication in spring 2026, decentralizing sampling in summer 2026, and introducing aggregations into the pipeline in fall 2026.
Background
Our pipeline starts with an internal service called Logfwdr, where we collect from highly distributed data sources (think: Workers, FL). We then feed this data to a set of centralized receivers, which eventually push them onto our buffering system, Buftee. Consumers fetch data from Buftee and distribute data to their final destinations, like ClickHouse, which we rely on heavily.
Unpacking the monolith
In 2022, we dismantled our one and only schema. Previously, there was a single stream packed with every product's fields, forcing Cloudflare-internal consumers to ingest everything and demux or discard records via filters. At the time, most of Cloudflare’s data products were built on HTTP, Security and CDN metadata. In 2021, our message schema looked like this:
Some fields here belonged under the same product, but some were completely irrelevant to each other. The hypothesis was that none of these teams require 100% of fields in the monolithic schema. In other words, we can create small messages for each product’s required fields. Although we were going to duplicate fields, some of them in every message, replacing this firehose with product-specific schemas actually reduced the backbone bandwidth usage by 35-40%, knocking out roughly a year’s worth of compressed traffic growth.
Compression
By 2024, as traffic steadily grew, we were tackling network congestion issues on a daily basis. To react to this, we changed our compression algorithm from LZ4 to zstd. We had already experimented with zstd compression before, but we noticed a higher CPU usage at the time. Therefore, we were careful to track the metrics to ensure the trade-off was worth it.
Initially, we rolled this change out to a few servers. To our relief, we didn’t observe a noticeable difference in CPU usage.
With more confidence, we gradually rolled out to our entire fleet, which also showed little impact to CPUs. In the end, there was nearly a 40% reduction in compressed traffic throughput. The uncompressed bytes remained at the same growth, meaning we could support more than 1.5x the amount of traffic with the same size pipe. Or another way to put it, the estimated growth-equivalent reductions put us at about 10 months prior.
Now, in 2026, we attempted three strategies to reduce uncompressed bytes (and thus, compressed bytes).
Load balancing
To make analytics resilient against regional disasters, our systems require redundant data to be stored in multiple centralized regions (data subject to Customer Metadata Boundaries is stored strictly within its designated region). Historically, the simplest way to achieve disaster resilience was double-writing: Logfwdr transmitted two full copies of every non-regional analytics event — one to each centralized region. Each region then independently processed a complete copy through to ClickHouse. We also apply sampling in each region, an incredibly scalable technique that works for all volumes of data during any traffic conditions. We downsample high-volume traffic while rare events are preserved.
This infrastructure was manageable when only a handful of streams used secondary regions. However, as we expanded disaster resilience across almost all analytics streams, Logfwdr traffic doubled across the board. Sending every event, twice, over wide-area transit was unsustainable against our exponential traffic growth.
We had already tackled a similar challenge for Logpush. For Logpush, Logfwdr treats the centralized data centers as a unified, shared pool of receivers: each message is sent to only one region, failing over to another destination if a machine or facility is unreachable. That model had already proven its worth during large incidents, shifting traffic seamlessly from one location to another without human intervention. This automatic failover was possible because Logpush delivery is stateless, as customer destinations do not care which centralized data center pushes the logs.
Analytics was trickier. Unlike stateless logs, ClickHouse clusters in both regions still need a full copy of non-regional data to allow instant, independent query failover. The breakthrough was decoupling pipeline transit from database redundancy:
1. Shared Ingest Pool: We adopted Logpush’s model to the analytics streams. Logfwdr dispatches each event exactly once across wide-area transit to whichever centralized receiver is available.
2. Late Replication from centralized regions: Instead of replicating traffic at source, replication happens as late as possible in the pipeline. Data lands in our distributed buffering layer, Buftee, and remote inserters stream cross-data-center copies downstream.
3. Resilient Failure Handling: If a centralized region goes down, Logfwdrs immediately routes all non-regional traffic to the surviving region. If the inter-data center connection blips, each cluster continues ingesting its local share without backpressure; remote inserters catch up from Buftee's retention buffer once the backbone recovers.
For the datasets we migrated, the cutover eliminated approximately 43 GB/s of compressed transit traffic while adding only ~7 GB/s of cross-data-center replication on our pipeline. Two architectural factors explain this asymmetry:
1. Replication happens downstream of sampling: In the old model, Logfwdrs transmitted two copies of raw, unsampled events over wide-area transit. In the new model, Logfwdrs send a single copy to centralized receivers, which immediately apply sampling before buffering into Buftee, carrying only this already-compacted stream.
2. Better compression through uniform partitioning: Data at source is fragmented across thousands of individual servers. After centralization, streams are aggregated and partitioned into uniform batches over wider time windows. This structural uniformity allows compression algorithms to achieve dramatically higher compression ratios than Logfwdr transit batches ever could.
Overall, this was a net reduction of 36 GB/s across wide-area networks. We rolled this out initially to two datasets, HTTP analytics and Ready-Analytics, our in-house one-click analytics product.
We’ve been actively migrating more datasets to this load-balanced architecture since the spring.
Sampling from the get-go
Another strategy we employed was further expanding our sampling mechanism so that we pulled critical processing earlier into the pipeline. Sampling was already used in our centralized services, particularly the receivers, easing pressure on downstream systems. We can be more resource efficient if we send less data downstream (without sacrificing data quality).
The solution here was to simply sample in Logfwdr, in addition to maintaining the sampling in centralized receivers. How the sampling algorithm works here, in short, is each dataset has a key that producer teams have chosen to index and sample the data. When sampling, we first shuffle the records for each key to eliminate bias. Then, for each group of records, we select a sample size equal to the square root of the total count of the records. The result is a representative sample, whether sampled once or twice. To produce estimates, we scale calculations against the sample rate. For example, if we sample 10 out of 100 records, the sample rate would be 10/100, and the unbiased estimate of the original count would be 10*10 = 100.
To ensure this approach was working well, we compared the number of rows written to ClickHouse against the estimated sum for total count using a variety of keys across a variety of traffic footprints, so that “least seen” keys to “most seen” keys were captured across the spectrum.
The result is that for keys with more data, the sample rate decreases. However, keys with less data were sampled comparably. Thus, we still kept a representative sample while delivering and storing fewer events. We’re not compromising the quality of data delivered, even when we deliver less in quantity.
If we look at this more closely, using power laws, we can observe that the double-sampled (red) grows at roughly x0.319 v. sampled-once/control (blue) at x0.485. Another way to picture this is, a key that has 100x more data than another key would have stored roughly 10x the number of rows if single-sampled. Now, it will only store roughly 4x the number of rows. Concretely, a total of 11.6 million events is represented by 18k rows in ClickHouse as opposed to 79k. Double sampling attenuates storage of the “most seen” keys, while still retaining the same detail per event for “least seen” keys.
We initially implemented this strategy against three of our top datasets. Every single one at least halved the amount of compressed data we were originally sending on the wire to centralized receivers. That’s 25GB/s altogether, or over 2PB/day.
Aggregating
Cloudflare offers several analytics datasets built on rollups: aggregates of the raw events computed at ingest time. This makes the opposite tradeoff to sampling: rather than answering any question approximately, we answer a fixed set of questions exactly, provided we choose the dimensions and metrics up front.
For example, in the HTTP dataset, we measure the number of unique occurrences of IP addresses during a given minute rather than the individual IPs themselves. Another example is we sum the total number of GET, POST, PUT, etc. requests for a given domain, for that minute, grouped by the HTTP method. None of these computations actually necessitate waiting until the tail-end of the pipeline to start calculating.
Historically, this aggregation occurred towards the end of the pipeline, inside the inserters which read from Buftee and insert into ClickHouse. Decentralizing this aggregation was an opportunity to spread out load and reduce the amount of data we centralize.
Hence, we built an aggregation functionality that is utilized every step of the way, creating repeated opportunities to combine matching partial aggregates as data converges. Much like sampling, records are grouped by a key, which determines which records can be combined. We aggregate on each instance of Logfwdr. We aggregate again after the partially aggregated events reach the centralized receivers, which push these re-aggregated events onto dedicated partitioned buffers. Because these buffers bring together records from multiple receivers, we aggregate another time after they’ve been read in batches by the ClickHouse inserters. Finally, we aggregate in ClickHouse with aggregating table engines.
The first dataset we rolled this out to was for the HTTP traffic. In just this one dataset alone, we dropped from 9+ GB/s to <2 GB/s in compressed bytes traffic. Even though this is currently the highest cardinality dataset, the aggregations on it still gave us an approximate 80% reduction on the wire.
This aggregation feature is powerful for datasets that can collapse easily, especially for use cases like usage metrics where accuracy on the sums and counts is paramount. It also means we can offer producer teams another option to reduce resource usage besides sampling, which we did. Like Ready-Analytics, we created a generic in-house one-click aggregating analytics product, called Ready-Aggregates. As we continue to iterate on this new feature in the pipeline, we expect to see savings continue to mount.
Impact
The starkest proof of this exponential growth is how rapidly traffic growth consumes headroom.
Take Ready-Analytics for example, where two of the three mechanisms, load balancing and sampling techniques, were applied. In mid-May, load balancing dropped traffic by 50%, plunging from ~26 GB/s to ~13 GB/s. Two months later, traffic had already started surging back up to ~20 GB/s. That’s about half of the reduction, erased by organic traffic growth. We then created even more headroom by reducing this dataset’s throughput rate to the single digits, ~8GB/, when sampling rolled out.
Without both interventions, Ready-Analytics alone would have breached 60 GB/s by September. By processing less data in centralized data centers, we also save a significant amount of CPUs and memory. The following graphs show the impact of load-balancing and sampling in Logfwdr on the CPU and memory usage of just the Ready-Analytics receivers: a ~50% reduction, regaining ~750 CPUs and 3.5 TiB of memory.
Across the entire pipeline altogether, from spring to fall, load balancing (~38 GB/s saved), sampling (~25 GB/s saved across top datasets), and aggregating (~7+ GB/s so far), eliminated ~70 GB/s of compressed traffic from our backbone. These cliff drops provide immediate relief.
If we zoom out such that we look at five years from now, the changes made in this year alone have just as much impact as the short-term benefits. We’ve halved the amount of data we’d be processing in another half a decade’s time. The structural and algorithmic optimizations we have and will continue to make are essential to keep hardware demands sustainable.
If you’re interested in helping us solve these challenges at scale, we’re hiring!

articles.title: Refrigeration Controller Hack Spoils Food Across European Supermarkets
articles.text:
A cyberattack hit hundreds of supermarkets across Europe, setting refrigerators and freezers to defrost overnight.
Exploiting a vulnerability in refrigeration controllers, hackers reportedly raised temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), spoiling food products and causing significant monetary damages.
The attack hit several supermarket chains across Europe, including Auchan, Carrefour, E.Leclerc, Intermarché (owned by Groupement Mousquetaire), and Monoprix, Reuters reports.
Most of the damage was done in France, but food retailers in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, and Spain were also affected.
Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher confirmed on X that several stores were affected. Cooperative U operates supermarkets under the Hyper U, Super U, and U Express and Utile brands.
“Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack,” an automated translation of Schelcher’s post reads.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” Schelcher added.
According to French news outlet BFM TV, more than 300 supermarket locations across France were affected. The losses are estimated to reach millions of euros.
Roughly 5% of Monoprix stores have been affected, Groupe Casino, which owns the French retail chain, told SecurityWeek, adding that no other brands it owns have been impacted. Monoprix operates over 600 locations.
“The food safety of our customers is our top priority. Any product whose storage conditions are no longer guaranteed is withdrawn from sale,” a Groupe Casino spokesperson said.
The hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers from Danish company Danfoss and tampered with refrigerator and freezer settings in the middle of the night. The temperature in some equipment reportedly rose for six hours before employees discovered the issue.
“Someone remotely took over refrigeration controllers and made them defrost. Target temperature set to 50°C. Staff opening freezers in the morning were hit by a wave of hot air,” security researcher Lukasz Olejnik commented.
The large-scale attack occurred roughly two months after cybersecurity firm Claroty disclosed vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A management platform that could allow attackers to bypass authentication, execute arbitrary code remotely, and inject arbitrary configuration directives.
Claroty said it identified thousands of publicly accessible AK-SM 800A management interfaces, urging customers to upgrade their systems to firmware version R4.3.1, which contains the necessary patches.
“Because these systems provide centralized management of refrigeration equipment, compromising the management interface can have significant operational consequences,” Claroty warned.
It’s unclear whether the attackers exploited the flaws Claroty disclosed.
*Updated with statement from Groupe Casino.

articles.title: El ex de Hayden Panettiere pide al tribunal que actúe como representante de su hija para proteger la herencia
articles.text:
Wladimir Klitschko ya tiene la custodia de su hija Kaya, pero eso no le da ningún poder sobre lo que la niña hereda de su madre. Por eso ha ido al tribunal de sucesiones del condado de Los Ángeles: pide que lo nombren tutor temporal de su patrimonio. El escrito se presentó el jueves 24 de septiembre y la vista está señalada para hoy.
Hayden Panettiere murió el 16 de agosto, a los 36 años, en un apartamento de Greenville, en Carolina del Sur. El forense del condado habló de una sobredosis accidental de varias sustancias, entre ellas fentanilo; la policía de la ciudad investiga y, según lo publicado, la DEA se habría sumado a la investigación. Kaya es, según el escrito, su única heredera.
Tiene la custodia, ¿para qué quiere una tutela?
Son dos cosas distintas. Por un lado, la custodia decide dónde vive la niña y quién la cuida. Lo que es la tutela del patrimonio decide quién firma por ella cuando hay dinero de por medio, porque, como es normal, una menor no puede administrarlos.
En el primer caso, Klitschko decide el colegio; para firmar en su nombre un papel del banco, necesita otro tipo de autorización.
Por eso mismo, Klitschko pide ser tutor temporal, no definitivo, y el escrito define la medida como “urgent and essential”. Lo que dice buscar es proteger lo que hereda Kaya hasta que el tribunal designe a alguien que administre el patrimonio de la actriz, y según la petición, también quiere estar legitimado para impulsar ese nombramiento.
Todo esto viene porque, según varias informaciones de la prensa del corazón, Panettiere no dejó testamento.
Joyas, correos y cerraduras: lo que dice el escrito
En toda esta historia se ha dado una situación que puede resultar especialmente preocupante. Según parece, una persona sin identificar habría entrado sin permiso en la propiedad de Los Ángeles antes de la muerte de la actriz; por eso, contrataron seguridad. Según parece, faltaban joyas y otras pertenencias.
Pero eso no es todo; se dice que personas ajenas a la familia habrían accedido a correos electrónicos de la actriz y los habrían borrado. Tras su muerte, se habrían cambiado las cerraduras y trasladado ropa y accesorios a unidades de almacenamiento.
Nada de esto está verificado de forma independiente. Lo único comprobado: hay una petición, está en un tribunal de Los Ángeles y tiene vista. El escrito no dice quién es la persona que preocupa a Klitschko y, según uno de los resúmenes que se han publicado, parte de lo que dice le ha llegado de oídas.
Una casa de empeño, 26.800 euros y una petición a la policía
Poco después de conocerse la petición, salió a la luz una ampliación: Klitschko quiere que su nombramiento incluya la autoridad de pedir una investigación policial sobre los bienes.
Lo que parece es que piensa que una persona no familiar vinculada a la actriz pudo vender joyas en una casa de empeño (no se sabe si de las desaparecidas o no), aunque la tienda, dice, no da datos sin intervención policial.
El 7 de octubre se conoció otro argumento. Klitschko dice que adelantará de su bolsillo unos 30.000 dólares (unos 26.800 euros) por los impuestos de 2025 de la actriz, que vencen el 15 de octubre. Eso sí, seguidamente pedirá a la herencia que se los devuelva.
¿Quién puede leer los correos de alguien que ha muerto?
Este tipo de nombramiento provisional existe en California. El artículo 2250 del Código de Sucesiones pide que se presenten hechos que acrediten una causa justificada y, mientras tanto, deja al tutor temporal en funciones hasta que se resuelva la petición.
En el caso del patrimonio de la fallecida, hay otra figura relevante, la del administrador especial del artículo 8540, con poderes limitados a conservar los bienes.
Respecto a los correos. La ley californiana separa dos cosas. Según el artículo 876, el proveedor solo entrega al representante del patrimonio el contenido de los mensajes si el difunto lo consintió o lo ordena un tribunal.
En este caso se desconoce qué proveedor está implicado ni que alguien haya pedido nada. A nivel práctico, lo mejor es dejarlo preparado en vida: Google permite designar hasta diez contactos de confianza en su administrador de cuentas inactivas, y Apple da a su contacto de legado tres años de acceso una vez aprobada la solicitud.

articles.title: Windows 10 : à partir de juin 2027, ces PC ne recevront plus rien, absolument plus rien, de Windows Update
articles.text:
Windows 10 : à partir de juin 2027, ces PC ne recevront plus rien, absolument plus rien, de Windows Update
Privés de correctifs de sécurité depuis octobre 2025, les PC restés sous Windows 10 sans le programme de sécurité étendue (ESU) gardent encore un fil avec Microsoft. Le 19 juin 2027, il cassera net, et la porte de sortie, pourtant gratuite en France, pourrait se refermer plus tôt qu'annoncé.
Depuis la fin du support de Windows 10, le 14 octobre 2025, un PC non inscrit aux mises à jour de sécurité étendues (ESU) ne reçoit plus le moindre correctif pour Windows. Il reste pourtant branché sur Windows Update. Par ce canal transitent notamment les définitions de l'antivirus Microsoft Defender, que l'éditeur s'est engagé à fournir sur Windows 10 jusqu'en octobre 2028. Ce dernier lien a désormais une date de fin. Dans une note publiée le 8 octobre, Microsoft explique que les certificats permettant aux PC de vérifier qu'ils dialoguent avec ses véritables serveurs expirent les 17 mai et 19 juin 2027. Une machine privée de leurs remplaçants cessera alors de recevoir "tous les types de mises à jour" par Windows Update.
Windows Update en 2027 : quels PC risquent la coupure
Les nouveaux certificats ont déjà été glissés dans les correctifs mensuels. Windows 11 25H2 et ses successeurs n'ont rien à faire. Windows 11 24H2 doit avoir reçu au moins la mise à jour de septembre 2025, et les autres versions encore suivies de Windows 11 et de Windows 10 celle de juillet 2026, détaille le centre de messages Windows. Un PC pris en charge mais resté en retard pourra encore se rattraper après l'échéance, en téléchargeant le correctif requis sur le catalogue Microsoft Update.
	
Les appareils exécutant des versions non prises en charge de Windows perdront l'accès aux services Windows Update et ne recevront donc pas de mises à jour.
Windows 10 sans ESU : mieux vaut s'inscrire avant juin 2027
Le couperet vise d'abord les PC Windows 10 jamais inscrits aux ESU, qui n'ont reçu aucun correctif depuis octobre 2025. D'après StatCounter, Windows 10 animait encore 24,4 % des PC Windows en France en septembre. Les versions de Windows 11 abandonnées, comme la 23H2 Famille ou Pro, sont logées à la même enseigne.
La parade reste gratuite, puisque Microsoft a prolongé les ESU grand public jusqu'au 12 octobre 2027. L'inscription, proposée dans Paramètres > Mise à jour et sécurité > Windows Update, ne coûte rien à qui se connecte avec un compte Microsoft et le conserve. La machine reçoit ensuite toutes les mises à jour critiques publiées depuis octobre 2025, nouveaux certificats compris.
Officiellement, l'inscription reste ouverte jusqu'en octobre 2027. Elle passe pourtant par Windows Update, et un PC coupé du service en juin risquerait de ne plus pouvoir la mener à bien. Mieux vaut ne pas attendre l'été.
Pour vérifier où en est votre machine, ouvrez l'historique des mises à jour, dans Paramètres > Windows Update sous Windows 11 ou Mise à jour et sécurité sous Windows 10. Une mise à jour datée de juillet 2026 ou plus récente vous met à l'abri.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6

articles.title: Apple launches a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI and remote-free voice commands | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple launched a new $299 Apple TV 4K streaming device today, with an upgraded chip, integration with the updated version of Siri AI for content discovery, and mics that allow users to issue voice commands directly without using the remote.
The refreshed Apple TV 4K comes with an upgraded A19 chip to enable various AI features. Hardware-wise, the new streaming box comes with three far-field microphones, letting users talk with Siri without a remote or a paired HomePod.
The company said that users can now have a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2 speakers.
The remote also gets a welcome update: It now includes a small speaker. This helps users find the remote easily when it gets lost in the nooks and corners of the couch or when they leave the remote in another room while doing a chore. (Apple added a way to find the remote with Siri and Find My in 2023, but it hinged on showing directions in the app rather than an audible sound.)
With Siri AI now rolling out to all Apple platforms, the big draw for Apple is to utilize it for better personalization and content recommendations. On the Apple TV, viewers can ask questions like “Which Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” to search for content, or ask for more information about shows with questions like “Where was ‘Pluribus’ filmed?”
Rivals Google and Amazon have also added AI for content suggestions in the past few years.
The device is not updated as often as other Apple hardware, given this long-pending upgrade comes four years after the launch of Apple TV 4K in 2022. Bloomberg reported that the company wanted to launch the new device in 2024, but delays in launching the AI-powered Siri forced Apple to push the launch of new home devices as well.
Consumers can preorder the new Apple TV 4K starting today, and the device will be available on November 13.

articles.title: Google makes it easier to launch your vibe-coded apps
articles.text:
The next time you vibe-code a custom app with Google’s AI Studio, you won’t have to connect your phone to a computer to install it. On Tuesday, Google announced a new feature in the US that will allow you to launch personal apps directly through the Play Store.
Google makes it easier to launch your vibe-coded apps
You can now launch your vibe-coded app directly from the Google Play Store.
Google first launched the ability to vibe-code personal Android apps in May. Even though you can now launch your custom apps in Google Play, the company notes it will continue to keep them “secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog.” You can also launch them using a standard Google account, and the company will soon add the ability to share your app with a select group of people, too.
Though this might make it easier to play around with experimental apps, Google is positioning it as an on-ramp of sorts for fledgling developers. “If you want to share your app with the world, Google Play helps you graduate to a professional developer account with the same Trust & Safety reviews and high-quality standards as professional developers,” Sam Bright, Google’s vice president and general manager of Google Play, writes in the announcement.

articles.title: Should Carney give Canadian tech a (tax) break?
articles.text:
Two years ago, Canada’s then-governing Liberal Party proposed a capital gains tax inclusion rate hike, and much of the country’s tech sector freaked out. While this plan was scrapped after Mark Carney replaced Justin Trudeau as party leader, the surprise decision and the message it conveyed had severely hurt the Liberals’ relationship with Canadian tech. As Roadmunk co-founder Latif Nanji told me last year, “The damage [was] done.”
Today, many of the same industry leaders have penned an open letter asking Carney’s Liberals for a capital gains rollover and a US QSBS-style tax incentive in the upcoming federal budget to better retain Canada’s entrepreneurs, talent, and capital. The key difference this time around is that both parties seem more receptive to working together.
As NACO CEO Claudio Rojas told BetaKit, “We want to see Canadian companies succeed, we want to control our own destiny, and that aligns quite well with the signals that we’re seeing from this government that they’re willing to take action.”
Hundreds of Canadian CEOs, investors, and other business leaders have signed the open letter. Its authors frame these measures as a means of derisking investments in domestic firms and incentivizing the reinvestment of associated profits in Canada.
As CVCA CEO Ben Bergen noted, it will take more than a single investment summit, budget, or prime minister swap to transform Canada. Others say it will also require more than just tax reform. Community builder Jesse Rodgers singled out removing personal guarantees on business loans and leases as another logical step.
These calls to do more signal how much has changed since 2024, when a large portion of Canadian tech was ready to run the Liberals out of town. Now, instead of regime change, Canadian tech feels emboldened to ask the new(ish) Liberals for sizeable tax breaks. With Canada’s latest budget expected to drop next month, BetaKit will be watching to see whether Carney heeds them.
Josh Scott, 
Reporter

Edmonton-based SenseHuman AI is developing a hardhat with machine vision to give construction workers 360-degree worksite surveillance. It vibrates when it detects risks like trenches, ledges, or tripping hazards.
Bad signals on Bill C-22
Secure messaging platform Signal reaffirmed that it would shut down Canadian operations rather than comply with Canada’s controversial Lawful Access Act. The bill, which is currently before the Senate, would compel companies like Signal to keep user data and give law enforcement more power to collect it.
Deals and dollars
Who cashed in, or out, this week:
- Mecka AI revealed a $60-million USD Series B round backed by Sequoia Capital, Nvidia, and others. (Toronto)
- Autonomous vehicle maker CyberWorks landed a $1-million Canadian Armed Forces contract. (Markham, Ont.)
- Xanadu announced a multi-year strategic partnership with semiconductor manufacturer GlobalFoundries to produce quantum chips. (Toronto)
- Scotiabank-owned Tangerine Bank launched a business banking platform for entrepreneurs. (Toronto)
- Polygrade emerged from stealth with $6.3 million USD in seed funding to solve home warranty claims with AI. (Toronto)
- Screen-free educational tech startup Tokidos closed $3.15 million CAD to accelerate growth in Canada and abroad. (Montréal)
- Cohere signed a partnership with defence company Thales to bring agentic AI to the Royal Canadian Navy. (Toronto)
- BioRender released an AI agent to help users build scientific research images. (Toronto)
- Fund management tech companies Brio and Losange Finance merged and rebranded as Stellé. (Montréal)
- Eskasoni First Nation and Aeon Blue created a joint venture for a facility to make jet fuel out of seawater. (Cape Breton)

Artificial or ‘Super Intelligent’?
You may have heard that US President Donald Trump is now calling artificial intelligence “super intelligence,” and a number of powerful tech execs have fallen in line. To track how we got here, Tech Policy Press has a deep dive into the origins of the term and how there’s no perfect, all-encompassing term to capture what we now call AI.

articles.title: Nikolas Bullwinkel, Circus Group founder & CEO, joins the EU-Startups Summit 2027 | EU-Startups
articles.text:
We’re excited to announce that Nikolas Bullwinkel, Founder and CEO of Circus Group, will join us at the EU-Startups Summit 2027, taking place on May 13-14 in sunny Malta! Nikolas will deliver the keynote AI robotics and how Europe can scale DeepTech from lab to market.
Nikolas is a serial entrepreneur currently building at the intersection of artificial intelligence, robotics, and autonomous infrastructure. Through Munich-based Circus, he is working to automate one of the world’s most fundamental activities: producing meals.
The company develops AI-powered robotic systems designed to autonomously prepare food for enterprise customers across commercial, industrial, and defence environments.
Drawing on his experience building both Flink and Circus, he’ll explore what it takes to turn ambitious European technology into commercially viable products, move from prototypes to industrial production, and compete globally in the emerging field of Physical AI.
His Story
Before founding Circus, Nikolas was one of the co-founders of Flink, the Berlin-based quick-commerce company that became one of Europe’s fastest-growing delivery startups. During its rapid expansion, Flink grew to around 12,000 employees and more than 140 locations, while a €669 million ($750 million) funding round in December 2021 valued the company at €2.5 billion ($2.85 billion) post-money.
Nikolas subsequently turned his attention towards AI and robotics.
He founded Circus in 2021 alongside Carsten Wille, Helge Plehn, and Fabio Haebel. The company initially set out to rethink food production and delivery through technology, automation, and its own micro-kitchen infrastructure.
By 2022, EU-Startups reported that Circus had secured €11 million in investment and expanded its services across several German cities.
A major step in its evolution came with the acquisition of Berlin-based culinary robotics startup Aitme in 2023, bringing robotics expertise and automated cooking technology directly into Circus. The following year, Circus completed its Xetra listing and began trading on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, marking its transition into a publicly listed European DeepTech company.
Today, Circus is focused on its CA-1 autonomous food-production robot, combining robotics, proprietary AI, software, and automation into a system capable of producing meals with minimal human intervention. Its technology is being developed for a range of civilian and defence applications, with Nikolas continuing to lead the company as CEO.
EU-Startups Summit
On May 13-14, 2027, we’ll be bringing the European startup ecosystem together once again for the EU-Startups Summit in sunny Malta. We’re expecting around 2,500 founders, investors, startup enthusiasts, and ecosystem players for two packed days of networking, inspiration, and learning.
The event will showcase many of Europe’s hottest startups and bring attendees face-to-face with some of the most successful entrepreneurs and innovators of our time. With inspiring keynotes, fireside chats, workshops, a buzzing exhibition hall, and plenty of opportunities to make valuable connections, it is set to be another unmissable edition.
Ready to join us?: Secure your ticket to the EU-Startups Summit 2027 today!
